1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

User programs can't touch hardware directly. They open a special file like /dev/mycam0 and call ordinary file functions on it. The kernel routes each call to your driver's matching function. Because user programs can pass garbage, a driver never dereferences a user pointer. It copies data in and out with helpers that check the address is valid.

Character device
A device accessed as a stream of bytes through a /dev file, identified by major/minor numbers.
file_operations
A struct of function pointers (open, read, unlocked_ioctl…) that the VFS calls.
VFS
Virtual File System, the kernel layer that turns file syscalls into driver calls.
`__user`
A pointer annotation meaning "this address belongs to user space". sparse warns if you dereference it.
copy_from_user
Safely copies bytes from user memory. Returns the number of bytes not copied (0 means success).
misc device
A simple way to register a single char device with a dynamic minor number.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A character device exposes a driver through a file in /dev. When user space calls open, read, write, mmap or ioctl, the VFS dispatches to function pointers in your struct file_operations. Data never crosses the boundary through raw pointers: copy_from_user and copy_to_user validate and copy it, and fail cleanly on bad addresses. ioctl command numbers encode direction, type and size with _IOR, _IOW and _IOWR.

MAKE IT STICK

A bank teller window. Customers (user processes) never walk into the vault. They pass forms through the slot (syscalls), the teller checks every field (copy_from_user plus validation), does the work in the back (driver), and slides results back out (copy_to_user).

INTERACTIVE LAB
ioctl path with hostile input
IN PLAIN WORDS

A bouncer checking IDs at the door. Every request from outside is checked for size, numbers and permissions before it gets in.

Try this: Send a valid request, then hostile ones, and see where the driver stops each one and with which error.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Send valid and malicious inputs and see where the driver stops them and with which errno.

User passes
Valid config
Bad pointer
Huge width
Unknown cmd
ioctl(fd, cmd, &cfg) user space
VFS → f_op->unlocked_ioctl dispatch
copy_from_user fault-safe copy
validate values never trust input
mutex_lock process context
program hardware readl/writel
return 0 / -errno back to user
The request was copied in safely, checked, applied under a lock, and the answer is "all good" (0).
Term: returns 0; copied, validated, locked, applied; returns 0
START WITH THE INCIDENT
A fuzzer crashes the kernel with one ioctl

A fuzzer throws bad inputs at your driver, like a crash-test dummy, to find what breaks. syzkaller (Google's kernel fuzzer) sends CAM_IOC_SET_CFG with a pointer into unmapped memory, then a valid pointer with width = 0xFFFFFFFF. The first version of the driver did memcpy(&cfg, (void*)arg, ...) and later used width * height * 2 to size a buffer. One call oopses the kernel; the other overflows the size calculation and corrupts the heap.

1 · Follow the path from syscall to driver

Here is the path an app's request takes into your driver. ioctl(fd, cmd, &cfg) → syscall entry → do_vfs_ioctl → file->f_op->unlocked_ioctl(file, cmd, arg). read and write get a char __user *buf and a size_t count, and must return the number of bytes or a negative errno. open usually finds the device with container_of and stores it in file->private_data; release runs on the last close.

2 · Treat every user value as hostile

Use copy_from_user, copy_to_user, get_user and put_user. Check every length, index and multiplication (check_mul_overflow, array_size). Re-validate state under the lock, because another thread may have changed it (TOCTOU). Copy a structure once and validate the kernel copy; reading user memory twice invites double-fetch bugs.

3 · Design the UAPI to last forever

User-space ABI can't break. Use fixed-width __u32/__u64 types, explicit padding, a size or version field, and reserved fields that must be zero. Prefer existing subsystems (V4L2, IIO, input, DRM, hwmon) over private ioctls: you get standard tools and an ABI that's already reviewed.

4 · Concurrency and lifetime

Several processes may open the device, and the device may be unplugged while a file is open. Protect state with a mutex (process context), take references (kref, get_device), and make operations on a removed device return -ENODEV instead of touching freed memory.

LESSON 10.2 · C · LINUX KERNEL + DTS · NEW
Platform drivers, Device Tree & probe
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

The kernel needs to know what hardware is on your board and where. On ARM boards that's written in a Device Tree file (.dts). Each hardware block has a node with a compatible string, like "acme,cam-bridge". Your driver lists the strings it supports, and when the kernel finds a match it calls your probe() function to set the device up.

Device Tree (DT)
A tree of nodes describing non-discoverable hardware, compiled to a .dtb and passed by the bootloader.
compatible
A string (vendor,device) used to match a DT node with a driver.
probe()
The driver function called when a device matches. It acquires resources and registers interfaces.
devm_*
Device-managed resource helpers, freed automatically when the device unbinds or probe fails.
-EPROBE_DEFER
"A dependency isn't ready; retry my probe later."
reg / interrupts
DT properties giving the MMIO address range and interrupt specifier.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Many chips can't announce their own devices, so a map file tells Linux what is on the board. On SoCs, most devices aren't discoverable like PCI; the board's Device Tree describes them: register address, interrupts, clocks, regulators, GPIOs. At boot the kernel creates platform_devices from DT nodes. A platform_driver declares an of_match_table of compatible strings, and when one matches, the driver core calls probe(). Managed (devm_*) APIs tie resources to the device, so they're released automatically on probe failure or removal. Deferred probe (-EPROBE_DEFER) handles dependencies that aren't ready yet.

MAKE IT STICK

A wedding seating chart. The Device Tree is the chart (who sits where, with which needs). Each driver is a guest looking for a place card with its name (the compatible string). When it finds a match, it sits down (probe) and claims its plate, glass and chair (registers, IRQ, clocks). devm_ is the caterer clearing everything when the guest leaves.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Device Tree match & probe
IN PLAIN WORDS

A wedding seating chart: a guest sits only if their name card matches a seat, the seat is not blocked, and the people they depend on have arrived. Otherwise they wait or never sit.

Try this: Change the name match, the status and whether the supplier is ready, and see if the driver binds, waits or never runs.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Change compatible, status and supplier readiness, and see whether probe binds, defers or never runs.

DT compatible
"acme,cam-bridge"
"acme,cambridge" (typo)
v2 + fallback
status = "okay"
PMIC regulator driver ready
bridge@4a000000 {
  compatible = "acme,cam-bridge";
  status = "okay";
  vdd-supply = <&pmic_ldo3>;
};
Names match, the part is switched on, and its power is ready. The driver sets up the hardware and is now in charge of it.
Term: matched → probe(): map regs, get clocks/regulators, read ID, request IRQ, register subdevice; bound
START WITH THE INCIDENT
The bridge chip driver never probes on the new board revision

On rev B, /sys/bus/platform/drivers/cam-bridge/ shows no bound device and there's no error in dmesg. The hardware team moved the bridge's power rail to a new PMIC regulator. The DT references vdd-supply = <&pmic_ldo3>, but the PMIC node has status = "disabled" on rev B, so its driver never probes. The bridge's probe returns -EPROBE_DEFER silently, forever.

1 · How matching happens

Here is how a device on the map gets matched to its driver. Bootloader passes the DTB → kernel unflattens it → of_platform_populate creates platform devices for nodes with status = "okay" → when a driver registers (or a device appears), the bus match compares compatible strings → really_probe calls your probe. Check bindings in /sys/firmware/devicetree/base/ and /sys/bus/platform/devices/.

2 · probe acquires, in a safe order

Start a device in a safe order: get power and clocks, prove you can talk to it, and only then accept its interrupts. Typical order: allocate state → map registers → get clocks, resets, regulators and GPIOs → power up (enable regulator, deassert reset, enable clock) → read an ID register to prove bus access → request the IRQ (devm_request_threaded_irq) → register with a subsystem (V4L2, net). Request the IRQ only once the handler's data is ready, because the interrupt may fire immediately.

3 · Deferred probe and dependencies

If a part your driver needs isn't ready yet, Linux will simply try again later. If a supplier (clock, regulator, GPIO controller, PHY) isn't ready, its getter returns -EPROBE_DEFER, and the core retries after other drivers probe. Check /sys/kernel/debug/devices_deferred for the reason. fw_devlink builds supplier/consumer links from DT phandles to order probing and runtime PM.

4 · DT bindings are an ABI

Bindings live in Documentation/devicetree/bindings/ as YAML schemas validated with make dtbs_check. Don't encode driver policy in DT; describe hardware. Upstream reviewers will push back on vendor-specific properties that duplicate standard ones (clocks, resets, *-supply, *-gpios).

text:
LESSON 10.3 · C · LINUX KERNEL · NEW
Kernel concurrency: contexts, spinlocks, mutexes & deferred work
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

In the kernel, the most important question about any line of code is: can this sleep? Interrupt handlers and code holding a spinlock can't sleep (no mutex_lock, no kmalloc(GFP_KERNEL), no copy_from_user). So the interrupt handler does the minimum (acknowledge the device, grab the status) and schedules the rest to run later in a thread that can sleep.

Process context
Running on behalf of a task (syscall, kthread). May sleep.
Atomic context
Hard IRQ, softirq, or holding a spinlock or with preemption off. Must not sleep.
Spinlock
A lock that busy-waits. spin_lock_irqsave also disables local interrupts.
Threaded IRQ
A handler split into a fast hard-IRQ part and a kernel thread that may sleep.
Workqueue
Kernel threads that run deferred work items in process context.
lockdep
Kernel lock validator that detects lock-order and context bugs at runtime.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Some kernel code is allowed to wait, and some must never wait. That decides which lock you may use. Kernel code runs in different contexts: process context (syscalls, kthreads; may sleep), and atomic context (hard IRQ handlers, softirqs and tasklets, or any code holding a spinlock or with preemption disabled; must not sleep). The context decides the tools: mutex only where sleeping is allowed; spinlock (with _irqsave if an IRQ handler shares the data) in atomic context. Heavy work moves out of the hard IRQ into a threaded IRQ, a workqueue or NAPI polling.

MAKE IT STICK

A hospital. The hard IRQ is an emergency-room triage nurse: assess in seconds, never leave to fetch coffee (can't sleep). Workqueues and threaded IRQs are the ward doctors who can take their time. A spinlock is holding a door shut with your body (you can't leave, so keep it short). A mutex is a key you can take with you to lunch.

💤 = may stop and wait (sleep). Some places must never wait. One is an interrupt handler. Another is any code holding a spinlock. A third is anywhere task switching is turned off.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
"BUG: sleeping function called from invalid context"

After adding I2C reads to fetch sensor status "right when the frame-done IRQ fires", the device logs that splat and occasionally hard-locks. The I2C transfer (i2c_transfer) sleeps waiting for the bus, and it's called from the hard-IRQ handler. On a single-core build it deadlocks outright.

1 · Know which context you're in

Hard IRQ: in_hardirq(). Softirq or tasklet: bottom halves, including network RX. Process context: syscalls, kthreads, workqueues, threaded IRQs. might_sleep() annotations plus CONFIG_DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP catch violations. Any call that can block (mutex, GFP_KERNEL allocation, I2C or SPI transfers, msleep, copy_from_user) is process-context only.

2 · Pick the right lock

Data shared only among process-context paths: mutex. Shared with a hard IRQ: spin_lock_irqsave in process context and spin_lock in the handler. Shared with a softirq: spin_lock_bh. Read-mostly data with rare updates: RCU. Single counters: atomic_t or refcount_t. Keep spinlock sections tiny and never sleep inside one.

3 · Defer the heavy work

There are a few ways to push slow work out of an interrupt to later. Threaded IRQs (simplest for drivers), workqueues (queue_work, with system_highpri_wq or dedicated alloc_workqueue for latency), tasklets (legacy, avoid in new code), and timers or hrtimers for timed work. For network RX, NAPI polling switches from interrupts to polling under load (Lesson 4.7).

4 · Let tools find bugs

Turn on the kernel's checking tools; they warn about lock mistakes before they bite. Enable lockdep (CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING) to detect lock-order inversions and IRQ-safety violations. It reports the potential deadlock even if it never happened. KCSAN finds data races. CONFIG_DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP flags sleeping in atomic context. Run your driver's stress tests on a debug kernel before release.

DMA API, IOMMU & cache coherency
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A camera's DMA engine writes pixels straight into RAM. Two problems: the device may use different addresses than the CPU, and the CPU's cache may hold stale copies of that RAM. Linux's DMA API solves both: you ask it to map a buffer for the device, it hands back the address the device should use, and it handles cache flushing at the right moments.

DMA
Direct Memory Access: the device moves data to and from RAM itself.
dma_addr_t
The address as the device sees it (IOVA if an IOMMU is present). Not a CPU pointer.
IOMMU / SMMU
MMU for devices: translates IOVAs and isolates devices from memory they shouldn't touch.
Coherent mapping
A buffer where CPU and device always see the same data (uncached or HW-coherent).
Streaming mapping
A per-transfer mapping with explicit ownership hand-offs and cache maintenance.
Scatter-gather (sg)
A list of physically discontiguous chunks presented as one transfer.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

DMA lets a device read or write memory without the CPU. Devices see bus (DMA) addresses, which may differ from CPU physical addresses because of an IOMMU or offsets. The DMA API hides this: dma_alloc_coherent gives long-lived buffers that both sides see consistently; streaming mappings (dma_map_single/dma_map_sg) map existing buffers for one transfer, and on non-coherent SoCs they clean or invalidate CPU caches. Ownership is the whole game: between map and unmap (or sync_for_cpu), the device owns the buffer.

MAKE IT STICK

A shared whiteboard behind frosted glass. The CPU writes in its notebook (cache) and must copy it to the board (clean/flush) before the device reads. After the device writes on the board, the CPU must tear out its stale notebook page (invalidate) before reading. The IOMMU is a receptionist who translates room numbers and refuses visitors to rooms they weren't given.

INTERACTIVE LAB
DMA ownership protocol
IN PLAIN WORDS

Lending a notebook to a helper who writes in it directly. While they have it, you must not read your old photocopy. Wait until they hand it back.

Try this: Try the map, transfer, unmap and read steps in different orders and see when old data appears.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Map, DMA, unmap and read in different orders, and see when stale data appears.

Hardware cache-coherent SoC
owner: CPU
dma_map
device writes
dma_unmap
CPU reads
Reset
Safe order: lend it, let the device write, take it back, then read.
Term: map → device writes → unmap → CPU reads
START WITH THE INCIDENT
Green stripes in every 30th frame

On the new SoC, captured frames sometimes show 64-byte stripes of old pixel data. The driver uses kmalloc buffers, passes virt_to_phys(buf) to the DMA engine, and reads the buffer after the frame-done IRQ. On the old (cache-coherent) SoC it worked. On the new non-coherent one, the CPU's dirty cache lines are evicted after the DMA write, overwriting fresh pixels, and the CPU reads stale cached lines.

1 · Addresses: virtual, physical, bus

CPU code uses virtual addresses. The device uses DMA addresses: a physical address plus an offset, or an IOVA translated by the IOMMU or SMMU. Only the DMA API knows the mapping. virt_to_phys bypasses the IOMMU, bounce buffers and offsets, and breaks on many platforms.

2 · Coherent vs streaming

Coherent: descriptor rings, mailboxes, small control structures touched by both sides constantly. Streaming: bulk data buffers in one direction per transfer (DMA_TO_DEVICE, DMA_FROM_DEVICE, DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL). On non-coherent ARM, a TO_DEVICE map cleans (writes back) caches and a FROM_DEVICE map invalidates them. Respect the ownership hand-offs exactly.

3 · IOMMU: isolation and contiguity

The IOMMU is like a translator and bouncer for devices: it maps addresses and blocks places the device shouldn't touch. The IOMMU makes discontiguous pages look contiguous to the device (great for big camera buffers via dma_map_sg), confines the device to buffers it was given (a buggy or malicious device can't scribble on the kernel), and enables device assignment to VMs (VFIO). Faults show up as SMMU or IOMMU fault logs with the faulting IOVA, which is your best clue.

4 · Use the frameworks

Big subsystems wrap these helpers, so buffers can be shared between devices without copying. Subsystems wrap the DMA API: V4L2 videobuf2-dma-contig/dma-sg, networking page pools, DRM GEM. Buffers shared between devices (camera → GPU → encoder) use dma-buf file descriptors with fences for synchronization: zero-copy pipelines across drivers.

Camera pipelines: MIPI CSI-2, V4L2 & the media controller

PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Camera sensors send pixels over a fast serial link called MIPI CSI-2 (a few differential 'lanes'). Linux describes each chip in the path as a 'sub-device' with input and output 'pads'. Every pad has a format, like 1920x1080 RAW10. For streaming to work, every connected pad must agree. Applications then ask for buffers, queue them, and get frames back one at a time.

MIPI CSI-2
Camera Serial Interface: packetized pixel data over 1–4 (or more) D-PHY/C-PHY lanes.
V4L2
Video4Linux2, the kernel video capture and output API.
Sub-device
A V4L2 object for a non-memory block (sensor, bridge, CSI receiver) with pads and ops.
Pad / link
Pad: an input or output port. Link: a connection between two pads in the media graph.
Media bus code
The on-wire format, e.g. MEDIA_BUS_FMT_SRGGB10_1X10 (RAW10 Bayer).
vb2
videobuf2, the kernel framework managing buffer queues and DMA for V4L2.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A camera path is an assembly line, from sensor to memory, and Linux models each station. A modern camera path is a graph: sensor → (optional bridge/serializer, e.g. HDMI-to-CSI or GMSL/FPD-Link) → CSI-2 receiver (D-PHY/C-PHY) → ISP → memory. Linux models each block as a V4L2 sub-device with pads, connected by links in the media controller graph. Each pad negotiates a format (resolution plus media bus code). User space configures the graph (media-ctl), then streams from a /dev/videoN node using buffer queues (VIDIOC_REQBUFS, QBUF, DQBUF, STREAMON), usually via libcamera.

MAKE IT STICK

A water-treatment plant. Sensor = river intake, bridge = pipe adapter, CSI-2 receiver = the plant inlet, ISP = filtration, memory = storage tanks. Every pipe joint (pad) must have the same diameter and flow format, or nothing comes out. The media controller is the plant's piping diagram.

INTERACTIVE LAB
CSI-2 link budget
IN PLAIN WORDS

A highway between the camera and the processor. Each lane carries so many cars per second. If the picture needs more cars than the lanes can carry, the picture breaks.

Try this: Pick a camera mode, number of lanes and lane speed, and find setups that overflow or don't match.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Configure mode, lanes and link rate; catch bandwidth and lane-mismatch bugs.

Term: link budget OK; endpoints agree; verify receiver error counters
START WITH THE INCIDENT
STREAMON succeeds but no frames ever arrive

A new 4K HDMI input via a Lontium-class bridge into the SoC's CSI-2 receiver. VIDIOC_STREAMON returns 0, but DQBUF blocks forever. The receiver's error register shows SoT (start-of-transmission) sync errors. The DT says data-lanes = <1 2 3 4> on the bridge endpoint but <1 2> on the receiver endpoint, and the link frequency doesn't match the 4K60 bandwidth.

1 · The bandwidth math

Required bit rate = width × height × fps × bits-per-pixel × (1 + blanking overhead). 3840×2160×60×16 bpp ≈ 7.96 Gbps raw, plus blanking, spread across lanes: with 4 lanes that's about 2+ Gbps per lane, which needs a D-PHY rate (e.g. 2.5 Gbps/lane) both sides support. A mismatched lane count or link frequency gives sync errors or no frames at all.

2 · DT endpoints must agree

The graph is described by port/endpoint nodes with remote-endpoint phandles, data-lanes, clock-lanes, link-frequencies and bus-type. Both ends must be consistent. Drivers parse them with v4l2_fwnode_endpoint_parse. Async notifiers bind sub-devices together as they probe.

3 · Debug top-down, then bottom-up

Top-down: media-ctl -p (links enabled? formats agree on every pad?), v4l2-ctl --all, v4l2-compliance. Bottom-up: is the sensor or bridge streaming (status registers, a scope on the clock lane)? Does the receiver see LP→HS transitions? Check receiver error counters (ECC, CRC, SoT sync), then ISP and DMA overflow flags.

4 · Buffers and timing

A helper library manages the queue of frame buffers; your driver just fills them and hands them back. vb2 handles queues: drivers implement queue_setup, buf_queue, start_streaming and stop_streaming, and complete buffers from the frame-done IRQ with timestamps. Return all buffers on stop (with the ERROR state) or STREAMOFF hangs. libcamera sits above this for complex ISPs, handling 3A control loops in user space via IPAs.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Every PCIe card describes itself: who made it, what it is, and how much memory-mapped space it needs. The kernel assigns that space and calls your driver's probe. You then 'map' the space so you can read and write the card's registers like memory, turn on its ability to do DMA, and set up interrupts, ideally one per queue so different CPUs can handle them.

Config space
A per-function register block (256 B, or 4 KiB extended) with IDs, BARs and capabilities.
BAR
Base Address Register: describes a MMIO (or I/O) window. The driver maps it to access device registers or memory.
Bus mastering
Permission for the device to initiate DMA. Enable it with pci_set_master().
MSI-X
Message Signaled Interrupts: up to 2048 vectors per function, each with its own address and data, steerable to CPUs.
TLP
Transaction Layer Packet: PCIe's unit of reads, writes and completions.
BDF
Bus:Device.Function address, e.g. 0000:01:00.0 in lspci.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

PCIe devices are discoverable. Firmware and the kernel walk the bus tree, read each function's configuration space (vendor and device ID, class, capabilities), size and assign its BARs (Base Address Registers: windows of MMIO the driver maps), and match a pci_driver by ID table. Drivers enable the device, request regions, map BARs (pcim_iomap_regions), enable bus mastering for DMA, and allocate MSI-X vectors: per-queue interrupts delivered as memory writes. GPUs, NICs and NVMe all follow this pattern.

MAKE IT STICK

Moving into an office building. Enumeration is the building manager walking every floor, asking each tenant "who are you and how much space do you need?" (config space and BAR sizing), then assigning suite numbers (addresses). MSI-X is giving each department its own doorbell instead of one shared fire alarm.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The accelerator times out only after a warm reboot

A PCIe AI accelerator works from cold boot, but after reboot the driver's first command times out and BAR reads return 0xFFFFFFFF. The device didn't complete its reset before enumeration; reads to a device that isn't responding complete with all-ones. The driver had no check, and treated 0xFFFFFFFF as a valid status.

1 · Enumeration and resources

The root complex sits at the top, with switches and endpoints below. Firmware or the kernel scans config space, sizes BARs (write all-ones, read back the size mask), and assigns addresses in bridge windows. lspci -vvv shows BARs, capabilities, link speed and width (LnkSta), and the MSI-X table. /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/ exposes resources and config.

2 · MMIO semantics

Device registers aren't normal memory: writes may be delayed, so read back to be sure they landed. BAR space is uncached device memory. readl/writel include ordering barriers, and _relaxed variants skip them for hot paths when you reason about ordering yourself. PCIe writes are posted (fire-and-forget): read back a register to flush posted writes before relying on their effect. A read returning all-ones often means the device dropped off the bus or is in reset.

3 · Interrupts and queues

Fast devices have many queues, each with its own doorbell and its own CPU, so they don't fight. Modern devices (NVMe, NICs, GPUs) have many submission and completion queues, each with an MSI-X vector affined to a CPU. That gives no shared-IRQ contention and cache-local completion handling. pci_irq_vector(pdev, i) gives the Linux IRQ number for vector i, and managed affinity spreads vectors across CPUs.

4 · Errors, reset and power

PCIe can report and recover from its own errors, and a slow link is often a cable or slot problem. AER (Advanced Error Reporting) logs correctable and uncorrectable errors. Implement err_handler callbacks to recover. Reset methods: FLR (function-level reset), secondary bus reset. Link issues show as reduced speed or width (LnkSta: Speed 8GT/s, Width x4 (downgraded)). Runtime PM and ASPM trade power for latency. GPUs add huge BARs (Resizable BAR) and peer-to-peer DMA.

1

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Memory doesn't arrive one byte at a time. It arrives in 64-byte chunks called cache lines. If your loop walks memory in order, every chunk you fetch is fully used and the CPU fetches the next one ahead of time. If it jumps around, every access can wait ~100 ns for RAM. The same algorithm can be 10× faster just by touching memory in the order it's laid out.

Cache line
The 64-byte unit (on most x86 and ARM CPUs) moved between memory and caches.
Spatial locality
Using data stored near recently used data.
Temporal locality
Reusing the same data soon.
Prefetcher
Hardware that detects access patterns and fetches lines before they're requested.
Row-major
C/C++ arrays store rows contiguously: a[i][j] and a[i][j+1] are neighbours.
AoS / SoA
Array of Structs vs Struct of Arrays, two layouts with very different cache behavior.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

CPUs are fast and DRAM is slow (~100 ns, or hundreds of cycles). Caches (L1 ~1 ns, L2 ~4 ns, L3 ~10–40 ns) bridge the gap by holding recently used 64-byte cache lines. Performance follows locality: spatial (use neighbouring bytes from the same line) and temporal (reuse data while it's still cached). Sequential access lets the hardware prefetcher stream data. Random pointer-chasing defeats it. Data layout (array-of-structs vs struct-of-arrays, row-major traversal) often matters more than instruction count.

MAKE IT STICK

Cooking. L1 is the cutting board, L2 the counter, L3 the fridge, DRAM the grocery store across town. You never fetch one grain of rice; you bring the whole bag (a cache line). A good cook preps ingredients in the order they're needed (sequential access) so the helper can fetch the next bag in advance (prefetcher).

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 'optimized' image filter got slower

A colleague converted a camera de-noise filter from per-pixel structs (struct Px { uint8_t r,g,b,a; float weight; ... }, 32 bytes) to a cleaner object design, and processed columns first "to match the algorithm description". Throughput dropped from 120 fps to 18 fps on the ARM SoC. The instruction count barely changed; perf stat shows the L1 miss rate went from 2% to 45%.

1 · Know the latency ladder

Memory has layers, like a desk, a shelf and a basement: the further away, the slower. Rough numbers to memorize: L1 hit ≈ 1 ns (4 cycles), L2 ≈ 4 ns, L3 ≈ 10–40 ns, DRAM ≈ 80–120 ns, a cross-socket NUMA hop adds more. One DRAM miss costs as much as hundreds of simple instructions. Out-of-order execution hides some latency, but not a dependent chain of misses (linked lists, trees).

2 · Layout for the access pattern

Traverse row-major arrays with the last index innermost. Choose SoA when hot loops touch one field of many elements (it uses every byte fetched and vectorizes well). Choose AoS when you touch all fields of one element together. Pack hot fields together and move cold ones out. Prefer contiguous containers (std::vector) over node-based ones (std::list, std::map) in hot paths.

3 · Blocking (tiling)

Work on small tiles that fit in the fast memory, like doing a jigsaw one corner at a time. For 2D work (matrix multiply, image filters, transposes), process tiles that fit in L1 or L2, e.g. 64×64, so data is reused before it's evicted. This is the same idea as CUDA shared-memory tiling (Lesson 12.2): move a working set into fast memory, reuse it, move on.

4 · Measure, don't guess

perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses gives IPC and miss rates. Low IPC (< 1) with high misses means memory-bound. Compare against the roofline (Lesson 7.4). Hardware counters on ARM (via perf, or vendor tools like Arm Streamline) work the same way.

LESSON 11.2 · C++ · NEW
False sharing, contention & lock-free basics
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Each CPU core has its own cache. When one core writes to a cache line, every other core's copy of that line becomes invalid, so they have to fetch it again. If two threads write two different counters stored next to each other, they fight over the same line constantly. Putting each counter on its own 64-byte line removes the fight.

Cache coherence
The hardware protocol (MESI/MOESI) keeping every core's view of a line consistent.
False sharing
Independent variables on the same line causing coherence traffic.
alignas(64)
C++ specifier forcing an object to start on a 64-byte boundary.
Contention
Many threads competing for the same lock or variable.
Lock-free
At least one thread always makes progress; built with atomics and CAS, no mutex.
CAS
Compare-and-swap: atomically replace a value only if it still equals the expected one.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Two cores writing to different things on the same cache line keep stealing it from each other, like two people sharing one pen. Caches are kept coherent per line (MESI-style protocols). If two cores write different variables that happen to share one 64-byte line, the line ping-pongs between their caches: false sharing. Each write invalidates the other core's copy, and throughput can collapse 10× with no logical sharing at all. Fix it with padding or alignment (alignas(64), std::hardware_destructive_interference_size) or per-thread data merged at the end. True contention (many cores updating one counter or lock) needs sharding, batching, or a different design.

MAKE IT STICK

Two people editing different paragraphs of the same Google Doc page, where the rule says only one person can hold the page at a time. They aren't editing the same words, but they keep yanking the page from each other. Give each their own page (padding) and they both fly.

IN PLAIN WORDS

Term: false sharing: coherence invalidations on one cache line
START WITH THE INCIDENT
Adding threads made the packet counter slower

Picture eight people writing tallies on one small notepad: they spend all their time passing it around. A telemetry module counts frames per camera stream in uint64_t stats[8] (one slot per thread, made atomic after a TSan report). Going from 1 to 8 threads, total throughput dropped from 400 M increments/s to 60 M. perf c2c shows one cache line with heavy HITM (hit-modified) traffic: all eight counters live in it.

1 · Coherence in one minute

A line is Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid (MESI). To write, a core needs exclusive ownership, which invalidates every other copy. Two cores alternately writing the same line force a transfer every time (tens of ns, more across sockets). That's why one shared atomic counter scales negatively with cores.

2 · Detect it

Symptoms: throughput falls as threads increase; high cycles on simple stores. Tools: perf c2c record/report (Linux) pinpoints contended lines and the offsets each thread writes; Intel VTune 'memory access'; on ARM, the SPE or CMN counters. TSan finds races, not false sharing; those are separate problems.

3 · Fix it

Pad or align per-thread data to 64 bytes (128 on some CPUs where adjacent-line prefetch pairs lines). Use thread-local accumulation and merge at the end. Shard hot counters per CPU (the kernel's percpu counters). Separate read-mostly fields from frequently written ones in shared structs (e.g. the producer index and consumer index of a ring on different lines).

4 · Lock-free with care

Lock-free code avoids waiting but is hard to get right; use it only when measurements say so. Lock-free structures (SPSC ring from Lesson 4.6, Treiber stack via CAS) avoid blocking but not coherence costs, and bring ABA problems, memory reclamation (hazard pointers, epochs) and subtle ordering. Use them when measurement shows lock contention matters and the structure is well understood. Often sharding plus a plain mutex wins.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Instead of guessing what's slow, let the CPU tell you. perf interrupts the program thousands of times a second and records which function (and which callers) was running. Functions that show up in many samples are where time goes. A flame graph draws this as stacked boxes: the wider a box, the more time it costs.

Sampling profiler
Periodically records the current stack. Low overhead and statistical.
IPC
Instructions per cycle. Low IPC often means stalls (memory, branches).
Flame graph
A visualization of sampled stacks: x = sample share (not time order), y = stack depth.

A register chain that makes stack unwinding cheap. Compile with -fno-omit-frame-pointer.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Measure before you optimise. A flame graph shows where time goes, like a map of a busy city. Optimization starts with measurement. perf stat gives whole-program counters (cycles, instructions, IPC, cache and branch misses). perf record -g samples call stacks thousands of times per second, and flame graphs visualize where time goes: width = share of samples, stacks grow upward, and wide plateaus at the top are your hot spots. START WITH THE INCIDENT
"The encoder is slow" (it wasn't)

The video pipeline drops frames at 4K30. The team blames the hardware encoder and starts tuning bitrate parameters. A 10-second system-wide perf record -a -g shows 38% of CPU in memcpy called from a user-space color-conversion step and 12% in a kernel __arch_copy_from_user path: frames are copied twice before reaching the encoder.

1 · Start broad

First find out what kind of slow it is: busy CPU, slow memory, waiting on I/O, or the GPU. Before profiling functions, classify the bottleneck: CPU-bound (high utilization, perf stat IPC), memory-bound (low IPC, high cache misses), I/O or lock-bound (low CPU, threads blocked), or GPU and accelerator-bound. top/htop, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1 and pidstat -t answer this in a minute.

2 · Read flame graphs correctly

In a flame graph, wide means "took a lot of time"; left to right is not a timeline. The x-axis is not time; boxes are sorted alphabetically and merged. Width = how often that frame appeared. Look for wide towers and wide plateaus (self time at the top). Click to zoom. Compare before and after with differential flame graphs. Missing frames usually mean no frame pointers or stripped symbols.

3 · Don't forget off-CPU and the kernel

If CPU is low but latency is high, the time is off-CPU: locks, I/O, scheduling. Use perf sched, bcc/bpftrace offcputime, or perf trace. Include the kernel (-a, privileges) when drivers, syscalls, IRQs or copies matter, which in camera and network stacks they usually do.

4 · Close the loop

Change one thing at a time, measure again, and write it down, like a careful lab experiment. Form a hypothesis from the profile, change one thing, re-measure with the same workload, and keep a log. Watch for observer effects and noise (pin CPU frequency, repeat runs, report variance). Here the fix was zero-copy dma-buf import into the encoder: CPU dropped 45% and 4K30 became stable.

LESSON 12.1 · CUDA C++ · NEW
Streams, events & overlapping copies with compute
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

The GPU has separate engines for copying data and for computing. If you copy everything, then compute, then copy back, each engine waits for the others. Instead, cut the work into chunks and give each chunk its own queue (stream). Then chunk 2 can copy in while chunk 1 computes and chunk 0 copies out. For copies to really run in the background, the CPU memory must be 'pinned' so the GPU can DMA it directly.

Stream
An ordered queue of GPU operations. Different streams can overlap.
Pinned memory
Page-locked host memory the GPU can DMA directly; required for truly async copies.
Copy engine
Dedicated DMA hardware on the GPU for host↔device transfers (often 2+).
cudaMemcpyAsync
Enqueues a copy in a stream and returns immediately.
Event
A marker in a stream used for timing or cross-stream waits.
Default stream
Stream 0. Legacy behavior synchronizes with other streams, so avoid it for overlap.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Keep the GPU busy by copying the next batch while it works on the current one. A CUDA stream is an in-order queue of GPU work (kernels, copies). Work in different streams may run concurrently. Overlap comes from splitting data into chunks and pipelining H2D copy → kernel → D2H copy across streams, so the copy engines and SMs work at the same time. Truly async copies need pinned (page-locked) host memory (cudaMallocHost); pageable memory forces a staging copy and serializes. Events mark points in a stream for timing and cross-stream dependencies (cudaStreamWaitEvent). CUDA Graphs capture a whole sequence to cut launch overhead.

MAKE IT STICK

Think of a laundromat with a washer, a dryer and a folding table. A laundromat with a washer (H2D copy engine), a dryer (SMs) and a folding table (D2H engine). Doing one giant load means two machines sit idle. Split the laundry into loads and pipeline them: while load 2 washes, load 1 dries and load 0 gets folded. Pinned memory is having your clothes already sorted at the door, so nobody waits for you to empty the basket.

INTERACTIVE LAB
CUDA stream timeline
IN PLAIN WORDS

Doing laundry with one washer and one dryer. While load 2 washes, load 1 can dry. Doing one load at a time leaves a machine idle.

Try this: Add streams and turn on pinned memory to overlap copies with work.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Add streams and pinned memory to overlap copies with kernels.

Streams / chunks
1

H2D
0

0
D2H
0
Total 52.0 units. One queue: copy in, work, copy out, one after another.
Term: one stream: H2D, kernel, D2H run serially
START WITH THE INCIDENT
Four streams, zero overlap

The work was split into four queues, yet everything still ran one at a time. An inference preprocessing service split a batch across 4 streams, but Nsight Systems shows copies and kernels running strictly one after another. The host buffers came from std::vector<float> (pageable), and one helper used cudaMemcpy (synchronous, default stream) for a small lookup table in the middle of the loop.

1 · Why pageable memory blocks overlap

The GPU can only DMA from physical pages that won't move. With pageable memory, the driver copies through an internal pinned staging buffer, and the call behaves synchronously with respect to the host. Pin the buffers you stream (cudaMallocHost or cudaHostRegister), and reuse them; pinning is expensive.

2 · Implicit synchronization

The legacy default stream synchronizes with all blocking streams. cudaMemcpy, cudaMalloc, cudaFree and some other calls can serialize everything. Use non-blocking streams or per-thread default streams (--default-stream per-thread), preallocate memory (or use the stream-ordered allocator cudaMallocAsync), and keep sync calls out of the hot loop.

3 · Read the timeline

Nsight Systems shows rows for each stream and the copy engines. Healthy overlap looks like staggered blocks: H2D(i+1) under Kernel(i) under D2H(i-1). Gaps between kernels mean CPU launch overhead (use CUDA Graphs) or a host-side sync.

4 · Dependencies across streams

Use events: cudaEventRecord(e, producer) then cudaStreamWaitEvent(consumer, e). That expresses a GPU-side dependency without blocking the CPU. In multi-GPU or NCCL setups the same ideas apply to communication streams overlapping compute.

text:
LESSON 12.2 · CUDA C++ · NEW
Shared memory, tiling, reductions & warp shuffles
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Thousands of GPU threads can't all add into one variable at once. Instead, each block of threads adds its numbers in pairs, then pairs of pairs, halving the active threads each round, using a small fast scratchpad called shared memory. The last 32 threads (one warp) finish by passing values directly between registers. Each block then adds its single result to the global total.

Shared memory
Fast on-chip memory shared by a thread block. Explicitly managed.
__syncthreads()
A barrier: every thread in the block waits until all reach it. Shared memory writes are then visible.
Warp
32 threads executing in lockstep (SIMT) on an SM.
__shfl_down_sync
Read a register from the lane offset higher in the same warp.
Bank conflict
Several threads in a warp accessing different addresses in the same shared-memory bank, which serializes them.
Tiling
Loading a sub-block of data into shared memory to reuse it many times.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Global memory (HBM/GDDR) is high-bandwidth but high-latency. Each SM has fast shared memory (tens to hundreds of KB, ~20–30 cycles) that a thread block uses as a programmer-managed cache: load a tile once with coalesced reads, __syncthreads(), reuse it many times. A reduction (sum, max) combines values in a tree: log2(n) steps instead of n. Inside a warp (32 threads), shuffle intrinsics (__shfl_down_sync) exchange registers directly, with no shared memory and no barrier. Watch for bank conflicts (32 banks; threads hitting the same bank serialize).

MAKE IT STICK

Counting votes in a stadium. Instead of one person walking every row (serial), each row's neighbours pair up and add their counts, then pairs of pairs, and so on, until one number remains: a tree. Shared memory is the whiteboard each section shares. Warp shuffles are 32 people in one row whispering numbers directly to each other without using the whiteboard.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Tree reduction stepper
IN PLAIN WORDS

Adding up 16 numbers in a classroom: pair up and add, then pair the pairs, until one person holds the total. It takes 4 rounds instead of 15 steps in a row.

Try this: Step through the rounds until one number is left.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Step a 16-element shared-memory reduction to its sum.

3

Next tree step →
Reset
Half the workers drop out each round. On a real GPU, the last 32 numbers are finished by passing values between neighbors directly.
Term: active threads halve each step; finish the last 32 with warp shuffles
START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 'parallel' sum is slower than the CPU

A first CUDA attempt sums 100M floats with atomicAdd(out, in[i]) from every thread. It runs at a fraction of memory bandwidth, slower than a vectorized CPU loop. Every thread hammers one address; atomics on the same location serialize in the memory system.

1 · Why the tree wins

n atomics on one address serialize to O(n). A tree reduction does O(n) total adds but only O(log n) dependent steps, with most work in registers and shared memory. Then one atomic per block (or a second kernel pass) combines block results.

2 · Memory hierarchy on the GPU

GPU memory goes from tiny and fast to huge and slow. Fetch from the slow layer once and reuse it from the fast one. Registers (fastest, per thread) → shared memory and L1 (per SM) → L2 (shared) → HBM (TB/s but hundreds of cycles). Kernels should read global memory once, coalesced, and do repeated access in shared memory or registers. Tiled matrix multiply loads A and B tiles into shared memory and reuses each element TILE times.

3 · Bank conflicts and divergence

Shared memory has 32 banks of 4 bytes. If two lanes access different addresses in the same bank, the accesses serialize. Sequential addressing (tid and tid + s) avoids this, while interleaved 2*s*tid patterns cause conflicts and divergence. Padding tiles ([TILE][TILE+1]) fixes transposes.

4 · Use the libraries, understand the pattern

In production, use CUB (cub::DeviceReduce::Sum), Thrust or cooperative groups, which are tuned per architecture. Interviewers still expect you to write and explain this kernel: barriers, coalescing, bank conflicts, shuffles and why __syncthreads() can't be inside divergent branches.

The GPU driver stack: UMD, KMD, contexts, GPU VM & channels
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Your program doesn't talk to the GPU directly. A user-space driver library turns 'launch this kernel' into GPU command bytes and places them in shared memory. A kernel driver set that up earlier: it gave your process its own GPU address space and a command queue. Submitting work is then often just writing the queue entry and poking a doorbell register, with no system call per launch. The GPU signals completion by writing a fence value.

UMD
User-mode driver: libcuda, Vulkan or GL drivers. Builds command streams in user space.
KMD
Kernel-mode driver (e.g. nvidia.ko, amdgpu, nouveau): privileged setup, memory, scheduling and faults.
Context
A GPU-side process equivalent: its own virtual address space and state.
Channel / ring
A command queue that a context submits work into (GPFIFO on NVIDIA, rings on AMD).
Doorbell
An MMIO register written to notify the GPU that new entries are in a ring.
Fence / semaphore
A memory value the GPU writes on completion; the CPU or other engines wait on it.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A kernel launch crosses several layers. The user-mode driver (UMD) (CUDA runtime/driver library, or Vulkan/GL drivers) validates the call, encodes commands into a push buffer in memory the GPU can read, and submits by writing an entry into a channel's ring (e.g. a GPFIFO) and ringing a doorbell (an MMIO write), often without a syscall. The kernel-mode driver (KMD) handles what needs privilege: creating contexts and channels, managing GPU virtual memory (page tables, allocations, pinning), scheduling and time-slicing between contexts, interrupts, fault handling and recovery. Fences/semaphores report completion back.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant. The UMD is the waiter who writes orders in kitchen shorthand (commands) on a ticket rail (push buffer and ring) and rings the bell (doorbell). The KMD is the restaurant manager: assigns tables (contexts), controls which pantry shelves each table may use (GPU VM), decides which orders the kitchen works on (scheduling), and handles the fire alarm (faults and recovery). The kitchen (GPU engines) reads tickets on its own.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Put it in order
IN PLAIN WORDS

START WITH THE INCIDENT
"Xid" errors and a hung GPU after a driver update

After an update, some jobs crash and others hang. The logs tell you which kind of bug each one is. After a rollout, some training nodes log GPU fault errors (on NVIDIA, 'Xid' messages in the kernel log) and jobs hang. One class shows MMU faults at a GPU virtual address just past a buffer: a kernel bug reading out of bounds. Another shows channel timeouts caused by a long-running kernel that never completes, so the watchdog resets the channel.

1 · Who does what

A GPU driver comes in two halves: one inside your app and one inside the kernel. UMD: API validation, JIT and module loading (PTX → SASS), command encoding, user-space submission, and sync primitives built on fences. KMD: device init and firmware (on modern NVIDIA, the GSP runs much of the resource manager on the GPU), memory management (VRAM plus system memory, page tables, migration for Unified Memory), channel and context scheduling, interrupts, fault and error handling, power, and display.

2 · GPU virtual memory

Each context has its own GPU page tables, so an out-of-bounds access faults instead of corrupting another process. Unified Memory relies on GPU page faults to migrate pages on demand. Pinning host memory means the KMD locks pages and maps them into the GPU's address space for DMA (ties back to Lessons 10.4 and 12.1).

3 · Scheduling and isolation

Many programs can share one GPU by taking turns, merging, or splitting the chip into parts. Many contexts share the GPU via time-slicing and runlists managed by the KMD or firmware. MPS (Multi-Process Service) merges clients into one context for concurrency. MIG partitions an A100/H100-class GPU into hardware-isolated instances. Preemption granularity affects latency for interactive or real-time work.

4 · Debugging the stack

There are good tools for finding GPU faults and slow spots, and the open-source drivers are worth reading. Kernel logs (fault codes, channel IDs), nvidia-smi and DCGM health metrics, compute-sanitizer for out-of-bounds or race bugs in kernels, Nsight Systems for submission gaps, and reading open-source drivers (NVIDIA's open GPU kernel modules, nouveau, amdgpu) to understand ioctls, channels and page tables.

text:
LESSON 13.1 · C++ · NEW
Feedback control: PID loops that don't oscillate
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A robot joint needs to reach and hold an angle. Each loop, the controller computes the error (target minus actual) and adds three things: a push proportional to the error, a slowly growing push if the error persists, and a brake proportional to how fast things are moving. Too much push and it overshoots and oscillates; too little and it's sluggish. Limits keep the motor command within what the hardware can do.

Setpoint
The target value (desired angle, speed).
Error
Setpoint minus measurement.
Integral windup
The I term keeps growing while the output is saturated, causing big overshoot later.
Derivative kick
A spike in D output when the setpoint jumps. Avoided by differentiating the measurement.
Cascade control
An outer loop (position) feeding the setpoint of a faster inner loop (velocity, current).
Loop rate
How often the controller runs (e.g. 1 kHz for joints, 10–40 kHz for current loops).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A controller is like a thermostat: measure, compare with the target, and adjust, many times a second. A controller repeatedly measures a state (joint angle, motor speed), compares it to a setpoint, and outputs a command (torque, PWM duty). PID combines three terms: P reacts to the current error, I removes steady-state error by accumulating it, and D damps motion by reacting to the rate of change. Tuning trades rise time, overshoot and stability. Real controllers add output limits, anti-windup (stop integrating when saturated), derivative on measurement (no 'kick' on setpoint steps), filtering and a fixed, jitter-free loop rate. Humanoid joints use cascaded loops: position → velocity → current (torque) at increasing rates.

MAKE IT STICK

Steering a car into a lane. P: turn harder the further you are from the centre. I: if a crosswind keeps pushing you off, slowly add a constant correction. D: if you're approaching the centre fast, ease off so you don't overshoot. Anti-windup: if the wheel is already at full lock, stop 'saving up' more steering you can't use.

INTERACTIVE LAB

IN PLAIN WORDS

Term: steady-state error: add integral gain (Ki)
START WITH THE INCIDENT
The elbow joint overshoots after lifting a box

A test arm holds a 5 kg box at full torque for two seconds (it's at its limit), then the box is removed. The elbow flies up 25° past its target and rings for a second. The controller had no anti-windup: the I term kept accumulating error while the motor was saturated, and released it all at once.

1 · What each term does

P alone: faster with higher kp, but leaves steady-state error against constant loads (gravity) and oscillates if too high. I removes steady-state error but adds lag and overshoot. D adds damping and anticipation but amplifies sensor noise, so filter it. Start with P, add D for damping, add a little I last.

2 · Tuning in practice

Begin with ki = kd = 0 and raise kp until it responds briskly with slight overshoot. Add kd to damp the overshoot, then a small ki to remove the remaining offset. Use step-response plots (rise time, overshoot, settling time). Ziegler–Nichols gives starting points; model-based tuning or frequency response (Bode, gain and phase margin) is used for serious systems.

3 · Real-world must-haves

Real controllers need extra guards: limits, filters, a good first guess and safety stops. Output saturation with anti-windup, derivative on measurement with a low-pass filter, feedforward (gravity, inertia, friction) so feedback handles only the residual, rate limits on setpoints, a fixed dt with measured jitter, and safety: torque limits, watchdogs and fault states when encoders disagree.

4 · Humanoid context

A humanoid like Optimus has dozens of actuators. Each typically runs a current or torque loop in motor-driver firmware at 10+ kHz, velocity and position loops around 1 kHz, and whole-body controllers (balance, impedance control, MPC) at 100 Hz to 1 kHz. Latency and jitter in this chain directly limit achievable gains and stability.

text:
LESSON 13.2 · C++ · NEW
State estimation: sensor fusion with Kalman filters
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

You never know a robot's true state exactly; you only have guesses from a model and from noisy sensors. A Kalman filter keeps a best guess plus 'how unsure am I'. Each tick it predicts forward (and gets more unsure), then corrects with a sensor reading, trusting it more or less depending on how noisy that sensor is.

State x
What we estimate (position, velocity, orientation, bias).
Covariance P
Uncertainty of the estimate (a variance in 1D).
Process noise Q
How much the motion model may be wrong per step.
Measurement noise R
How noisy the sensor is.
Kalman gain K
The blend factor between prediction and measurement, 0 to 1.
EKF
Extended Kalman Filter: linearizes nonlinear models around the current estimate.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Sensors are noisy and incomplete: encoders drift relative to the world, IMUs integrate bias, cameras are slow and occasionally wrong. A Kalman filter keeps an estimate x and its uncertainty P. Predict moves the estimate forward with a motion model (uncertainty grows by process noise Q). Update blends in a measurement z weighted by the Kalman gain K = P/(P+R), so trusted measurements (small R) pull harder. Nonlinear robots use the EKF/UKF or complementary filters. Humanoid balance relies on fused IMU, joint encoders and foot contact.

MAKE IT STICK

Walking to the kitchen in the dark. You predict where you are from your steps (motion model), getting less sure with every step. When your hand touches the door frame (measurement), you snap your belief toward it, more strongly if you trust your touch more than your step counting.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Sensor fusion lab
IN PLAIN WORDS

Walking in the dark with a step counter that slowly drifts and a GPS that jumps around. Combine both: trust the step counter short-term and the GPS long-term.

Try this: Change how much you trust each sensor and watch the blended estimate.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Fuse a drifting gyro with a noisy absolute sensor; tune Q and R.

R (sensor noise)
4
Q (model trust)
0.01
Gyro bias

— true angle — turn sensor only (drifts) — blended estimate. A position reading arrives every 5 steps.

Average error 0.87. The guess is smooth, and each position reading pulls it back, so drift never builds up.
Term: balanced Q and R: bounded drift (RMSE)
START WITH THE INCIDENT
The robot's heading drifts 20° per minute

A mobile base estimates heading by integrating the gyro. After a minute it believes it's facing a different wall. The gyro has a small bias (0.3°/s) that integration turns into unbounded drift. A magnetometer or camera heading is noisy but doesn't drift, and the team never fused them.

1 · Predict and correct

Prediction uses fast, smooth, drifting sources (IMU, odometry). Correction uses slow, noisy, absolute ones (camera landmarks, GPS, magnetometer, foot contact). Fusion gets the best of both: smooth and drift-free.

2 · Tuning Q and R

R comes from sensor datasheets or measurement variance at rest. Q expresses model error (unmodeled accelerations, slip). Too small a Q makes the filter overconfident and slow to react. Too large makes it noisy. Watch the innovation sequence: it should look like zero-mean white noise with the predicted variance.

3 · Estimate biases too

Augment the state with the gyro bias: x = [angle, bias]. The filter learns the bias from absolute measurements and subtracts it in prediction, which fixes the drift story above. Real systems also handle outliers (innovation gating) and timestamps (late camera measurements need a delay-compensated update).

4 · Humanoid state estimation

To balance, a robot needs to know how it is tilted and moving, and sensors must agree on the time. Balance needs base orientation and velocity: IMU propagation plus leg kinematics when feet are in contact (contact-aided EKF), often with vision for global position. Timestamps across sensors must be precise (hardware sync, PTP), which ties directly to driver timestamping and camera sync work.

ROS 2, DDS & QoS: moving robot data reliably
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL

CODE, LINE BY LINE

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A robot runs many programs (nodes): camera driver, perception, planner, motor controller. They talk by publishing messages to named topics. Each publisher and subscriber chooses delivery rules: retry until delivered, or just send the latest and drop old ones. If the rules on both sides don't match, they silently don't connect, which is the #1 ROS 2 surprise.

Node
A process or component with publishers, subscribers, services and timers.
Topic
A named, typed pub/sub channel, e.g. /camera/image_raw.
DDS
Data Distribution Service, the middleware standard ROS 2 uses for discovery and transport.
QoS
Quality of Service policies: reliability, history, depth, durability, deadline.
Best effort
Send without retransmission. Drops are allowed.
Transient local
The publisher keeps the last samples for subscribers that join later.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

ROS 2 structures robot software as nodes exchanging messages over topics (pub/sub), services (request/response) and actions (long-running goals with feedback). Underneath is DDS (a data-distribution middleware) with QoS policies per endpoint: reliability (reliable vs best-effort), history/depth (keep last N), durability (volatile vs transient-local for late joiners) and deadline/liveliness. Publisher and subscriber QoS must be compatible or no data flows. Sensor streams usually want best-effort, keep-last-1 (fresh beats complete). Commands and maps want reliable. Large data (images, point clouds) benefit from zero-copy intra-process or shared-memory transports.

MAKE IT STICK

Live TV vs registered mail. A camera feed is live TV: if you miss a frame, you want the next one, not a replay (best-effort, keep last 1). A 'stop now' command or a map is registered mail: it must arrive, and late arrivals should still get the latest copy (reliable, transient-local).

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The perception node receives nothing

A new perception node subscribes to /camera/image_raw with default (reliable) QoS. The camera driver publishes with best-effort. ros2 topic list shows the topic, the camera is clearly publishing, but the callback never fires. Reliable subscribers are incompatible with best-effort publishers, and DDS reports an 'incompatible QoS' event that nobody logged.

1 · QoS compatibility rules

Reliability: a best-effort publisher can't satisfy a reliable subscriber (no data); a reliable publisher can serve both. Durability: a volatile publisher can't satisfy a transient-local subscriber. Deadline and liveliness must also be compatible. Debug with ros2 topic info -v /topic (shows each endpoint's QoS) and incompatible-QoS event callbacks.

2 · Choose QoS per data type

Camera and LiDAR streams: best-effort, keep-last small (fresh beats complete; retransmitting old frames adds latency). Commands: reliable, keep-last, plus deadline monitoring. Maps and static TFs: reliable plus transient-local so late joiners get them. Logs: reliable with a larger depth.

3 · Latency and big messages

Images are big; copying them for every listener is slow, so share them instead. A 1080p RGB image is about 6 MB; serializing and copying it per subscriber is costly. Use intra-process communication (components in one process with unique_ptr messages for zero-copy), shared-memory transports offered by some DDS implementations, or loaned messages. Keep callbacks short and choose executors and threads deliberately.

4 · Real-time considerations

ROS 2 isn't hard real-time by itself. Robots split it: hard RT control loops (1 kHz+) in dedicated RT threads or MCU firmware, ROS 2 for perception, planning and coordination. Use bounded allocations, RT-safe executors, and keep DDS traffic off the RT cores.

LESSON 13.4 · C · LINUX REAL-TIME · NEW
Real-time Linux & motor control: PREEMPT_RT, jitter & EtherCAT
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A robot joint loop running at 1000 times per second must run every 1 ms, every time. A normal Linux system usually does, but occasionally a long kernel operation or page fault delays it by several milliseconds, and the robot jerks. Real-time Linux and careful programming (highest priority, memory locked in RAM, sleeping until exact times, a dedicated CPU) keep the worst-case delay down to tens of microseconds.

Jitter
Variation in when a periodic task actually runs.
PREEMPT_RT
Real-time Linux configuration: preemptible kernel, threaded IRQs, sleeping spinlocks.
SCHED_FIFO
A real-time scheduling policy: the highest priority runs until it blocks or yields.
mlockall
Locks the process's memory in RAM to prevent page-fault delays.
cyclictest
The standard tool to measure scheduling latency and jitter.
EtherCAT
An industrial Ethernet fieldbus with deterministic cycles and distributed clocks.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Control loops need determinism: the worst-case latency matters more than the average. On Linux, PREEMPT_RT (merged into mainline in 6.12) makes almost all kernel code preemptible and threads IRQ handlers, so a high-priority SCHED_FIFO thread can preempt nearly anything. An RT loop locks its memory (mlockall), preallocates, avoids blocking syscalls, sleeps to absolute deadlines (clock_nanosleep with TIMER_ABSTIME) and runs on isolated CPUs. Measure with cyclictest. Motor drives sit on deterministic fieldbuses like EtherCAT (sub-ms cycles with distributed clocks) or CAN-FD; the innermost current loops run in MCU or FPGA firmware.

MAKE IT STICK

A metronome for an orchestra. It doesn't matter that it ticks on time on average; one late tick throws off every musician. PREEMPT_RT lets the conductor interrupt anyone instantly. Isolated CPUs give the metronome its own quiet room. mlockall makes sure its sheet music is always on the stand, never fetched from storage mid-song.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Real-time jitter tuner
IN PLAIN WORDS

A train timetable. Most trains are on time, but the rare late one is what breaks your connection. Fixes aim to shrink the worst delay, not the average.

Try this: Turn on each real-time fix and watch the worst-case delay shrink.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Enable RT mitigations and watch the worst-case latency shrink.

mlockall + prefault

Worst-case wakeup latency
9.0 ms
Sometimes the task wakes a whole millisecond late. A loop that must run 1,000 times a second will miss beats. Turn on the fixes one by one. Sleeping "for 1 ms" instead of "until the next tick" also lets small delays add up.
Term: millisecond wake-up latency spikes; relative sleeps add cumulative drift
START WITH THE INCIDENT
A 1 kHz walking controller stumbles twice an hour

The robot's balance loop runs at 1 kHz on Linux. 99.99% of cycles are on time, but twice an hour a cycle is late by 4–8 ms and the robot visibly stumbles. Traces show the loop thread blocked behind a page fault (memory wasn't locked) and, separately, preempted by a long non-threaded IRQ from a USB camera driver.

1 · Average is irrelevant, the tail is everything

Measure the worst case over hours under load: cyclictest -m -S -p 90 -i 1000 -h 400 while running stress (stress-ng, network, storage and GPU load). Plot the latency histogram. Typical tuned PREEMPT_RT systems reach tens of µs worst case on suitable hardware; stock kernels can show milliseconds.

2 · Remove sources of latency

Prepare everything in advance and keep the real-time loop's CPU free of distractions. Lock and prefault memory, preallocate everything, avoid syscalls that may block (file I/O, logging: use a lock-free queue to a non-RT logger thread), isolate CPUs (isolcpus/nohz_full, cpusets), move IRQs off RT cores (irq affinity), disable deep C-states and frequency scaling on RT cores, and watch SMIs and firmware interrupts on x86.

3 · Priority inversion and locking

A low-priority task holding a lock can block an urgent one, like a slow car in a one-lane tunnel. If the RT thread shares a mutex with a low-priority thread, a medium-priority thread can starve the holder (priority inversion; Mars Pathfinder is the classic case). Use priority-inheritance mutexes (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT; rt-mutexes in PREEMPT_RT) or, better, lock-free single-producer/single-consumer buffers between RT and non-RT code.

4 · The actuator side

The fastest motor loops run on small chips beside the motor, and Linux sends them targets. Torque or current loops at 10–40 kHz run in motor-driver MCUs or FPGAs (field-oriented control, PWM). The Linux RT loop sends setpoints over EtherCAT or CAN-FD each cycle, with distributed clocks aligning sampling across joints. Safety: watchdogs that cut torque if setpoints stop, limits enforced in firmware, and a safe-stop state.

LESSON 14.1 · C++ · NEW
Two pointers & sliding windows
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Instead of re-checking every possible substring, keep a 'window' between two positions. Move the right edge forward one character at a time. When the window becomes invalid (for example, a letter repeats), move the left edge forward until it's valid again. Track the best window seen. Because both edges only move forward, the work is proportional to the string length.

Window
The current range [left, right] under consideration.
Invariant
A rule the window always satisfies after each step (e.g. no repeated characters).
O(n)
Time grows linearly with input size.
std::array<int, 256>
A fixed-size array on the stack: one slot per possible byte value.
unsigned char
A byte from 0 to 255, safe to use as an array index (a plain char may be negative).
std::max
Returns the larger of two values (from <algorithm>).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Many array and string problems ask for the best contiguous range. Brute force checks every (start, end) pair in O(n²). A sliding window keeps two indices: right expands the window one step at a time, and left advances only when the window breaks a rule (a duplicate, a sum over budget). Each index moves at most n times, so the whole scan is O(n). Two pointers from both ends solve sorted-array problems (pair sums, container with most water) the same way.

MAKE IT STICK

A caterpillar crawling along a branch. Its head (right) reaches forward to take in the next leaf. When it's holding something it can't have (a repeat), its tail (left) pulls in until the problem is gone. It never backs up, so it crosses the branch in one pass.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Sliding-window animator
IN PLAIN WORDS

A sliding window on a train: the view grows on the right, and when you see a repeat, the left edge jumps forward past it.

Try this: Step the right edge and watch the left edge jump. Try the text "abba".

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Advance the right pointer and watch left jump past duplicates; try 'abba'.

String
abcabcbb
abba

Advance right →
Reset
Press Advance. The right edge moves one letter at a time. The left edge only jumps when a letter repeats inside the window.
Term: two pointers: right advances; left jumps past a duplicate
START WITH THE INCIDENT
Find the longest clean stretch of sensor data

A camera log records a status byte per frame. You need the longest run of frames with no repeated error code (an interview disguise of 'longest substring without repeating characters'). A nested-loop solution passes small tests but times out on a 10M-frame log.

1 · Spot the pattern

Think of a window sliding along a train, letting you look at a few cars at a time. Signals: 'contiguous subarray or substring', 'longest or shortest', 'at most K distinct', 'sum ≤ budget'. If the validity of a window changes monotonically as you extend or shrink it, a sliding window works.

2 · State the invariant aloud

Say: 'After each step, s[left..right] contains no duplicates.' Then each line of code either extends the window or restores the invariant. That's how you convince an interviewer it's correct, and how you avoid off-by-one errors.

3 · Variants

Fixed-size window (moving average over k samples: add the new value, subtract the outgoing one). Variable window with counts (at most K distinct: shrink while the distinct count exceeds K). Two pointers on sorted input (pair sum: move left up if the sum is too small, right down if too big).

4 · Complexity and tests

State time O(n) and space O(alphabet). Test with the empty string, all-same, all-unique, the duplicate at the boundary ('abba'), and non-ASCII bytes. 'abba' catches the bug of moving left backwards, which the >= left check prevents.

3 · CODE, LINE BY LINE

C++ · line by line
Copy code
1
int longestUnique(const std::string& s) {
2
  std::array<int, 256> last;                // last index where each byte was seen
3
  last.fill(-1);                            // -1 = never seen
4
  int best = 0, left = 0;
5
  for (int right = 0; right < (int)s.size(); ++right) {
6
    unsigned char c = s[right];
7
    if (last[c] >= left) left = last[c] + 1;  // duplicate inside window: shrink
8
    last[c] = right;                          // record latest position
9
    best = std::max(best, right - left + 1);  // window size
10
  }
11
  return best;
12

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A graph is just things (nodes) and connections (edges). To find an order for tasks with dependencies, count for each task how many prerequisites it still has. Start with tasks that have none, and whenever you finish one, reduce the count of the tasks that depended on it. Any task whose count hits zero is ready. If tasks remain that never become ready, the dependencies form a loop.

Adjacency list
For each node, a list of its neighbours. Memory O(V + E).
In-degree
The number of edges coming into a node (unmet prerequisites).
DAG
Directed Acyclic Graph: directed edges, no cycles.
BFS
Breadth-first search using a FIFO queue. Gives shortest hop-count paths.
DFS
Depth-first search using recursion or a stack.
Kahn's algorithm
BFS-style topological sort using in-degrees.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Graphs model dependencies, networks, grids and state spaces. Store them as an adjacency list (vector<vector<int>>). BFS (queue) explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS (stack or recursion) explores deep first, for connectivity, cycle detection and backtracking. Topological sort orders a DAG so every edge u→v has u before v. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly takes nodes with in-degree 0; if not all nodes get output, there's a cycle. All run in O(V + E).

MAKE IT STICK

Driver init order at boot. The I2C controller must come up before the camera bridge, the regulator before the sensor. Topological sort is writing the boot order so every device starts after everything it depends on, and spotting the impossible case where two devices wait for each other (a cycle, like a deferred-probe loop).

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Service startup deadlocks after adding a dependency

A device's init system starts services in a fixed hand-written order. After the camera service gained a dependency on the network-time service (for timestamps), which already depended on a config service that waits for the camera, boot hangs. A topological sort over the dependency graph would have reported the cycle immediately.

1 · Recognize graph problems in disguise

Many problems are graphs in disguise: things (nodes) connected by links (edges). Build orders, course prerequisites, driver probe dependencies, word ladders (BFS over words), islands in a grid (DFS or BFS over cells), network reachability and shortest hops. Ask: what are the nodes, what are the edges, directed or not, weighted or not?

2 · BFS vs DFS

BFS: shortest path in unweighted graphs, level order, minimum steps. DFS: connectivity, cycle detection (three colours: unvisited, in-progress, done), backtracking and exhaustive search. Weighted shortest paths need Dijkstra (heap, non-negative weights).

3 · Implementation hygiene

Mark visited when you push (BFS), not when you pop, to avoid duplicates. Watch recursion depth in DFS on big graphs (use an explicit stack). Represent grids implicitly with direction arrays instead of building an adjacency list.

4 · Systems connections

Real systems use the same ordering trick to start things in the right order. Linux deferred probe and fw_devlink order drivers by supplier/consumer graphs. Build systems (make, Bazel) topologically order targets. Kubernetes controllers and DAG schedulers (Airflow) do the same. Mentioning these makes your answer memorable.

1

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

An LRU cache remembers a fixed number of items and throws out the one used longest ago when full. To make both lookup and reordering instant, keep the items in a linked list ordered by recent use, plus a hash map that jumps straight to any item's position in that list. Using an item moves it to the front; adding to a full cache removes the item at the back.

LRU
Least Recently Used, an eviction policy.
std::list
A doubly linked list: O(1) insert, erase and splice given an iterator; iterators stay valid.
splice
Moves list nodes within or between lists without copying or invalidating iterators.
Iterator
A position handle into a container (like a smart pointer to an element).
std::optional<int>
Either an int or 'nothing' (std::nullopt), cleaner than magic values like -1.
Sharding
Splitting one structure into N independent ones by key hash to reduce lock contention.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A cache that throws out the item used longest ago is like a desk that only keeps your most recent papers. Senior coding rounds often combine data structures with design: 'implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put', then 'make it thread-safe'. The classic solution pairs a doubly linked list (recency order; O(1) move-to-front and evict-from-back via splice) with a hash map from key to list iterator. Thread safety starts with one mutex guarding both structures (they must change together), then scales with sharding (N independent caches by key hash) to cut contention. Note that get mutates recency order, so it needs an exclusive lock, not a shared one.

MAKE IT STICK

A desk with a stack of papers. Whatever you touch goes on top (most recent). When the desk is full, the bottom paper goes in the bin (evict least recent). The hash map is an index card telling you exactly where each paper sits in the stack, so you never search through it.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The model-metadata cache melts under 64 threads

A "read" that secretly reorders the list is really a write, so it needs the full lock. An inference gateway caches model metadata in an LRU guarded by a std::shared_mutex. Someone used shared_lock in get() 'because it's a read'. Under load, TSan reports a data race on the list (get splices nodes!), and after fixing it with an exclusive lock, p99 latency jumps because all 64 threads serialize on one mutex.

1 · Get the single-threaded version right

Write down the rules that must always hold, like "the map and the list always have the same items". Invariants: map size == list size ≤ capacity; every map iterator points to a live node with the same key; the list front is most recent. splice keeps iterators valid, which is why std::list (not vector) is used. Erase from the map before pop_back so you still have the key.

2 · Make it thread-safe correctly

Both structures change together on get and put, so one mutex must guard both, and get is a writer (it reorders). A reader/writer lock doesn't help unless gets stop updating recency (e.g. approximate LRU with per-entry timestamps or CLOCK).

3 · Then make it scale

Shard: N independent LRUs, chosen by hash(key) % N, each with its own mutex. Contention drops about N×; the eviction policy becomes per-shard (approximately global LRU), which is usually fine. Pad shard locks to separate cache lines (Lesson 11.2). Alternatives: CLOCK or segmented LRU, or concurrent hash maps with approximate eviction.

4 · What interviewers listen for

A strong answer covers speed, the rules, tricky cases, thread safety and how you'd test it. Complexity (O(1) average for both operations), invariants, edge cases (capacity 0 or 1, updating an existing key, repeated gets), the thread-safety reasoning above, and testing: unit tests, a randomized test against a simple reference model, and TSan under concurrent load.
