1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Text, images and sounds can be turned into lists of numbers called vectors, where similar things get nearby vectors. Search means finding the stored vectors nearest to a query vector. Doing it exactly means measuring the distance to every one, which is simple but costs a full pass over the data for every question.

Embedding vector
A list of numbers (for example 768 of them) that represents an item so that similar items are close together.
k-nearest neighbours (kNN)
The k stored vectors closest to a query. Exact kNN checks every vector.
Squared L2 distance
The sum of squared differences between two vectors. It ranks the same as normal distance but skips the square root.
Inner product
Multiply matching numbers and add them up (q·x). Bigger means more similar for normalized vectors.
GEMM
General matrix multiply: the core operation behind batched distance computation and most deep-learning math.
Top-k selection
Keeping only the k best scores out of many, usually with a small heap or a GPU selection kernel.
Memory-bound
Limited by how fast data can be read, not by how fast the chip can do math.
Ground truth
The exact answers, used to grade approximate methods.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Vector search answers one question: which stored vectors are closest to this query vector? The exact answer compares the query against every stored vector. On a GPU you rewrite squared distance as ‖q‖² + ‖x‖² − 2·q·x: the norms are precomputed once, and the q·x part for a whole batch of queries is one big matrix multiply (GEMM), the operation GPUs are best at. After that, a top-k selection keeps only the k smallest distances per query. Small batches are memory-bound (you stream the entire dataset for little math); large batches become compute-bound. Exact search is also the ground truth every approximate index is graded against.

MAKE IT STICK

Finding the five songs most like the one you hum. The honest way is to compare your tune with every song in the library. A GPU is a hall of 10,000 judges, so comparing is cheap. The slow part is wheeling the whole library past them. Bring many hummed tunes at once and each trip of the library cart does more useful work.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The demo that melted at launch

A retrieval demo searches 2 million 768-number vectors with exact search, one query at a time, and feels instant. At launch the library grows to 200 million vectors and traffic arrives as thousands of single queries. Latency jumps from 4 ms to over 300 ms and the GPU shows 3% math utilization, while its memory bus sits at 95%.

1 · Why it got slow: arithmetic intensity

Each query streams the whole dataset (200M × 768 × 4 bytes ≈ 614 GB, which no longer even fits on one card) to do 2 flops per byte read. A GPU can do roughly 30–100 flops in the time it reads one byte from HBM. With batch size 1 you leave almost all the math idle. Batch B queries together and each byte read feeds 2·B flops. That's why GEMM-shaped search wins and why the posting stresses "benchmarking and performance analysis".

2 · How GPU libraries do it

GPU libraries do exactly this. FAISS-GPU and NVIDIA's cuVS brute-force index compute the q·x block with a tuned GEMM (cuBLAS or a fused kernel), add the norms, and run a GPU top-k selection per query (radix select or warp select), often fused so the full distance matrix never hits memory. For very large k, selection becomes the bottleneck. For fp16 or int8 data, bandwidth halves or quarters.

3 · When exact search is still the right call

Small collections (under a few million), strict 100% recall needs (legal, dedup), filtered queries that leave few candidates, and computing ground truth for every benchmark. Everything else moves to an approximate index (IVF, graph) that skips most of the data.

4 · Distance choices

Inner product, cosine (inner product on normalized vectors) and L2 rank items differently unless vectors are normalized. Mixing them up is a silent recall bug: the index was built for L2 but the model was trained for cosine.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Searching everything is too slow for hundreds of millions of vectors. So you sort vectors into buckets and only search the nearest few buckets. You also compress each vector into a few bytes, so far more fit in memory and each comparison is just a few table lookups.

Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)
Search that returns most, not always all, of the true nearest vectors, much faster than exact search.
IVF (inverted file index)
Vectors grouped into buckets around k-means centroids; queries scan only the closest buckets.
nlist
How many IVF buckets (clusters) the index has.
nprobe
How many of the closest buckets a query scans. Higher means better recall and slower search.
Product quantization (PQ)
Compression that splits a vector into M chunks and stores one small code per chunk.
Codebook
The list of chunk-centroids for one chunk position, learned with k-means.
ADC (asymmetric distance computation)
Distance from a full-precision query to compressed vectors, computed with per-query lookup tables.
Recall@k
The fraction of the true k nearest neighbours that the search returned.
Re-ranking
Recomputing exact distances for the best few candidates to fix the order.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An IVF (inverted file) index first clusters all vectors with k-means into nlist buckets, each with a centroid. A query is compared with the centroids, and only the nprobe closest buckets are scanned. Product quantization (PQ) then shrinks each stored vector: split it into M chunks, and replace each chunk with the id of its nearest chunk-centroid (one byte for 256 choices). Search builds a small lookup table per query (distance from each query chunk to every chunk-centroid), so the distance to any stored vector becomes M table lookups and adds, called asymmetric distance computation (ADC). Knobs: nlist and nprobe trade recall for speed; M trades memory and recall. Re-ranking the best few hundred with full vectors recovers precision.

MAKE IT STICK

A huge library. IVF puts books on shelves by topic and you only walk to the few shelves nearest your question. PQ replaces each book with a short catalogue card, a few codes describing it. You skim cards quickly instead of reading books. Then you pull the top few real books off the shelf to double-check.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Recall fell off a cliff after a 'harmless' resize

A team grows its collection from 10M to 400M vectors and rebuilds IVF-PQ with nlist raised from 4,096 to 65,536 for speed. They keep nprobe at 32. Recall@10 drops from 0.93 to 0.61 and nobody notices for a week, because latency improved and no recall dashboard existed.

1 · What nlist and nprobe really mean

With 65,536 buckets, 32 probes cover only 0.05% of the data. Neighbours of a query often sit just across a bucket boundary, so with many small buckets you must probe more of them. Rule of thumb from FAISS guidance: nlist around √N to 16·√N, then sweep nprobe until recall@k hits your target, and record the curve.

2 · Where PQ loses accuracy

Each chunk is snapped to one of 256 centroids, so distances are approximations. Close calls (two candidates at nearly the same distance) get mis-ordered. Fixes: more bytes per vector (bigger M), encoding residuals (vector minus its bucket centroid, which is what IVF-PQ does), training codebooks on representative data, and re-ranking the top 100–1,000 with full vectors kept on host memory or SSD.

3 · GPU specifics (cuVS / FAISS-GPU)

The per-query lookup table must fit in fast shared memory: M × ksub × 4 bytes (96 × 256 × 4 = 96 KB, near the limit). Libraries offer fp16 tables or 4-bit codes (ksub 16) to fit. Scanning buckets is memory-bound on code bytes, so smaller codes mean faster scans. Building the index (k-means on hundreds of millions of points) is itself a GPU workload.

4 · Make recall observable

Keep a held-out query set with exact ground truth (from brute force, lesson 15.1). Measure recall@k in CI on every index rebuild and parameter change, and alert on drops. Latency without recall is half a benchmark.

LESSON 15.3 · C++17 · BEST-FIRST GRAPH SEARCH · NEW Graph indexes: HNSW and CAGRA, walking links to the nearest points WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS NVIDIA · Senior System Software Engineer, ML & Vector Search "Graph and IVF indexes" are named; CAGRA is cuVS's GPU graph index. 1 PLAIN LANGUAGE 2 MENTAL MODEL 3 CODE, LINE BY LINE 4 PRACTICE 5 INTERVIEW + JOB 1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST Instead of buckets, connect each item to a handful of similar items, like a social network of look-alikes. To search, start somewhere and keep hopping to whichever neighbour is closer to what you want. You only measure a few hundred distances, even in a huge collection. Proximity graph A graph where each vector links to some of its nearest vectors. HNSW Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a multi-layer proximity graph, the most common CPU ANN index. CAGRA A GPU-built, fixed-degree graph index in NVIDIA cuVS, searched by many threads at once. efSearch How many candidate results the walk keeps. Bigger means higher recall and slower search. M (graph degree) How many links each node keeps. More links means better recall and more memory. Entry point The node where the walk starts. HNSW gets it from its top layer. Filtered search Search that only returns items matching a condition (for example, same customer). Hard for graphs if the filter removes most nodes. 2 · MENTAL MODEL A proximity graph links each vector to a few of its near neighbours. Search starts at an entry point and does a best-first walk: keep a frontier of candidates sorted by distance, expand the closest, add its unseen neighbours, and stop when the frontier can no longer beat the worst of your current best ef results. HNSW stacks several layers (sparse top layers for long jumps, a dense bottom layer for precision). Its knobs are M (links per node), efConstruction (build quality) and efSearch (search width). CAGRA, in NVIDIA cuVS, builds a fixed-degree graph on the GPU and searches many queries in parallel, with each thread block keeping its own candidate list in shared memory. Graphs give excellent recall per distance computed, but they use more memory than PQ and handle filters and deletes awkwardly. MAKE IT STICK Finding a café in a strange city by asking people. Each person knows a few nearby places. You start at the station, ask, walk toward whoever points closest, and repeat. You keep a short list of the best leads so one bad tip doesn't strand you. HNSW adds a highway map for the first long jumps. INTERACTIVE LAB Graph walk search IN PLAIN WORDS Finding a café in a strange city by asking people. Each person knows a few nearby places, and you keep walking toward whoever points closest. Try this: Lower the links per point to two and watch the walk miss. Then widen the search until all five green dots appear. THE TECHNICAL VERSION Watch a real greedy walk over a link graph find the nearest points, and see what links and width change. Links per point 4 Search width 5 New question point Square: the question. Dashed ring: start point. Amber: checked. Green: returned. Red: a true match that was missed. Distances computed 47 of 80 True top 5 found 5 / 5 All five true neighbours found after checking only 47 of 80 points. Walking the links skips most of the data. Term: recall@5 = 1.0 with 47 distance computations START WITH THE INCIDENT Filtered search returned three results instead of ten A multi-tenant service stores all customers in one HNSW graph and filters results to the caller's customer after the walk. Small customers (0.1% of vectors) get 2–3 results instead of 10, and sometimes wrong ones, because the walk's ef candidates almost never include their vectors. 1 · Why graphs work Real embeddings have structure, so a node's neighbours' neighbours are often near the query too. Each hop roughly halves the distance early on, then the walk polishes locally. HNSW's upper layers act like express trains, so the walk starts close. Typical cost: a few hundred to a few thousand distance computations per query, even for a billion vectors. 2 · The knobs and their costs M (degree) of 16–64: memory ≈ N × M × 4 bytes of links on top of the vectors. efConstruction (100–500) buys a better graph with a longer build. efSearch is the runtime dial: sweep it to draw the recall-vs-QPS curve. On GPUs, CAGRA fixes the degree (for example 32 or 64) so every thread block does predictable work, and searches thousands of queries at once. 3 · Filters, deletes and updates Post-filtering fails for selective filters (the story above). Options: pre-filter with a bitset and let the walk skip non-matching nodes while still traversing them (works down to a few percent selectivity), separate indexes per large tenant, or fall back to brute force on the filtered subset when it is small. Deletes are usually tombstones plus periodic rebuilds, because removing nodes can disconnect the graph. 4 · IVF-PQ or graph? Graphs give the best recall per query time when the vectors fit in memory. IVF-PQ wins when memory is tight (billions of vectors on few GPUs) or when updates are frequent. Many systems combine them: a graph over compressed vectors, with re-ranking from full vectors. 1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Clustering means finding natural groups in data without labels. k-means is the simplest method and also builds the buckets for IVF and the codebooks for PQ. PCA is a different tool: it finds the few directions where data varies most, so you can keep fewer numbers per item.

k-means
Clustering into k groups by alternating 'assign to nearest centroid' and 'move centroid to the mean'.
Centroid
The average point of a cluster.
Lloyd's algorithm
The standard k-means loop of assign and update steps.
Inertia
Sum of squared distances from points to their centroids: the cost k-means lowers each round.
k-means++
Seeding that picks each new starting centroid with probability proportional to squared distance from existing ones.
PCA
Principal component analysis: projects data onto the directions of greatest variance.
Closed-form
Solved directly by a formula or matrix factorization, not by repeated improvement.
Reduction
Combining many values into one (sum, mean, max), a core GPU pattern.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

k-means groups points into k clusters with Lloyd's algorithm. Assign each point to its nearest centroid, move each centroid to the mean of its points, and repeat until assignments stop changing. It is iterative (each round improves a cost, the sum of squared distances or inertia) and finds a local optimum that depends on the start, so k-means++ seeding picks spread-out starting points. On a GPU, the assign step is a batched distance plus argmin (the same GEMM trick as lesson 15.1) and the update step is a reduction. PCA finds the directions of greatest variance and projects data onto the top few. It is closed-form (from an eigen or singular value decomposition), and it is used to shrink vectors before indexing or to visualize them. The posting's "iterative vs closed-form" phrase is exactly this contrast.

MAKE IT STICK

Placing k ice-cream stands on a beach. Everyone walks to the closest stand; then each stand moves to the middle of its crowd; repeat until nobody switches. Where you put the stands on day one changes where they end up, so you spread them out at the start.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
IVF build takes six hours

Building IVF on 500M vectors runs k-means with nlist 65,536 on the CPU and takes six hours. Every index rebuild blocks a release. The team moves training to the GPU and samples the data, cutting the build to minutes with the same recall.

1 · k-means as GPU work

The assign step is n×k distances: a GEMM between points and centroids, then a row-wise argmin. The update step is a sum per cluster, done with atomics (simple, but contended on popular clusters) or by sorting points by cluster and running a segmented reduction. cuML and cuVS provide both k-means and balanced hierarchical k-means for very large k.

2 · Training tricks that matter

Train on a sample (FAISS warns when there are fewer than about 39 points per centroid; 256 or more per centroid is a comfortable target). Use k-means++ or random-subset seeding. Cap the number of rounds (10–25 is common for IVF). Handle empty clusters by splitting the largest one. Use balanced k-means when bucket sizes must be even, which is good for GPU load balance.

3 · PCA and friends

PCA finds the directions along which the data spreads out most. Technically it centers the data, then takes the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (or a truncated SVD). Projecting 768 numbers to 256 can cut memory 3× with a small recall loss, and it often helps PQ. For visualization, UMAP and t-SNE preserve local neighbourhoods better than PCA but are iterative and non-linear. cuML accelerates both.

4 · Iterative vs closed-form, the interview phrasing

Iterative methods improve an answer round by round. k-means, UMAP and gradient descent work this way: they need stopping rules, seeds and convergence checks, and they can get stuck in a local optimum. PCA and least squares are closed-form: one factorization, the same answer every run (up to sign). Be ready to say which you'd choose for reproducibility and which for scale.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Fast search is easy if you're allowed to return wrong answers. So every speed number must come with an accuracy number, measured against exact answers. Shipping the library also means giving Python and Java users a thin, safe wrapper that shares memory instead of copying it.

QPS
Queries per second: throughput.
Latency percentile (p99)
The time under which 99% of queries finish. It shows the slow tail that averages hide.
Pareto curve
The set of best trade-offs: no point is both faster and more accurate than another on the curve.
Warm-up
Running untimed queries first so caches, memory pools and lazy setup don't distort timings.
Python bindings
A layer that lets Python call C++ code (Cython, pybind11, nanobind).
DLPack
A standard for sharing tensors between libraries without copying (PyTorch, CuPy, cuVS).
JNI
Java Native Interface: how Java calls C or C++ code.
Memory pool
Pre-allocated memory handed out quickly, avoiding slow device allocations (RMM in RAPIDS).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An ANN result is meaningless without its recall. Fair benchmarks fix the dataset, metric and k, compute exact ground truth once, build each index (recording build time and memory), warm up, then sweep search knobs and plot recall@k against QPS (or latency percentiles). Compare libraries at equal recall, never at default settings. The NVIDIA team ships C++/CUDA cores to Python (via Cython or pybind11-style bindings and CUDA Array Interface/DLPack zero-copy tensors) and Java (via JNI or the newer Panama Foreign Function API). It also uses memory pools so repeated allocations don't stall the GPU. Measurement hygiene: synchronize the device before stopping timers, report p50/p95/p99, and pin clocks or record them.

MAKE IT STICK

Comparing cars by top speed alone is useless if one of them skips half the route. You must check that every car visited the same stops (recall) and then compare times. Also start timing after the engines are warm, not at the cold start.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
"10× faster" that wasn't

A pull request claims a new search kernel is 10× faster. The benchmark ran with nprobe 1 for the new code and nprobe 32 for the old, timed without device synchronization, and reported the mean. At equal recall@10 of 0.95, the gain is 1.4×, still good, but the reviewer only found out after asking for the recall curve.

1 · The ANN-benchmarks method

Public benchmarks (ann-benchmarks, big-ann-benchmarks) plot recall on one axis and QPS on the other for many parameter settings, then keep the Pareto front. Compare libraries at the same recall (for example 0.95). Report build time, index size and hardware. Batch size changes GPU results enormously, so state it: single query (latency) or large batch (throughput).

2 · Timing GPUs correctly

Kernel launches are asynchronous, so synchronize before reading the clock, or use CUDA events. Warm up to trigger lazy module loading and memory-pool growth. Pin or record GPU clocks (thermal throttling shifts results). Run several repetitions and report the spread. Profile with Nsight Systems to see whether time goes to kernels, copies or the host.

3 · Bindings without copies

Python users pass NumPy, CuPy or PyTorch arrays. Accept anything exposing __cuda_array_interface__ or DLPack and wrap the pointer without copying. Release the GIL during long C++ calls. For Java, JNI needs careful pinning of arrays (or direct ByteBuffers); Panama (Java 22+) can call C APIs with less glue. Keep a stable C API underneath so every language binds to the same core.

4 · Open source habits

cuVS, RAFT and cuML are developed in the open on GitHub. Expect benchmarks in pull requests, CI on several GPU architectures, API deprecation cycles, and reviews from users at vector-database companies. Clear issue write-ups and reproducible benchmarks are a visible hiring signal.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Robots and cars ship their own custom Linux, built from source so every byte is known and repeatable. A build system called Yocto assembles it from recipes. At power-on, each piece of software checks the digital signature of the next before running it, so nobody can slip in modified code.

Yocto Project
A toolkit for building custom embedded Linux images from source, using BitBake and layers of recipes.
BitBake
Yocto's build engine. It reads recipes and runs tasks (fetch, compile, package).
Layer (meta-*)
A folder of related recipes and settings, such as a vendor BSP layer or your product layer.
Recipe (.bb)
Instructions for fetching, building and packaging one piece of software.
BSP
Board support package: bootloader, kernel, device trees and firmware for a specific board.
Kernel config fragment
A small .cfg file that turns kernel options on or off on top of a base config.
Chain of trust
Each boot stage verifies the signature of the next before running it, starting from keys fused in the chip.
dm-verity
A Linux feature that checks every block of a read-only filesystem against a signed hash tree.
FIT image
U-Boot's signed bundle of kernel, device tree and initramfs.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A fleet vehicle doesn't run a desktop distro. It runs an image you build from source with Yocto: layers (BSP layers from the silicon vendor such as meta-tegra for Jetson, your distro policy layer, your application layer) contain recipes that BitBake turns into packages and a bootable image. The kernel config is managed as small fragments (for example enabling PREEMPT_RT or forcing module signatures). The device tree tells the kernel what hardware is on the board (sensors on I2C, camera lanes, GPIOs) so drivers can probe. Secure boot builds a chain of trust: ROM verifies the first bootloader with a key hash burned into fuses, each stage verifies the next, the kernel is verified (for example inside a signed FIT image), and the root filesystem is checked block by block with dm-verity. A/B slots keep a known-good copy for updates.

Building a car from a parts catalogue instead of buying one off the lot. Yocto is the factory: each recipe is a work order, each layer is a supplier's binder. Secure boot is the guard at each gate who checks the next person's badge before letting them in. If any badge is forged, the line stops.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The robot that booted on the bench but not in the field

A new camera board works on the bench. In the field, units intermittently fail to find the camera after an OTA update. The cause: the update shipped a new kernel, but the device tree overlay for the camera stayed in the old slot, and the driver never probed. There was no boot-health check, so the unit didn't roll back.

1 · Layers keep the image reproducible

Pin everything so two builds match. Lock every layer to a commit (with a manifest tool such as repo or kas), pin each recipe's source revision (SRCREV), and use a shared state cache so builds are fast and identical. Keep vendor BSP layers unmodified; put changes in bbappends in your own layer, so vendor upgrades stay mergeable. Generate an SBOM and license manifest per image, which security and legal reviews will ask for.

2 · Device trees and overlays

The device tree describes buses, addresses, interrupts, clocks and regulators. Drivers match on compatible strings and read properties in probe. Overlays add hardware variants (a different camera) without forking the base tree. Ship kernel, device tree and overlays together in one signed bundle (a FIT image) so they can't drift apart, which is exactly the story's bug.

3 · The chain of trust in practice

ROM verifies the first bootloader against a public-key hash in one-time fuses. Each stage verifies the next (U-Boot verifies a signed FIT; UEFI platforms verify signed kernels). The kernel enforces module signatures and mounts a dm-verity root filesystem. Anti-rollback counters (also in fuses or secure storage) stop downgrades to old, vulnerable images. On NVIDIA Jetson and DRIVE, the vendor documents its own secure-boot flow; follow it rather than inventing one.

4 · A/B updates and boot health

Write the update to the inactive slot, switch, and boot with a counter. If the new slot doesn't confirm health (services up, sensors probed) within N attempts, the bootloader falls back. Tools like RAUC, Mender or SWUpdate integrate with Yocto. Health checks must include hardware, not just 'kernel booted'.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Programs on the same computer normally exchange data by copying it. For big messages like camera frames, the copying itself becomes the bottleneck. Shared memory lets several programs see the same bytes, so the sender only passes a small number that says which slot to read.

IPC
Inter-process communication: how separate programs exchange data.
Shared memory
Memory mapped into several processes so they see the same bytes (shm_open + mmap).
Zero-copy
Passing a reference to data instead of copying the data.
Loan
Borrowing a free slot from the middleware to write a message in place.
Acquire/release ordering
Atomic ordering that makes writes before a release visible to a thread that acquires the same variable.
SPSC queue
Single-producer, single-consumer queue: simple and lock-free.
iceoryx
An open-source zero-copy shared-memory IPC middleware used in automotive and robotics.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A camera frame is several megabytes. At 30 Hz with several subscribers, copying it through sockets burns gigabytes per second of memory bandwidth and whole CPU cores. Zero-copy IPC puts fixed-size slots in shared memory mapped by every process. The publisher loans a free slot, writes the frame in place, and publishes only its index through a lock-free queue; subscribers read in place and release the slot. Correctness hinges on memory ordering (release when publishing, acquire when taking) and on ownership rules (a slot is never written while loaned to a reader). Frameworks such as Eclipse iceoryx, and ROS 2 with loaned messages over iceoryx- or shared-memory-capable DDS, work this way.

MAKE IT STICK

A shared whiteboard in a hallway instead of photocopying a poster for every colleague. You reserve a board, draw on it, then put its number on the notice list. Colleagues walk up and read it. When everyone is done, the board is wiped and becomes free again. Nobody photocopies anything.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Four cameras, eight subscribers, two cores gone

A robot streams four 6 MB camera frames at 30 Hz to perception, logging, a visualizer and a health monitor. With socket-based serialization, profiling shows about 2 CPU cores doing memcpy and memory bandwidth at 40% before any perception runs. Moving the camera topics to shared-memory loans drops the copy cost to near zero.

1 · Where copies hide

Count the copies in a normal path. Serialize into a buffer (copy 1), write to a socket (copy into the kernel), read on the other side (copy out), deserialize (another copy), and repeat per subscriber. For 6 MB × 30 Hz × 4 cameras × several subscribers, that is several GB/s of pure copying. The lab shows the arithmetic.

2 · How loans work in real middleware

Real middleware works like the code above. iceoryx keeps a shared-memory pool (managed by a central RouDi process in iceoryx 1; iceoryx2 needs no central process), with publishers loaning chunks and subscribers holding references until released. ROS 2 offers borrow_loaned_message() when the RMW (for example Cyclone DDS with iceoryx, or other DDS vendors' shared-memory transports) supports it. The message type must be fixed-size (no std::string or unbounded vectors) to live in shared memory.

3 · Failure modes

A crashed subscriber holds slots forever, so the middleware must reclaim slots of dead processes (heartbeats or robust ownership records). A slow subscriber should lose old samples rather than block the publisher. Version the message layout: two processes compiled with different struct layouts will read garbage. Security: any process mapping the segment can read it, so set permissions per topic.

4 · Across chips and engines

Zero-copy between CPU processes is the first step. On NVIDIA DRIVE and Jetson, the same idea extends to GPUs, cameras and accelerators with shared buffer objects and sync objects, which is the NvSci team's area (next lesson, described generically).

7

8
static_assert(std::atomic<uint32_t>::is_always_lock_free, "atomics must work across processes");
9
struct Shm {
10
  std::atomic<uint32_t> state[kSlots];     // 0 free, 1 loaned, 2 ready, 3 reading
11
  std::atomic<uint32_t> head, tail;        // published-index queue (SPSC)
12
  uint32_t queue[kSlots];
13
  alignas(64) unsigned char data[kSlots][kSlotBytes];
14
};
15
Shm* shm_create() {
16
  void* p = mmap(nullptr, sizeof(Shm), PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
17
  if (p == MAP_FAILED) return nullptr;
18
  return new (p) Shm{};
19
}
20
int loan(Shm* s) {                         // publisher: find a free slot
21
  for (int i = 0; i < kSlots; ++i) {
22
    uint32_t want = 0;
23
    if (s->state[i].compare_exchange_strong(want, 1, std::memory_order_acquire)) return i;
24
  }
25
  return -1;                                // all busy: drop, wait, or apply backpressure
26
}
27
void publish(Shm* s, int slot) {
28
  s->state[slot].store(2, std::memory_order_relaxed);
29
  uint32_t h = s->head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
30
  s->queue[h % kSlots] = (uint32_t)slot;
31
  s->head.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_release);
32
}
33
int take(Shm* s) {                         // subscriber
34
  uint32_t t = s->tail.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
35
  if (t == s->head.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) return -1;
36
  int slot = (int)s->queue[t % kSlots];
37
  s->tail.store(t + 1, std::memory_order_release);
38
  s->state[slot].store(3, std::memory_order_relaxed);
39
  return slot;
40
}
41
void release(Shm* s, int slot) { s->state[slot].store(0, std::memory_order_release); }

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

The team's mission: buffer sharing, cross-engine synchronization, streaming and IPC across GPUs, CPUs and accelerators.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Different parts of a chip each have their own rules about where a picture can live in memory. Instead of copying the picture between formats, you agree on one layout that works for all of them. Then each part tells the next one 'frame 42 is ready' with a small signal, so nobody waits longer than needed.

Engine
A hardware block on the chip: GPU, camera input, video encoder, AI accelerator, display.
Pitch (stride)
Bytes from the start of one image row to the next, often padded for alignment.
Physically contiguous
One unbroken block of real memory, needed by engines without an IOMMU.
Buffer handle
A token (for example a file descriptor) that lets another process or engine access the same buffer.
Fence
A one-shot 'this work is done' signal another engine or thread can wait on.
Timeline semaphore
A counter that only goes up. Waiters wait for it to reach a value, such as frame N.
DMA-BUF
Linux's mechanism for sharing buffers between drivers and processes via file descriptors.
NvSci
NVIDIA's buffer and sync middleware on DRIVE and Jetson (NvSciBuf, NvSciSync, NvSciStream, NvSciIpc).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

One frame often visits several parts of a chip. It may be written by the camera input engine, processed by the GPU, read by an AI accelerator and encoded by a video encoder. Each engine has constraints: address alignment, row pitch alignment, whether it needs physically contiguous memory (no IOMMU), and whether the CPU must map it (cache coherency). A buffer-sharing middleware lets each user state its needs, reconciles them into one layout that satisfies everybody, allocates once, and exports a handle to other processes and engines. Synchronization uses fences or timeline semaphores: the producer signals value N when frame N is done, and each consumer waits for exactly N, so engines run concurrently without the CPU in the loop. This is the general pattern behind NVIDIA's NvSciBuf and NvSciSync, and behind Linux DMA-BUF with dma-fence and Vulkan's external memory with timeline semaphores. The exact NvSci APIs aren't in the posting; this lesson teaches the concepts.

MAKE IT STICK

A shared kitchen counter used by a baker, a decorator and a packer. Before buying the counter, each states what they need: deep enough for trays, wide enough for boxes, near the oven. You buy one counter that fits everyone. Then each worker rings a numbered bell when their batch is done, so the next worker starts on exactly that batch.

Term: attribute reconciliation (max alignment, LCM pitch) + per-frame fence; zero-copy across engines
START WITH THE INCIDENT
The pipeline that copied every frame three times

A perception pipeline captures camera frames, converts them on the GPU, runs a network on an accelerator and encodes a preview. Each stage allocates its own buffers in its own format and copies between them, and the CPU calls 'wait for device idle' between stages. Frame latency is 48 ms; after switching to reconciled shared buffers with per-frame fences, it is 21 ms and the CPU is mostly idle.

1 · Negotiate, then allocate once

Each consumer and producer submits its requirements (alignment, pitch, layout such as linear or block-linear, cache coherency, security domain). The middleware reconciles them, or fails early if they conflict (for example, one engine needs a tiled layout another can't read). One allocation serves the whole pipeline. NVIDIA's NvSciBuf documents an attribute-list model of this kind; Linux has no single equivalent, so drivers negotiate via DMA-BUF and format modifiers.

2 · Sync without the CPU

Each engine signals a sync object when it finishes frame N and waits on its producer's object for N before starting. On Linux this is dma-fence and sync_file; in Vulkan it is timeline semaphores; NvSciSync plays this role across engines on DRIVE. The CPU sets up the graph once and then stays out of the per-frame path, which cuts latency and jitter.

3 · Streams: producer, pool, consumers

A streaming layer manages a pool of shared buffers that cycle between a producer and its consumers. Examples are NvSciStream on DRIVE, and similar ideas in GStreamer or EGLStream; the pool can span processes, VMs or chips. Each packet carries its buffer handle and fences. Consumers return packets when done, and backpressure appears naturally when the pool runs dry.

4 · Safety and security angle

On a safety-certified platform, the middleware must prove that a misbehaving consumer can't corrupt another's memory (freedom from interference), that timeouts are bounded, and that handles crossing VMs are validated. That's why the posting pairs this work with ISO 26262, ASPICE, fuzzing and static analysis (next lesson).

13
bool reconcile(const BufReq *r, int n, uint32_t width_bytes, uint32_t rows, BufPlan *out) {
14

15

16
    if (!pow2(r[i].align) || !pow2(r[i].pitch_align)) return false;
17

18

23

24

25

26

27

28

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Car software is rated by how badly a failure could hurt someone. Higher ratings demand more careful design, testing and paperwork. Security has its own standard. In daily coding, this shows up as strict coding rules, automatic checkers, and fuzzing, which hammers code with random inputs to find crashes.

ISO 26262
The functional-safety standard for road-vehicle electrical and electronic systems.
ASIL
Automotive Safety Integrity Level, A to D, set by severity, exposure and controllability. QM means no special safety measures.
HARA
Hazard analysis and risk assessment: the step that assigns ASILs to safety goals.
MC/DC
Modified condition/decision coverage: tests show each condition in a decision independently changes the outcome.
ASPICE
Automotive SPICE: a process-maturity model for automotive software development.
ISO/SAE 21434
The road-vehicle cybersecurity engineering standard.
TARA
Threat analysis and risk assessment under ISO 21434.
MISRA C
Coding guidelines that restrict risky C features in safety-related code.
Fuzzing
Feeding huge numbers of generated inputs to code to find crashes and undefined behaviour.
Freedom from interference
Proof that lower-rated software can't corrupt or delay higher-rated software.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

ISO 26262 is the road-vehicle functional-safety standard. A hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA) rates each hazard by Severity, Exposure and Controllability, giving an ASIL from A (lowest) to D (highest), or QM (no special safety measures). The ASIL sets how rigorous requirements, design, coding, verification and independence must be. For example, ISO 26262-6 highly recommends MC/DC structural coverage for ASIL D units. ASPICE assesses process maturity (traceable requirements, reviews, V-model testing). ISO/SAE 21434 is the cybersecurity counterpart, built around a TARA (threat analysis and risk assessment). In code this means MISRA C/C++ rules, static analysis (Coverity, Polyspace), sanitizers in testing, fuzzing of every parser that touches untrusted input, and sometimes formal verification of critical pieces.

MAKE IT STICK

Building codes for a house. A garden shed (QM) needs common sense; a hospital (ASIL D) needs licensed engineers, inspections at every stage, and paperwork showing who checked what. ISO 21434 is the burglar-proofing code; fuzzing is hiring people to rattle every door and window thousands of times a minute.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A diagnostic port that could reboot the car

A security assessment for ISO 21434 finds that a diagnostic service trusts the length byte in incoming frames. A crafted frame overflows a stack buffer in the middleware process that also forwards brake-health messages. Fuzzing would have found it in seconds; MISRA review missed it because the code 'looked bounded'.

1 · From hazard to ASIL to code rules

HARA rates a hazard such as 'unintended braking at highway speed' as S3 (life-threatening), E4 (high exposure) and C3 (difficult to control), giving ASIL D. The safety goal flows into technical requirements, then software requirements per component. Each carries the ASIL, which sets methods: for ASIL D units, MC/DC coverage is highly recommended, and so are more independence in reviews and stronger static analysis. Lower-ASIL or QM code sharing a processor must be shown not to interfere.

2 · ASPICE in daily life

Every requirement has an ID; every design element, code change and test traces back to it. Reviews are recorded. Tests exist at each level of the V (unit, integration, qualification). Tools like Jira plus a requirements tool (Polarion, codebeamer, DOORS) keep the traces. Assessors sample artifacts and ask you to show the trace.

3 · Security: TARA, fuzzing and hardening

ISO 21434's TARA lists what must be protected (keys, brake commands), how attackers could reach it (faked diagnostic frames) and the attack paths. It then rates risk and chooses controls: authenticated messages (AUTOSAR SecOC is one example), input validation, least privilege, secure boot. Every parser on an external interface gets a fuzz target in CI (libFuzzer or AFL++ with sanitizers), and crashes become regression tests.

4 · Tools named in the posting

Coding rules are checked by tools, not by eye. MISRA C:2012 and C++ guidelines are enforced by Coverity, Polyspace, PC-lint or clang-tidy profiles. Coverity also finds resource leaks and data races. Formal verification (model checking, or proving the absence of runtime errors with tools such as Polyspace Code Prover or Frama-C) is used on small, critical modules. Record deviations from MISRA with written justifications; that's normal, not failure.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

Named: QNX distributions, QNX or another RTOS valued.
NVIDIA · Senior Software Engineer, Embedded Platform Middleware

Embedded operating systems.
1

2

3
CODE, LINE BY LINE

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Some car software must never be late or crash; other software just needs to be useful. A small real-time operating system runs the critical parts, and Linux runs the rest. A hypervisor splits one chip so they can't disturb each other. QNX, common in cars, passes messages between programs in a strict request-and-reply style.

RTOS
Real-time operating system: designed for bounded, predictable response times.
Microkernel
A tiny kernel that does only scheduling, IPC and memory protection; drivers run as normal processes.
QNX Neutrino
A commercial microkernel RTOS widely used in vehicles, with a safety-certified variant.
Resource manager
A QNX user-space server (often a driver) that exposes a path such as /dev/can0.
Synchronous message passing
The sender blocks until the receiver replies, as with QNX MsgSend/MsgReceive/MsgReply.
Priority inheritance
A server or lock holder temporarily runs at the priority of the highest waiting client.
Hypervisor
Software that splits a chip into isolated virtual machines.
Mixed criticality
Software of different safety levels sharing one chip with proven isolation.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

QNX Neutrino is a microkernel RTOS: the kernel does scheduling, IPC and memory protection, while drivers, filesystems and network stacks run as separate user-space resource managers. A crashed driver can be restarted without rebooting. Its core IPC is synchronous message passing: MsgSend blocks the client until the server's MsgReceive and MsgReply, and the server can inherit the client's priority, which avoids priority inversion across processes. Linux is a monolithic kernel with a huge ecosystem (CUDA, ROS 2), real-time via PREEMPT_RT, but harder to certify. Vehicles often mix both on one chip with a hypervisor or separation kernel: a small certified partition for ASIL functions and a Linux VM for perception, infotainment and logging. This is mixed criticality, and it relies on spatial isolation (MMU and IOMMU) and temporal isolation (CPU budgets).

MAKE IT STICK

A hospital with an operating theatre and a waiting room. The theatre (safety RTOS) is small, sterile and strictly controlled. The waiting room (Linux) is busy and full of useful things. The hypervisor is the wall and the door rules between them: nothing from the waiting room can wander into surgery or make the surgeon wait.

INTERACTIVE LAB

IN PLAIN WORDS

A hospital with a small, strict operating room and a busy waiting room. A wall and door rules keep the waiting room from slowing the surgeons.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Infotainment froze, and the brake monitor missed a deadline

A prototype ran everything in one Linux system: brake-health monitoring, perception and the media screen. A media app leaked memory, the kernel started reclaiming pages, and the brake monitor's 10 ms task ran 60 ms late. The production design moves the monitor into a small RTOS partition under a hypervisor, with its own CPU core and memory.

1 · Why microkernels suit safety

Less code runs in kernel mode, so there's less to certify. Drivers are processes: if the CAN driver crashes, the OS restarts it and clients see an error instead of a kernel panic. QNX OS for Safety is certified to ISO 26262 ASIL D; Green Hills INTEGRITY and others offer similar certified kernels. The trade-off is IPC cost: every driver call is a message.

2 · Message passing and priorities

QNX lends the client's priority to the server. When a high-priority client sends to a driver, the driver runs at that priority for the request, so a low-priority job can't keep it busy while an urgent request waits. The model above shows the blocking states; the real kernel adds priority-ordered queues, pulses (asynchronous notifications) and direct copies between address spaces.

3 · Hypervisors and partitions

A hypervisor hands each VM its own cores, memory and devices. Type-1 hypervisors (QNX Hypervisor, NVIDIA's DRIVE OS hypervisor, Xen, Bao and others) also use the IOMMU so a VM's DMA can't reach another's memory. Temporal isolation needs dedicated cores or scheduled budgets, plus attention to shared caches and memory bandwidth (cache partitioning, memory-bandwidth regulation). Inter-VM communication goes through validated shared-memory channels.

4 · Linux in the picture

Linux with PREEMPT_RT handles soft and firm real-time robotics well (Wayve's posting mentions Linux and QNX distributions), and it is where CUDA, ROS 2 and machine-learning stacks live. Hard ASIL D functions usually stay on a certified RTOS or a safety MCU. Being fluent in both, and in the boundary between them, is the skill these postings want.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Wayve · Senior Software Engineer, OS (Robot Software)
Named: code observable and debuggable on a device 2000 km away with limited connectivity; stack traces, core dumps, disk I/O, CPU, memory, threading.
Google · Staff Software Engineer, Drivers & Systems Engineering
Testing and launching at fleet scale.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Robots in the field crash where you can't attach a debugger. So the software must record what happened by itself, safely and cheaply, and send the most useful part first over a slow connection. A crash handler is a small function that runs when the program crashes and writes down where it was.

Core dump
A file holding a crashed process's memory and registers, for later debugging with gdb.
Minidump
A small crash file with thread stacks, registers and selected memory (Breakpad or Crashpad format).
Async-signal-safe
Functions that are safe to call inside a signal handler, such as write() and _exit(), but not malloc() or printf().
Build ID
A unique hash embedded in each binary, used to find the matching debug symbols.
Symbolization
Turning raw addresses in a crash into function names and line numbers using debug symbols.
Flight recorder
A fixed-size in-memory ring of recent logs and events, saved when something goes wrong.
Watchdog
A timer that resets or alerts if software stops checking in, which catches hangs.
sigaltstack
A separate stack for signal handlers, so a crash from stack overflow can still be handled.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

When a vehicle fails far away on a weak cellular link, you get one shot at the evidence. Design for it: a crash handler that writes a small record using only async-signal-safe calls, a minidump (thread stacks and registers plus a little memory) that uploads first, and a full core dump kept locally for later retrieval. Every artifact carries the build ID so you can symbolize it against archived debug symbols. Add a ring-buffer flight recorder of recent logs and metrics, watchdogs for hangs, and remote, rate-limited tools to pull disk, CPU, memory and thread stats on demand. A planning process crashes on about one vehicle in 200 every few days. Vehicles have 2–3 hours of patchy cellular connectivity per day. 1 · Layers of evidence

Keep evidence in layers, smallest first. Crash record (bytes, sent immediately), minidump (megabytes, sent within hours), full core (gigabytes, kept on disk and pulled on demand or at the depot), and a flight-recorder ring (last N seconds of logs and metrics, saved on crash or trigger). Prioritize uploads by value per byte, and budget the link so diagnostics never starve operational traffic.

2 · Symbols and build IDs

Ship stripped binaries; archive full debug info per build ID in a symbol server (debuginfod is a standard option). Every crash artifact carries build IDs for every loaded module. Without this, field crashes are just addresses.

3 · Beyond crashes: hangs and slowdowns

Watchdogs detect stuck threads. On timeout, capture all thread stacks before restarting, for example by sending a signal that makes each thread record its stack, or with an external tool like eu-stack. Remote tools pull targeted stats: per-thread CPU (top -H, perf on demand), disk latency (iostat, blktrace), memory (smaps, PSI pressure). All remote actions are authenticated, rate-limited and audited.

4 · Linux core dump plumbing

kernel.core_pattern can pipe cores to a program (for example |/usr/lib/systemd/systemd-coredump ...), which can compress, cap size and record metadata. coredumpctl lists and extracts them. Set per-service limits (LimitCORE=) and make sure crash storage can't fill the root filesystem.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Self-driving software is tested in simulated worlds millions of times. For a failure to be fixable, rerunning it must give exactly the same result. That means every source of randomness and timing must be controlled by the simulator itself, not by the computer it happens to run on.

Log replay (open loop)
Feeding recorded sensor data into the stack; the stack's outputs don't change what happens next.
Closed loop
The stack's decisions move the simulated car, so the world reacts.
SIL
Software-in-the-loop: the stack runs on ordinary servers against the simulator.
HIL
Hardware-in-the-loop: the real vehicle computer runs against simulated sensors and actuators.
Sim clock
Simulated time advanced by the simulator in fixed steps, independent of real time.
Seed
The starting value of a random number generator; the same seed gives the same sequence.
Determinism
Same inputs always give bit-identical outputs.
Real-time factor
How fast the sim runs compared with real time (2× means one simulated minute takes 30 seconds).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An AV simulation platform runs the autonomy stack under test against a world model: scenario actors, roads, and sensor models (camera, lidar, radar) or object-level inputs. It runs in several modes. Log replay (open loop) feeds recorded sensor data and compares outputs. Closed-loop SIL lets the stack's decisions change the world. HIL puts the real vehicle computer in the loop with simulated sensors. A result is only useful if it's reproducible: same scenario, same build and same seed must give bit-identical results. That means a sim clock in integer ticks (never wall time), a per-actor seeded RNG with a portable algorithm, a fixed execution order (no thread races or hash-map iteration order), and attention to floating-point settings across machines. With determinism, a single failing run can be replayed, bisected and debugged.

A chess game recorded move by move. Replay the moves and you get the exact same board every time, so you can study the blunder. If the pieces sometimes moved by themselves (a wall clock, a shared dice, players racing), the replay would differ and the blunder would vanish when you looked.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The failure nobody could reproduce

A nightly suite reports a near-collision in an unprotected-left-turn scenario on 1 run in 400. Engineers rerun it 50 times and never see it. The simulator read the wall clock for sensor timestamps, perception ran in a thread pool whose finishing order varied, and a pedestrian model shared one global random generator. After fixing all three, the failing seed fails every time and the bug is found in an afternoon.

1 · Architecture of a sim platform

A sim platform has six main pieces. They are the scenario description (actors, behaviours, parameter ranges), the world and physics engine, sensor models (from object lists to ray-traced camera and lidar), the stack under test wrapped in a harness that controls its clock and inputs, metrics evaluators, and a result store. Middleware (often ROS-style topics) connects them, with the sim controlling time. GM's posting describes infrastructure for test organization, triggering, execution and result analysis around such a simulator.

2 · Sources of nondeterminism

Randomness leaks in from many places. Wall-clock reads and timeouts, thread scheduling (who finishes first), hash containers with no fixed order, memory read before it was set, floating-point differences (fast-math, fused multiply-add, different CPUs or GPU kernels, library versions), network or file-system timing, and random distributions that differ between libraries. Each needs a control: sim clock, ordered merges, sorted iteration, sanitizers, pinned compiler flags and images, and seeded per-component RNGs.

3 · Replay modes and their limits

Open-loop log replay is perfectly realistic for perception but can't show what would happen if the car acted differently. Closed-loop SIL can, but sensor models are imperfect, so trust in the simulation must itself be measured (the related GM posting talks about characterizing the trustworthiness of simulation tests). HIL adds real timing and hardware but costs rigs. Platforms use all three.

4 · Debugging with determinism

Record the digest every N ticks. When a run differs from a reference, binary-search for the first differing tick, then dump the state there. Combined with build bisection (git bisect over builds that run the same seed), you can find which commit changed behaviour. This is the payoff that justifies the discipline.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Running a test suite in simulation means launching a huge number of small jobs on many machines. Some machines disappear mid-job, so jobs must be safely retried. Each result is stored under a key made from its inputs, so retries never double-count.

Orchestrator
The service that turns a test suite into jobs, schedules them and collects results.
Idempotent write
Writing the same result twice leaves the same state as writing it once.
Preemptible (spot) machine
A cheap cloud machine that can be taken away at short notice.
Jittered backoff
Waiting a growing, randomized time between retries so they don't all hit at once.
Infra error
A failure caused by the platform (preemption, timeout, crash of the sim host), not by the code under test.
Semaphore
A counter that limits how many tasks run at once.
Sharding
Splitting work into many independent pieces that run in parallel.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A nightly evaluation might run hundreds of thousands of scenario × seed jobs against a new build. The orchestrator turns a test suite into jobs, schedules them on a cluster (Kubernetes, Batch or a custom scheduler) within quotas, and retries infrastructure failures (preempted machines, timeouts) with jittered backoff, while never retrying genuine test failures as if they were noise. Results are written idempotently, keyed by (scenario, build, seed), so a retried job overwrites rather than duplicates. Separate infra errors from test failures in every report. Capacity math (jobs × sim length ÷ real-time factor ÷ machines) decides whether the run fits its window and its budget, and cheaper preemptible machines are worth it only if retries are cheap.

A huge exam marked by thousands of temporary helpers. Each paper has a unique number. If a helper leaves halfway, someone else picks up the paper; because it's numbered, it's never marked twice. A smudged scan (infrastructure problem) is re-scanned; a wrong answer (real failure) is never re-marked hoping for a better grade.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The pass rate that dropped when the cloud got busy

A release gate reported the candidate build's pass rate falling from 97% to 91%. The build was fine: a spot-capacity crunch preempted thousands of jobs, the orchestrator recorded them as failures, and its retries also created duplicate rows that double-counted some scenarios. Separating infra errors and keying results by inputs fixed the report.

1 · From suite to jobs

A suite is a versioned list of scenarios with parameters and seeds, tagged by feature and risk. The orchestrator expands it into jobs, orders them (fail-fast critical scenarios first, long ones early to avoid a long tail), and shards across machines. Large scenarios can be split into segments if the simulator supports checkpoints.

2 · Retries without lying

Retry only errors you can prove are infrastructure (preemption, host crash, timeout before the stack started). A stack crash or wrong behaviour is a result. Cap retries and record infra errors explicitly; a rising infra-error rate is itself an alert. Idempotent result writes (unique key on scenario, build, seed, and attempt metadata kept separately) make retries safe.

3 · Capacity and cost

Jobs × simulated seconds ÷ real-time factor = machine-seconds, plus overhead for startup and preemption. Compare with the machines available in the window. Levers: faster sims (headless rendering, lower-fidelity sensors where valid), smarter selection (run the full suite nightly but a risk-based subset per commit), caching unchanged results, and preemptible machines with cheap retries. Track cost per thousand simulated miles.

4 · Observability for the platform itself

Dashboards for queue depth, job latency, infra-error rate by cause, machine utilization and cost. Trace each job from trigger to stored result. When the nightly run misses its window, you need to know if the queue, the sims or the result writer was the bottleneck. GM's posting stresses observability and incident learning.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A pass rate from a few hundred runs is a guess with a margin of error. Release decisions must account for that margin, or teams will chase noise and miss real regressions. The math is one formula; the engineering is storing every run so the formula can be applied by build, scenario and feature.

Metric
A number computed from a run, such as minimum time-to-collision.
Pass rate
Passed runs divided by finished runs.
Confidence interval
A range likely to contain the true value (for example 95% of the time).
Wilson score interval
A confidence interval for a proportion that stays accurate near 0% and 100%.
Release gate
An automatic check that must pass before a build is promoted.
Flaky test
A test whose outcome changes without any change to code or inputs.
dbt
A tool that builds warehouse tables from version-controlled SQL SELECT models, with tests and lineage.
Data warehouse
A database built for analytics over large tables (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Simulation produces numbers; the platform must turn them into decisions. Each run yields metrics (collisions, minimum time-to-collision, hard-braking events, rule violations, progress) that roll up into pass/fail per scenario. A pass rate from n runs is uncertain, so report a confidence interval: the Wilson score interval behaves well near 0% and 100%, where the simple normal approximation breaks. A release gate compares candidate against baseline and blocks only when the regression is statistically clear; overlapping intervals mean 'run more seeds', not 'ship' or 'block'. Flaky scenarios (same build, scenario and seed, different outcomes) point to nondeterminism and are tracked separately. Results live in a warehouse (BigQuery, PostgreSQL, DuckDB for local work) with versioned SQL models built by tools like dbt.

MAKE IT STICK

A basketball player who makes 9 of 10 free throws isn't proven better than one who makes 85 of 100. With only ten shots, luck is a big part of the score. Error bars show how much luck is in each number. You only declare a slump when even the best case of today is worse than the worst case of before.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Blocked by noise, shipped a real regression

A gate compared raw pass rates with a fixed 1-point threshold. It blocked a good build that scored 96.4% on 250 runs against a baseline of 97.5% on 4,000, which was pure luck. Two weeks later it passed a build whose pedestrian scenarios had regressed, because the overall rate hid the drop. The fix: Wilson intervals per scenario family, and a rule that 'overlap means run more'.

1 · From runs to metrics to pass/fail

Each run logs time series (positions, speeds, distances) and events. Evaluators compute metrics such as collision (yes or no), minimum time-to-collision, maximum deceleration, lane and rule violations, and route progress. Thresholds turn metrics into pass/fail per scenario, versioned like code so you can explain why a past result was a pass.

2 · Why Wilson

The simple interval p ± z·√(p(1−p)/n) collapses to zero width at 0% or 100% and can stray outside [0, 1]. AV pass rates often sit at 99% or higher, exactly where it fails. Wilson stays inside [0, 1], has sensible width at the extremes, and is cheap enough to compute in SQL for every group. For comparing two builds directly, a two-proportion test or a bootstrap gives a p-value; correct for many comparisons when gating dozens of scenario families.

3 · Gate design

Gate per scenario family (pedestrians, merges, unprotected turns), not only overall. Block if the candidate's upper bound is below the baseline's lower bound. If they overlap and the candidate is lower, schedule more seeds automatically. Track flaky scenarios with a query like: group by build, scenario and seed and flag where both pass and fail appear, then quarantine them and fix the determinism leak.

4 · Data modelling

Fact table: one row per run (build, scenario, seed, status, metrics, timestamps, sim version). Dimensions: scenarios (tags, owner, ODD), builds (commit, branch), simulator versions. dbt models build pass rates, trends and gate tables, with tests such as uniqueness of (build, scenario, seed) and not-null metrics. DuckDB runs the same SQL locally on Parquet files, which is handy for development and for the lab.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Teams keep a library of driving situations as reusable templates with adjustable numbers. Each template expands into many concrete test runs. The evaluation tools are usually written in Python, but heavy math is done in C++ and called from Python through a thin binding layer.

Scenario library
A versioned, tagged collection of test situations for the driving stack.
Parameterized scenario
A scenario template with ranges (speeds, gaps, timing) that expands into many concrete tests.
OpenSCENARIO
ASAM's standard format for describing driving scenarios (XML in 1.x; a domain-specific language in 2.0).
Sensor fidelity
How realistically simulated sensors behave, from object lists to physics-based rendering.
pybind11
A header-only C++ library for exposing C++ functions and classes to Python.
GIL
Python's global interpreter lock: only one thread runs Python code at a time.
Time-to-collision (TTC)
Gap divided by closing speed: seconds until impact if nothing changes.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A scenario library is the curated, versioned set of situations the stack must handle. Scenarios are often written as parameterized scenarios (ranges for speeds, gaps and timings) in a format such as ASAM OpenSCENARIO or an in-house scenario language. Sources are fleet events (disengagements, triggers), safety analyses and regulations. Parameter sweeps and seeded variation turn one scenario into thousands of concrete runs. Sensor simulation ranges from object lists (fast, no perception testing) to physically based camera, lidar and radar rendering (slow, tests perception), and fidelity must match what you're testing. Platform code is usually Python for orchestration and analysis with hot paths in C++, connected by bindings (pybind11, nanobind) that pass NumPy arrays without copies and release the GIL during long C++ work.

MAKE IT STICK

A driving instructor's notebook of tricky situations, each written as a template: 'a cyclist appears from behind a parked van, between 1 and 3 seconds ahead'. The instructor runs each template many ways. The fancy driving simulator with photo-real graphics is only needed when you're testing the student's eyes, not their decisions.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Ten thousand variations of one near-miss

A fleet vehicle braked hard for a cyclist emerging from behind a delivery van. The team turns the 20-second log into a parameterized scenario (van length, cyclist speed, emergence time, ego speed), sweeps 10,000 combinations overnight, and finds that 3% fail when the cyclist emerges within 1.4 s at ego speeds above 40 km/h. The scenario joins the library with a gate.

1 · Building the library

Scenarios come from several sources: fleet triggers and disengagements, safety analyses, regulations and test protocols (for example Euro NCAP test scenarios), and synthetic edge cases. Each scenario has an owner, tags (feature, ODD, risk), parameter ranges, pass criteria, and a version. Remove or merge duplicates; track coverage of the operational design domain, not just the count of scenarios.

2 · Trusting the simulation

Before a sim verdict counts, check the scenario reproduces the real event: replay the log open-loop and compare the stack's outputs, then check closed-loop behaviour is plausible. The related GM simulation posting mentions characterizing the trustworthiness of simulation tests. Sensor fidelity must match the question: object-level sim for planning logic, rendered sensors for perception, and real logs for the final word.

3 · Python/C++ boundary

Each language does what it is best at. Python orchestrates, queries and plots; C++ (or NumPy array math) does per-sample math over millions of rows. pybind11 converts types automatically, maps C++ exceptions to Python ones, and with py::array_t reads NumPy memory directly. Release the GIL in long loops, keep the binding layer thin, and test both sides. ROS 2 itself uses this split (rclpy over the C rcl library).

4 · Searching for failures

Grid sweeps waste runs on easy regions. Better: adaptive sampling (focus where outcomes change), optimization-based falsification (search for parameters that minimize TTC), and importance sampling to estimate rare-event rates. Every failure found becomes a concrete regression test with its parameters and seed.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

Minimum qualification: kernel drivers and GPU drivers.

Accelerator software stack above the firmware.
NVIDIA · Senior Software Engineer, Embedded Platform Middleware
Buffer sharing and cross-engine sync (dma-buf and fences are the Linux equivalents).
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

In Linux, graphics and accelerator drivers share a common framework called DRM. Programs allocate memory buffers through the driver, submit work that references those buffers, and get back a 'done' signal called a fence. Other drivers can share the same buffers and wait on the same fences, which is how camera, GPU and display cooperate without copies.

DRM
Direct Rendering Manager: the Linux kernel framework for GPU drivers (and the base of the accel subsystem).
GEM buffer object
A DRM-managed memory buffer referenced by a handle (Graphics Execution Manager).
ioctl
A device-specific system call used to send commands to a driver.
drm_sched
The shared DRM GPU scheduler: queues jobs, waits for dependencies, pushes to hardware rings, handles timeouts.
dma-fence
The kernel's 'this DMA or GPU work is done' object, with refcounting and callbacks.
sync_file
A file descriptor wrapping fences so user space and other drivers can wait on them.
accel subsystem
The Linux subsystem for compute accelerators (/dev/accel), built on DRM.
Kref
The kernel's reference-count helper: free the object when the last reference is dropped.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Upstream Linux GPU and accelerator drivers live in DRM (Direct Rendering Manager). User space opens /dev/dri/renderD* and talks through ioctls. Memory is managed as GEM buffer objects (BOs), created, mapped and passed by handle. A submit ioctl hands the driver a command buffer plus the list of BOs it uses; the driver validates and pins them, then creates a job with an out-fence. The shared DRM GPU scheduler (drm_sched) holds the job until its in-fences signal, then pushes it to a hardware ring. When the GPU finishes, an interrupt signals the job's dma-fence, which wakes waiters and runs callbacks. dma-buf exports a BO as a file descriptor so other drivers (camera, display, video) or processes can share it, and fences travel with it (sync_file) so consumers wait exactly as long as needed. Compute accelerators increasingly use the accel subsystem (/dev/accel), built on the same DRM core.

MAKE IT STICK

A print shop. You hand over a job ticket listing the papers it needs (buffer objects). The clerk checks the papers exist and locks them in a tray, then gives you a numbered receipt (the fence). The job waits in a queue until any jobs it depends on are done. When it's printed, your receipt number lights up on the board, and anyone holding that number knows it's ready.

IN PLAIN WORDS

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The compositor that froze once a week

A display compositor occasionally freezes forever. The camera driver exported frames as dma-bufs with fences; the compositor added a callback to each fence. Rarely, the fence had already signaled, dma_fence_add_callback returned -ENOENT, the code ignored it, and the callback never ran. One missing branch caused a weekly hang.

1 · The DRM driver skeleton

A DRM driver registers a struct drm_driver with feature flags (render, GEM, syncobj), file operations and ioctl tables. GEM helpers (shmem or DMA helpers, or TTM for VRAM) manage BOs. Hardware specifics live in the driver's submit path, MMU (GPU page tables) and interrupt handler. Drivers like amdgpu, i915/xe, nouveau and panfrost are open references; NVIDIA's open GPU kernel modules are also public.

2 · Scheduling and timeouts

drm_sched gives each ring a scheduler with entities (per-context queues) and priorities. A job runs only when its dependencies (in-fences) signal. A timeout handler detects hung jobs, triggers GPU reset, and resubmits or fails innocent jobs. Fences that never signal are the worst bug class: they hang every waiter, so every path must eventually signal, even on error (with an error code set on the fence).

3 · Sharing with dma-buf

Exporting a BO creates a dma-buf FD; importers attach and map it for their device (through the IOMMU). Implicit sync uses fences stored in the buffer's reservation object (dma_resv); explicit sync passes sync_file FDs with each submit. Modern Vulkan and Wayland stacks prefer explicit sync. Format modifiers describe tiling so producer and consumer agree.

4 · Testing GPU drivers

IGT GPU Tools is the standard DRM test suite (run in CI on real hardware); KUnit covers helpers; lockdep, KASAN and kmemleak catch locking and memory bugs. Fault injection (failing allocations, simulated hangs) tests error paths that never run normally, which is where fence leaks hide. Lesson 18.5 covers launch at scale.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Data centers can only deliver so much electricity to each rack. If every chip ran flat out, breakers would trip. So software caps each chip's power. Because power rises steeply with speed, a modest cap costs surprisingly little performance.

DVFS
Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: changing clock speed and voltage together to trade speed for power.
Power cap
A limit on average power that hardware or firmware enforces by lowering clocks.
powercap framework
The Linux sysfs interface (/sys/class/powercap) for power-limit zones such as Intel RAPL.
RAPL
Running Average Power Limit: Intel's energy counters and power limits per package and domain.
hwmon
The Linux hardware-monitoring subsystem for temperatures, voltages, currents and power (/sys/class/hwmon).
Thermal throttling
Hardware slowing itself down to stay under a temperature limit.
Runtime PM
Linux framework for suspending idle devices and resuming them on demand.
TDP
Thermal design power: the sustained power a cooling system is designed for.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An AI rack has a power budget set by its feed and cooling, and each accelerator can draw hundreds of watts. Software keeps the rack inside it. DVFS lowers voltage and frequency together; since dynamic power scales roughly with V²·f, and V must rise with f, power grows much faster than speed near the top. That makes power capping cheap: trimming the last 20% of power usually costs only a few percent of speed. Linux exposes limits through the powercap framework (for example Intel RAPL domains with energy_uj counters and constraint_*_power_limit_uw), hwmon for sensors, and vendor interfaces for GPUs and TPUs. The platform also handles thermal throttling, runtime PM (suspending idle devices), and rack-level coordination: when a power supply fails, every node must drop its cap within milliseconds to seconds.

MAKE IT STICK

Driving on the motorway. Going from 110 to 130 km/h burns far more fuel than going from 90 to 110, because drag climbs steeply. If your tank (the power budget) is limited, easing off the top speed a little saves a lot of fuel and only slightly delays arrival.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A power supply failed and the whole row tripped

A training cluster lost one of two power supplies in several racks. Racks drew more than the surviving supply could deliver, and breakers tripped, killing a multi-day training job. The fix: a rack power controller that, on a supply-failure event from the BMC, lowers every accelerator's cap within a second, then restores it when redundancy returns, costing about 8% speed instead of an outage.

1 · Why capping is cheap

Dynamic power ≈ C·V²·f. Near the top of the frequency range, each step up in f needs more voltage, so power rises close to f³. Dropping clocks 10% can cut power 20–30%. Many fleets run accelerators slightly capped all the time for efficiency (performance per watt) and to fit more devices per rack.

2 · Control loops at several levels

Inside the chip: firmware enforces fast limits (microseconds to milliseconds) against current and thermal sensors. On the host: drivers and agents set caps via vendor APIs or powercap (seconds). Rack and row: a controller divides the budget across nodes using telemetry, and reacts to supply failures (sub-second to seconds). Each level must be faster than the protection device above it (breaker trip curves).

3 · Telemetry and correctness

Energy counters wrap and some need root. Sampling intervals must be long enough to average out noise. Validate sensor readings against BMC (Redfish) power data, which is next lesson's topic. Log every cap change with a reason so performance regressions can be explained ('this job ran 7% slower because the rack was capped for 3 hours').

4 · Thermal and idle states

Thermal throttling can cut speed more than any cap, and it's uneven: one hot slot slows a whole synchronized training job (stragglers). Monitor temperature per device and fix airflow. Runtime PM and package C-states save power when idle but add wake-up latency, so latency-critical services may disable deep states.

2

3
CODE, LINE BY LINE

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Servers have many small chips that report voltage, current, temperature and power over simple two-wire buses. The operating system reads them through standard drivers, and a separate management computer on the board (the BMC) reads them too and reports them over the network. Standards from DMTF and OCP make chips from different vendors speak the same language.

I2C
A simple two-wire bus (clock and data) for low-speed chips on a board.
SMBus
System Management Bus: a stricter subset of I2C with defined timeouts and transactions.
PMBus
A command set on SMBus for power supplies and voltage regulators.
LINEAR11
PMBus number format: 5-bit signed exponent and 11-bit signed mantissa, value = mantissa × 2^exponent.
i2c-dev
Linux interface (/dev/i2c-N) that lets user space run I2C and SMBus transfers.
BMC
Baseboard management controller: a small computer on the server board for out-of-band monitoring and control.
Redfish
DMTF's REST API standard for managing servers through the BMC.
MCTP
Management Component Transport Protocol (DMTF): carries management messages over SMBus, PCIe or I3C.
PLDM
Platform Level Data Model (DMTF): message types for sensors, inventory and firmware update, usually over MCTP.
OCP
Open Compute Project: an industry group publishing open data-center hardware and management specs.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Every accelerator board is full of small management chips: voltage regulators, temperature sensors, small memory chips holding board IDs, and fan controllers. They talk over I2C or its stricter cousin SMBus. Power chips speak PMBus, a command set on SMBus (READ_VIN 0x88, READ_IOUT 0x8C, READ_TEMPERATURE_1 0x8D, READ_POUT 0x96) whose readings often use the LINEAR11 format: a 5-bit signed exponent and an 11-bit signed mantissa. Linux exposes these through hwmon drivers (/sys/class/hwmon), or raw access via i2c-dev. Out of band, the BMC monitors the same sensors and reports them over DMTF Redfish (a REST API). Inside the box, MCTP carries management messages over SMBus, PCIe VDM or I3C, and PLDM (also DMTF) defines messages for sensors, inventory and firmware updates on top. OCP (Open Compute Project) publishes open hardware and management specs that hyperscalers build on.

MAKE IT STICK

A building's caretaker system. Every room has small gauges (temperature, power) wired on a thin shared cable (I2C). The caretaker's office (BMC) reads them all, even when the building's main computers are off, and answers questions from headquarters over the phone (Redfish). MCTP and PLDM are the agreed phrasebook so gauges from different makers can be read the same way.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Decode a power-chip reading
IN PLAIN WORDS

A price tag written as a number and a shift: 100 shifted down two places is 25. The chip packs both into one short reading.

Try this: Move the scale and count sliders and watch the coloured boxes and the value change.
