Term: PMBus LINEAR11: 5-bit two's-complement exponent N, 11-bit two's-complement mantissa Y, value = Y·2^N
START WITH THE INCIDENT
The node that reported 32,000 watts

A fleet dashboard showed one accelerator node drawing 32 kW, triggering automated power capping across its rack. The voltage regulator's READ_POUT was decoded as a plain integer instead of LINEAR11, and the exponent bits turned 250 W into a huge number. A shared, tested decoder plus a sanity range check fixed it fleet-wide.

1 · I2C and SMBus in practice

Two wires, 7-bit addresses, 100 kHz to 1 MHz. SMBus adds timeouts (a stuck slave can't hang the bus forever), defined transactions (read byte, read word, block read) and optional packet error checking (PEC, a CRC-8). Bus hangs, address conflicts and muxes (PCA954x) are everyday bring-up problems; a logic analyzer is the best friend here.

2 · From chip to Linux to fleet

Linux does the decoding for you. Kernel PMBus drivers decode the formats and expose hwmon files like power1_input (in millionths of a watt) and temp1_input (thousandths of a degree). Node agents read hwmon; the BMC reads the same sensors out of band and publishes them via Redfish (/redfish/v1/Chassis/<id>/Sensors or the PowerSubsystem resource). Fleet systems compare in-band and out-of-band readings to catch broken sensors.

3 · MCTP and PLDM

Modern accelerators and network cards expose management through MCTP endpoints, carried over SMBus, PCIe vendor messages or I3C. PLDM Type 2 covers platform monitoring (sensors), and Type 5 covers firmware update; SPDM (also DMTF) handles device attestation. Linux has an in-kernel MCTP stack, and OpenBMC implements PLDM. This is the plumbing behind 'update GPU firmware across a fleet' and 'read accelerator temperature without the host OS'.

4 · Standards bodies on the résumé

Standards experience is a listed preference. Google's posting names PCI-SIG, the CXL Consortium, DMTF and OCP. In practice that means reading and implementing their specs (Redfish schemas, PLDM types, OCP hardware management specs), contributing feedback, and knowing which spec governs which interface. Name the specs you've implemented, not just the acronyms.

/* PMBus LINEAR11: bits 15..11 = signed exponent N, bits 10..0 = signed mantissa Y. */
7
double linear11(uint16_t w) {
8
  int exp = (int)(w >> 11) & 0x1F;          /* 5-bit field */
9
  if (exp & 0x10) exp -= 32;                 /* sign-extend: 0x1E means -2 */
10
  int man = (int)(w & 0x7FF);                /* 11-bit field */
11
  if (man & 0x400) man -= 2048;              /* sign-extend: 0x7FF means -1 */
12
  return ldexp((double)man, exp);            /* man * 2^exp */
13
}

15
int pmbus_read_word(int fd, uint8_t addr, uint8_t cmd, uint16_t *out) {
16
  union i2c_smbus_data data;
17
  struct i2c_smbus_ioctl_data args;
18
  args.read_write = I2C_SMBUS_READ;
19
  args.command = cmd;
20
  args.size = I2C_SMBUS_WORD_DATA;
21
  args.data = &data;
22
  if (ioctl(fd, I2C_SLAVE, addr) < 0) return -1;   /* select the device */
23
  if (ioctl(fd, I2C_SMBUS, &args) < 0) return -1;
24
  *out = data.word;
25
  return 0;
26

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

Named: PCIe integration, HPC systems and networking, PCI-SIG and CXL Consortium.

Hardware/firmware co-design on heterogeneous systems.
1

2

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

PCIe links connect accelerators to the host. In a big fleet, links quietly degrade: they come up slower than designed, or they start fixing more and more transmission errors. Software reads the link's status and error counters from Linux, spots trouble early, and takes the machine out of service before jobs fail.

Link speed and width
PCIe generation (for example Gen5 at 32 GT/s) and lane count (x16) that the link trained to.
Downtraining
A link coming up at lower speed or width than its maximum, often due to signal problems.
AER
Advanced Error Reporting: PCIe's error classification and logging (correctable, non-fatal, fatal).
Correctable error
An error the link fixed by itself (for example a retried packet); a high rate is a warning.
pci_error_handlers
Driver callbacks (error_detected, slot_reset, resume) used to recover from PCIe errors.
Hot-plug
Adding or removing a PCIe device while the system runs.
CXL
Compute Express Link: coherent memory and cache protocols on the PCIe physical layer.
Peer-to-peer DMA
One PCIe device reading or writing another's memory directly, without staging in host RAM.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Chapter 10 covered enumeration, BARs and MSI-X. At fleet scale, the questions change. Is each link running at the speed and width it should (current_link_speed and current_link_width vs the max_ values in sysfs)? Downtraining silently halves bandwidth. AER (Advanced Error Reporting) classifies errors as correctable (fixed by retry, but a rising rate means marginal signal integrity), uncorrectable non-fatal (one transaction lost) and fatal (the link is unreliable, so recovery or reset is needed). Drivers implement pci_error_handlers to recover. Hot-plug and surprise removal must not crash the kernel. CXL runs on the PCIe physical layer and adds cache-coherent memory semantics (CXL.mem for memory expansion and pooling). Accelerator clusters also use peer-to-peer DMA and RDMA (GPUDirect-style) so devices move data without bouncing through host memory.

MAKE IT STICK

A motorway with lanes. A link built for 16 lanes at full speed sometimes opens with only 8 lanes or at a lower speed limit, and nobody notices because traffic still flows. Correctable errors are potholes the cars swerve around: harmless one at a time, but a growing number means the road is breaking up.

INTERACTIVE LAB

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Training jobs 4% slower on one rack

One rack's training throughput was 4% lower than its neighbours, with no errors in job logs. A fleet scan found three accelerators linked at x8 instead of x16 after a maintenance visit reseated risers, and one link logging thousands of correctable BadDLLP errors per hour. Draining and repairing those nodes restored throughput; a link-health check now runs at every boot.

1 · Link health checks

At boot and periodically, compare current vs max link speed and width for every accelerator, NIC and switch port. Alert on any downtraining. Note that some devices drop link speed at idle to save power (ASPM or dynamic link speed), so check under load or read the expected state. Bandwidth math: Gen5 is about 3.9 GB/s per lane per direction, so x16 ≈ 63 GB/s and x8 ≈ 31.5 GB/s.

2 · AER and recovery

Correctable errors are fixed by the link itself, but their rate matters. Counters such as RxErr, BadTLP and BadDLLP should be tracked per device and trended. Uncorrectable errors invoke the driver's pci_error_handlers: error_detected decides whether to recover, slot_reset reinitializes, resume restarts I/O. DPC (Downstream Port Containment) can isolate a failing link. Many fleets drain a node when correctable rates cross a threshold, before fatal errors hit.

3 · Hot-plug, surprise removal and CXL

Drivers must handle a device vanishing: reads return all-ones (0xFFFFFFFF), so check for that and fail gracefully instead of looping. CXL adds three protocols on the PCIe PHY: CXL.io (PCIe-like), CXL.cache and CXL.mem. Memory expanders and pooled memory appear to Linux as NUMA nodes or DAX devices. The CXL Consortium and PCI-SIG publish the specs Google's posting mentions.

4 · Peer-to-peer and HPC networking

Accelerators send data to each other without going through the CPU. Inside a node they use PCIe switches (peer-to-peer DMA); across nodes they use RDMA network cards (GPUDirect RDMA-style), with collectives such as all-reduce on top. Topology matters: devices behind the same switch get far better peer bandwidth than those crossing CPU sockets. ACS and IOMMU settings can force peer traffic through the root complex and cut bandwidth, which is a classic misconfiguration.

Testing and launching kernel drivers at fleet scale: KUnit, selftests, fault injection and staged rollout
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Google · Staff Software Engineer, Drivers & Systems Engineering
Minimum qualification: 5 years testing and launching software products, plus kernel drivers.
Google · Senior Staff Software Engineer, Accelerator Platforms
Launch of the accelerator stack with SRE teams.

Automation, static analysis and fuzzing.
1

2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Kernel drivers can crash an entire machine, and a fleet has many thousands of them. So every change goes through layers of tests, including tests that deliberately make things fail, and is rolled out to a few machines first with automatic checks and an easy way back.

KUnit
The Linux kernel's unit-testing framework; tests run in-kernel or under user-mode Linux.
UML
User-mode Linux: the kernel compiled as a normal program, handy for fast KUnit runs.
kselftest
Kernel self-tests in tools/testing/selftests that exercise kernel interfaces from user space.
Fault injection
Deliberately making operations fail (for example memory allocation) to test error handling.
KASAN
Kernel Address Sanitizer: finds out-of-bounds and use-after-free bugs in the kernel.
syzkaller
A coverage-guided system-call fuzzer that finds kernel bugs.
Canary
A small first group of machines that gets a change before everyone else.
Health gate
An automated check of metrics that must pass before a rollout continues.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Driver code runs with full privileges on every machine in the fleet, so testing is layered. KUnit runs unit tests inside the kernel (or under UML, user-mode Linux, in seconds on a laptop) for pure logic like format decoding. kselftest and subsystem suites (IGT for DRM) exercise real interfaces on real hardware. Fault injection (failslab, fail_page_alloc, and driver-specific hooks) forces error paths that never run normally. Sanitizers (KASAN, KCSAN, lockdep, kmemleak) turn hidden bugs into reports. syzkaller fuzzes system calls and ioctls. Launch is staged: canary machines, then increasing percentages with health gates (crash rate, error counters, job throughput) and automatic rollback to the last good kernel. Launching safely is a minimum qualification in Google's posting.

MAKE IT STICK

Testing a new aircraft part. First the part is tested alone on a bench (KUnit). Then it's fitted to a test plane on the ground (selftests on lab hardware). Engineers break things on purpose to see if backups kick in (fault injection). Then one plane flies with it, then a few routes, and the whole fleet only after the numbers look good.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A driver update that only failed on 0.3% of machines

A driver change passed all lab tests and rolled to 5% of the fleet. Health gates noticed a 0.3% increase in machine crashes on one hardware revision: an allocation failure path under memory pressure freed a buffer twice. The rollout halted automatically and rolled back. Fault injection with failslab reproduced it in the lab within minutes, and a KUnit-plus-fault-injection test now guards that path.

1 · The test pyramid for drivers

Bottom: KUnit tests for pure logic (parsers, state machines, math), run on every commit in seconds under UML or QEMU. Middle: kselftests and subsystem suites (IGT for DRM, v4l2-compliance for media) on lab hardware. Top: soak and stress tests on production-like racks. Run debug kernels (KASAN, lockdep, KCSAN, kmemleak) in CI, plus syzkaller for ioctl fuzzing.

2 · Fault injection

The kernel can make chosen operations fail on purpose. Its fault-injection framework (CONFIG_FAULT_INJECTION with failslab, fail_page_alloc and fail_make_request, set up through debugfs) fails them with a probability or on the Nth call. Combine it with KASAN to catch double frees and leaks in error paths. Add driver-specific injection points (for example, simulate a firmware timeout) behind a debug config.

3 · Staged rollout and health gates

Kernels and drivers ship as fleet releases: canary machines first, then 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%, with soak time at each stage. Gates compare the new cohort against a control cohort on crash and panic rates, machine-check and AER errors, driver error counters and job throughput, normalized by hardware revision. A gate failure halts and rolls back automatically, with kdump captures collected for triage.

4 · Launch is a product skill

Google's posting asks for 5 years of testing and launching software products. Show you can plan a launch: compatibility matrix (kernel × firmware × hardware revision), rollback plan, metrics and owners, communication with SRE, and a postmortem habit. The Tesla OTA drill in this course covers the device-fleet version of the same thinking.

text:
LESSON 19.1 · C · LIBIBVERBS (ONE RDMA WRITE, THEN POLL THE COMPLETION QUEUE) · NEW
RDMA from the ground up: queue pairs, completions and registered memory
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
NVIDIA · Senior Solution Engineer, Networking (Austin)
InfiniBand and Spectrum-X both carry RDMA traffic. Field issues are often verbs-level: bad keys, unregistered memory, retry storms.
NVIDIA · Senior System Software Engineer, Performance (Austin)
HPC and AI workloads lean on RDMA for low CPU cost per byte.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

RDMA means remote direct memory access. A network card copies data from your memory straight into another machine's memory. Neither CPU copies the bytes, and the operating system is not in the middle of each transfer. You set things up once, then hand the card small job tickets and check a results tray.

RDMA
Remote direct memory access: a NIC reads or writes another machine's memory directly, without the remote CPU copying data.
Verbs
The standard low-level RDMA programming interface (libibverbs on Linux), named after the actions it defines.
Queue pair (QP)
A send queue plus a receive queue on the NIC. Each connection uses one QP on each side.
Work request (WR)
A small job ticket posted to a queue: which operation, which local buffer, and for RDMA, which remote address.
Completion queue (CQ)
Where the NIC reports finished work requests as work completions with a status code.
Memory region (MR)
A buffer registered with the NIC: pages are pinned and the NIC gets an lkey (local) and rkey (remote) to check access.
rkey
The key a remote peer must present to read or write your registered memory. Leaking it means granting access.
Kernel bypass
The application posts work to the NIC directly from user space, with no system call per message.
Reliable connected (RC)
The common RDMA transport: in-order, acknowledged delivery between exactly two queue pairs.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

RDMA lets one computer write straight into another computer's memory without the remote CPU copying anything. The application talks to the NIC through queues, not system calls. You register a buffer once (a memory region, which pins the pages and returns keys), create a queue pair (a send queue and a receive queue), and post work requests that point at your buffers. The NIC moves the bytes by DMA and later writes a work completion into a completion queue, which you poll. One-sided operations (RDMA WRITE and READ) need no code on the remote side once it has shared its address and rkey. Two-sided SEND needs the receiver to have posted a receive buffer first. The kernel sets everything up, then steps out of the data path. That is called kernel bypass, and it is where the low latency and low CPU cost come from.

MAKE IT STICK

Normal networking is posting a letter through the office mail room: clerks open it, copy it, and carry it to a desk. RDMA is giving a trusted courier a key to one filing drawer in the other office. The courier puts the papers straight into that drawer, and drops a note in your tray saying it's done.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The training job that hung at step one

A customer's 64-node training job hangs the first time GPUs exchange data. TCP tests between the same nodes pass. The NIC counters show the first RDMA WRITE retried 7 times, then the queue pair dropped into the error state with status RETRY_EXC_ERR.

1 · The QP state machine is the first clue

A queue pair walks RESET → INIT → RTR (ready to receive) → RTS (ready to send). Moving to RTR needs the peer's QP number, its port address (LID on InfiniBand, a GID on RoCE) and the path MTU. One wrong field and the QP still reaches RTS, but the packets go nowhere. The sender retries retry_cnt times and gives up with RETRY_EXC_ERR. TCP passing proves the cable works. It doesn't prove the RDMA addressing does.

2 · Where the RoCE version bit bites

On RoCE, the GID index picks both the IP address and the RoCE version (v1 or v2). A node using a v1 GID talking to a v2-only switch path silently drops. show_gids lists each index. The root cause in this story is a mismatched GID index in a config file on 3 of 64 nodes. That is very typical for field issues: one config edge, not a deep bug.

3 · Memory registration costs and pitfalls

Registering pins pages and fills the NIC's translation tables. It is slow (microseconds to milliseconds), so libraries register once and reuse a pool. Common faults: the buffer is freed while still registered, a fork() copy-on-write breaks the pinning, or a registration limit is hit because ulimit -l (locked memory) is too low. The last one shows up as ENOMEM from ibv_reg_mr.

4 · Reading the completion status

Map statuses to layers. LOC_PROT_ERR means your lkey or range is wrong (local bug). REM_ACCESS_ERR means the rkey or remote range is wrong, or the peer deregistered. RETRY_EXC_ERR means no ACKs came back (addressing, fabric or peer down). RNR_RETRY_EXC_ERR means the peer had no receive posted for a SEND. Each points to a different owner, so it speeds up triage.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Training clusters move huge bursts of data at the same moment. A lost packet forces slow resends and stalls every GPU waiting for it. So these networks either never drop (InfiniBand) or add pause and early-warning signals to Ethernet so drops almost never happen.

Lossless network
A network designed so that packets are never dropped because a buffer was full.
Credit-based flow control
InfiniBand's rule: send only when the receiver has advertised free buffer space (credits).
PFC
Priority flow control: an Ethernet switch pauses one traffic class on a link when its buffer for that class fills.
Head-of-line blocking
A paused or slow packet at the front of a queue blocks packets behind it that could have gone elsewhere.
ECN
Explicit congestion notification: a switch marks packets instead of dropping them, to warn the sender early.
CNP
Congestion notification packet: the RoCE receiver tells the sender 'you caused ECN marks, slow down'.
DCQCN
A widely used RoCEv2 congestion-control algorithm: cut rate on CNPs, then recover in steps.
Incast
Many senders hitting one receiver at once, overflowing the last switch port. Typical in all-to-all traffic.
RoCEv2
RDMA over Converged Ethernet version 2: RDMA packets carried in UDP/IP over Ethernet.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

AI training makes every GPU send at the same moment, and direct memory transfers recover badly from lost packets, so these networks are built to be lossless. InfiniBand never drops for lack of buffer space: it uses credit-based flow control, where a sender transmits only when the next hop has advertised free buffer space. Ethernet was designed to drop, so RoCEv2 adds PFC (priority flow control): a switch whose queue fills sends a PAUSE frame for one traffic class. PFC alone is dangerous: pauses spread backwards and block innocent flows (head-of-line blocking), and in rare loops they deadlock. So fabrics add ECN: switches mark packets when a queue passes a threshold, the receiver sends back a congestion notification packet (CNP), and the sender cuts its rate. DCQCN is the classic RoCE algorithm for that rate control. Newer fabrics such as NVIDIA's Spectrum-X add adaptive routing and their own congestion control (public product description).

MAKE IT STICK

A motorway with ramp lights. InfiniBand is a road where you may only enter when the next stretch has a free parking space reserved for you. PFC is a police officer stopping all lanes of one colour when traffic backs up, which works but jams nearby roads too. ECN is a sign that tells drivers early to slow down before the jam forms.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The all-to-all that froze a whole rack

A customer upgrades to a mixture-of-experts model with heavy all-to-all traffic. Training slows by 40%, and an unrelated storage job on the same switches times out. Switch counters show huge PFC pause durations on one uplink, and almost no ECN marks.

1 · Why pauses spread

With PFC alone, a full egress queue pauses its upstream port for that traffic class. That upstream queue fills and pauses its own upstream, and the pause spreads back toward every sender (a pause storm). Flows that never touched the hot port share those paused queues, so they stall too. That is the storage job in this story.

2 · ECN must act before PFC

The fix order matters: ECN marking thresholds must sit well below the PFC trigger, so senders slow down before buffers fill. If ECN is off, or its threshold is above PFC, you get pauses instead of rate control. Here ECN was enabled on the NIC but not on the switch's lossless class. Almost no marks and lots of pauses is exactly that signature.

3 · Tuning knobs and what they trade

ECN min and max thresholds (earlier marking → lower queues but less throughput), DCQCN gains (faster reaction vs oscillation), PFC headroom (buffer reserved for packets already in flight when a pause is sent, which grows with cable length and speed). Always change one knob, rerun the same collective benchmark, and compare pause time, marks and job step time.

4 · What InfiniBand does differently

InfiniBand's credits make the link itself lossless, and its fabric manager computes routes. It still needs congestion control (it has its own congestion notification), and adaptive routing spreads flows over many paths. The habit of debugging from counters transfers across fabrics: find where queues build, and why the senders didn't slow down.

11
void dcqcn_init(dcqcn_t *f, double line) {
12

16

17
  f->rt = f->rc;
18
  f->rc = f->rc * (1.0 - f->alpha / 2.0);
19
  f->alpha = (1.0 - g) * f->alpha + g;
20
  f->stages = 0;
21

22
 
23

24
void dcqcn_on_quiet(dcqcn_t *f, double g, double step) {
25
  f->alpha = (1.0 - g) * f->alpha;
26
  if (f->stages >= 5) f->rt += step;
27
  if (f->rt > f->line) f->rt = f->line;
28
  f->rc = (f->rc + f->rt) / 2.0;
29
  f->stages++;
30
}

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

When many GPUs train one model, they must add up their results and share the total after every step. How that adding-and-sharing is arranged decides whether the expensive GPUs spend their time computing or waiting on the network.

All-reduce
Every participant contributes an array and every participant ends up with the element-wise sum.
Reduce-scatter
First half of ring all-reduce: each rank ends with the full sum of one slice.
All-gather
Second half: every rank collects every slice from the others.
Alpha-beta model
Time ≈ α × number of steps + bytes ÷ β: per-step latency plus bandwidth cost.
NCCL
NVIDIA Collective Communications Library: GPU collectives over NVLink, PCIe, InfiniBand and RoCE.
NVLink / NVSwitch
NVIDIA's GPU-to-GPU links, and the switch chip that connects many GPUs all-to-all inside a node or rack.
GPUDirect RDMA
The NIC reads and writes GPU memory directly, skipping a copy through host memory.
Bus bandwidth (busbw)
algbw × 2(p−1)/p for all-reduce: a number comparable to the link's real speed.
Rank
One participant (usually one GPU) in a collective, numbered 0 to p−1.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

In data-parallel training every GPU computes gradients, then all GPUs must end up with the sum. That operation is all-reduce. A ring all-reduce splits the data into p chunks and passes them around a ring twice: first a reduce-scatter (each GPU ends with the full sum of one chunk), then an all-gather (everyone collects all summed chunks). Each GPU sends about 2·(p−1)/p of the data, almost independent of p. That makes rings bandwidth-optimal but latency-heavy, with 2·(p−1) steps. Tree algorithms take about 2·log₂p steps, which wins for small messages. A simple alpha-beta model predicts time: α per step (latency) plus bytes ÷ β (bandwidth). NCCL picks ring or tree per size and topology. It uses NVLink/NVSwitch inside a node and InfiniBand or RoCE between nodes, ideally with GPUDirect RDMA so the NIC reads GPU memory directly. Bus bandwidth (busbw) normalizes results so you can compare them with link speed.

MAKE IT STICK

Eight people each counted votes in part of a city, and everyone needs the city total. Passing partial sums around a circle is fair: everyone carries the same small load, but it takes many hand-offs. A phone tree is fewer rounds but each call carries more. For a few numbers, the tree is quicker. For a huge stack of ballots, the circle wins.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Half the bandwidth on the new cluster

A customer runs all_reduce_perf from nccl-tests across 16 nodes with 8 GPUs each. Large messages reach a bus bandwidth of 180 GB/s inside one node but only 21 GB/s across nodes, where they expected close to 45 GB/s per 400 Gb/s port. Their support ticket says the network is slow.

1 · Read algbw vs busbw correctly

nccl-tests prints algbw (bytes ÷ time) and busbw (algbw × 2(p−1)/p for all-reduce). Compare busbw with the slowest link in the path. 400 Gb/s is 50 GB/s raw, so ~45 GB/s is a realistic ceiling per port. Inside a node NVLink is much faster, so the inter-node links set the pace.

2 · First suspects: topology and GPUDirect

Run with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and read which transport each ring step uses. 'NET/IB' with 'GDRDMA' is good. Plain 'NET/IB' without it means data is copied through host memory. Check that each GPU uses the NIC on its own PCIe switch. A GPU crossing to a NIC on the other CPU socket halves bandwidth. In this story, the NIC-to-GPU mapping was wrong because a firmware update changed PCIe enumeration order.

3 · Then the fabric

If transports look right, check fabric counters during the test: port errors and link speed (a link trained at a lower rate), congestion marks, adaptive routing settings. Run the test over subsets of nodes to bisect: if one pair of nodes is slow, it's a link. If everything is uniformly slow, it's configuration.

4 · Small messages are a different problem

At 8 KB, time is dominated by α (latency per step), not bandwidth. Tree algorithms and fewer, larger messages help. Framework settings such as gradient bucket size decide the message sizes NCCL actually sees, so the fix may be in the training config rather than the network.

6

7

8

11

12

13
      sent += c;
14

15

16

17

18

20

21

23

24

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Getting packets from the network card into a program costs CPU time. At tens of millions of packets per second, even a tiny cost per packet adds up. These techniques cut that cost by skipping layers, batching work and giving each user its own slice of the card.

SR-IOV
Single-root I/O virtualization: one PCIe device exposes a physical function (PF) plus many virtual functions (VFs) assignable to VMs or containers.
Virtual function (VF)
A lightweight PCIe function with its own queues, owned by a guest or container.
DPDK
Data Plane Development Kit: user-space libraries and poll-mode drivers for fast packet processing.
Poll-mode driver (PMD)
A driver that checks the NIC queues in a loop instead of waiting for interrupts.
Burst
Moving many packets (for example 32) per call to amortize fixed overhead.
SPSC ring
A single-producer, single-consumer circular queue that needs only atomic loads and stores, not locks.
SmartNIC / DPU
A NIC with its own programmable cores and accelerators. NVIDIA calls its version a DPU (BlueField).
Interrupt moderation
Delaying or batching interrupts so the CPU handles many packets per interrupt.
Huge pages
2 MB or 1 GB memory pages that reduce address-translation misses for big packet buffers.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

The fastest network is useless if the host can't feed it. SR-IOV lets one physical NIC present many lightweight virtual functions (VFs) that VMs or containers own directly, bypassing the hypervisor's software switch. DPDK goes further for packet processing: a user-space poll-mode driver owns the NIC queues, dedicated cores spin on rx_burst() without interrupts, buffers come from huge-page memory pools, and work moves in bursts of 32 or so packets to amortize per-call costs. Between threads, DPDK uses lock-free single-producer/single-consumer rings. A SmartNIC or DPU (for example NVIDIA BlueField) puts Arm cores and accelerators on the NIC itself, so the virtual switch, storage and security work leave the host CPU. NVIDIA's SDK for that is DOCA. On normal Linux, NAPI blends interrupts and polling, and interrupt moderation batches interrupts to save CPU at some latency cost.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant kitchen. Interrupts are a bell that rings for every order: fine when it's quiet, chaos at rush hour. Polling is a cook who stands at the hatch and grabs orders in handfuls, always busy even when no one comes. SR-IOV gives each dining room its own hatch. A DPU hires a second kitchen just to handle deliveries.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Packet loss with the CPU only 30% busy

A customer's virtual router on a SmartNIC-equipped server drops 0.5% of packets at 40 Mpps, yet top shows the host only 30% busy. NIC counters show rx_missed (the NIC had no free descriptors) climbing on two queues out of sixteen.

1 · Averages hide hot queues

RSS (receive-side scaling) hashes flows to queues. A few elephant flows can land on one queue, so that core is pegged while others idle. rx_missed on specific queues is the tell. Check per-queue counters and per-core utilization, not host averages.

2 · Poll-mode realities

A DPDK core spinning on an empty queue shows 100% busy even when idle, so CPU % is meaningless there. The real metric is cycles per packet and empty-poll ratio. Stalls come from cache misses on packet data, cross-NUMA memory (the mempool on the wrong socket), or a burst size too small to amortize overhead.

3 · Where SR-IOV and DPUs change the picture

With SR-IOV, a VM's VF gets its own queues, but VF limits (queues, MAC filters, spoof checks) are set from the PF and can silently drop. With a DPU, switching rules are offloaded to hardware, and a missed offload (an unsupported tunnel or header combination) falls back to a slow software path on the DPU's Arm cores. That fallback shows up as a sudden throughput cliff for one traffic type.

4 · The fix in this story

Two queues received most elephant flows. The fixes were spreading flows with a better RSS key, adding queues, and moving the mempool to the NIC's NUMA node. Drops went to zero at the same core count. The write-up to the customer explained the per-queue view, with before and after counters.

#include <stdatomic.h>
2
#include <stddef.h>
3
#define RING_SZ 1024u  /* power of two */
4
typedef struct {
5
  _Alignas(64) _Atomic size_t head;  /* written by producer */
6
  _Alignas(64) _Atomic size_t tail;  /* written by consumer */
7

8

9
 
10
/* Producer: enqueue up to n items; returns how many fit. */
11
size_t ring_enq_burst(ring_t *r, void *const *objs, size_t n) {
12
  size_t h = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);
13
  size_t t = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);
14
  size_t free_slots = RING_SZ - (h - t);
15
  if (n > free_slots) n = free_slots;
16
  for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) r->slot[(h + i) & (RING_SZ - 1)] = objs[i];
17
  atomic_store_explicit(&r->head, h + n, memory_order_release);
18
  return n;
19
}
20
 
21
/* Consumer: dequeue up to n items; returns how many were taken. */
22
size_t ring_deq_burst(ring_t *r, void **objs, size_t n) {
23
  size_t t = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_relaxed);
24
  size_t h = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);
25
  size_t avail = h - t;
26
  if (n > avail) n = avail;
27
  for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) objs[i] = r->slot[(t + i) & (RING_SZ - 1)];
28
  atomic_store_explicit(&r->tail, t + n, memory_order_release);
29
  return n;
30
}

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Network software reacts to events: cables plugged in, timers expiring, messages arriving. It tracks where it is with a state machine. Bugs happen when events arrive in an order nobody planned for. Finding them means rebuilding the exact sequence from logs and counters.

Finite state machine (FSM)
A model where software is always in one named state and events move it to another along defined transitions.
Event loop
A loop that waits for the next event (packet, timer, message) and runs its handler, one at a time.
Debounce
Waiting a short time before believing a change, so brief glitches are ignored.
Stale event
An event that was valid when created but no longer matches the current state when it is handled.
Generation counter
A number bumped on every relevant change. Events carry it, and old numbers are ignored.
Race condition
Behaviour that depends on the timing or order of events or threads.
Link flap
A port going down and up repeatedly, often from a marginal cable, optic or signal.
Root cause analysis (RCA)
A written explanation of what failed, why, how it was proven, and how it is prevented.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Most network-software bugs found in the field aren't wrong formulas. They are ordering problems: an event arrives in a state nobody expected, or a stale timer fires after the world moved on. Network operating systems and NIC firmware are built from finite state machines (port link state, routing protocol neighbours, QP states) driven by an event loop that pulls events from queues. Classic failure: a link flaps down and up quickly, a debounce timer armed during the first 'down' fires late, and the port is declared down while the cable is fine. The fix pattern is a generation counter: every timer carries the generation it was armed in, and the handler ignores it if the generation has changed. Root-causing such bugs in the field follows a loop: reproduce, collect (counters, logs with timestamps, traces), narrow to one state machine and event sequence, read the source for the transition, then confirm with a targeted test.

MAKE IT STICK

You tell a friend 'if I don't call back in 5 minutes, assume I'm stuck'. Then you call back after 2 minutes, but forget to cancel the deal. At minute 5 your friend starts a search party. A generation number is like saying 'search only if you haven't heard from me since call #3'.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The port that kept coming back too early

A customer reports that after a switch reboot, about one port in 200 forwards traffic briefly, then drops it for 2 seconds, then recovers. Training jobs see a burst of RDMA retries each time. The logs show 'link up' confirmed only 10 ms after the latest PHY 'up', even though the debounce time is 300 ms.

1 · Reproduce with the exact sequence

From the timestamps: PHY up at t=0 (timer armed), PHY down at 120 ms, PHY up at 290 ms (a new timer armed), then the first timer fires at 300 ms. Without a generation check, the old timer confirms the link 10 ms into the new 'up' instead of 300 ms. The link then flaps again during training, which is exactly the observed pattern. Reproduce it in a unit test by feeding that event list.

2 · Read the source for the transition

Find the handler for the timer event and ask: what does it check before acting? Here it checked only timer_armed, and the new 'up' re-armed it, so the stale timer looked valid. The fix is one comparison plus a test, but the proof is the event trace matching the logs line for line.

3 · Collect the right evidence

Port FSM logs with monotonic timestamps, PHY counters (signal loss, symbol errors), timer arm and fire logs, and the firmware version. For RDMA impact: QP retry counters and NCCL warnings timed against the flaps. Ask the customer for a capture window that covers one full event, not just the end state.

4 · Write it up for two audiences

For the customer: what happened, impact, workaround (raise debounce, or apply the fixed firmware), and how to verify. For R&D: the exact event sequence, the faulty check, a failing unit test, and the patch. Clear RCAs are part of the job, not an afterthought.

Measuring performance you can trust: benchmarks, noise and statistics
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
NVIDIA · Senior System Software Engineer, Performance (Austin)
Named: "strong skills in performance analysis, data analysis and performance optimization".
Qualcomm · Enablement Software Engineer (Austin)
Enablement work proves each optimization on real and pre-silicon platforms.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Computers don't run the same code at exactly the same speed twice. Caches, clock speeds and other programs all add noise. Good performance work measures many times, reports a typical value with its wobble, and only believes differences bigger than the wobble.

Microbenchmark
A small, focused test that times one piece of code in isolation.
Warm-up
Running the code a few times before measuring so caches and predictors settle.
Median
The middle value of sorted results. One outlier can't drag it like it drags an average.
MAD
Median absolute deviation: the median distance from the median, a robust measure of spread.
Frequency scaling
The CPU changes its clock speed with load, temperature and power limits.
SMT
Simultaneous multithreading: two hardware threads share one core's units, so they disturb each other's timings.
Dead-code elimination
The compiler removes work whose result is never used, which can make a benchmark measure nothing.
perf stat
The Linux tool that counts hardware events (cycles, instructions, cache misses) for a command.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A performance claim is only as good as its measurement. Modern CPUs change speed on their own (frequency scaling and turbo), share caches and cores with other work (SMT), and warm up caches and branch predictors over time. So a single timing means little. A trustworthy microbenchmark pins the thread to a core, warms up first, repeats many times, and reports the median with a spread measure such as the MAD (median absolute deviation) or percentiles. It also stops the compiler deleting the work it measures (dead-code elimination) by consuming results. To claim a speedup, compare distributions, not two numbers. If the difference is smaller than the run-to-run noise, it isn't a result yet. On Linux, perf stat -r 10 repeats a command and prints the variance of each counter, which is a quick sanity check.

MAKE IT STICK

Timing a runner once on a windy day tells you little. You time several laps on a calm day, after a warm-up, on the same track, and report a typical lap with how much it varied. If a new shoe saves less than the normal lap-to-lap wobble, you can't say it helped.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Is the speed-up real?
IN PLAIN WORDS

Timing a runner on several calm laps after a warm-up, rather than once on a windy day.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 7% speedup that wasn't

A pull request claims a 7% speedup in a memory-copy routine on the new Arm server, based on one run before and one after. Reviewers ask for more data. Ten runs each show the old version ranging 96–109 ms and the new one 95–106 ms.

1 · Noise sources on servers

Turbo and power limits move the clock between runs. Other tenants and kernel threads steal time. Memory placement differs run to run (which NUMA node, which pages). SMT siblings share the core. Pin threads (taskset), fix the frequency governor where possible, disable SMT for the test or account for it, and record everything in the result.

2 · Report distributions

Medians with spread, or full percentile plots, beat means. Here the medians are 101 ms vs 100 ms with spread about ±4 ms: no real difference. A simple check: does one version beat the other in nearly every paired run? A rank test or bootstrap confidence interval makes that formal.

3 · Check what you measured

Inspect the generated code or use perf stat counters. If instructions per run dropped to near zero, the compiler deleted the work. If cycles stayed equal but time changed, the clock moved, not your code. Counters turn 'it got faster' into 'it retired 12% fewer instructions'.

4 · Make it reproducible

Save the command, machine config, kernel, compiler and flags, frequency settings and raw samples. A result someone else can rerun is worth ten that they can't. That is also what makes competitive comparisons credible.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Processors have built-in counters that record what happened inside them. They count finished instructions, times data wasn't in the cache, and wrong guesses about branches. Reading these counters tells you why code is slow, not just that it's slow.

PMU
Performance monitoring unit: the hardware counters inside each CPU core.
IPC
Instructions retired per cycle. Low IPC means the core is mostly waiting.
Top-down analysis
Splitting time into retiring, bad speculation, frontend bound and backend bound, then drilling into the biggest.
Frontend bound
The core couldn't fetch and decode instructions fast enough.
Backend bound
Instructions were decoded but waited on execution units or memory.
Bad speculation
Slots wasted on work thrown away after a mispredicted branch.
SPE
Arm's Statistical Profiling Extension: samples individual operations with latency and address.
perf_event_open
The Linux system call that opens a hardware or software counter for a thread or CPU.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Hardware performance counters (the PMU) count events like cycles, retired instructions, cache refills and branch mispredictions. IPC (instructions per cycle) is the first number to read. Top-down analysis splits every cycle's issue slots into four buckets. Retiring is useful work. Bad speculation is work thrown away after wrong branch guesses. Frontend bound means the core couldn't fetch or decode instructions fast enough (instruction cache, branch target misses). Backend bound means instructions were ready but stuck waiting for execution units or memory. Then you drill into the biggest bucket. On Arm Neoverse cores the events have names like CPU_CYCLES, INST_RETIRED, STALL_FRONTEND, STALL_BACKEND, L1D_CACHE_REFILL and BR_MIS_PRED_RETIRED. Arm publishes top-down methods for them. SPE (Statistical Profiling Extension) samples individual operations with their latency and data address. In code, you read counters with perf_event_open, the same system call perf itself uses.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant measuring a slow evening. Retiring is meals served. Bad speculation is meals cooked for the wrong table and thrown out. Frontend bound is waiters not bringing orders to the kitchen fast enough. Backend bound is the orders waiting because the oven or the pantry is the holdup.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Same code, different bottleneck

A database workload runs 25% slower on a new Arm server than on a competitor's x86 server at a similar clock. The team's first guess is 'the compiler isn't optimizing for Arm'. perf stat shows IPC of 0.9 on both machines, but cycles are 25% higher on the Arm system.

1 · Start with IPC and the top level

Equal IPC with more cycles means more instructions, or the same instructions taking more cycles somewhere. Here the instruction counts match, so the extra cycles are stalls. Top-down shows backend bound at 55% on Arm vs 40% on x86, mostly memory.

2 · Drill into memory

L1 refills are similar. Last-level cache misses are 2× higher on Arm. The workload's hot index is 48 MB; the Arm part's shared last-level cache is smaller per core in this configuration, so more accesses go to DRAM. SPE samples confirm the latency spike lands on index lookups.

3 · Turn evidence into options

Software options: shrink the index (compression), improve locality (cluster hot keys), use huge pages to cut TLB misses on the index, and prefetch the next lookup. Hardware and policy options: cache partitioning, larger LLC SKUs. Each option gets a predicted gain from the counters before anyone codes it.

4 · Communicate the comparison fairly

Report both machines' counters side by side with configs. 'Backend-memory bound due to LLC capacity; 30% fewer DRAM reads after index compression' is a result product and hardware teams can act on. 'Arm is slower' is not.

Virtual memory, TLBs, huge pages and NUMA
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

Named: virtual memory, caching, multicore hardware; datacenter-scale CPU+GPU systems.
Qualcomm · Enablement Software Engineer (Austin)

1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2

3
CODE, LINE BY LINE

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Programs use made-up addresses that the hardware translates to real memory locations. Translations are cached in a small table. When data is spread wide, translations miss and every access gets slower. On big servers, some memory is also physically farther from the CPU than other memory.

Virtual address
The address a program uses. Hardware translates it to a physical memory address.
TLB
Translation lookaside buffer: a small cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.
Page walk
Reading the page tables to translate an address after a TLB miss.
TLB reach
How much memory the TLB covers: number of entries × page size.
Huge pages
Larger pages (2 MB or more) so each TLB entry covers more memory.
NUMA
Non-uniform memory access: memory attached to another socket or die is slower to reach.
First-touch
Linux places a page on the NUMA node of the thread that first writes it.
Pointer chase
A benchmark where each load's address comes from the previous load, exposing true latency.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Every load uses a virtual address that must be translated to a physical one. The TLB caches recent translations. A miss triggers a page walk through the page tables, which costs tens to hundreds of cycles if those tables aren't cached. TLB reach is entries × page size: 2,048 entries of 4 KB cover only 8 MB, so a random-access working set of 1 GB misses constantly. Huge pages (2 MB, or on Arm64 64 KB base pages and larger blocks) multiply the reach. On Linux, transparent huge pages do it automatically, if memory isn't too fragmented. On multi-socket or multi-die servers, memory is NUMA: each CPU has local memory and slower remote memory. Linux uses first-touch placement, so the thread that first writes a page decides where it lives. A single-threaded initialization therefore puts all data on one node. numactl and mbind control placement. The classic way to measure memory latency is a pointer chase, where each load's address depends on the previous one.

MAKE IT STICK

The TLB is the speed-dial list on your phone. Calling someone on speed dial is instant. Anyone else means looking them up in a thick directory. Huge pages are like speed-dialling a whole office instead of each person. NUMA is your desk drawer vs the filing room down the hall: both work, one is slower.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Fast on one socket, slow on two

An in-memory analytics service scales well up to 64 threads on one socket, then gains only 15% with 128 threads across two sockets. Remote-memory access counters are high, and page-walk cycles are 8% of total cycles.

1 · First-touch caught everyone out

The service loads its 200 GB dataset with one thread at startup, so first-touch puts all of it on node 0. Threads on node 1 read everything remotely, at higher latency and through the socket link's limited bandwidth. Parallel initialization (each thread touches the part it will use) or numactl --interleave fixes placement.

2 · The TLB adds a second tax

Random lookups across 200 GB with 4 KB pages miss the TLB on nearly every access. Page-walk cycles of 8% confirm it. Enabling huge pages for the dataset region (THP with madvise, or explicit hugetlbfs) cut walk cycles to under 1%.

3 · Measure, don't assume

A pointer-chase sweep shows the latency curve: local DRAM vs remote DRAM, and the jump when the working set passes TLB reach. Counters for remote accesses and page walks confirm which effect dominates in the real service.

4 · Arm-specific notes

Arm64 Linux can use 4 KB, 16 KB or 64 KB base pages, chosen at kernel build time. 64 KB pages raise TLB reach 16× for everyone, at some memory overhead. Many Arm server distros choose 64 KB for this reason. That is a platform decision enablement engineers make and must measure.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Most requests are fast; a few are slow, and users notice those. The slow ones are often caused by the operating system: hardware interrupting the core, the core waking from a power-saving nap, or the clock speeding up too slowly. Fixing them means choosing where work and interrupts run, and how much power to spend.

Tail latency
The slow end of the response-time distribution, such as the 99th or 99.9th percentile.
Interrupt (IRQ)
A hardware signal that makes a CPU core stop and run a handler for a device.
IRQ affinity
The set of CPU cores allowed to handle a given interrupt.
Idle state
A low-power state a core enters when idle. Deeper states save more power but take longer to wake.
Frequency governor
The kernel policy that raises and lowers CPU clock speed with load.
isolcpus / nohz_full
Boot options that keep the scheduler and timer ticks away from chosen cores.
Performance per watt
Work done per unit of energy. Often the real target for datacenter products.
Housekeeping
Background kernel work like timers and deferred callbacks that can interrupt any core.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Average speed is easy. Tail latency (the slowest 1% or 0.1%) is where systems fail their promises, and it usually comes from the OS and power management, not your algorithm. Device interrupts land on whichever core their IRQ affinity allows. If that is the same core as a latency-critical thread, every packet steals time from it. Idle states (C-states on x86; WFI and deeper states on Arm) save power but take microseconds to wake from. Frequency governors ramp clocks up slowly after idle. Kernel housekeeping (timers, RCU callbacks, other tasks) adds random delays. Tools: /proc/interrupts shows where interrupts go. isolcpus and nohz_full keep a core quiet. Disabling deep idle states cuts wake-up time. Good engineers then measure performance per watt, because pinning everything at maximum frequency with no idle states wins latency and loses the power budget. The right answer is a policy per workload.

MAKE IT STICK

A receptionist (a CPU core) who also answers every phone call (interrupts), takes naps when it's quiet (idle states), and starts slow after a nap (frequency ramp). For an important visitor (a latency-critical request), you give them a receptionist with no phone, who stays awake, and route calls to someone else.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
p99 doubled after a 'harmless' kernel update

A latency-sensitive inference front-end on an Arm server sees p50 unchanged at 180 µs but p99 jump from 400 µs to 900 µs after a kernel update. CPU usage is identical. The update changed the default IRQ balancing policy and the cpuidle driver.

1 · Look at where interrupts land

Diffing /proc/interrupts shows the NIC's queue interrupts now spread over all cores, including the 8 cores running request threads. Each interrupt and its softirq processing steals 5–20 µs from a request on that core. Pinning NIC IRQs to separate housekeeping cores restores most of the tail.

2 · Idle states add wake-up time

The new cpuidle driver enables a deeper idle state with a long exit latency. Lightly loaded cores drop into it between requests, and the next request pays the wake-up. Limiting deep states on request cores (with a PM QoS latency request, or cpuidle settings) removes the rest of the regression.

3 · Then count the watts

Keeping 8 cores out of deep idle costs measurable power. Report it: p99 back to 410 µs for +6% package power. Product and platform owners decide whether that trade is right. The engineer's job is to make it visible with numbers.

4 · Make it a policy, not a hack

Encode the result as a tuned profile or boot configuration (IRQ affinity, isolcpus or cpusets, idle limits, governor) that ships with the product, and add a tail-latency test to CI so the next kernel update can't silently undo it.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Saying one processor is faster than another needs care. You must test them the same way, and decide what 'better' means: per chip, per core, per watt or per dollar. Each choice can change the winner, so you say which one you used.

Competitive analysis
Measuring your product against others on the same workloads under controlled, documented conditions.
Normalization
Dividing a result by something (cores, watts, price) so different systems compare fairly.
Geometric mean
The n-th root of a product of n ratios. The fair way to average speedups.
Rate vs speed
Rate runs many copies at once (throughput); speed runs one copy (single-thread latency).
Iso-power
Comparing systems at the same power draw.
TDP
Thermal design power: the sustained power a chip is designed to dissipate.
Baseline
The system every other result is divided by.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A competitive comparison answers a question like 'is our chip better for this customer's workload, by how much, and why?'. The honest version controls the setup: same compiler and flags (or each vendor's best, stated clearly), same memory configuration, SMT on or off for both, same OS and settings. It then chooses the normalization the question needs. Per chip answers 'which box does more?'. Per core answers 'whose core is faster?'. Per watt answers 'who does more within a power budget?'. Per dollar answers 'who is cheaper?'. Different normalizations can crown different winners, so state which one you use and why. Summaries across many benchmarks use the geometric mean of ratios, because an arithmetic mean of ratios is biased by which machine you call the baseline. Finally, explain the result with counters (IPC, cache misses, bandwidth), so the comparison drives design and software decisions. Rate results (many copies in parallel) and speed results (one copy) measure different things.

MAKE IT STICK

Comparing two delivery vans. 'Which carries more per trip' (per chip), 'which is faster on its own' (per core), 'which goes further per litre' (per watt), and 'which costs less per parcel' (per dollar) can each name a different winner. A fair review says which question it answers.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Two slides, two winners

Marketing wants a slide showing the new 72-core Arm CPU beats a competitor's 96-core x86 part. Engineering's data: on a 10-benchmark server suite, the competitor scores 8% higher per chip, but the Arm part draws 30% less power and each Arm core is 35% faster on single-copy runs.

1 · Each normalization tells a true story

Per chip: competitor +8%. Per core: Arm wins by a wide margin. Per watt: Arm wins by about 30%. All three are true. Picking one without saying so is how comparisons lose credibility with customers' own engineers.

2 · Control what you can

Same OS and kernel, same memory speed and channel count, SMT stated for both, compilers at their best documented flags, results as medians over repeated runs. Any deviation goes in a footnote. Customers will rerun your numbers.

3 · Explain, don't just rank

Counters explain the gaps. The competitor wins two memory-bandwidth-heavy tests because it has more memory channels. The Arm part wins branchy, cache-friendly code on IPC. That turns a scoreboard into guidance: which workloads to target, which software optimizations to push upstream.

4 · Write the conclusion carefully

'At equal power, the Arm system completes 1.3× more work on this suite; per chip, the competitor is 8% higher; memory-bound tests favour more channels.' Precise, reproducible, and useful to architects planning the next chip.

NVIDIA · Senior System Software Engineer, Performance (Austin)

CODE, LINE BY LINE

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Arm processors run code at different trust levels: apps at the bottom, then the operating system, then a hypervisor, then secure firmware at the top. Code asks a higher level for help with a special instruction. The first job when enabling a new chip is identifying exactly which core and revision you are running on.

Exception level (EL0–EL3)
Arm's privilege levels: apps, kernel, hypervisor, secure monitor.
Hypervisor
Software that runs virtual machines and controls what they can touch.
VHE
Virtualization Host Extensions: lets a host kernel run at EL2 so KVM avoids extra transitions.
Secure monitor
The EL3 firmware that switches between normal and secure worlds and handles SMC calls.
SVC / HVC / SMC
Instructions that trap into EL1, EL2 or EL3 respectively.
System register
A CPU control or ID register accessed with MRS (read) and MSR (write).
MIDR_EL1
Main ID register: implementer, variant, architecture, part number and revision of the core.
Erratum
A documented hardware bug in a specific core revision, usually with a software workaround.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An Arm 64-bit CPU runs software at four privilege rings called exception levels. EL0 runs applications. EL1 runs the OS kernel. EL2 runs a hypervisor (or the kernel itself, with VHE, so KVM hosts avoid an extra hop). EL3 runs the secure monitor firmware (usually Trusted Firmware-A), which switches between the normal and secure worlds. Software moves up a level only through an exception: SVC asks EL1 (a system call), HVC asks EL2, SMC asks EL3. Interrupts and faults are routed to a level by configuration bits (for example in HCR_EL2 and SCR_EL3). Each level has its own system registers, read with MRS and written with MSR, such as SCTLR_EL1 (MMU and caches on or off) or VBAR_EL1 (where the exception vector table lives). Bring-up starts by identifying the core: MIDR_EL1 holds the implementer (0x41 is Arm Ltd, 0x51 is Qualcomm), part number, variant and revision. The kernel uses it to apply errata workarounds and to print the CPU in boot logs. On Linux you can read it without privilege from sysfs or through emulated MRS in user space.

MAKE IT STICK

An office building with four floors. The lobby is for visitors (apps), the second floor for staff (the kernel), the third for building management (the hypervisor), and the top floor has the vault and the master keys (secure firmware). You can't take the stairs up: you call the floor above through a specific phone line (SVC, HVC, SMC), and they decide whether to help.

IN PLAIN WORDS

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Secondary cores never come online

On early boards of a new custom-CPU server, Linux boots on CPU 0, but the log shows 'CPU1: failed to come online' for every other core. The same kernel boots fine on a reference Arm server.

1 · Who wakes the other cores?

On Arm servers, Linux doesn't wake cores itself. It asks the EL3 firmware with an SMC call (PSCI CPU_ON, covered next lesson). So the failure lives on the line between EL1 and EL3, or in what EL3 does next.

2 · Follow the exception

Add a print in the firmware's SMC handler: the call arrives, so routing works. The firmware writes the core's start address and releases it from reset, but the core takes an exception immediately at EL3 because its vector base register (VBAR_EL3) was never set for secondary cores on this new part.

3 · Identify the part

The fix is per-core code that only runs on this implementer and part number. Firmware and kernel both decode MIDR_EL1 to choose part-specific setup. Getting the ID right (implementer 0x51, new part number, revision r0p0) is the first line of any enablement patch.

4 · Make it permanent

Upstream the CPU's MIDR definition to the kernel and firmware, add it to errata tables when issues are confirmed, and add a CI boot test on the virtual platform that checks every core comes online.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

An Arm server starts with secure firmware, then general firmware that sets up devices, then the operating system. The firmware gives the OS a standard description of the hardware, so one generic OS image can boot on many machines. A certification program checks that the hardware and firmware follow the rules.

TF-A
Trusted Firmware-A: Arm's reference secure boot firmware. BL31 stays resident at EL3.
PSCI
Power State Coordination Interface: standard firmware calls to power cores on/off, suspend and reset.
UEFI
Unified Extensible Firmware Interface: the standard firmware that initializes devices and loads the OS.
ACPI
Advanced Configuration and Power Interface: tables that describe hardware to the OS.
RSDP / XSDT
The root pointer and the list of all other ACPI tables.
MADT / GTDT / SPCR / IORT / PPTT
ACPI tables for interrupts and CPUs, timers, the serial console, IOMMU mapping, and cache topology.
SBSA / BBR
Server Base System Architecture (hardware rules) and Base Boot Requirements (firmware rules).
SystemReady
Arm's certification that generic OS images boot on a platform.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An Arm server boots in stages. Boot ROM loads Trusted Firmware-A: BL1 and BL2 set up memory and load the next images; BL31 stays resident at EL3 as the secure monitor. BL31 implements PSCI (Power State Coordination Interface), the standard SMC calls the OS uses to turn cores on and off, suspend, reset and power off. Next, UEFI firmware (often EDK2) at EL2 initializes PCIe and devices, offers boot services, and hands the OS a set of ACPI tables describing the hardware. Key tables for Arm servers: MADT (interrupt controller and CPUs), GTDT (timers), SPCR (serial console), IORT (how PCIe and devices map through the IOMMU, called SMMU on Arm, and to interrupt translation), PPTT (cache and core topology), MCFG (PCIe config space). Linux finds them through the RSDP pointer and the XSDT list. Arm SystemReady is a certification program: a platform that follows SBSA (hardware rules) and BBR (firmware rules) boots generic, unmodified OS images. Enablement engineers write and fix this firmware and the kernel code that reads it.

MAKE IT STICK

Moving into a new office building. Security guards (TF-A) unlock the building and keep the master keys. Facilities (UEFI) switches on lights and lifts. Then you're handed a floor plan (ACPI tables) showing every room, desk and exit. A standard floor plan format (SystemReady) means any tenant (any OS) can move in without a custom map.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A generic distro hangs with no console output

A SystemReady pre-certification run boots a stock Linux distribution image from USB. The firmware menu works, GRUB appears, then the screen and serial port go silent. A vendor-built kernel with a hard-coded console works.

1 · Where does the console come from?

A generic kernel learns which UART to use for early messages from the ACPI SPCR table. The vendor kernel had it on the command line, so it never needed SPCR.

2 · Dump the tables

From the UEFI shell, acpiview shows an SPCR table, but its checksum fails, and its interface type says a 16550 UART while the board has an Arm PL011. Linux ignores a table with a bad checksum, so the kernel boots blind.

3 · Check the rest with the test suite

The Arm SystemReady test suite (ACS) also flags the IORT: one PCIe root complex is missing, so devices behind it will get no MSI interrupts once the console works. Two firmware bugs, not kernel bugs.

4 · Fix and prove

Fix both tables in the firmware build, rerun ACS and boot three unmodified distributions. Add a firmware CI step that validates checksums and required tables on every build, using code like this lesson's walker.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

Named: "working knowledge of weak memory models" for server platforms.
NVIDIA · Senior System Software Engineer, Performance (Austin)
Named: multicore concurrency on Arm datacenter CPUs.

Functional models must reproduce what orderings a CPU allows.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Processors can make memory writes visible to other cores in a different order than the program wrote them. Arm allows more reordering than x86, so some shared-memory code that seemed fine on PCs breaks on Arm servers. You fix it by marking which writes and reads must stay in order.

Memory model
The rules for which orders of memory operations other cores may observe.
TSO
Total store order, x86's model: only a later load may pass an earlier store.
Store buffer
A per-core queue holding stores before they reach the cache, visible to that core first.
Weakly ordered
A model, like Arm's, where independent accesses can be reordered unless a barrier or ordered instruction says otherwise.
Release / acquire
A release store makes earlier writes visible before it; an acquire load keeps later reads after it.
Barrier (DMB)
An instruction that orders memory accesses around it.
Litmus test
A tiny multi-threaded program used to test which outcomes a memory model allows.
Data race
Two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, with no ordering between them. Undefined behaviour in C/C++.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Each CPU core may reorder its own loads and stores for speed, as long as the result looks the same to that core. Other cores can see the difference. A memory model says which orderings other cores may observe. x86 uses TSO (total store order): stores sit in a store buffer, so a later load may pass an earlier store, but stores appear in order and loads appear in order. Arm is weakly ordered: without barriers, independent loads and stores to different addresses can appear in almost any order. Code that 'worked for years' on x86 can fail on Arm. The classic test is message passing: thread A writes data then sets a flag; thread B sees the flag, then reads stale data. The fix is ordering, not delay. In C11 or C++11, write the flag with release and read it with acquire. On Arm these compile to STLR and LDAR (or LDAPR). Kernel code uses smp_store_release / smp_load_acquire or barriers like DMB ISH. Some patterns, like store buffering (Dekker-style mutual exclusion), need a full sequentially consistent fence even on x86. Small tests that show which outcomes are allowed are called litmus tests; tools like herd7 check them against the formal Arm model.

MAKE IT STICK

Two people sending postcards. One writes 'the parcel is on your porch' and posts the parcel, but the postcard arrives first, and the friend finds an empty porch. Release/acquire is a rule: the postcard only goes out after the parcel has been delivered.

START WITH THE INCIDENT

A logging library's lock-free ring buffer has run on x86 fleets for six years. On the new Arm server platform, about one in ten million log records arrives as garbage or zeros. Nobody can reproduce it on x86.

1 · Suspect ordering, not the algorithm

The producer fills a slot and then bumps the head index with a plain store. On x86 (TSO), stores appear in order, so the consumer never sees the new head before the slot contents. On Arm, the head store can become visible first.

2 · Prove it

Write a litmus test with the same shape (message passing), run it with herd7 against the Arm model: the 'stale data' outcome is allowed. Run the real code under ThreadSanitizer on any machine: it reports a data race on the slot.

3 · Fix with the weakest correct ordering

Make the head index atomic: release on the producer's store, acquire on the consumer's load. A full fence would also work but costs more on every message.

4 · Prevent recurrence

Add TSan runs to CI, run stress tests on Arm hardware or a model in CI, and add a porting checklist: any 'volatile flag' or plain-store publication must be reviewed.

LESSON 21.4 · C · RUNTIME DISPATCH ON HWCAP BITS WITH A PORTABLE FALLBACK · NEW
Pre-silicon enablement, feature detection and errata workarounds
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Qualcomm · Enablement Software Engineer (Austin)
Named: software virtual platforms, pre-silicon debug tools, and drivers and optimizations for new CPUs.
AMD · Senior Virtual Platform Functional Modeling Engineer (Austin)
Virtual platforms exist so software teams can start before silicon.
NVIDIA · Senior System Software Engineer, Performance (Austin)
Named: pre- and post-silicon performance work.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Software for a new chip is written before the chip exists, using simulated versions of it. When real chips arrive, software checks at run time which features each chip has and works around known hardware bugs.

Shift-left
Moving software work earlier, before silicon, so it's ready at launch.
Virtual platform
A software model of a whole system that runs real firmware and OS images.
Emulator / FPGA prototype
Hardware that runs the chip's real design (RTL), slower than silicon but more accurate than a model.
HWCAP
Linux bitmask of CPU features given to each process (AT_HWCAP, AT_HWCAP2).
ifunc
A glibc mechanism that picks a function implementation once, at load time, based on CPU features.
LSE atomics
Armv8.1 Large System Extensions: single-instruction atomics like LDADD, much faster under contention than load/store-exclusive loops.
Erratum workaround
A software change that avoids a known hardware bug on specific core revisions.
A0 silicon
The first manufactured version of a chip.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

New chips take years to design, so software must be ready on day one. Shift-left means starting software work before silicon exists, on pre-silicon platforms: fast virtual platforms (instruction-accurate models like Arm FVPs or QEMU, running at tens to hundreds of MIPS) for firmware and OS bring-up; emulators (cycle-accurate hardware emulation boxes) and FPGA prototypes (much slower than silicon, but running real RTL) for driver and performance checks. When silicon arrives, the goal is booting Linux in days, not months. Software must also adapt at run time to what each CPU supports. Feature detection on Linux uses HWCAP bits from getauxval(AT_HWCAP), backed by the ID registers. Libraries like glibc pick optimized routines (for example, LSE atomics or SVE string functions) with ifunc resolvers. Hardware bugs found late become errata: the kernel and firmware match MIDR ranges and apply workarounds (an extra barrier, a disabled feature, a different instruction sequence). START WITH THE INCIDENT
Linux in 3 days on first silicon

A new custom-CPU server SoC is 9 months from first silicon. Leadership asks the enablement team to boot a generic distribution within a week of A0 parts arriving.

The architecture team provides a functional model of the SoC (a virtual platform). The team brings up TF-A, UEFI and Linux on it, writes ACPI tables, and adds the new MIDR and features upstream. CI boots the model nightly.

2 · Move to emulation for real RTL

Six months out, the same images run on the hardware emulator, at a few MHz. It catches what the model got wrong: a register reset value, an interrupt routed to the wrong GIC line, a cache maintenance quirk. Each is fixed in both the firmware and the model.

3 · Silicon arrives

Firmware boots in hours. One problem remains: under heavy contention, an atomic instruction sequence occasionally returns a wrong value on r0p0. It becomes an erratum (fictional example for teaching): the kernel matches the MIDR revision range and disables that path, and libraries fall back via feature checks.

Generic Linux booted on day 3. The team logs which bugs were found on the model, the emulator and silicon, to argue for more model investment next time.

Virtual platforms: abstraction levels and device register models
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
AMD · Senior Virtual Platform Functional Modeling Engineer (Austin)
Named: functional models, model interfaces and adapters for software-visible behaviour, early software bring-up.
Qualcomm · Enablement Software Engineer (Austin)
Named: software virtual platforms for pre-silicon enablement.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A virtual platform is a software copy of a computer that can run real software before the chip exists. It can be fast and rough, or slow and exact. For drivers, the most important part is that each device register looks and behaves exactly like the real one.

Virtual platform (VP)
A software model of a full system that runs real software images.
Functional model
Models what the hardware does, not how long it takes.
Instruction-accurate
Each instruction has the right effect; timing is not modelled precisely.
Approximately-timed
Adds estimated timing per transaction, for performance studies.
Cycle-accurate
Matches the hardware's timing cycle by cycle. Very slow.
Programmer's view
Everything software can see: registers, memory map, interrupts and their behaviour.
W1C
Write-1-to-clear: writing 1 to a bit clears it; writing 0 leaves it alone.
Side effect
An action caused by a register access, such as raising an interrupt or starting a transfer.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A virtual platform (VP) is a program that pretends to be a whole computer well enough to run real firmware, OS and drivers. It is built from models: CPU models, memory, interconnect and device models. Choosing the abstraction level is the main design decision. Functional / instruction-accurate models (QEMU, Simics, Arm Fast Models, SystemC loosely-timed) run hundreds of millions of instructions per second and boot Linux in seconds, but timing is approximate. Approximately-timed models add per-transaction timing for performance studies. Cycle-accurate models and RTL simulation are exact but thousands to millions of times slower. Most VPs mix levels. A device model must match the programmer's view: every register's address, reset value, access type and side effects, as the spec says. Common access types: read-only, read/write, write-1-to-clear (W1C, typical for interrupt status), read-to-clear, and write-only command registers. Side effects (raising an interrupt, starting a DMA) happen on register writes or on internal events. If a model gets these wrong, drivers developed on the VP break on silicon.

MAKE IT STICK

A flight simulator. A cheap one shows the cockpit switches and what they do, good enough to learn procedures. An expensive one models the airflow over the wings, needed for aircraft design but far too slow for practising checklists. A virtual platform picks the right simulator for the job, and every switch must do exactly what the real one does.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The driver works on the VP and storms on silicon

A timer driver was developed entirely on the virtual platform and passed every test. On first silicon, the CPU locks up in an interrupt storm a few seconds after boot.

1 · Compare the programmer's view

The driver clears the interrupt by writing 0 to STATUS. The VP's model treated STATUS as read/write, so writing 0 cleared it. The spec, and silicon, say STATUS is W1C: writing 0 does nothing, the line stays high, and the handler runs forever.

2 · Fix both sides

The driver writes 1 to clear, as the spec says. More importantly, the model is fixed to W1C, because the VP must fail exactly where silicon fails, or it hides bugs.

3 · Stop it happening again

Generate register models from the same machine-readable spec as the RTL (IP-XACT or SystemRDL), so access types can't drift. Add a conformance test that checks every register's reset value and access type against the spec.

4 · Choose the right level

For this bug, an instruction-accurate VP was the right level: it's a programmer's-view bug. Timing bugs (a driver assuming a register update is instant) would need an approximately-timed model or emulation.

// A tiny timer-like device: CTRL (RW), STATUS (W1C), IRQ_EN (RW), ID (RO).
5
class TimerRegs {
6
 public:
7
  static constexpr uint32_t CTRL = 0x0, STATUS = 0x4, IRQ_EN = 0x8, ID = 0xC;
8
  static constexpr uint32_t ID_VALUE = 0x0001'2A01;  // fixed device ID
9
  std::function<void(bool)> irq_line;              // wired by the platform
10
 
11
  void reset() { ctrl_ = 0; status_ = 0; irq_en_ = 0; update_irq(); }
12
 
13
  uint32_t read(uint32_t off) const {
14
    switch (off) {
15
      case CTRL: return ctrl_;
16
      case STATUS: return status_;
17
      case IRQ_EN: return irq_en_;
18
      case ID: return ID_VALUE;
19
      default: return 0;  // unmapped offset: reads as zero (check the spec!)
20
    }
21
  }
22
 
23
  void write(uint32_t off, uint32_t v) {
24
    switch (off) {
25
      case CTRL: ctrl_ = v & 0x3u; break;          // only bits 1:0 exist
26
      case STATUS: status_ &= ~v; break;           // W1C
27
      case IRQ_EN: irq_en_ = v & 0x1u; break;
28
      case ID: break;                              // read-only: ignore writes
29
      default: break;
30
    }
31
    update_irq();
32
  }
33
 
34
  // Called by the platform when the modelled timer expires.
35
  void expire() { if (ctrl_ & 0x1u) { status_ |= 0x1u; update_irq(); } }
36
 
37
 private:
38
  void update_irq() {
39
    bool level = (status_ & 0x1u) && (irq_en_ & 0x1u);
40
    if (level != line_ && irq_line) irq_line(level);
41
    line_ = level;
42
  }
43
  uint32_t ctrl_ = 0, status_ = 0, irq_en_ = 0;
44
  bool line_ = false;
45
};
