LESSON 22.2 · C++17 + SYSTEMC 3.0 · AN LT INITIATOR WITH A QUANTUM KEEPER AND A MEMORY TARGET · NEW
SystemC and TLM-2.0: transactions, timing annotation and the quantum
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
AMD · Senior Virtual Platform Functional Modeling Engineer (Austin)
Named: SystemC/TLM-2.0, Arm Fast Models, Simics or QEMU.
Qualcomm · Enablement Software Engineer (Austin)
Software virtual platforms are often built on SystemC/TLM.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

SystemC is a C++ toolkit for building simulations of hardware. Parts of the system talk by passing transaction objects. To run fast, each part works ahead on its own clock and only re-syncs with the others now and then. The trade-off is speed versus how precisely events line up in time.

SystemC
An IEEE-standard C++ library for modelling hardware and systems with simulated time.
TLM-2.0
SystemC's transaction-level modelling standard: generic payloads, sockets and transport calls.
Generic payload
The standard transaction object: command, address, data pointer, length, response status.
b_transport
Blocking transport call: the target completes the transaction and adds its latency to a delay argument.
Loosely-timed (LT)
A TLM style where initiators run ahead of global time and annotate delays.
Temporal decoupling
Letting a process run ahead of simulation time to avoid frequent context switches.
Global quantum
The maximum time a process may run ahead before it must sync.
DMI
Direct memory interface: a raw pointer to model memory that skips transactions for speed.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

SystemC is a C++ library for modelling hardware. It provides modules (components), ports and sockets (connections), processes (threads that model concurrent hardware), and a discrete-event simulation kernel that advances simulated time. TLM-2.0 (transaction-level modelling) standardizes how models talk: an initiator (like a CPU) sends a generic payload (command, address, data pointer, length, response status) to a target (like memory) over a socket. In loosely-timed (LT) style, the initiator calls b_transport(payload, delay): the target does the work immediately and adds its latency to delay, instead of waiting. The initiator keeps running ahead of the global simulation time by up to a global quantum. This temporal decoupling avoids a context switch per transaction and makes LT models fast. The quantum keeper tracks the local time offset and calls sync() when the quantum is used up. A bigger quantum means faster simulation, but threads see each other's events late, so timing (for example, how fast an interrupt is noticed) gets less exact. DMI (direct memory interface) goes further: the initiator gets a raw pointer to memory and skips transactions entirely.

MAKE IT STICK

Office workers doing their own tasks and only checking the shared calendar every hour (the quantum). Work flies, but if someone's meeting moved at 9:05, the others only find out at 10:00. Check every minute and nobody misses anything, but everyone spends the day checking calendars.

INTERACTIVE LAB
The quantum dial
IN PLAIN WORDS

Office workers checking the shared calendar every minute, or once an hour.

Try this: Drag the quantum from smallest to largest. Find where it's fast and still accurate.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Move the global quantum and see wall-clock time, sync points and timing error between models.

Teaching model: 1 s of simulated time, 5 billion instructions at 200 MIPS, about 2 µs of host time per sync.

Global quantum
1 µs
Initiator threads (cores modelled)
4
Timer and watchdog models use transaction timestamps
Wall-clock time
33 s
Worst timing error between models
1 µs
Sync points
4,000,000
A good balance: fast, with timing errors small enough for this platform.
Term: quantum balances speed and accuracy
START WITH THE INCIDENT
Linux boots in 40 seconds, but the watchdog fires

A team speeds up their SystemC virtual platform by raising the global quantum from 1 µs to 1 ms. Linux boot drops from 6 minutes to 40 seconds. But a firmware watchdog test now fails: the watchdog fires even though software kicks it on time.

1 · What changed is not the software

With a 1 ms quantum, the CPU model runs up to 1 ms ahead of the watchdog model. The kick write reaches the watchdog with a timestamp, but the watchdog's own thread already ran its timeout check at an earlier global time and saw no kick.

2 · Understand the trade

Temporal decoupling is safe for code that doesn't depend on precise timing between models. Tight timing between models (watchdogs, timers, handshakes) needs those models to sync more often.

3 · Fix it locally, not globally

Keep the big quantum for speed, but make the watchdog model handle timing correctly: compute timeouts from transaction timestamps (sc_time_stamp() plus the annotated delay), or have the CPU sync before accesses to timing-critical devices.

4 · Test both settings

Run regression at both a small and a large quantum. Results that change with the quantum point to models that depend on timing they don't handle properly.

Distributed simulation: synchronization, message ordering, credits and determinism
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

Named: distributed multi-node functional models; message ordering, flow control, protocol state machines; scheduling, synchronization, deterministic execution and replay.

Ordering and determinism matter in distributed robot fleets too.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Big chip models can be split across several computers. Each part keeps its own clock. They must never get a message timestamped earlier than where they've already got to, and messages that arrive together must always be handled in the same order. Then the whole run can be repeated exactly.

Simulation node
One process or machine running part of a distributed model, with its own simulated clock.
Causality violation
Receiving a message with a timestamp earlier than your current simulated time.
Conservative synchronization
Never advancing past the earliest time a peer could still send you a message.
Lookahead
How far into the future a node can promise it won't send messages. Often the link latency.
Optimistic synchronization
Running ahead and rolling back when a late message arrives.
Credit-based flow control
A sender may only send as many messages as it holds credits; the receiver returns credits as it frees buffers.
Deterministic execution
Same inputs give exactly the same results, every run.
Replay
Re-running a recorded execution exactly, for debugging.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A very large system (many chiplets, sockets or nodes) may not fit in one simulator process, so the model is split across processes or machines. Each simulation node has its own clock. To stay correct, no node may receive a message 'from the past' (a causality violation). Conservative synchronization guarantees this: each node advances only up to the earliest time any peer could still send it something. That bound is the peer's current time plus the lookahead, usually the minimum link latency. Big lookahead means nodes can run far apart and fast. Lock-step (every node syncs every step) is simple and slow. Optimistic methods run ahead and roll back on violations, which is complex. Messages between nodes need a deterministic ordering rule when timestamps tie, such as (time, source node, sequence number), or results change from run to run. Links need flow control: credit-based schemes let a sender transmit only as many messages as the receiver has buffer slots, and the receiver returns credits as it frees slots. With deterministic ordering and recorded inputs, a run can be replayed exactly to debug a failure.

MAKE IT STICK

Several kitchens cooking one banquet, each with its own clock. A kitchen may cook ahead only as far as it's sure no other kitchen will send it an ingredient it needs earlier. Deliveries that arrive at the same moment are always unpacked in the same order, so tomorrow's rehearsal goes exactly like today's.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A 4-socket model fails one run in fifty

A functional model of a 4-socket server is split into 4 processes, one per socket, connected over the network. A coherency test fails about once every 50 runs with the same inputs. Nobody can reproduce a failure on demand.

1 · Look for non-determinism

Two messages from different sockets sometimes arrive with the same timestamp. The receiver handles them in network arrival order, which varies with host load. Different order, different protocol outcome.

2 · Define a total order

Order messages by (time, source, sequence). Now the receiver's behaviour depends only on simulated events. The 1-in-50 failure becomes either 50 in 50 or 0 in 50 with the same seed.

3 · It's 50 in 50, and that's good

The ordering now always produces the failing case, which turns out to be a real protocol bug: a snoop response and a new request crossing at the same instant. Deterministic replay lets the team step through it in a debugger.

4 · Guard the sync

Add a causality-violation counter (it must stay zero), credit-based flow control on each link so a slow node can't be flooded, and CI runs with different host loads that must give identical traces.

LESSON 22.4 · C++17 · A MESI MODEL OF N CACHES ON A SNOOPING BUS WITH AN SWMR CHECKER · NEW
Cache coherency and SoC interconnects: MESI, snoops, AXI/CHI, CXL and UCIe
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
AMD · Senior Virtual Platform Functional Modeling Engineer (Austin)
Named: memory hierarchies, cache coherency, interconnects and fabrics; PCIe, CXL, AXI, CHI, ACE, UCIe, HBM, DDR.
NVIDIA · Senior System Software Engineer, Performance (Austin)
Coherency traffic is a top cause of multicore slowdowns.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Each processor core keeps copies of memory in its cache. When one core changes data, the others' copies must not go stale. A coherency protocol tracks who holds which copy and whether it may be changed. The chip's internal network and links between chips carry these messages.

Coherency
Keeping every cache's copy of a memory location consistent.
SWMR
Single writer, multiple readers: the invariant coherency protocols enforce for each line.
MESI
Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid: a common per-line state protocol.
Snoop
A request to other caches to check, share or invalidate a line.
Directory / snoop filter
Structures that track which caches hold a line, so snoops go only where needed.
AXI / ACE / CHI
Arm AMBA interconnect protocols: basic, coherent extension, and coherent packet-based hub.
CXL
Compute Express Link: coherent memory and cache protocols over PCIe's physical layer.
UCIe
Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express: a standard die-to-die link between chiplets.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

When several cores cache the same memory, a coherency protocol keeps their copies consistent. The key invariant is SWMR (single writer, multiple readers): at any time, a cache line has either one writer or any number of readers, never both. MESI names four states per cached line. Modified (only copy, dirty). Exclusive (only copy, clean, can be written silently). Shared (clean, others may hold it). Invalid. A write to a Shared line must first invalidate the other copies. A read that finds another cache holding the line Modified gets the data from that cache (a snoop hit) and both end up Shared after the dirty data is written back. Real systems add states like Owned (MOESI) or Forward (MESIF) and use a directory or snoop filter to avoid broadcasting to every cache. On Arm SoCs, AXI is the basic non-coherent bus, ACE added coherency, and CHI is the packet-based coherent interconnect for many-core designs. Off-chip, PCIe connects devices, CXL adds coherent memory and cache semantics on top of the PCIe physical layer, and UCIe connects chiplets inside one package. HBM and DDR are the memory types behind it all. A functional model must get the states and messages right; a performance model also counts how many and how long.

MAKE IT STICK

A shared document with several people holding printed copies. Anyone can read their copy. To edit, you must first collect and shred everyone else's copy (invalidate), and while you edit, nobody else may. If someone asks for the document while you're editing, you hand over your latest version first.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A chiplet model passes boot but fails a lock test

A functional model of a two-chiplet CPU (two core complexes joined by a die-to-die link) boots Linux, but a spinlock stress test reports two threads in the critical section at once, about once per hour of simulated runtime.

1 · Check the invariant, not the symptom

Add an SWMR checker on every coherency transaction. It fires: a line is Modified in chiplet A while chiplet B still holds it Shared.

2 · Find the missing message

The trace shows A upgraded the line from S to M. The upgrade's invalidation reached only A's local caches. The cross-chiplet adapter dropped invalidations when its credit pool was empty, instead of stalling.

3 · Fix the adapter

Invalidations must never be dropped. The adapter now stalls the upgrade until it gets a credit, and the protocol uses a separate credit pool for snoops so they can't be blocked behind ordinary requests (avoiding deadlock).

4 · Keep the checker on

SWMR and 'no lost messages' checkers run in every regression. Fault-injection tests deliberately exhaust credits to make sure the adapter stalls rather than drops.

10
 
11

12
    if (st_[c] != St::I) return;                    // hit: no bus traffic
13
    ++bus_msgs;                                     // BusRd
14
    bool others = false;
15
    for (std::size_t o = 0; o < st_.size(); ++o) {
16
      if (o == c || st_[o] == St::I) continue;
17
      if (st_[o] == St::M) ++writebacks;            // dirty owner supplies data
18
      st_[o] = St::S;                               // everyone downgrades to S
19
      others = true;
20

21
    st_[c] = others ? St::S : St::E;               // alone? get Exclusive
22
  }
23
 
24
  void write(std::size_t c) {
25
    if (st_[c] == St::M) return;                    // already owner
26
    if (st_[c] == St::E) { st_[c] = St::M; return; } // silent upgrade
27
    ++bus_msgs;                                     // BusRdX or Upgrade
28
    for (std::size_t o = 0; o < st_.size(); ++o) {
29
      if (o == c) continue;
30
      if (st_[o] == St::M) ++writebacks;
31

32
    }
33

34

35

37
  bool swmr_ok() const {
38

39

40
    return writers == 0 || (writers == 1 && valid == 1);
41
  }
42

43

44

LESSON 22.5 · C++17 · FIRST-DIVERGENCE TRACE COMPARISON WITH A TIMING TOLERANCE · NEW
Validating models: trace comparison, regression, fault injection and HW/SW co-validation
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
AMD · Senior Virtual Platform Functional Modeling Engineer (Austin)
Named: validation, regression testing, trace-based debug, CI/CD; fault injection; HW/SW co-validation.
Apptronik · Staff Systems Engineer, Robot-as-a-Service Platform (Austin)
Named: failure semantics and reliability for distributed systems.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

To trust a model, compare what it does with a trusted reference, step by step, and find the first place they disagree. Run these checks on every change. Also break things on purpose to test that errors are handled properly.

Validation
Checking a model behaves like its reference (spec, RTL or silicon).
Trace
A time-ordered log of events, such as transactions or register writes.
First divergence
The earliest point where two traces disagree; usually the root cause.
Regression suite
Tests rerun on every change to catch things that used to work and now don't.
Fault injection
Introducing errors on purpose to test detection and recovery.
Co-validation
Running the same software on model and hardware to check they agree.
Seed
The starting value for random tests, recorded so a failing case can be rerun exactly.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A model is only useful if it's right, and stays right as everyone changes it. Validation compares the model against a reference: the spec, RTL simulation, an emulator or real silicon. A practical method is trace comparison: both sides log events (instruction retired, register write, transaction) in a common format; a tool walks the traces in lockstep and reports the first divergence, the earliest point where they disagree. Later differences are usually consequences. Timing fields are compared with a tolerance, or ignored for functional models. Regression runs a suite (boot tests, directed tests, random tests with fixed seeds) on every change in CI, and keeps results comparable over time. Fault injection deliberately breaks things (drop or corrupt a message, stall a link, flip a memory bit, fail a power state transition) to test the error handling paths of models, firmware and drivers that are hard to reach otherwise. HW/SW co-validation runs real firmware and drivers on the model and the RTL or silicon and checks they behave the same, so software teams and hardware teams catch each other's bugs early.

MAKE IT STICK

Proofreading a translated book against the original. You read both side by side and stop at the first sentence that differs, because everything after it may just follow from that one mistake. Fault injection is a fire drill: you set off the alarm on purpose to check people know what to do.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Fault injection bench
IN PLAIN WORDS

A fire drill: set off the alarm on purpose to see if people know what to do.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A screen shows a new picture at fixed moments, many times per second. Each picture has to be ready before its moment, or the old one stays up and the motion stutters. Smooth car screens come from making every single frame on time, not just the average.

Refresh rate
How many times per second the display can show a new image, e.g. 60 Hz.
Vsync
The moment the display starts showing the next frame. Frames must be ready before it.
Render pipeline
The stages a frame passes through: input, update, draw commands, GPU rendering, composition.
Compositor
The system service that combines app windows into the final screen image (Weston, SurfaceFlinger).
Jank
Visible stutter caused by frames missing their vsync deadline.
Double / triple buffering
Using two or three image buffers so drawing and display can overlap.
Frame budget
The time available per frame: 16.7 ms at 60 Hz.
Present timestamp
When a frame actually reached the screen; the right input for jank measurement.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A display refreshes at a fixed rate, for example 60 Hz, so a new image can appear only every 16.7 ms, at vsync. A UI frame passes through a render pipeline: the UI thread handles input and updates state, builds a list of drawing commands, the render thread or GPU draws them into a buffer, and the compositor (Wayland/Weston on Linux, Screen on QNX, SurfaceFlinger on Android) combines app buffers onto the screen. If any stage misses its deadline, the old frame stays on screen for another refresh: a dropped frame, seen as jank (stutter). Double buffering lets the GPU draw the next frame while the current one is shown; triple buffering absorbs occasional slow frames but adds a frame of latency. The UI thread must never block on disk, network or slow IPC. Car screens add more: multiple displays (cluster, centre stack, passenger) with different refresh rates, safety-relevant content like the instrument cluster, and cheaper GPUs than phones. Measuring means timestamps per frame (present time), not averages: a 60 fps average can hide a 200 ms freeze.

MAKE IT STICK

A train that leaves the station exactly every 16.7 minutes. Passengers (frames) who arrive late just miss it and wait for the next one, and the platform display keeps showing the old departure. Triple buffering is an extra waiting room: fewer missed trains, but everyone boards a bit later.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The map scroll stutters every two seconds

On a new centre-stack display, scrolling the navigation map averages 58 fps, which looks fine on the dashboard. Drivers and testers still report a regular hitch every couple of seconds.

1 · Measure per frame

Present timestamps show 59 frames on time, then one 85 ms gap, repeating every 2 s. The average hides it completely: that's five missed vsyncs in a row.

2 · Trace the UI thread

A system trace shows the UI thread blocked in a synchronous IPC call to the vehicle-data service every 2 s, waiting for a batch of traffic data. The service takes 70–80 ms to reply.

3 · Fix the architecture

Make the call asynchronous: request on a worker thread, deliver results back to the UI thread as a queued event (lesson 23.4). The UI thread now only does UI work. No more hitch.

4 · Guard it

Add an automated scroll test that records present timestamps and fails CI if missed vsyncs or the worst gap exceed budget. Track p99 and worst frame time, not average fps.

15

16
  r.frames = static_cast<int>(present_us.size());
17
  if (present_us.size() < 2 || refresh_hz <= 0) return r;
18
  const double period_us = 1e6 / refresh_hz;
19
  std::vector<double> gaps;
20

21
    double gap = static_cast<double>(present_us[i] - present_us[i - 1]);
22
    gaps.push_back(gap / 1000.0);
23
    long periods = std::lround(gap / period_us);
24
    if (periods > 1) r.missed_vsyncs += static_cast<int>(periods - 1);
25

26
  r.worst_ms = *std::max_element(gaps.begin(), gaps.end());
27
  std::sort(gaps.begin(), gaps.end());
28
  std::size_t idx = static_cast<std::size_t>(std::ceil(0.99 * gaps.size())) - 1;
29
  r.p99_ms = gaps[std::min(idx, gaps.size() - 1)];
30
  return r;
31
}

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A car screen must show certain things very quickly after starting, especially the backup camera. A full computer system can't boot that fast, so engineers start the important parts first, keep the system half-asleep when parked, and delay everything else.

FMVSS 111
US federal motor vehicle safety standard for rear visibility; sets a 2.0 s limit for showing the rear-view image.
Power moding
Managing the system's power states (off, standby, on) in step with the vehicle's states.
Suspend-to-RAM
A sleep state that keeps memory powered so the system resumes in about a second.
Critical path
The longest chain of dependent steps that decides when a goal can be reached.
Staged startup
Starting the system in priority order rather than all at once.
Lazy loading
Loading a feature only when it's first needed.
Early camera path
Showing the camera before the main OS is up, using the bootloader, an RTOS or a hypervisor guest.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

When you open a car door or press start, the infotainment system must come alive fast, and some features have hard limits. US rule FMVSS 111 requires the rear-view camera image to be shown within 2.0 seconds of the start of a backing event (the driver selecting reverse). Automakers design every startup path, including right after the car wakes, around that limit. A full Linux or Android system can take 10–30 s to boot, so engineers use power moding and staged startup. The vehicle has power modes (off, accessory, run, crank), and the head unit has its own states (off, suspend-to-RAM, running). Suspend-to-RAM resumes in about a second, but costs standby battery drain, so it has time limits. For cold boots, the critical path is shortened: an early-boot rear-camera path in the bootloader, a small RTOS, or a hypervisor guest; parallel service start; lazy loading of non-essential apps; precompiled QML and shaders; and a splash screen. The skill is finding the true critical path (the longest chain of dependent steps to a goal), not just making everything a bit faster.

MAKE IT STICK

Opening a shop in the morning. The fire exit sign must be lit within seconds of the door opening. Everything else (the coffee machine, the music, restocking shelves) can follow. You plan the opening so the exit sign doesn't wait for the coffee.

A new head unit shows the rear camera in 0.9 s from suspend-to-RAM, but after a long park (when the system falls back to a full cold boot to save battery), it takes 2.4 s. The limit is 2.0 s.

1 · Build the task graph

From boot traces: bootloader 300 ms, kernel 700 ms, camera driver 250 ms, display driver 200 ms, compositor 400 ms, camera app 500 ms. The camera app waits for the compositor, which waits for the display driver and the kernel.

2 · Find the critical path

The path is bootloader → kernel → display → compositor → camera app = 2.1 s, plus the camera stream start. The camera driver isn't on the critical path; making it faster changes nothing.

3 · Shorten the right links

Options: show the camera on a hardware overlay plane directly from a small early service, skipping the full compositor; trim the kernel (built-in drivers, no unused probing); start the camera stream in parallel with the compositor.

4 · Prove it at the limits

Measure across 1,000 cold boots, at cold temperature and with a weak battery, and report the worst case. Add a power-moding test: suspend expiry → cold boot → reverse. The requirement is a worst case, not an average.

std::vector<int> earliest_finish(const std::vector<Task> &t) {
13
  std::vector<int> fin(t.size(), 0);
14
  for (std::size_t i = 0; i < t.size(); ++i) {
15
    int start = 0;
16

18

23
std::vector<int> critical_path(const std::vector<Task> &t, int goal) {
24
  auto fin = earliest_finish(t);
25
  std::vector<int> path;
26
  for (int cur = goal; cur >= 0; ) {
27
    path.push_back(cur);
28

29
    for (int d : t[static_cast<std::size_t>(cur)].deps)
30

31
    cur = next;
32
  }
33
  std::reverse(path.begin(), path.end());
34
  return path;
35

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Car screens show information sent by other computers in the vehicle over in-car networks. Each message is packed tightly and must be unpacked with a description file. The screen must update at a sensible rate, and must show clearly when information stops arriving.

ECU
Electronic control unit: one of the many computers in a vehicle.
CAN / CAN FD
Controller Area Network, the classic in-vehicle bus; FD allows larger, faster frames.
DBC file
A text database describing CAN messages and how to decode each signal.
Scale and offset
Physical value = raw value × factor + offset.
SOME/IP
Scalable service-Oriented MiddlewarE over IP: automotive service protocol over Ethernet.
VHAL
Android Automotive's Vehicle Hardware Abstraction Layer, exposing vehicle properties to apps.
VSS
COVESA Vehicle Signal Specification: a standard tree of signal names like Vehicle.Speed.
Staleness
When a value is too old to trust because updates stopped.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Infotainment screens show data that comes from other computers in the car (ECUs): speed, gear, door state, battery level. Classic transport is CAN: short frames (8 bytes; up to 64 with CAN FD) identified by an ID, with signals packed as bit fields. A DBC file describes each signal: start bit, length, byte order, scale and offset (physical = raw × factor + offset), units and range. Newer cars add Ethernet with SOME/IP, a service-oriented protocol with events, methods and fields. On the head unit, a vehicle abstraction layer (Android's VHAL, or a service built on the COVESA VSS signal catalogue) turns these into named properties like Vehicle.Speed. UI code must handle signal rates (some arrive 100 times a second; screens need about 30 updates a second at most), staleness (a signal that stops arriving must show as unknown, not freeze on the last value), invalid or out-of-range values, and units. Updating UI on every message wastes CPU; updating too rarely makes gauges look laggy.

MAKE IT STICK

A newsroom receiving reports from many correspondents. Each report is in a compact code that needs a decoding sheet (the DBC). Some correspondents send updates constantly; the TV screen only needs refreshing a few times a second. If a correspondent goes silent, the screen must say 'no update', not keep showing yesterday's news as live.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The fuel gauge froze, and nobody noticed

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

One thread runs the user interface and must never wait on slow work. Slow jobs run on helper threads, which send their results back as messages to the interface thread. Tools then check for crashes, races between threads, and memory that slowly leaks during a long drive.

UI thread
The single thread that owns UI objects and handles input and drawing.
Event loop
A loop that takes queued events and runs their handlers one at a time.
Worker thread
A thread for slow work, so the UI thread stays responsive.
Queued connection
Qt's way of delivering a signal by posting it to the receiver thread's event loop.
IPC
Inter-process communication, such as D-Bus, Binder or QNX message passing.
Valgrind / ASan / TSan
Tools for memory errors and leaks, address bugs, and data races.
Static analysis
Tools that find defects by examining code without running it (Coverity, Parasoft, clang-tidy).
MISRA C++
A coding standard for safety-related C++ in vehicles.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

UI frameworks (Qt, Android, browsers) have one UI thread (in Qt, the main or GUI thread) that owns UI objects. Only it may touch them, and it must stay free to handle input and frames. Slow work (IPC calls, file I/O, decoding images, parsing) runs on worker threads, which hand results back by posting an event to the UI thread's event loop. In Qt this is a queued connection: emitting a signal from a worker to a UI object queues the call on the UI thread. In QML, C++ models (QAbstractListModel) expose data to the UI, and must emit change notifications from the UI thread. IPC between processes (D-Bus, Binder, QNX messages, gRPC, or SOME/IP) should be asynchronous from the UI's point of view. Memory problems show up as slow growth over long drives: tools include Valgrind (memcheck, massif), AddressSanitizer and heaptrack. ThreadSanitizer finds data races, and GDB handles crashes and core dumps. Static analysis (Coverity, Parasoft, SonarQube, clang-tidy) with coding standards like MISRA C++ or AUTOSAR C++14 catches defects before testing.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant host at the door (the UI thread) greets every guest promptly. If the host goes to the kitchen to cook (slow work), the queue at the door stops moving. Cooks (workers) prepare dishes and put them on the pass (the event queue); the host only carries them out.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The media app crashes after 3 hours of driving

A Qt/QML media app occasionally crashes on long drives. Crash dumps point to different places each time inside the album-art list model. Memory use also creeps up by about 80 MB per hour.

1 · Random crash sites suggest a race

A TSan build in the lab reports a data race: a worker thread decoding album art writes directly into the list model's data while the UI thread reads it to draw. Qt models must only be changed from the UI thread.

2 · Fix with posting

The worker decodes, then posts the finished image to the UI thread (a queued signal in Qt, or the UiQueue pattern). The UI thread updates the model and emits dataChanged. TSan is now clean.

3 · Find the leak

heaptrack shows decoded images cached by URL with no limit. Each new streaming track adds one. A size-bounded cache (an LRU with a byte limit) flattens memory use.

4 · Keep it fixed

TSan and ASan builds run in CI on UI tests. A 12-hour soak test records memory and fails on growth. Static analysis rules flag model writes outside the UI thread.

Requirements, availability math and architecture decisions for robot fleets
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Apptronik · Staff Systems Engineer, Robot-as-a-Service Platform (Austin)
Named: define functional and non-functional requirements; capture constraints (latency, availability, security, data ownership, failure semantics); write clear design docs.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Before building a robot service, write down exactly what it must do and how reliable, fast and secure it must be. Reliability can be calculated: parts that all must work make the whole less reliable, and backups make it more reliable. Designing robots to keep working when the internet drops is often the biggest improvement.

RaaS
Robot-as-a-Service: customers pay for robot work or uptime instead of buying robots.
Functional requirement
What the system must do.
Non-functional requirement
How well it must do it: latency, availability, security, cost.
Availability
The fraction of time a service works, e.g. 99.9%.
SLO / error budget
A reliability target, and the downtime it allows (43 min/month at 99.9%).
Failure semantics
What a component does when something it depends on fails.
Data ownership
Who controls data and where it may be stored or sent.
ADR
Architecture decision record: a short document of a decision, its options and why.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS) means customers pay for robot work (hours, tasks, uptime) rather than buying robots, so the vendor owns uptime. A platform for it starts with requirements. Functional ones say what it does: dispatch tasks, stream telemetry, update software, report usage for billing. Non-functional ones say how well: latency (a stop command reaches the robot within 100 ms on site), availability (the customer's robots can keep working 99.9% of shift hours), security, data ownership (camera data from a customer's site may not leave it without consent), and failure semantics (what each part does when another fails). Availability is a number you can calculate. Parts in series (all needed) multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 = 0.998. Redundant parts in parallel fail only if all fail: 1 − (1 − 0.99)² = 0.9999. A 99.9% SLO allows about 43 minutes of downtime per 30-day month: the error budget. The biggest win usually comes from removing hard dependencies: if robots keep working safely when the cloud is down (local autonomy), cloud availability drops out of the series chain. Decisions and their reasons go into short architecture decision records (ADRs).

MAKE IT STICK

A delivery company promising 'parcels arrive on time 99.9% of days'. If each day needs the truck, the driver and the depot all working, each must be far better than 99.9%. Giving drivers a backup route when the depot is down removes the depot from the chain.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 99.9% promise that couldn't be kept

Sales wants to promise RaaS customers 99.9% robot availability during shifts. The first design has each robot call the cloud for every task assignment. Measured: robot hardware 99.95%, site Wi-Fi 99.5%, site gateway 99.8%, internet link 99.7%, cloud task service 99.95%.

1 · Do the math

In series: 0.9995 × 0.995 × 0.998 × 0.997 × 0.9995 ≈ 0.989. That's about 8 hours of lost work per month, not 43 minutes. The design can't meet the promise.

2 · Remove hard dependencies

Give the site gateway a task queue for the next few hours of work. Robots keep working when the internet or cloud is down. Now the internet and cloud mostly drop out of the chain.

3 · Add redundancy where it pays

Two gateways with automatic failover (two 99.8% units ≈ 99.9996%), and Wi-Fi roaming between two access points. New estimate: about 99.9%, inside the promise with a small margin.

4 · Write it down

An ADR records the options (cloud-dependent, edge queue, fully autonomous robots), the decision (edge queue with 4-hour autonomy), the reasons and the risks (queue staleness, conflicting edits when reconnecting). Requirements list the failure semantics for each part.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Robots, customer systems and dashboards talk to the platform through defined interfaces. Messages can be repeated when networks are flaky, so each command carries a unique key and is only carried out once. Robots run different software versions at the same time, so interfaces must stay compatible.

API contract
The agreed format and behaviour of an interface: messages, states, errors and timing.
Idempotent
Repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once.
Idempotency key
A unique ID per command, so duplicates can be recognised.
Semantic versioning
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: major means breaking, minor adds features compatibly, patch fixes bugs.
Backward compatible
New versions still accept and correctly handle messages from old versions.
Version skew
Different parts of a system running different versions at the same time.
Schema
A machine-readable definition of message formats, such as Protobuf.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A RaaS platform has three kinds of API. Robot-facing APIs carry commands and telemetry between cloud or site and robots. Integration APIs let customers' warehouse or factory systems submit work. Operator-facing APIs drive dashboards and teleoperation. Good contracts share rules. Commands are idempotent when repeated delivery has the same effect as one: each command carries a unique idempotency key, and the robot remembers recent keys, so a retry after a timeout can't make it do the task twice. Commands have explicit states (accepted, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled) and deadlines. Versioning follows semantic versioning and backward-compatible changes: add optional fields, never remove or repurpose them. Robots in a fleet run different software versions for weeks during rollouts, so servers must handle version skew: each side advertises a version and supported features, and both use the highest common one. Schemas (Protobuf, JSON Schema) with compatibility checks in CI catch breaking changes before release.

MAKE IT STICK

Ordering food by phone when the line keeps dropping. If you give an order number each time, the restaurant knows a repeat call is the same order, not a second one. And if the menu changes, old menus still work for a while.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The robot moved the same pallet twice

During a Wi-Fi dropout, the cloud sent 'move pallet P-112 to dock 3' to a robot. The robot started, but the acknowledgement was lost. The cloud timed out and resent. The robot treated it as a new task and moved a second pallet it believed was P-112's replacement.

1 · At-least-once delivery is normal

Networks lose replies. Retrying is correct; doing the work twice is not. The contract was missing an idempotency key.

2 · Add keys and states

Each command now carries a UUID created once by the sender and reused on retries. The robot remembers recent keys and returns the existing state for duplicates. The cloud can query a command's state instead of guessing.

3 · The rollout reveals skew

Half the fleet gets the new firmware first. Old robots ignore the new key field. The cloud checks each robot's advertised version and features, and only relies on idempotency for robots that support it; for old ones it queries state before retrying.

4 · Guard the contract

Protobuf schemas live in one repository; CI runs a breaking-change check. Integration tests replay lost-reply and duplicate scenarios against every supported robot version.

Edge and cloud: store-and-forward, MQTT QoS, the outbox pattern and consistency
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

NVIDIA · Senior Solution Engineer, Networking (Austin)

1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Robots often lose their internet connection. They keep working and save outgoing messages locally, sending them when the connection returns. Important messages are never thrown away; less important ones can be when space runs out. Messages are numbered so repeats are ignored.

Edge
Computing on or near the robots, on the customer's site.
Store-and-forward
Saving messages locally and sending them when the connection returns.
MQTT
A lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol common in IoT and robotics.
QoS 0 / 1 / 2
MQTT delivery levels: at most once, at least once, exactly once (to the broker).
Transactional outbox
Saving a state change and its outgoing event in one transaction, then publishing from that table.
Network partition
When parts of a system can't talk to each other.
CAP theorem
During a partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability.
Reconciliation
Merging local and cloud state after reconnecting.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Robots live at the edge: on customer sites with Wi-Fi gaps and internet links that drop. The platform must keep working through that. Store-and-forward means robots and site gateways write outgoing data to a local, durable queue and send it when the link returns. Queues need limits and priorities: safety events and billing records must never be dropped; high-rate telemetry can be thinned when the buffer fills. Messaging often uses MQTT, a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol with three QoS levels: 0 (at most once, may lose), 1 (at least once, may duplicate, so receivers must be idempotent), and 2 (exactly once between client and broker, slower). The transactional outbox pattern avoids losing or duplicating events when a service updates its database and publishes a message: write both the state change and the outgoing event in one local transaction, and a separate relay publishes from the outbox table. When the site is cut off, the system must choose: keep working on local data (availability) and reconcile later, or stop until it can confirm with the cloud (consistency). The CAP theorem says during a network partition you can't have both. RaaS sites usually choose availability for work and consistency for things like billing totals and safety configuration.

MAKE IT STICK

A field reporter with no signal writes stories in a notebook and files them when back in range: urgent ones first. If the notebook fills, they cut the weather notes, never the breaking news. Each story is numbered, so the editor doesn't print one twice.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A 6-hour internet outage at a customer warehouse

A construction crew cuts the fibre to a warehouse running 40 robots. The site is offline for 6 hours. Customers expect robots to keep working, and the next morning's invoice must be right.

1 · Keep working locally

The site gateway holds the task queue and a copy of the site map and safety configuration. Robots continue their work. Safety configuration can't be changed from the cloud during the outage, by design (consistency for safety settings).

2 · Buffer by priority

Each robot produces 2 MB/min of telemetry. 6 hours × 40 robots × 2 MB/min would be about 29 GB, far more than the gateway's 8 GB buffer. It thins telemetry, keeps all events and every billing record.

3 · Reconnect without a flood

When the link returns, the gateway sends critical records first, then events, then telemetry, rate-limited so it doesn't saturate the link and delay live commands. Sequence numbers let the cloud ignore duplicates from QoS 1 retries.

4 · Reconcile

Task results recorded locally are merged into the cloud's records. Conflicts (a task cancelled in the cloud during the outage but completed on site) follow a rule written in advance: what happened physically wins, and the customer is notified.

Fleet management, data pipelines and security for robots at customer sites
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Apptronik · Staff Systems Engineer, Robot-as-a-Service Platform (Austin)
Named: data pipelines (collection, inference, fleet management), security, and modern C++ multithreading on Linux.
NVIDIA · Senior Solution Engineer, Networking (Austin)

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A robot fleet needs a system that knows each robot's health and location and gives tasks to the best one. It also updates software safely and moves data without breaking customers' privacy rules. Every robot proves its identity, and all software is signed.

Fleet management
Tracking, updating and controlling many robots as one system.
Dispatch
Choosing which robot does which task.
OTA / canary rollout
Over-the-air updates sent to a small group first, then widened if healthy.
Data pipeline
The steps that move data from collection through processing to storage and use.
Edge inference
Running ML models on the robot or site instead of in the cloud.
Mutual TLS (mTLS)
Encrypted connections where both sides prove identity with certificates.
Secure element / TPM
A tamper-resistant chip that stores a device's private keys.
Least privilege
Giving each person or service only the access it needs.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Running robots as a service needs a fleet management layer that keeps track of every robot. It holds an inventory of robots with identity, software version, health and location. Dispatch assigns tasks based on capability, battery and distance. OTA updates roll out in stages (canary robots first, automatic rollback on health regressions), and alerts flag problems. Data pipelines move data from robots for operations, billing and model training: collection on the robot, filtering and inference at the edge or in the cloud, storage and labelling. Where each step runs is a trade-off between latency (stopping for a person must happen on the robot), bandwidth (camera streams can't all go to the cloud), cost, and data ownership (customer video may need to stay on site, or be anonymised first). Security is end to end: each robot has a unique identity (a certificate in a secure element or TPM), all links use mutual TLS, software is signed and verified at boot and on update, operators get least-privilege roles, teleoperation sessions are audited, and secrets never ship in images. Modern C++ services on the robot and gateway use thread pools and lock-free queues for these pipelines.

MAKE IT STICK

Running a taxi company with cars parked at many customers' garages. You need a list of every car and its health, a dispatcher, a way to update all the cars' maps safely, and keys only the right drivers can use. Dash-cam footage is the customer's: it stays in their garage unless they agree.

A new navigation release passed all lab tests. It is scheduled to go to 400 robots across 12 customer sites overnight.

1 · Stage the rollout

Instead of all at once, the release goes to 2% of robots at 3 sites (canaries), chosen to cover different floor types and robot hardware revisions.

2 · Watch health automatically

Canary health metrics are compared with the rest of the fleet: task success, interventions per hour, localisation errors. After 4 hours, interventions are 3× higher at one site with reflective floors.

3 · Roll back and investigate

Automatic rollback restores the previous signed image on the A/B partitions. The pipeline pulls only the relevant anonymised sensor snippets from those robots (the customer's data agreement allows this) for the team to reproduce the issue.

Every image was signed and verified at boot; each robot authenticated with its own certificate; the operator who approved the rollout had rollout rights but not teleoperation rights. Audit logs record every step.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Before choosing new servers, measure what the existing ones really spend their time on. Weight each program by how much of the fleet it uses. Then build small test programs that behave like the big ones, and check that they predict real results.

Fleet
All the servers a company runs, often millions of machines.
Workload characterization
Measuring how programs use the hardware, using the same counters everywhere.
IPC
Instructions per cycle: how much useful work a core does each clock tick.
MPKI
Cache misses per thousand instructions: a common measure of memory pressure.
Front-end bound
The core waits for instructions to arrive, typical of very large code.
Representative benchmark
A small test program whose hardware behaviour matches a real service class.
Fidelity
How closely a benchmark's behaviour matches the real workload it stands for.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A fleet is all the servers a company runs, and the first co-design job is to learn what that fleet actually spends its cycles on. Workload characterization means measuring each big service with the same hardware counters: IPC (instructions per cycle), cache misses per thousand instructions (MPKI), front-end stalls (time waiting for instructions), memory bandwidth, and core count. Weight each service by the cores it uses, because a 2% win on a service using 30% of the fleet beats a 20% win on one using 0.5%. Services cluster into workload classes by their main bottleneck: front-end bound (huge code, like web servers), memory bound (caches, feed ranking), or compute bound (ML inference, compression). A representative benchmark reproduces a class's counter profile closely enough that a result on new hardware predicts the fleet result. Popular suites often don't: they have small code and hot caches, so they flatter wider cores and hide front-end and memory problems. You check a proxy's fidelity by comparing its counter profile with the fleet-weighted profile, and by checking past predictions against what the fleet actually did after deployment.

MAKE IT STICK

Planning a new kitchen by watching what the restaurant actually cooks all week, weighted by how many plates of each, instead of by timing the chef on one fancy dessert.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The benchmark said 25%. The fleet said 6%.

A vendor's next CPU scores 25% higher on a popular compute benchmark. Leadership asks whether to buy it for the whole web tier next year.

1 · Profile the fleet

You pull counters for the top 40 services by cores. The web tier (35% of cores) is front-end bound: 38% of slots wait for instructions. Feed ranking (25%) is memory bound at 14 L2 MPKI. Only 20% of cores look like the benchmark.

2 · Check the proxy

The benchmark's code fits in the instruction cache, so it shows 4% front-end stalls versus the fleet's 27%. Its fidelity error is over 80%. It mostly measures the new core's wider execution, which the web tier can't use.

3 · Build better proxies

You build three proxies, one per class, from replayed production traffic and real binaries. Each lands within 12% of its class profile on every counter. On the new CPU they predict 6% fleet-weighted cores saved.

4 · Turn it into a roadmap ask

The front-end class would gain most from a bigger instruction cache and better branch prediction. You take that data to the vendor, and to the compiler team for code layout optimizations. That is co-design.

LESSON 25.2 · C++17 · TCO, PERF PER TCO, AMDAHL SPEEDUP WITH TRANSFER OVERHEAD, AND AN OFFLOAD DECISION · NEW
Pathfinding: performance, power and total cost models for next-generation platforms
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Meta · Software Engineer, HW/SW Co-Design (Menlo Park)
Named: conduct pathfinding to quantify the value proposition, drive roadmap definition, find HW/SW co-design opportunities, and influence vendor roadmaps.
Google · Staff Software Engineer, AI and Infrastructure (Borglet, Sunnyvale)
Capacity fungibility and GPUs/TPUs in Borg are decided with this kind of cost model.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

To decide on new hardware, compare work done per dollar over its whole life, including electricity and cooling. For a special-purpose chip, only the part of the job it speeds up gets faster. Moving data to it also costs time.

Pathfinding
Studying a future hardware or software option with models before building it.
TCO
Total cost of ownership: purchase price plus power, cooling and operations over the server's life.
PUE
Power usage effectiveness: total data-centre power divided by the power the servers use.
Perf per TCO
Useful work delivered per dollar of total cost, the usual yardstick for platform choices.
Amdahl's law
Overall speedup is limited by the part of the job that is not sped up.
Accelerator / offload
A special-purpose chip that does one kind of work faster than the CPU.
Co-design
Changing hardware and software together so each fits the other.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Pathfinding is answering 'should we build or buy this?' with numbers before anyone builds it. The yardstick is performance per TCO. TCO (total cost of ownership) is purchase price plus power and cooling over the server's life, scaled by PUE (power usage effectiveness: data-centre power divided by server power). A faster chip that burns much more power can lose. For an accelerator or offload, Amdahl's law sets the ceiling: if a function takes a fraction f of the time and gets s times faster, the whole job speeds up 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s). With f = 0.3, even an infinitely fast accelerator gives at most 1.43×. Moving data to the device costs time too, and can erase the gain. Co-design means changing both sides: rewriting software so f grows (batching small calls, changing data layouts) while asking hardware for features that serve the fleet's hot paths. A model is only useful if it is checked: predict, measure on early silicon or a simulator, and correct.

MAKE IT STICK

Deciding whether to buy a dishwasher for a café: it only helps with the share of the night spent washing, it costs electricity, and carrying dishes to it takes time. If washing is 30% of the work, even a magic dishwasher only makes the night 1.43× faster.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The compression accelerator pitch

A vendor pitches a compression accelerator card. In your fleet, the storage service spends 30% of CPU time compressing. The card is 10× faster than a core, adds 15% to server TCO, and data must cross PCIe.

1 · Amdahl first

With f = 0.3 and s = 10, the best case is 1 / (0.7 + 0.03) = 1.37×. Even infinite speed would give 1.43×. That is the ceiling for the whole idea.

2 · Count the data movement

Small 4 KB blocks mean many tiny transfers. Measured transfer overhead is 8% of job time, so the speedup falls to 1.23×. That is still above the 1.15× cost bar, but only just.

3 · Co-design the software

The storage team batches blocks into 1 MB requests. Transfer overhead drops to 2%, and moving checksums onto the card too raises f to 0.4. Speedup is now about 1.52× for 15% more cost: a clear win.

4 · Influence the roadmap

You ask the vendor to build the engine into the next CPU's package, removing the PCIe hop. You show the fleet numbers as evidence. Pathfinding has become a roadmap request.

9
 
10
double tco_usd(const Platform &p, double usd_per_kwh, double pue) {
11
  double hours = p.life_years * 365.0 * 24.0;
12
  double kwh = p.watts / 1000.0 * hours * pue;
13
  return p.capex_usd + kwh * usd_per_kwh;
14

15
 
16

17
  double t = tco_usd(p, usd_per_kwh, pue);
18
  return t > 0 ? p.perf / t : 0.0;
19

// Amdahl: fraction f of time sped up s times, plus a per-job transfer cost.
22
double offload_speedup(double f, double s, double transfer) {
23
  if (s <= 0) return 0.0;
24
  double t = (1.0 - f) + f / s + transfer;
25
  return 1.0 / t;
26
}
27
 
28
// Does adding the accelerator improve perf per TCO?
29
bool offload_pays(double f, double s, double transfer, double base_tco, double added_tco) {
30
  double sp = offload_speedup(f, s, transfer);
31
  return sp / (base_tco + added_tco) > 1.0 / base_tco;
32
}

35
long servers_needed(double demand, double perf_per_server, double target_util) {
36
  if (perf_per_server <= 0 || target_util <= 0) return -1;
37
  return static_cast<long>(std::ceil(demand / (perf_per_server * target_util)));
38
}

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Fast memory is expensive, and cheap storage is slow. Most programs use a small part of their data most of the time. Keep that hot part in fast memory and the rest in cheaper tiers, and the average stays fast.

Tier
One level of memory or storage, with its own speed and cost per byte.
DRAM
The main memory next to the CPU, about 100 nanoseconds per access.
CXL memory
Extra memory attached over a fast link, larger but somewhat slower than local DRAM.
Flash / SSD
Solid-state storage, about 100 microseconds per random read.
HDD
A spinning hard disk, cheapest per terabyte but about 10 milliseconds per random read.
IOPS
Input/output operations per second a drive can serve.
Skew
Uneven access: a small share of data gets most of the requests.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Memory and storage come in tiers: each one down is cheaper per byte but slower. Local DRAM answers in about 100 ns. CXL memory (extra DRAM attached over a PCIe-based link) adds capacity at roughly 200–300 ns. Flash (SSDs) answers in about 100 µs and delivers hundreds of thousands of random reads per second. HDDs (spinning disks) take about 10 ms per random read but are the cheapest per terabyte. Workloads are usually skewed: a small fraction of data gets most accesses. Tiering keeps the hot pages or blocks in the fast tier and the cold ones below, so the average access time stays close to the fast tier while most bytes sit in cheap media. The average is a weighted sum: hits in the fast tier times its latency, plus the rest times the slow latency. Sizing storage has two limits: you need enough drives for the capacity and enough for the IOPS (operations per second). HDDs often run out of IOPS long before capacity, which is why hot data goes on flash.

MAKE IT STICK

A kitchen with a counter, a fridge and a basement pantry. The few things you use constantly sit on the counter. The rest waits further away. As long as the counter holds the right things, cooking stays fast.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

An inference server answers requests by running AI models on GPUs. GPUs are much more efficient with many requests at once. So the server waits a tiny moment to group requests, but never so long that users notice.

Inference server
A program that loads trained models and answers prediction requests over the network.
Model repository
A folder tree holding each model's files, configuration and versions.
Backend
A plug-in that runs models from one framework, such as TensorRT or PyTorch.
Dynamic batching
Merging separate requests that arrive close together into one GPU batch.
Max queue delay
The longest the oldest request may wait for a batch to fill.
Instance group
Several copies of one model running at once, on one or more GPUs.
KServe v2
A standard HTTP/gRPC protocol for inference requests and model metadata.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An inference server loads trained models and answers requests over the network, and its main job is keeping GPUs busy without making users wait. NVIDIA's Triton Inference Server (public docs) shows the standard design. Models live in a model repository: one folder per model, a config.pbtxt describing inputs, outputs and limits, and numbered version folders. Each model runs on a backend, a plug-in library for one framework (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, Python, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM). Clients call HTTP or gRPC endpoints that follow the KServe v2 protocol. The dynamic batcher holds requests for a moment and merges them into one GPU batch, because a batch of 8 often costs barely more than a batch of 1. Two settings control it: the largest batch, and the max queue delay, how long the oldest request may wait for company. Instance groups run several copies of a model on one or more GPUs so one copy can compute while another is loading inputs. Other schedulers handle stateful sequences and ensembles (pipelines of models). Inside, it is a C++ server: thread-safe queues, condition variables, request lifetimes and careful memory reuse.

MAKE IT STICK

A shuttle bus at an airport. It leaves when it's full, or when the first passenger has waited five minutes, whichever comes first. More buses help when the line is long. Each terminal has its own kind of bus.

An image model serves 400 requests per second on one GPU with batching off. Each run takes 8 ms plus 1 ms per image. p99 latency is climbing and GPU utilization looks low.

1 · Find the waste

Without batching, each request costs 9 ms, so one copy handles about 111 per second. Requests queue up even though the GPU's math units sit mostly idle in each tiny run.

2 · Turn on the dynamic batcher

With max batch 16 and a 2 ms max queue delay, batches average about 8. Each costs 16 ms for 8 images, so one copy handles about 500 per second. The queue drains.

3 · Add a second instance

Two instances on the same GPU overlap one batch's input copy with the other's compute. p99 drops again. A third adds nothing, because the GPU is now really busy.

Named: unify Triton and NVIDIA Dynamo for LLM and non-LLM workloads; high-scale distributed systems; Rust; GPU memory and cache management, high-performance networking.

2

3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

An AI chat model first reads your whole message, then writes the answer one word-piece at a time. The two steps need different hardware strengths. Splitting them across machines, and sending repeat conversations back to the machine that remembers them, makes answers start sooner and stream smoothly.

Prefill
Reading the whole prompt in one pass; compute-heavy.
Decode
Generating output one token per step; limited by memory bandwidth.
TTFT
Time to first token: how long until the answer starts.
ITL
Inter-token latency: the gap between streamed tokens.
KV cache
Saved attention state for every earlier token, so it is not recomputed each step.
Disaggregated serving
Running prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and moving the KV cache between them.
KV-aware routing
Sending a request to the worker that already holds the most of its prompt's KV cache.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Serving a large language model has two very different phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt at once; it is compute-heavy and sets TTFT (time to first token). Decode then makes one token per step; it is memory-bandwidth-heavy and sets ITL (inter-token latency, how smoothly text streams). On one GPU they interfere: a long prefill stalls every decode step behind it, so streaming stutters. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and ships the prompt's KV cache between them over fast links, so each pool can be sized and tuned for its own phase. NVIDIA Dynamo (public docs; open source, largely Rust and Python) adds this on top of engines like vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. It also adds a KV-aware router. Prompts that share a beginning (a system prompt, a chat history) produce the same KV blocks. The router hashes the prompt in blocks and sends the request to the worker that already holds the longest matching prefix, balanced against that worker's load. A planner scales each pool to meet TTFT and ITL targets.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant where one cook reads a long order and preps everything (prefill), and another plates one dish at a time (decode). Put them at separate stations and they stop bumping elbows. The host seats returning guests at the table that already has their bread.

INTERACTIVE LAB

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Change prompt length and shared beginnings, then try prefix routing, separate GPU pools and chunking against two targets.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Answers start fast, then stutter

A chat service runs prefill and decode together on 8 GPUs. Most prompts share a 4,000-token system prompt plus chat history. Users complain that answers pause mid-sentence, and TTFT is high whenever long documents are pasted in.

1 · Measure both phases

Traces show decode steps normally take 20 ms. But whenever a 16k-token prefill lands on the same GPU, steps behind it wait about 1.6 s. That is the stutter.

2 · Route by prefix

Requests were spread round-robin, so the shared system prompt was recomputed on 7 of 8 GPUs. A KV-aware router sends each conversation to the worker holding its prefix. Prefill work falls by more than half.

3 · Disaggregate

Two GPUs become a prefill pool, six do decode. Long uncached prompts go to the prefill pool and their KV cache is copied over the fast GPU network (about 40 ms for 8k tokens). Decode steps stay near 22 ms.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Each conversation keeps a memory of earlier words on the GPU, and that memory fills up fast. Storing it in small equal pieces, sharing identical pieces between conversations, and reusing the oldest unused pieces lets one GPU serve far more people.

Paged KV cache
Storing attention state in fixed-size blocks instead of one big slab per request.
Block table
A request's list of which blocks hold its tokens, in order.
Reference count
How many running requests are using a block right now.
Prefix sharing
Several requests with the same beginning use the same cached blocks.
LRU eviction
Reusing the least recently used free block first when memory runs out.
Preemption
Pausing a running request and freeing its memory so others can proceed.
Offload
Moving cold blocks to CPU memory or SSD to reload later instead of recomputing.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Saved memory for past tokens is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve. Its size per token is 2 (keys and values) × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes per number: about 128 KiB per token for an 8-billion-parameter model in 16-bit numbers. Reserving one contiguous slab per request for the maximum length wastes most of it, because few requests reach the limit. Paged KV caches (popularized by vLLM's PagedAttention) split it into fixed-size blocks of, say, 16 tokens, like virtual-memory pages. A request holds a block table of block numbers and grows one block at a time, so waste is at most one partly filled block. Blocks with identical content can be shared: requests with the same prefix point at the same blocks, tracked with reference counts. When a request finishes, its blocks can stay cached for future prefix hits and are only reused when memory runs short, oldest first (LRU eviction). If every block belongs to a running request, the server must queue new work or preempt a request. Systems such as Dynamo's KV block manager also offload cold blocks to CPU memory or SSD so they can be reloaded instead of recomputed.

MAKE IT STICK

A parking garage with numbered spaces instead of a reserved row per company. Cars take spaces as they arrive. Carpools share one space. When the garage is full, the oldest unattended car gets towed to the overflow lot.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
40 GB of KV memory, 9 users

A team reserves KV memory for the full 32k-token context per request: 32,768 × 128 KiB = 4 GiB each. With 40 GB free on the GPU, only 9 users fit, though the average conversation is 2,000 tokens.

1 · Page it

With 16-token blocks, a 2,000-token conversation needs 125 blocks, about 250 MB. The same memory now holds around 150 conversations, with at most 15 tokens wasted per request.

2 · Share prefixes

Every request starts with the same 1,500-token system prompt. Sharing those blocks with reference counts means they're stored once, not 150 times. Capacity roughly quadruples again.

3 · Keep finished blocks

When conversations pause, their blocks stay cached on the LRU list. When the user replies, most blocks are still there, so the history isn't prefilled again.

4 · Plan for full

Under a spike, every block is in use. The scheduler stops admitting new requests and preempts the newest one, offloading its blocks to CPU memory to resume later. No crash, no out-of-memory error.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Rust is a systems language that stops whole kinds of crashes before the program ever runs. Each piece of data has one owner. Others may borrow it to read, or one may borrow it to change, and the compiler checks the rules.

Ownership
Each value has one owner; it is freed automatically when the owner goes away.
Move
Passing a value transfers ownership; the old variable can't be used afterward.
Borrow
Lending a reference: many read-only (&T) or one mutable (&mut T), not both.
Borrow checker
The part of the compiler that proves borrows never outlive or conflict with owners.
Send / Sync
Marker traits: Send can move to another thread; Sync can be shared between threads.
Arc<Mutex<T>>
A thread-safe shared pointer to data protected by a lock.
unsafe
A block where the programmer, not the compiler, guarantees memory safety.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Rust gives C++-level control without a garbage collector, and the compiler proves memory safety and freedom from data races. Three rules do most of the work. Ownership: every value has exactly one owner, and the value is freed when the owner goes out of scope, like C++ RAII with std::unique_ptr, but enforced. Assigning or passing a value moves it, and the old name can no longer be used. Borrowing: you can lend a value as many shared references (&T, read-only) or exactly one mutable reference (&mut T), never both at once. The borrow checker checks this at compile time, so dangling pointers and iterator invalidation become compile errors. For threads, two marker traits decide what is allowed. Send means a value may move to another thread, and Sync means it may be shared by reference between threads. Rc (a non-atomic shared pointer) is neither, so sharing it across threads won't compile. Arc is the atomic version. To mutate shared data, you wrap it: Arc<Mutex<T>>. Channels (mpsc) move ownership of messages between threads. unsafe blocks switch off some checks for FFI and low-level code, and must be small and justified.

MAKE IT STICK

A library book: one person owns it. You can let several friends read it at once, or let one friend write notes in it, but not both at the same time. The librarian (the compiler) checks every loan before you leave.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The race that couldn't compile

A C++ engineer ports a request router to Rust. Their first version shares a counter between threads with a plain pointer, as they would in C++.

1 · The compiler says no

Sharing Rc<RefCell<Stats>> with a spawned thread fails: Rc isn't Send. In C++ this would have compiled and lost counts under load.

2 · Pick the right wrapper

Switching to Arc<Mutex<Stats>> compiles. Arc's count is atomic, and the Mutex makes changes one at a time. The type now documents the threading design.

3 · Ownership through channels

Requests move into a channel. After tx.send(r), using r is a compile error, so no thread can touch a request after handing it off. That rules out a whole class of use-after-free bugs.

4 · Keep unsafe tiny

The CUDA bindings need unsafe for FFI calls. The team wraps them in a small safe module with documented rules, and the rest of the router has no unsafe at all.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Go makes it easy to run many tasks at once, and just as easy to run too many or leave some stuck forever. Cap how many run together, stop all of them when one fails, and let slow steps slow down fast ones.

Goroutine
A lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime.
Semaphore
A counter that limits how many tasks run at once; in Go, often a buffered channel.
Context
A value carrying a deadline and cancellation signal through a call tree.
Goroutine leak
A goroutine blocked forever, holding memory and never finishing.
Backpressure
A slow consumer slows the producer instead of letting a queue grow without limit.
Race detector
go test -race: finds unsynchronized access to the same memory from two goroutines.
pprof
Go's profiler for CPU, memory, goroutines and blocking.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Chapter 2 introduced goroutines, channels and context. Production services need a few patterns on top. Bounded parallelism: never start one goroutine per item for a million items. Use a semaphore (a buffered channel of size N) or a fixed worker pool, so memory and downstream load stay capped. Cancel on first error: when one part of a fan-out fails, cancel the shared context so the others stop early (the pattern the errgroup package provides). Each goroutine writes only its own slot of a results slice, so no lock is needed. Goroutine leaks happen when a goroutine blocks forever on a channel nobody reads. Every blocking send or receive in a long-lived goroutine should select on ctx.Done() too. Backpressure means a slow consumer slows the producer through a bounded channel, instead of letting a queue grow until memory runs out. Prove it with tools: `go test -race` runs the race detector, which reports two goroutines touching the same memory without synchronization. pprof shows goroutine counts, CPU and heap, so a leak shows up as a goroutine count that only grows.

MAKE IT STICK

A kitchen with exactly four burners (the bound). If one dish burns, the head chef shouts 'stop' and everyone turns off their burner (cancellation). Waiters only bring new orders when a burner frees up (backpressure).

Kubernetes operators in Go: reconcile loops, work queues, finalizers and storage drivers
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
NVIDIA · Senior Distributed Software Engineer, Golang, DGX Cloud (Santa Clara)
Named: Go programs deployed to Kubernetes; automate the distributed storage service end to end (deployment, management, monitoring); Kubernetes and cloud provider integrations.
Google · Staff Software Engineer, AI and Infrastructure (Borglet, Sunnyvale)

1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2

3

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

An operator is a program that keeps a service in the state you asked for. It compares what you want with what exists, makes one fix at a time, and repeats. Because it always looks at the current state, missed events and restarts don't break it.

Operator
A program that automates running a complex service on Kubernetes.
Custom resource
A new Kubernetes object type, such as Volume, that describes what you want.
Reconcile
Compare desired with actual state and take a step toward desired.
Level-triggered
Acting on the full current state, not on individual change events.
Work queue
A queue of object keys to reconcile, with duplicate removal and retry backoff.
Finalizer
A marker that delays an object's deletion until cleanup has finished.
CSI
Container Storage Interface: the plug-in standard for creating and mounting volumes.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An operator is a program that runs a complex service on Kubernetes the way a skilled human operator would. You describe the service with a custom resource (CR): a YAML object such as kind: Volume with a spec like 'three replicas of 100 GiB'. A controller watches those objects through informers (cached watches on the API server) and puts changed object keys on a work queue. Worker goroutines take keys and call Reconcile, which compares the desired spec with the actual state, takes a step toward it, and writes the result to the object's status. Reconcile is level-triggered: it looks at the whole current state, not at which event happened, so it is safe to run repeatedly and it heals after missed events or crashes. The queue removes duplicate keys and retries failures with exponential backoff. Finalizers block deletion until cleanup is done, for example deleting the replicas on storage nodes. observedGeneration in the status tells users which spec version the controller has acted on. For storage, the CSI (Container Storage Interface) driver is the plug-in that creates, attaches and mounts volumes for pods.

MAKE IT STICK

A thermostat that doesn't care how the room got cold. Every few seconds it compares the target with the actual temperature and nudges the heater. If it misses a reading, the next one fixes things anyway.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The volume that wouldn't die, and the one that leaked

A storage team's first operator reacted to events: 'on create, make 3 replicas; on delete, remove them'. After a controller restart during a burst of changes, some volumes had 2 replicas forever, and deleted volumes left data on storage nodes.

1 · Make it level-triggered

The rewrite reads the actual replica count every pass and takes one step toward the spec. Missed events no longer matter: the next resync fixes any drift.

2 · Add a finalizer first

Deleting a Volume now waits until the operator has removed every replica, and only then drops its finalizer. Orphaned data stops appearing.

3 · Back off failures

When a storage node is down, Reconcile fails and the key comes back after 5 ms, 10 ms, 20 ms and so on. A broken node can't make the operator spin the CPU.

4 · Report honestly

Status shows ReadyReplicas, Phase and observedGeneration. Users and automation can tell whether the operator has seen the latest spec yet.

Designing a distributed storage service: chunks, placement, replication vs erasure coding, durability
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
NVIDIA · Senior Distributed Software Engineer, Golang, DGX Cloud (Santa Clara)
Named: lead the architecture of a distributed storage service optimized for AI/ML; availability and reliability for large-scale deployments; multi-petabyte to exabyte clusters.
LinkedIn · Staff Software Engineer, Systems and Infrastructure (Mountain View)
Distributed data storage and storage systems are core to the role.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2

3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Big storage systems cut files into pieces and spread them over many machines. Copies must sit in different racks so one failure can't destroy them all. Full copies are simple but costly; coded pieces save space but make repairs heavier.

Chunk
A fixed-size piece of a file, the unit of placement and repair.
Consistent hashing
Placing data on a hash ring so adding a node moves only a small share of data.
Virtual node
One of many ring positions owned by a single real node, to even out load.
Failure domain
A group of machines that can fail together, such as a rack or power feed.
Replication
Storing several full copies of each chunk.
Erasure coding
Storing k data pieces plus m parity pieces; any k rebuild the chunk.
Durability
The chance that stored data is never lost, often quoted as a number of nines per year.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A distributed storage service splits files into chunks (often 4–64 MB) and spreads them across many storage nodes. It keeps a separate metadata service that maps file names to chunks and chunks to nodes. Placement decides where each chunk lives. Consistent hashing puts nodes on a hash ring, with many virtual nodes each, so load stays fairly even and adding a node moves only about 1/N of the data. Copies must land in different failure domains (racks, power feeds, zones), because one rack switch failing must not take out every copy. Redundancy comes in two kinds. Replication stores 3 full copies: simple and fast to read and repair, at 3× the storage. Erasure coding (EC) splits data into k pieces plus m parity pieces, for example 10+4. Any 10 of the 14 rebuild the data, so it survives 4 losses at only 1.4× storage, but repairs read from many nodes. Durability depends on how fast you repair: data is lost only if enough pieces fail within one repair window. Faster repair, spreading repair work across many nodes, and more parity all cut loss. Many systems keep hot data replicated and move cold data to EC.

Keeping important papers: three photocopies in three different buildings, or a puzzle cut into 14 pieces in 14 buildings where any 10 pieces rebuild it. The puzzle uses less paper but takes more trips to rebuild.
