START WITH THE INCIDENT
One rack switch, 0.3% of the data gone

An early AI-dataset store placed 3 replicas by plain hashing over 600 nodes in 20 racks. A rack's top switch failed during a firmware update. Some chunks became unreadable, and the bill for 3× storage was growing fast.

1 · Spread across failure domains

Plain hashing sometimes put 2 or 3 copies in one rack. Rack-aware placement on a consistent-hash ring guarantees 3 different racks. A whole rack failing now loses no data.

2 · Even out load

With 1 ring point per node, some nodes held 3× the average. With 150 virtual nodes each, the fullest node is within about 20% of the mean. Adding 60 nodes moved only about 9% of chunks.

3 · Code the cold data

Training datasets older than 30 days move to 10+4 erasure coding: 1.4× instead of 3×. That frees more than half the raw capacity. Hot data stays replicated for fast reads and cheap repair.

4 · Repair fast

Repair work is spread across all nodes, so a failed 20 TB disk is rebuilt in about 1 hour instead of 1 day. Estimated yearly loss for each group falls by orders of magnitude.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A partitioned log is a set of ordered lists of events that many programs can read at their own pace. Events with the same key stay in order. Readers note how far they got, so after a crash they resume, and the output is built so repeats don't count twice.

Partition
One ordered, append-only list within a topic.
Offset
A record's position in its partition.
Key
The value that picks a record's partition, keeping related events in order.
Consumer group
Readers sharing a topic; each partition goes to exactly one of them.
Commit
Saving how far a consumer has processed, so it can resume after a crash.
At-least-once
Nothing is lost, but some records may be processed more than once.
Idempotent
Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A partitioned log is the backbone of streaming platforms such as Apache Kafka, which began at LinkedIn. A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an append-only, ordered list of records, and each record gets an offset, its position in that list. Producers choose the partition from the record's key, so every event for one member or one order lands in the same partition and stays in order. Order is guaranteed only within a partition, not across the topic. Readers form a consumer group: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, so adding consumers (up to the partition count) adds parallelism. A consumer remembers progress by committing offsets. If it commits only after processing, a crash means some records are processed again: at-least-once delivery. If it commits before processing, a crash loses records: at-most-once. Exactly-once results come from making the effect idempotent (write with a unique key, so a repeat does nothing) or from transactions that commit output and offsets together. Partitions are replicated across brokers, with a leader and in-sync followers, so a broker failure doesn't lose acknowledged writes.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Members were notified twice, and some events arrived out of order

A notification pipeline reads member events from a 12-partition topic. After a deploy, some members got the same notification twice, and some saw 'connection accepted' before 'connection requested'.

1 · Fix the order

Producers keyed events by a random request ID, scattering one member's events across partitions. Keying by member ID puts them in one partition, where order holds.

2 · Explain the duplicates

Consumers commit after processing. The deploy killed them mid-batch, so up to 500 records per partition were reprocessed. That's at-least-once working as designed.

3 · Make the effect idempotent

The notification store now uses partition plus offset as a unique key. Replays become no-ops. Members see each notification once, and nothing is lost.

4 · Scale the group

Lag grows at peak. Adding consumers up to 12 helps, but a 13th would sit idle. The team raises the partition count for the next topic version and plans the key remapping.

Stream processing: event time, watermarks, windows, state and checkpoints
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Streaming jobs count things as events flow in. Events can arrive late, so count them by when they happened, not when they arrived. Wait a set time for stragglers, then close each time slot and publish its total.

Event time
When the event actually happened, stamped at the source.
Processing time
When the server processes the event.
Window
A group of events by time, such as one minute.
Watermark
A claim that no events older than a given time are still coming.
Allowed lateness
How long the processor waits for late events before closing a window.
State
Running values, such as counts per key, that the processor keeps between events.
Checkpoint
A consistent snapshot of all state plus input positions, used to recover from crashes.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A stream processor (Apache Flink is one) keeps updating results over endless event streams, for example 'profile views per member per minute'. Two clocks matter. Event time is when something happened on the device. Processing time is when the server sees it. Mobile events can arrive minutes late, so correct results need event time. A window groups events by event time. A tumbling window is a fixed, non-overlapping slice, such as each minute. But when is a minute complete? A watermark is the processor's claim that no more events older than time T will arrive. A simple one is the largest event time seen minus an allowed lateness. When the watermark passes a window's end, the window fires and its result is emitted. Events arriving after that are late: they are dropped, sent to a side output, or used to update the result. Per-key running totals are state, kept by the processor. Checkpoints periodically snapshot all state together with the input offsets. After a crash, the job restores the snapshot and rewinds the input to match, so results come out as if nothing failed.

MAKE IT STICK

Counting votes by the day they were cast, not the day they arrived. You wait a few extra days for postal ballots (allowed lateness), then declare each day's count final. Ballots arriving after that go to a 'late' pile.

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Trade waiting time against dropped stragglers, and see what a quiet input does to the watermark.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The dashboard that undercounted mobile users

A 'views per minute' dashboard grouped events by server arrival time. Mobile apps batch events and send them when the phone wakes, so mobile minutes looked 30% low and evening peaks appeared shifted.

1 · Switch to event time

Grouping by the device's timestamp puts each view in the minute it happened. The peaks line up with reality.

2 · Pick a watermark

Arrival-delay data shows 99.5% of events arrive within 2 minutes. Allowed lateness is set to 2 minutes, so each minute's count is final about 3 minutes after it starts.

3 · Handle stragglers

The 0.5% later than that go to a side output. A nightly batch job corrects stored totals, and the dashboard notes that recent minutes may still change slightly.

4 · Survive restarts

Checkpoints every 30 seconds save window state with the input offsets. After a crash, the job restores and replays from those offsets. No minute is double-counted or lost.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Some databases make writing fast by always adding new records instead of changing old ones. They tidy up in the background. Small summaries of each file let reads skip files that can't hold the answer.

LSM tree
A storage design that buffers writes in memory, then writes sorted immutable files.
Memtable
The in-memory sorted buffer that receives new writes.
SSTable
An immutable sorted file of keys and values on disk.
Tombstone
A marker that records a delete until compaction removes the old data.
Bloom filter
A compact bit array that says a key is definitely absent or maybe present.
Compaction
Merging files to remove old versions and deleted keys.
Write amplification
Bytes written to disk for each byte the user wrote.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Databases with many writes often keep data in sorted layers that get merged over time. This design is a log-structured merge tree (LSM tree), used by Cassandra and RocksDB. Writes go to an in-memory sorted memtable (and a write-ahead log for safety). When it fills, it is flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable. Deletes write a tombstone marker instead of erasing. Reads check the memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest, so the newest value wins. Many files make reads slow, so a Bloom filter per file answers 'definitely not here' or 'maybe here' using a few bits per key, letting most reads skip most files. Compaction merges files in the background, keeping only the newest version of each key and dropping tombstones once nothing older can resurface. Every design trades three costs. Write amplification is bytes written to disk per byte the user wrote. Read amplification is files checked per read. Space amplification is stale data kept around. Analytics tables use a related idea one level up. Table formats such as Apache Iceberg keep immutable data files plus metadata snapshots listing which files make up the table. A commit atomically swaps in a new snapshot, which gives readers consistent views and time travel.

MAKE IT STICK

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Reads got slower every hour

A member-settings store on an LSM engine handles 50,000 writes per second. p99 read latency climbs all afternoon. After a mass account cleanup, disk usage didn't go down.

1 · Count the files

Compaction had fallen behind, and reads were checking up to 40 SSTables. The Bloom filters were sized for far fewer keys, so false positives forced real disk reads.

2 · Resize the filters

Building filters at 10 bits per key, sized to each file, cuts false positives to about 1%. Most misses now skip almost every file.

3 · Rebalance compaction

Moving to levelled compaction caps the files checked per read, at the cost of more write amplification. Writes rise from about 3× to about 10×, which the SSDs can sustain.

4 · Understand tombstones

The cleanup wrote millions of tombstones. Space comes back only when compaction reaches the bottom level and drops them along with the old values. The team schedules that compaction overnight.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Each server runs a small manager program that starts tasks and limits how much processor and memory each may use. Linux enforces the limits and reports when tasks are waiting. The manager uses those signals to protect important tasks and squeeze less urgent ones.

Node agent
The program on each machine that runs tasks and enforces their limits (Borglet, kubelet).
cgroup v2
Linux control groups: a tree of groups with files that set and report resource limits.
cpu.max
A hard CPU cap: quota microseconds per period microseconds.
Throttling
Pausing a group that used its CPU quota until the next period starts.
memory.high / memory.max
Soft memory limit that triggers reclaim, and hard limit that triggers the OOM killer.
OOM killer
The kernel routine that ends a process when memory runs out.
PSI
Pressure stall information: share of time tasks waited for CPU, memory or I/O.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Every machine in a cluster runs a manager program called a node agent. Google's is the Borglet; Kubernetes' is the kubelet. It starts and stops tasks, sets their resource limits, watches their health and reports back. The kernel mechanism underneath is cgroup v2: a tree of control groups, one per task, each with files that set limits. cpu.weight shares CPU in proportion when the machine is busy. cpu.max (quota and period, such as 50000 100000 for half a core) is a hard cap: a task that uses its quota early is throttled until the next period, which can add tens of milliseconds of latency. memory.high is a soft limit: above it the kernel reclaims the task's memory aggressively and slows it down. memory.max is the hard limit: past it the kernel's OOM killer ends a process in that group. PSI (pressure stall information, in files like cpu.pressure) reports the share of time tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O. It is a better early warning than usage. Mixing latency-sensitive serving with batch jobs on one machine raises use of the hardware. The agent protects serving tasks by giving them weight and guarantees, letting batch use the slack, and squeezing or evicting batch first when pressure rises.

MAKE IT STICK

START WITH THE INCIDENT
p99 doubled, yet CPU use was only 40%

A search frontend task has cpu.max set to 4 cores. Average CPU use is 40% of that, but p99 latency doubled after batch jobs were added to the same machines.

1 · Look at throttling, not averages

cpu.stat shows nr_throttled climbing. Bursts of requests use the whole 4-core quota in the first 30 ms of each 100 ms period, then the task waits. Average use hides it.

2 · Use weights for sharing

The agent switches serving tasks to high cpu.weight with a generous cap, and gives batch jobs low weight. When serving bursts, the kernel gives it the CPU and batch slows down.

3 · Watch pressure

Memory PSI 'some' crosses 10% on a few machines as a batch job grows. The agent lowers that job's memory.high to force reclaim, and evicts it before serving tasks feel pressure.

4 · Prefer eviction to OOM

When eviction is needed, the agent picks the lowest-priority task most over its request and restarts it elsewhere. The kernel's OOM killer, which might pick a serving process, is never reached.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A cluster scheduler chooses a machine for every task. Packing tasks snugly leaves room for big ones later. Spreading them out leaves headroom but can strand small leftovers. GPU jobs also need their GPUs close together.

Scheduler
The service that decides which machine runs each task.
Bin packing
Fitting tasks of different sizes onto machines with fixed capacity.
Best fit / worst fit
Place where the least room is left, or where the most room is left.
Fragmentation
Free resources split into pieces too small to use.
Preemption
Evicting lower-priority tasks to make room for higher-priority ones.
Topology
How accelerators are connected; GPUs in one fast domain talk much faster.
Capacity planning
Deciding how many machines are needed for future demand plus headroom.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A cluster scheduler decides which machine runs each task. Every task asks for resources (CPU, memory, GPUs) and has a priority. Placing tasks is a bin-packing problem. Best fit puts a task where it leaves the least room, keeping big empty machines for big tasks. Worst fit spreads load and leaves headroom on each machine. Leftover pieces too small for anything useful are fragmentation: the cluster has free resources in total but can't place the next big task. Accelerators add topology. A job needing 4 GPUs runs far faster if all 4 share one fast interconnect domain (NVLink, or a TPU slice), so the scheduler must place it in one domain, not just on one machine. When no machine fits a high-priority task, preemption evicts lower-priority tasks to make room, and batch work restarts elsewhere. Capacity planning sets how many machines to buy. Forecast demand, add headroom for growth, failures (N+1 per failure domain) and maintenance, then remove what overcommit can safely reclaim: tasks rarely use their full request. Google's Borg paper (public, 2015) reports that sharing machines between serving and batch work this way saved many machines.

MAKE IT STICK

Packing a moving truck. Put each box where it fits most snugly and the big empty space stays free for the sofa. Scatter boxes everywhere and there's room in total, but nowhere for the sofa. A sofa that must stay in one piece is like a 4-GPU job that needs one connected group.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
200 free GPUs and nowhere to put a 4-GPU job

A cluster of 100 servers, each with 8 GPUs in two 4-GPU NVLink domains, reports 200 free GPUs. Yet 4-GPU training jobs wait for hours in the queue.

1 · Find the strands

Single-GPU inference tasks were placed by worst fit, one or two per domain across the cluster. stranded_gpus(…, 4) shows 170 of the 200 free GPUs sit in domains with fewer than 4 free.

2 · Pack small tasks

Switching small GPU tasks to best fit, at both the machine and the domain level, fills partly used domains first. Whole domains stay free for 4-GPU jobs.

3 · Preempt with care

High-priority training jobs may preempt batch inference that's packed into a domain. Evicted tasks restart elsewhere within a minute. Queue time for 4-GPU jobs falls from hours to minutes.

4 · Plan capacity

Forecast GPU demand grows 40% over the next two quarters. With N+1 spare capacity per failure domain and 5% for maintenance, the team orders 150 more servers instead of the 200 a naive count suggested.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A virtual machine runs a whole operating system on shared hardware. It runs at full speed until it needs something only the host can provide. Each of those hand-offs costs time, so fast designs avoid them.

KVM
The Linux kernel feature that lets it run virtual machines using CPU hardware support.
VMM
Virtual machine monitor: the user-space program that sets up the VM and emulates devices.
VM exit
The CPU leaving the guest and returning to the host to handle an event.
EPT
Extended page tables: hardware translation from guest physical to host physical memory.
virtio
A standard for fast virtual devices using shared-memory queues instead of frequent exits.
VFIO
A Linux framework for giving a VM direct, IOMMU-protected access to a real device.
gVisor
A sandbox that runs container system calls in a user-space kernel for isolation.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Containers share the host kernel; virtual machines don't. On Linux, KVM turns the kernel into a hypervisor. A user-space VMM (QEMU, Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor) creates a VM through /dev/kvm and runs each virtual CPU in a loop with the KVM_RUN call. The guest runs directly on the CPU until it does something the hardware must hand back to the host, such as touching an emulated device's I/O port or MMIO address, or halting. That hand-back is a VM exit. The VMM handles it and resumes the guest. Exits cost about a microsecond or more each, so frequent exits are the main overhead. Memory uses two-level translation: guest virtual to guest physical through the guest's page tables, then guest physical to host physical through EPT (Intel) or NPT (AMD) tables. A TLB miss can then take up to 24 memory references instead of 4, which is why huge pages matter even more in VMs. For speed, virtio devices batch work through shared-memory queues to avoid exits, and VFIO passes a real device such as a GPU straight to the guest, using the IOMMU to keep its DMA inside the guest's memory. Between containers and VMs sit sandboxes: gVisor intercepts a container's system calls in a user-space kernel, and microVMs like Firecracker boot tiny VMs in milliseconds.

MAKE IT STICK

A guest chef in your kitchen cooks freely, but must call you whenever they need the locked pantry (a VM exit). Every call interrupts both of you, so you stock their station in advance (virtio queues) or give them their own pantry key for one cupboard (passthrough).

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The VM that was 30% slower than the container

A team moves a network-heavy service from containers into VMs for stronger isolation. Throughput drops 30% and host CPU rises, though the guest looks idle.

1 · Count exits

KVM's exit statistics show 300,000 exits per second, mostly MMIO writes to an emulated network card. At about 2 µs each, that's 60% of a core lost to exits.

2 · Use virtio

Switching to a virtio-net device batches packets through shared-memory queues and only notifies occasionally. Exits fall to about 20,000 per second.

3 · Fix memory translation

Profiles show many TLB misses, and each costs up to 24 memory references under EPT. Backing guest memory with huge pages on the host cuts the walk cost.

4 · Pass through the accelerator

For the GPU tier, VFIO passes each GPU straight into its VM with the IOMMU fencing its DMA. Performance nearly matches bare metal, and tenants are still isolated.

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Version control stores each file and folder under a fingerprint of its contents. A folder's fingerprint depends on everything inside it. So unchanged folders are spotted instantly, identical files are stored once, and history can't be silently changed.

Content addressing
Storing each object under the hash of its bytes.
Blob
An object holding one file's contents.
Tree
An object listing a directory's entries and their IDs.
Commit
An object pointing to a root tree, its parents and metadata.
Merkle tree
A tree where each node's hash covers its children's hashes.
Change ID
jj's stable identity for a change, kept when the commit is rewritten.
Operation log
jj's record of every repository operation, which makes undo possible.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Modern version control is built on content addressing: every object is stored under the hash of its bytes. So identical content is stored once and any change produces a new ID. Git has four object types. A blob holds a file's bytes. A tree lists a directory's entries (name, type, ID). A commit points to one root tree, its parent commits, the author and a message. Tags name commits. Because each tree's ID covers its children's IDs, the structure is a Merkle tree. Two snapshots with the same root ID are identical, and a diff can skip any subdirectory whose ID didn't change. That is why comparing two huge trees can be fast. Branches are just movable names pointing at commits. jj (Jujutsu), an open-source VCS that Google's Source Client team works on, stores data in Git-compatible form but changes the model. The working copy is itself a commit, snapshotted automatically, so there's no staging area. Each change has a stable change ID that survives rewrites, while its commit ID changes every time it's amended or rebased. Descendants are rebased automatically. Conflicts are first-class: they can be committed and resolved later. An operation log records every repository operation, so any command can be undone.

MAKE IT STICK

A library where every page is filed under a fingerprint of its text. A chapter is a list of page fingerprints, and a book is a list of chapter fingerprints. If two editions have the same book fingerprint they're identical, and comparing editions only means opening chapters whose fingerprints differ.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Why 'what changed?' is instant in a giant repository

A monorepo snapshot has 2 million files in 200,000 directories. A tool needs the files that changed between two snapshots a few commits apart.

1 · Compare the roots

The root tree IDs differ, so something changed. Only the root's entries are loaded and compared, not 2 million files.

2 · Follow only changed IDs

Of 40 top-level directories, 39 have identical IDs and are skipped. Diff descends only into the one that changed, then into its changed children, and so on.

3 · Count the work

For 12 changed files in one area, Diff opens about 30 trees. A file-by-file comparison would read millions of entries. The Merkle property makes the cost track the size of the change, not the repository.

4 · Rewrite safely in jj

The developer amends a commit in the middle of a stack. jj gives it a new commit ID but keeps its change ID, rebases the descendants automatically, and records the operation so jj undo can reverse it.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Huge code repositories can't be copied to every laptop. A virtual filesystem shows every file but downloads one only when it's opened, and keeps your edits locally. Caching the answers to 'does this exist?' and 'how big is it?' keeps it fast.

Monorepo
One repository holding most of a company's code.
Virtual filesystem
A folder that looks normal but fetches file contents on demand.
FUSE
Filesystem in Userspace: the kernel sends file operations to a normal program.
Overlay
A local layer holding only the files you've changed.
Lazy fetch
Downloading a file's contents only when it's first read.
Negative caching
Remembering that a file does not exist, to avoid asking again.
Sparse checkout
Materializing only chosen directories of a repository on disk.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A monorepo can hold billions of lines of code, far too much to copy to each laptop. Public descriptions of Google's setup (Piper with the CitC workspace, CACM 2016) and other big companies' tools share one answer: a virtual filesystem. The repository appears as an ordinary folder, but files are fetched only when something opens them. On Linux this is usually built with FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace): the kernel forwards file operations such as lookup, getattr, readdir and read to a user-space daemon, which answers from caches or the server. Writes go to a local overlay that holds only the files you changed, so 'what did I modify?' is instant. Speed comes from caching at every level. Directory listings and file metadata go in a metadata cache, including negative caching of 'this file doesn't exist', which build tools ask about constantly. Content goes in a local cache keyed by hash, so it's shared across workspaces. Metadata for whole directories is fetched in one bulk call. Each kernel-to-daemon round trip costs microseconds, and each server round trip costs milliseconds, so the design goal is fewer of both. Sparse checkout is the simpler alternative: materialize only the directories you choose, at the cost of rebuilding the set when you need more.

MAKE IT STICK

A streaming music library. Every song appears in your list, but a song downloads only when you press play, and it stays on the phone afterwards. Your own recordings are kept separately on the device.

The build that made 400,000 network calls

Engineers move to a FUSE-based workspace for a 3-million-file monorepo. Checkouts become instant, but the first build takes 20 minutes instead of 4.

1 · Count round trips

Daemon metrics show 400,000 metadata calls to the server during the build. Most are build tools checking for files that don't exist, one path at a time.

2 · Cache 'not found'

Negative caching remembers missing paths for the snapshot. Since a snapshot never changes, the answer stays valid until the workspace syncs. Metadata calls fall by 70%.

3 · Fetch directories in bulk

When a build first touches a directory, the daemon fetches metadata for all its entries in one call. Remaining calls fall from about 120,000 to 9,000.

4 · Share content by hash

File contents are cached locally by content hash, shared across workspaces. The second workspace's build fetches almost nothing. Build time drops to 5 minutes the first time and 3 after that.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Google · Staff Software Engineer, Source Client (San Jose)
Preferred: operating system internals (Linux/macOS) and file system design; integrating agents and AI tools whose edits must be picked up instantly.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2

CODE, LINE BY LINE
4

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Finding changed files by checking each one gets slow in big projects. The operating system can announce changes instead, and a tool keeps a numbered log of them. If any announcements were lost, the safe fix is one full check.

inotify
The Linux interface that reports file changes in watched directories.
Watch
A registration asking the kernel to report changes in one directory.
IN_Q_OVERFLOW
inotify's signal that its queue filled and events were lost.
Rescan
Checking every file directly, needed after lost events.
Journal
A log of changed paths kept by the watching tool.
Clock
An increasing counter that lets clients ask what changed since their last query.
fsmonitor
Git's hook for asking a file watcher what changed, instead of scanning.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Commands like status, builds and editor plug-ins all ask the same question: what changed since last time? Scanning every file's metadata (stat) works for small trees but takes seconds or minutes in a large one. Operating systems can push changes instead. On Linux, inotify delivers events (created, modified, deleted, moved) for watched directories through a file descriptor. macOS has FSEvents and Windows has ReadDirectoryChangesW. inotify has hard limits. You need one watch per directory (capped by max_user_watches). The event queue is bounded, and when it fills the kernel sends IN_Q_OVERFLOW: events were lost and the only safe response is a full rescan. Tools such as Watchman keep a journal of changed paths, stamped with an increasing clock. A client remembers the clock of its last query and asks 'what changed since clock 1234?', getting a short list instead of rescanning. A fresh instance or overflow resets the clock and tells clients to do a full scan. Git's fsmonitor uses this to make git status fast in big repositories. It matters more now that AI agents edit many files quickly and tools must see every change.

MAKE IT STICK

A doorman with a logbook. Instead of searching every room for changes, you ask: 'what happened since entry 1,234?' If the logbook ran out of pages, he says so, and you search the building once.

INTERACTIVE LAB
Fast and correct status

START WITH THE INCIDENT
git status took 14 seconds

In a 1.5-million-file checkout, git status has to stat every file and takes 14 seconds. An AI coding agent runs status after each edit, so every turn feels sluggish.

1 · Add a watcher

A daemon watches the tree with inotify and keeps a clocked journal. Git's fsmonitor asks it for changes since its last clock, and status drops to 0.3 seconds.

2 · Hit the limits

The checkout has 180,000 directories, more than the default max_user_watches allowed. The team raises the limit and documents it in setup.

3 · Handle overflow

A big branch switch rewrites 300,000 files, the queue overflows, and an early version silently missed changes. The fix: on IN_Q_OVERFLOW, mark the journal 'fresh instance' so every client does one full scan.

4 · Agents and tools

The agent and the editor both query the same daemon with their own clocks. Each sees exactly the files changed since it last asked, including edits made by the other.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Big training jobs use thousands of machines at once. With that many machines, something breaks every few hours. The job saves its progress regularly, so a crash only loses the work since the last save. This lesson works out how often to save and how much time is really useful.

MTBF (mean time between failures)
The average running time between failures, for one machine or a whole job.
Checkpoint
A saved copy of the model and training state, so a job can restart from it.
Goodput
The share of time spent on useful training that is kept, after losses from failures, restarts and saving.
Young's formula
A rule of thumb for the checkpoint interval: the square root of 2 × checkpoint cost × MTBF.
Restart time
Time from a failure until training is running again: replacing nodes, loading state, warming up.
Hot spare
A healthy machine kept ready so a failed one can be replaced at once.
Binomial distribution
The chance of exactly k failures among n independent machines that each fail with probability p.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A training job that needs every one of its machines fails whenever any of them fails. If one node fails on average every 50,000 hours, its MTBF (mean time between failures) is 50,000 h. A job on 4,096 such nodes sees a failure about every 50,000 / 4,096 ≈ 12 hours. At 16,384 nodes it is about every 3 hours. So at frontier scale, failure is the normal case, and the design question becomes how much useful work survives. Jobs save a checkpoint (model and optimizer state) every interval τ. Each failure loses, on average, half an interval of work plus the restart time (find spare nodes, reload, warm up). Writing checkpoints also costs time. Young's formula gives a good interval: τ ≈ √(2·C·M), where C is the time a checkpoint blocks training and M is the job MTBF. Goodput is the share of wall-clock time spent on training that is kept. A first-order model: waste ≈ C/τ + (τ + C)/(2M) + R/M. Three levers move it: make checkpoints cheaper to block on (asynchronous, sharded writes), make restarts faster (hot spare nodes, cached data and images), and raise node MTBF (catch bad hardware before it joins a job). Spare capacity follows from the same math. A 4,096-node job on a fleet where 1% of nodes are down needs enough spares that it can almost always start.

MAKE IT STICK

A relay team of 4,000 runners where the race restarts from the last checkpoint flag whenever anyone trips. Flags cost a moment to plant. Plant them too often and you crawl; too rarely and every trip throws away a long stretch.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 16,000-GPU run that kept rewinding

A team scales a training run from 2,048 to 16,384 accelerators (2,048 nodes of 8). Throughput per step looks great, but after a week the model has trained only 61% as many tokens as planned.

1 · Do the math

Nodes average about 20,000 hours between failures, so the job sees one roughly every 10 hours. Checkpoints block training for 12 minutes and run every 4 hours; restarts take 40 minutes. The model predicts about 78% goodput. Measured goodput is lower because failures cluster in a few bad racks.

2 · Cheaper checkpoints

Switching to asynchronous, sharded checkpoints cuts blocking to 40 seconds: snapshot to host memory, then upload in the background. Young's formula now says about every 45 minutes, so a failure loses far less.

3 · Faster restarts

Keeping 2% hot spares with images and datasets pre-cached cuts restart time from 40 to 8 minutes. The spare math says 2% covers the job 99.9% of the time at the observed 0.5% node-down rate.

4 · Fewer failures

Burn-in tests and health gates before nodes join jobs (chapter 32) raise node MTBF by about a third. Goodput reaches about 93%, and the run catches up within two weeks.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Saving a huge model means many machines each write their own piece at the same time. The save only counts once a small list of all pieces is written last. If anything crashes earlier, the old save is still the one used.

Shard
One piece of a checkpoint, written by one worker.
Manifest
A small file written last that lists every shard and its checksum; its presence marks the checkpoint as complete.
Checksum
A short fingerprint of data (here SHA-256) used to detect corruption.
Atomic commit
A change that is either fully visible or not at all, never half done.
Asynchronous checkpoint
Copy state quickly, resume training, and upload in the background.
Resharding
Loading a checkpoint into a different number of workers than wrote it.
Retention
Rules for which old checkpoints to keep and safely delete.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

The saved state of a big AI system is huge, often many million megabytes. It holds the weights, the optimizer state (often 2–3× the weights) and data-loader positions. One machine can't write that quickly, so every worker writes its own shard in parallel to object storage. The hard part is atomicity. A crash mid-save must never leave a half-written checkpoint that looks valid. The standard pattern: write all shards under a step-specific prefix, then write a small manifest last, listing each shard with its size and checksum. A step counts as valid only if its manifest exists and every shard matches. That is a commit point, like a database commit record. Asynchronous checkpointing splits the save in two. A quick snapshot copies state to host memory, so training continues. A background upload then sends the snapshot to storage. Keep at most one upload in flight, or uploads pile up and memory runs out. Restore picks the newest valid step, verifies checksums and loads shards in parallel. Each worker reads only the shards it needs, which helps when the restart uses a different number of workers (resharding). Retention deletes old steps safely: delete the manifest first, then the shards, so a half-deleted step can never be loaded.

MAKE IT STICK

Moving house with 500 boxes. Each mover carries their own boxes (shards), and only when all are inside do you sign the delivery note (manifest). If the truck crashes halfway, there's no signed note, so nobody mistakes a half-empty house for the finished move.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The checkpoint that looked fine

A job restarts after a power event and loads the newest checkpoint folder. Loss jumps to a value from weeks ago. Half the optimizer shards in that folder were from an interrupted save.

1 · What went wrong

The old code picked the newest folder by name. A crash during save left some new shards next to missing ones, and the loader filled gaps with zeros.

2 · Commit with a manifest

Now shards go first and the manifest last. The loader ignores any step without a manifest and checks every shard's SHA-256. The interrupted step is invisible, and the previous one loads.

3 · Stop blocking training

SaveAsync copies state to host memory in 30 seconds. The upload then takes 9 minutes in the background with 64 parallel writers, capped so it doesn't starve data loading.

4 · Delete safely

Retention once deleted shards before the manifest, and a restart during cleanup loaded a broken step. Deleting the manifest first closes that window.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Training jobs need all their machines at the same time, and many teams share one cluster. The scheduler starts a job only when all its machines are free, gives each team a guaranteed share, and takes back borrowed machines when the owners need them.

Gang scheduling
Starting all of a job's workers together, or none of them.
Quota
The capacity a team is guaranteed.
Borrowing
Using idle capacity beyond your quota, which can be taken back.
Preemption
Stopping a running job to free resources for a higher-claim job.
Fair share
A rule for whose job runs next when demand exceeds capacity.
Backfill
Running small jobs in gaps while bigger jobs wait.
Starvation
A job that never runs because others keep taking the resources it needs.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Chapter 29 placed single tasks. Training jobs are different in three ways. A distributed job is useful only if all its workers run at once, so it needs gang scheduling: start all N or none. Half-started gangs waste GPUs while they wait for the rest, and two half-started gangs can deadlock each other. Second, many teams share one cluster. Each team gets a quota (a guaranteed share), and may borrow idle capacity beyond it. When an owner needs its quota back, the scheduler preempts borrowed work. That is fine for jobs that checkpoint (lesson 31.2). Third, fair share decides who goes next when demand exceeds supply. A common rule picks the team using the smallest fraction of its guarantee. Dominant resource fairness generalizes this to several resources. Big gangs risk starvation. If small jobs keep backfilling into gaps, a 512-node job may never find 512 free nodes at once. Schedulers add a reservation: after a big job has been skipped too often, hold freed nodes for it. In Kubernetes this logic lives in batch schedulers and queueing add-ons (Volcano, Kueue, YuniKorn), not the default scheduler.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant with tables for big parties. A party of 12 is only seated when all 12 chairs are free (gang). Each club has booked chairs (quota) but may use empty ones (borrowing) until the owners arrive (preemption). If you keep seating walk-in couples, the party of 12 waits forever, so after a while you hold tables for them (reservation).

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 512-node run that never started

A research team submits a 512-node pretraining job on a 2,000-node cluster shared by four teams. Two days later it still hasn't started, although the cluster is never more than 80% busy.

1 · Death by backfill

Small evaluation jobs keep landing in every gap, so 512 nodes are never free at the same moment. The utilization graph looks healthy while the most important job starves.

2 · Reserve

After the big job is skipped 20 times, the scheduler stops backfilling and holds freed nodes. It starts within 40 minutes; utilization dips briefly while capacity drains.

3 · Quotas and borrowing

The research team owns 800 nodes, but another team borrowed 300 of them overnight. Reclaim preempts the borrowed, low-priority jobs (they resume from checkpoints) without touching anyone's guarantee.

New dashboards show queue wait by job size, preemptions per team and nodes idle because of reservation. The policy becomes a documented contract that every team signs off on.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Anthropic · Staff+ Software Engineer, Infrastructure (Distributed Systems) (SF / Seattle)
POSTED: 'some of the largest Kubernetes clusters in the world'; Kubernetes and IaC required. RELATED postings: hyperscale (100+ clusters, 10K+ nodes), Kubernetes internals.

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Huge clusters keep all their state in one replicated database, behind one front door. If thousands of machines ask for everything at once, the front door falls over. Spreading retries out, answering from memory and giving important callers their own lane keeps it standing.

etcd
The replicated key-value store that holds every Kubernetes object.
API server
The front door to cluster state; every client reads and writes through it.
Watch
A long-lived request that streams changes after a given version.
resourceVersion
A version number for cluster state, used to resume a watch where it left off.
List storm
Many clients re-listing large collections at the same moment, overloading the API server.
Jitter
Random spread added to retry delays so clients don't retry in lockstep.
API Priority and Fairness (APF)
Kubernetes' admission control: concurrency shares per priority level and fair queuing per client flow.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Chapter 27 wrote one controller. At tens of thousands of nodes, the control plane is the bottleneck. Every object lives in etcd, a Raft-replicated key-value store with a modest size limit (about 8 GB is a common recommended maximum) and finite write throughput. The API server sits in front of etcd. It keeps a watch cache so most reads and watches are served from memory, not etcd. Clients (kubelets, controllers, daemons on every node) use list-then-watch. They list once, then watch for changes from that list's resourceVersion. If a watch breaks and the client's version is too old (compacted away), the server answers 410 Gone and the client must re-list. The classic outage is a list storm. Something makes every node's agent restart at once, and 20,000 full lists of all pods hit the API server together. Memory spikes, the server falls over, clients retry, and it gets worse. Defenses come in layers. Clients use exponential backoff with jitter, so retries spread out. Lists are served from the watch cache and paginated. Large clusters split heavy object types across separate etcd instances. API Priority and Fairness (APF) gives each priority level its own concurrency share and queues requests fairly per flow, so a misbehaving client can't starve the node heartbeats and system controllers that keep the cluster alive. Beyond one cluster's limits, you run many clusters with a fleet layer on top.

MAKE IT STICK

A library with one front desk. Normally people ask 'what changed since Tuesday?' (watch). After a fire drill, everyone rushes back at once asking for the full catalogue (list storm). The fix: staggered return times (jitter), a photocopy of the catalogue at the desk (watch cache), and separate lines so staff with urgent errands aren't stuck behind the crowd (priority and fairness).

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The daemonset rollout that took down the control plane

A config change restarts a logging daemon on all 18,000 nodes within two minutes. Each instance lists every pod in the cluster on startup. The API servers run out of memory and restart, and node heartbeats start failing.

1 · Why it cascades

Each restart triggers fresh lists from every client, including kubelets whose watches broke. Retries with fixed 1-second delays arrive in synchronized waves.

2 · Stop the stampede

Clients switch to full-jitter backoff, and the daemon lists only pods on its own node (a field selector), served from the watch cache. Load per restart drops by more than 1,000×.

3 · Protect the vital traffic

APF puts node heartbeats and system controllers in their own priority level. The daemon's flow is limited to its own queue, so it can be slow without starving the cluster.

4 · Make rollouts safe

Daemon rollouts now go out in waves (max unavailable 2%), and the team adds an API-server load SLO that pauses rollouts automatically.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Graphics cards in a big fleet report errors all day. Some errors are the program's fault and some mean the card is breaking. This lesson sorts each signal into keep, watch, take out of service, or send for repair.

XID error
A numbered error message the NVIDIA driver writes to the kernel log; NVIDIA documents what each number means.
ECC (error-correcting code)
Extra bits in memory that fix single-bit errors and detect double-bit errors.
Row remapping
Replacing a bad memory row with a spare row; takes effect after a GPU reset.
Drain
Stop placing new work on a node and move or finish the work already there.
Hysteresis
Requiring a clean period before going back to normal, so a node doesn't flap in and out.
Burn-in
Stress tests run on a node before it rejoins production work.
BMC / Redfish
The baseboard management controller and its standard web API for power, fans and temperature, reachable even if the OS is down.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A large group of GPUs reports errors all day long. The job is to turn each signal into one of four steps: keep, watch, drain (stop new work, let jobs finish or move) and repair (send to a technician or vendor). The NVIDIA driver logs XID errors to the kernel log. Each XID number has a meaning in NVIDIA's XID documentation; check it for your driver version. Some XIDs usually mean the application did something wrong, such as XID 13 (graphics engine exception) or XID 31 (GPU memory page fault). Others point at hardware: XID 48 (double-bit ECC error), XID 79 (GPU has fallen off the bus), XID 64 (row-remapper failure) and XID 95 (uncontained ECC error). On recent data-center GPUs, memory with a bad row is fixed by row remapping. A pending remap needs a GPU reset, so the right action is drain and reset, not repair. NVLink errors show up as rising CRC or replay counters; a slow rise means a flaky link, and a jump means a failing one. Good triage has three habits. Separate app-caused errors from hardware by checking whether the same GPU fails across different jobs. Use hysteresis, so a node needs a clean period before it returns. Send drained nodes through a burn-in test before rejoining, so a bad GPU never re-enters a 4,000-node training job. Tools like DCGM expose these signals as metrics; out-of-band BMC data (power, fans, temperatures via Redfish) catches failures the OS can't see.

MAKE IT STICK

A hospital triage desk. A cough after one bad meal is the food's fault; the same cough every day, whatever the meal, means the patient needs a doctor. Nobody is sent home until they've been fine for a while.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The node that kept coming back

A 1,000-node GPU cluster runs inference and training. One node is drained after a double-bit ECC error, auto-reset, and returned within minutes. It fails again two days later, killing a 512-GPU training job.

1 · What the logs show

The node logged XID 48, then XID 63 (remap pending). The reset applied the remap, which is correct, but it also logged XID 31 three times in the past week, each from a different job. Nobody linked them.

2 · Better triage

The classifier now treats the same app-type XID across three different jobs as a hardware hint and drains the node. A pending remap triggers drain and reset, not a repair ticket.

3 · Hysteresis and burn-in

Nodes return only after six clean windows and a burn-in run: memory stress, an NCCL all-reduce test across NVLink, and a thermal soak. The flapping node fails burn-in and goes to the vendor.

Track drains per day, repeat-failure rate within 7 days of return, and training jobs killed by hardware. The repeat rate is the number that shows the gate is working.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Updating software on thousands of machines at once is risky. Update a few first, wait, compare them with machines you haven't updated, and only then go wider. Never take too many machines from one group at the same time.

Canary
A small first group that gets a change before everyone else.
Wave
One stage of a rollout, covering a set share of the fleet.
Bake time
How long to wait and watch after a wave before starting the next.
Health gate
A check that must pass before the rollout continues.
Blast radius
How much of the system a bad change can hurt at once.
Control group
Untouched nodes used as the comparison for the updated ones.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Changing the GPU driver or firmware on thousands of machines is one of the most dangerous jobs a GPU platform team does. The same goes for the CUDA version. A bad version can break every node at once. Safe rollouts have four parts. Waves: update a small canary set first (say 1%), then 10%, 50% and 100%, with a bake time at each step. Health gates: compare the updated nodes against similar untouched nodes on the metrics that matter (error rate, XID rate, job failures, throughput). Don't compare against a fixed threshold, because the fleet's normal level drifts. Blast-radius limits: never take more than a set share of any pool out of service at once, so a pool keeps serving traffic and no training job loses too many nodes. Automatic halt and rollback: a failed gate stops the rollout and, if the old version is still available, reverts the affected wave. Pick nodes for each wave in a stable order (a hash of the node ID), so reruns are predictable and canaries cover every hardware type. A gate needs enough data to be meaningful; with few events, use a minimum sample size or a longer bake.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant chain changing its recipe: try it in one kitchen, then ten, then everywhere, comparing complaints against kitchens still on the old recipe, and never closing more than a few kitchens in one city on the same day.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The driver update that passed every test

A new GPU driver passes the test lab. Rolled to 10% of a 2,000-node fleet, it looks fine for an hour, so the team goes to 100%. Six hours later, XID 79 errors spike on one GPU model under sustained load.

1 · What went wrong

The canary was only 10 nodes, all the same GPU model, and the bake was shorter than the failure's onset time. There was no control group, so the slow rise looked like noise.

2 · Stratified waves

Waves now come from a stable hash within each hardware model, so every model has canaries. Bake time is set from past failure onset data: 24 hours for drivers.

3 · Comparative gates

Each wave's failure rate is compared with untouched nodes of the same model over the same window. A ratio above 1.5× halts the rollout; too few jobs means keep baking.

4 · Blast radius

No pool loses more than 5% of its nodes to updates at once, and training jobs are drained at checkpoint boundaries. The next bad driver is caught at the 1% wave on 20 nodes.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Small AI models don't need a whole graphics card. A card can be shared by taking turns, by running together, or by splitting it into walled-off parts. This lesson packs many small models onto as few cards as possible.

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU)
Splitting one GPU into isolated instances, each with its own compute and memory.
MPS (Multi-Process Service)
NVIDIA service that lets several processes run kernels on one GPU at the same time.
Time-slicing
Processes take turns on the whole GPU.
Profile
A fixed MIG instance size, such as 1g.10gb or 3g.40gb.
Fragmentation
Free capacity split into pieces too small or badly placed to use.
First-fit decreasing
Packing method: sort items largest first, place each into the first bin where it fits.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Many inference models are far smaller than one GPU, so running one model per GPU wastes most of it. There are three ways to share. Time-slicing lets processes take turns; it's simple but gives no memory isolation and adds context-switch delay. MPS (Multi-Process Service) runs kernels from several processes at the same time on one GPU; throughput is good, but a fault in one client can affect the others and memory isn't hard-partitioned. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU, on A100, H100 and later) splits a GPU into hardware-isolated instances, each with its own compute slices and memory. On an H100 80GB, profiles include 1g.10gb, 2g.20gb, 3g.40gb and 7g.80gb. Instances must sit at allowed start positions, so the order you create them in matters: the wrong mix leaves slices you can't use (fragmentation). Then the scheduler packs models into instances. A standard approach is first-fit decreasing: sort models by size, largest first, and place each into the first GPU with a valid free spot. Good packing can cut GPU count by half or more for small models. It also changes failure blast radius: one bad GPU takes down every model packed on it.

MAKE IT STICK

An apartment building. Time-slicing is one flat with a rota for the kitchen; MPS is flatmates cooking at once in one kitchen; MIG is splitting the floor into separate flats with their own doors. Fitting tenants well means placing the large families first.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

POSTED: CI and build systems, developer productivity at scale. PUBLIC (Roblox 2025 tools blog): time-to-land and CI speed are tracked metrics. Bazel is NOT named in the posting.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Builds repeat a lot of work that hasn't changed. A build cache remembers each step's result under a fingerprint of exactly what went into it. If the fingerprint matches, it reuses the result instead of doing the work again.

Action
One build step: a command with its inputs and outputs.
Digest
A content hash of a file, such as SHA-256.
Content addressing
Storing data under the hash of its content.
Hermetic
A build step that depends only on its declared inputs, nothing else on the machine.
Cache poisoning
A wrong result stored under a key that later builds trust.
Hit rate
The share of actions answered from the cache.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Most test-server time goes into building and testing again things that haven't changed. That test server is called CI (continuous integration). A remote build cache fixes that by remembering results. The trick is the cache key. A build step (an action) is a command plus everything it reads. Hash the command line, the relevant environment variables, the toolchain version and the digest (content hash) of every input file. Two actions with the same key must produce the same output, so the second one can just download the result. This is content addressing: outputs are stored by their hash, so identical files are stored once. It only works if actions are hermetic: they depend only on declared inputs. Hidden inputs break it in two ways. A timestamp or absolute path baked into the output makes keys differ every time (cache misses). An undeclared input, such as a header read from the machine, makes keys match when the outputs shouldn't (cache poisoning, which is worse). Build systems such as Bazel, Buck2 and others implement this with a remote cache and remote execution protocol. Only cache successful actions, and treat the cache as untrusted when keys come from developer machines: CI should write, laptops should read. Track hit rate by action type; a sudden drop usually means a new non-hermetic input.

MAKE IT STICK

A bakery that labels every cake with its exact recipe and ingredient batch numbers. If someone orders the same recipe with the same batches, hand over the cake already made. If a baker secretly adds an unlisted ingredient, two different cakes get the same label.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The cache that stopped hitting

A monorepo's CI takes 25 minutes on average. A remote cache was added a year ago, but its hit rate has fallen from 85% to 30%, and nobody knows why.

1 · Find the miss

Compare action keys from two CI runs of the same commit. The code-generation step's key differs: the generator stamps the build time into a header, which changes the inputs of everything downstream.

2 · Fix hermeticity

Remove the timestamp (or pass a fixed one), strip absolute paths from compiler flags, and pin the toolchain by digest. Keys now match across runs.

3 · Guard the cache

Only CI workers write; laptops read. A nightly job rebuilds a sample of actions without the cache and compares outputs, catching undeclared inputs.

4 · Watch the number

Hit rate is tracked per action type on a dashboard with an alert on drops. Median CI time returns to 9 minutes.

LESSON 33.2 · GO 1.22+ · BATCH TESTING WITH RECURSIVE BISECTION ON FAILURE, COUNTING CI RUNS · NEW
Merge queues: batching, bisection and keeping main green
WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Roblox · Principal Software Engineer, Engineering Acceleration (San Mateo)
POSTED: code review and CI systems, developer velocity. PUBLIC (Roblox 2025 tools blog): P75 time to land tracked.
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Two changes can work alone but break things together. A merge queue tests changes in order on top of the newest code. It tests groups to save time, and splits a failing group to find the bad change.

Main (trunk)
The shared branch everyone builds on; it should always pass tests.
Merge queue
A line of approved changes, each tested on top of main and those ahead of it before merging.
Batch
Several queued changes tested together in one CI run.
Bisection
Splitting a failing batch in halves to find the change that broke it.
Time to land
Time from approval until a change is merged.
Speculative testing
Testing later batches in parallel, assuming earlier ones will pass.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

In a busy repository, two changes can each pass CI alone and still break main together. A merge queue prevents that: it tests each change on top of the latest main plus everything ahead of it in the queue, and merges only what passes. Testing one change at a time is safe but slow; with a 20-minute CI run, only three changes land per hour. Batching tests several queued changes together. If the batch passes, all of them merge at once. If it fails, bisection splits the batch in half and tests each half, repeating until the bad change is found and removed. With failure rate p and batch size B, batches fail more often as B grows, so the best batch size depends on p. Speculative queues run several batches in parallel, each assuming the ones ahead will pass, trading compute for latency. The metric developers feel is time to land: from approval to merge. Track it at p50 and p75, not just averages, because the slow tail is what frustrates people.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Main is red every afternoon

A 600-engineer monorepo merges directly after per-change CI. Every afternoon, main breaks from semantic conflicts between changes, and fixing it blocks everyone for an hour.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails with the same code. That makes people stop trusting test results. This lesson finds flaky tests, takes them out of the way, and makes sure someone fixes them.

Flaky test
A test that passes and fails on the same code.
Same-commit disagreement
A test both passed and failed on one commit: strong evidence of flakiness.
Flake rate
Share of a test's commits where it disagreed with itself.
Quarantine
Running a test without letting it block merges, while it gets fixed.
Retry
Running a failed test again automatically.
Order dependence
A test that only passes when run before or after certain other tests.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Flakiness destroys trust in CI: developers rerun until green, merge queues reject good changes, and real failures get ignored. The cleanest signal is same-commit disagreement: if a test both passed and failed on one commit, it is flaky, whatever the code does. Count that across many commits to get a flake rate per test. Common causes are timing (sleeps, timeouts), shared state between tests, test order dependence, network calls and random seeds. Policy has three parts. Retries hide flakes from developers but can also hide real bugs; retry at most once and record that it happened. Quarantine removes a test from blocking CI once its flake rate crosses a threshold, while still running it and reporting to the owner. Ownership and deadlines: each quarantined test has an owner and a date, or it's deleted. A healthy CI tracks the share of runs failed by flakes and the time spent on reruns.

MAKE IT STICK

A smoke alarm that sometimes goes off when you make toast. If you just keep resetting it, you'll ignore it during a real fire. Instead, log every false alarm, move the alarm while you fix it, and give someone a deadline.

Rerun until green

Developers rerun CI an average of 1.8 times per change. The merge queue rejects about 1 in 10 batches for failures that disappear on retry.

1 · Find the flakes

CI already reruns failures, so the data exists. Grouping results by test and commit finds 140 tests that both passed and failed on the same commit last month.

2 · Quarantine

Tests with a flake rate above 2% over at least 20 commits stop blocking merges. They still run, and their results go to the owning team's dashboard.

3 · Fix the causes

Half of the flakes are timing (fixed sleeps), a quarter are shared temp directories, the rest are network calls. Each pattern gets a lint rule or helper.

4 · Keep it fixed

Quarantined tests have an owner and a 30-day deadline. Reruns per change fall to 1.1 and merge-queue false rejections drop sharply.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Searching a huge codebase line by line is too slow. A search index records which files contain each three-letter piece. A search checks only files that contain every piece, then confirms the real matches.

Trigram
Three characters in a row, such as 'mut' in 'mutex'.
Posting list
The sorted list of file IDs that contain one trigram.
Intersection
Keeping only the IDs present in every list.
Candidate
A file that might match because it contains all the trigrams.
Verification
Checking a candidate's text to confirm the real match.
Sharding
Splitting the index across machines.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Searching every file for a string doesn't scale to a large repository. Code search engines such as Zoekt and Google's Code Search build a trigram index. A trigram is any three consecutive characters: "mutex" contains "mut", "ute" and "tex". The index maps each trigram to a posting list: the IDs of files that contain it. To search for a literal, take its trigrams and intersect their posting lists. Any file containing the string must contain all its trigrams, so the intersection is a superset of the real matches. These are candidates; then verify each by actually searching its text, which removes false positives (files that have the trigrams in different places). Regular expressions work by turning the regex into a query of required trigrams. Intersect shortest lists first to keep work small. A production system adds sharding across machines, incremental updates as commits land, ranking (definitions before uses), and access control.

MAKE IT STICK

A library index that lists, for every three-letter combination, which books contain it. To find a phrase, look up its three-letter pieces, keep only books on every list, then open those few books to check.

Engineers search a 40 GB repository with a grep-based tool that takes over a minute per query, so they stop searching and duplicate code instead.

A trigram index over all text files fits in memory on a few shards. Queries now intersect posting lists and verify a few hundred candidates.

A car must still start after a software update, even a bad one. It keeps two copies of its software and updates the one not running. If the new copy fails to start a few times, it switches back to the old one.

A/B slots
Two copies of the system software; one runs while the other is updated.
OTA (over-the-air) update
Software delivered and installed over a network connection.
Tries remaining
How many more times the bootloader will attempt a new slot before giving up on it.
Mark successful
A step after boot that confirms the new slot works.
Anti-rollback
Refusing older software versions, even if properly signed, because they may have known flaws.
RPMB (replay protected memory block)
A small area of eMMC/UFS storage that only accepts authenticated writes.
Boot-time budget
The maximum allowed time from power-on until key services are ready.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A car's connected control box must never be left unable to start after new software arrives. This box is the telematics unit. The standard design is A/B slots: two copies of the bootloader-loaded images (kernel, root filesystem). The running slot stays untouched while an OTA update writes the other. Boot control metadata, often a small structure in a dedicated partition, records per slot a priority, a tries remaining counter and a successful flag. The bootloader picks the highest-priority slot that is either marked successful or still has tries left, and decrements tries before booting it. After boot, a health check in user space (services up, modem reachable) marks the slot successful. If the new slot keeps failing, its tries run out and the bootloader falls back to the old slot automatically: rollback. Separately, anti-rollback protection stops an attacker from installing an older, vulnerable but validly signed image. Each image carries a security version, and the device stores a minimum version in tamper-resistant storage (fuses or RPMB), raising it only after the new version is confirmed good. Automotive units also have a boot-time budget: some services must be ready within a fixed time after ignition, so you measure each stage and move non-critical work later.

MAKE IT STICK

A pilot with two identical planes. You refuel and update one while flying the other. On switching, you get three attempts to take off in the new plane; if it can't, you go back to the old one. And nobody may swap in a plane with an outdated safety certificate.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The update that left cars without connectivity

A telematics unit's OTA update boots fine on the bench, but in some vehicles the new modem firmware can't register on the network. The unit still boots, so it never rolls back, and eCall connectivity is gone.

1 · What 'successful' meant

The slot was marked successful as soon as Linux reached user space. Booting isn't the same as working.

2 · Real health checks

Mark-successful now waits for core services, a modem link check and a watchdog-supervised self-test, with a timeout. Failure reboots, consuming a try, and three failures roll back.

3 · Protect the floor

The anti-rollback minimum is raised only after mark-successful, so a rollback to the previous version is still allowed. Versions with known security holes have their floor raised on purpose.

4 · Keep the boot fast

Stage timing shows the health check pushed critical services past the budget. Non-critical checks move after the fast path, and the budget is tested on every build.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

The cheap memory chips in many car units slowly develop errors. The boot code skips bad areas, fixes small errors, and rewrites data that is getting weak. It also keeps spare copies of the most important parts.

Raw NAND
Flash memory without a built-in controller; software handles errors and bad blocks.
Bad block
A flash block that can't be used reliably and must be skipped.
ECC (error-correcting code)
Extra data stored with each page that can fix a limited number of bit errors.
Read disturb
Bit errors caused in nearby pages by many repeated reads.
Data retention
How long flash keeps data before charge leaks; shorter at high temperature.
Scrubbing
Rewriting weakening data to fresh blocks before it becomes unreadable.
eMMC / UFS
Flash storage with a built-in controller that manages errors and wear.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Many car control boxes start from cheap flash memory chips that are far from perfect. This kind is called raw NAND flash. Blocks can be bad from the factory (marked by the manufacturer) and more go bad over time. Every page has spare bytes holding ECC codes that correct a limited number of bit errors per chunk. Three things make NAND boot robust. First, bad block skipping: early boot code builds a map from logical to physical blocks, skipping blocks marked bad, so the image continues in the next good block. Second, ECC margins: if a read needed close to the maximum correctable bits, the data is still fine now but is degrading. Read disturb (many reads slowly flip nearby bits) and data retention loss (charge leaking over years, faster when hot) cause this. The fix is scrubbing: rewrite the data to a fresh block before it becomes uncorrectable. Third, redundant copies: keep two or more copies of the earliest boot stages in separate blocks, so an uncorrectable error in one still boots from another. Managed storage (eMMC, UFS) hides most of this inside its controller but has its own wear and power-loss behaviors. A car's ten-plus year life and wide temperature range make these issues real, not theoretical.

MAKE IT STICK

A paper map left in a hot glovebox for ten years. The ink fades, so you keep a second copy, and whenever a page looks faint you redraw it before it becomes unreadable. Torn pages are skipped, and the index tells you where each section really starts.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Cars in Arizona stop booting after four years

A fleet of vehicles in hot climates starts failing to boot after several years. The units boot from raw NAND with a single copy of the first-stage bootloader.

1 · Root cause

Heat speeds up charge loss. The bootloader block, read on every start and never rewritten, crossed the ECC limit. One uncorrectable block meant no boot.

2 · Redundant copies

The boot ROM can try several copies, so the first stage now has copies in different blocks. One unreadable copy no longer stops the boot.

3 · Scrubbing

When a read needs at least 6 of 8 correctable bits, a background service rewrites that block's data to a fresh block and updates the map.

4 · Proving it

Accelerated aging tests at high temperature and a read-disturb stress loop show the margin. Field telemetry reports corrected-bit counts per block so drift is visible years early.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS

POSTED: verified boot, disk integrity, full-disk encryption, MAC and threat analysis (TARA) for the telematics platform.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

The car checks each piece of software before running it, starting from code that can't be changed. For the large system disk, it keeps a tree of fingerprints. Each block is checked against the tree when it is read, so tampering is caught.

Chain of trust
Each boot stage checks the signature of the next before running it.
Root of trust
The first unchangeable code and key, usually in the chip's ROM and fuses.
Merkle tree
A tree of hashes where each parent is the hash of its children; one root hash covers everything.
dm-verity
Linux feature that checks each block read from a read-only partition against a Merkle tree.
Full-disk encryption
Encrypting stored data so it can't be read without the key.
MAC (mandatory access control)
System-enforced rules limiting what each process may access, such as SELinux.
TARA
Threat analysis and risk assessment, the automotive security analysis in ISO/SAE 21434.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Verified boot builds a chain of trust. The boot ROM, which can't be changed, holds or references a public key fused into the chip. It verifies the signature on the first bootloader, which verifies the next stage, and so on up to the kernel. Each stage only runs code signed by a trusted key. The kernel then has to trust the root filesystem, which is too big to check at boot. dm-verity solves this with a Merkle tree: split the filesystem into 4 KB blocks, hash each block, hash groups of hashes, and so on up to a single root hash. The root hash is part of the signed boot data. When a block is read, the kernel hashes it and checks it against its parent hash, up the tree, so any change is detected at read time, cheaply. Verity makes a read-only partition tamper-evident. Writable data needs other tools: full-disk encryption for confidentiality, and integrity protection for data that must not be altered. MAC (mandatory access control, such as SELinux) limits what each process can touch even if it's compromised. In automotive, a TARA (threat analysis and risk assessment, from ISO/SAE 21434) decides which protections each asset needs.

MAKE IT STICK

A sealed library. Each shelf has a label listing a fingerprint for every book on it, each room lists the fingerprints of its shelf labels, and the front door has one signed master fingerprint. Swap a page anywhere and the fingerprints stop matching on the way up.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A modified root filesystem on a returned unit

A unit returned from the field has an extra binary on its root filesystem. The bootloader chain was verified, but the root filesystem was only mounted read-only, not verified.

1 · The gap

Read-only isn't tamper-proof: an attacker with physical access rewrote the flash directly. Nothing checked the filesystem's contents.

2 · Add verity

The build now generates a Merkle tree for the root filesystem and puts the root hash in the signed kernel command line. Any modified block fails on read.

3 · Writable data

Configuration and logs live on an encrypted data partition with its key bound to the device. SELinux policy limits which services can write where.

4 · Tie it to the TARA

The threat analysis lists physical flash access as a threat; verity, encryption and MAC are the recorded controls, with tests for each.

4
 
5

6
#define H SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH       /* 32 bytes */
7
 
8
static void hash_pair(const unsigned char *a, const unsigned char *b, unsigned char *out) {
9
  unsigned char buf[2 * H];
10
  memcpy(buf, a, H); memcpy(buf + H, b, H);
11
  SHA256(buf, sizeof buf, out);
12
}
13

/* Build a binary Merkle tree. n must be a power of two. tree has 2n-1 entries:
15
   leaves at [n-1 .. 2n-2], root at [0]. */
16
void build(const unsigned char *data, int n, unsigned char (*tree)[H]) {
17
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) SHA256(data + (size_t)i * BLK, BLK, tree[n - 1 + i]);
18
  for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) hash_pair(tree[2 * i + 1], tree[2 * i + 2], tree[i]);
19
}
20
 
21
/* Verify block i using only the sibling hashes on its path, against a trusted root. */
22
bool verify(const unsigned char *block, int i, int n, unsigned char (*tree)[H], const unsigned char *root) {
23
  unsigned char cur[H];
24
  SHA256(block, BLK, cur);
25
  for (int node = n - 1 + i; node > 0; node = (node - 1) / 2) {
26
    bool left = (node % 2) == 1;
27
    int sib = left ? node + 1 : node - 1;
28
    unsigned char up[H];
29
    if (left) hash_pair(cur, tree[sib], up); else hash_pair(tree[sib], cur, up);
30
    memcpy(cur, up, H);
31
  }
32
  return memcmp(cur, root, H) == 0;
33
}

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

The main computer and the mobile-network chip pass messages through a shared ring of slots. One side writes and moves a marker, and the other reads and moves its own marker. The order of these steps matters, or the reader gets half-written messages.

Application processor (AP)
The main processor running Linux and applications.
Modem
The chip that handles the mobile network connection.
Ring buffer
A fixed array used in a circle, with head and tail positions.
Doorbell
A signal, such as a register write, telling the other side new data is ready.
Release / acquire
Memory-order rules that make data written before a release visible after the matching acquire.
SPSC
Single producer, single consumer: exactly one writer and one reader.
Link recovery
Detecting a crashed or reset peer and bringing the connection back cleanly.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Many telematics units pair an application processor (AP, running Linux) with a modem chip, joined by PCIe, USB or Ethernet. Qualcomm calls this kind of pairing fusion; the posting lists those three links. Over PCIe, the two sides typically share memory and pass messages through ring buffers: one side writes entries and advances a head index, the other reads and advances a tail index, and doorbells (register writes or interrupts) say that new entries exist. A single-producer single-consumer ring needs no lock: each index has exactly one writer. Correctness depends on memory ordering. The producer must make the entry's data visible before publishing the new head, and the consumer must read the head before the data. In C11 that's a release store and an acquire load. Real links add more: framing with lengths and sequence numbers, checksums for links without hardware integrity, and link recovery. If the modem crashes or the link resets, both sides must detect it (timeouts, sequence gaps), reset their rings and renegotiate, without the AP hanging. Power management matters too: the link may enter low-power states, so waking it costs time on the first message.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Corrupted messages once a day

The AP–modem control channel occasionally delivers messages with garbage in the payload, roughly once per day per thousand units. It never happens on x86 test benches, only on the ARM-based units.

1 · Find the race

The producer wrote the head index with a plain store. On ARM, the store to head could become visible before the payload, so the consumer read a half-written slot.

2 · Fix ordering

Head and tail become C11 atomics with release stores and acquire loads. On real shared memory with a device, the matching barriers and cache maintenance for DMA apply too.

3 · Detect the rest

Each message carries a sequence number. A gap triggers resynchronization, and a timeout with no doorbell triggers link recovery.

4 · Prove it

A stress test with ThreadSanitizer and millions of messages runs in CI, plus a hardware soak with forced modem resets.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Large robot AI models think slowly, but robot arms need commands many times a second. So the model plans a short burst of moves at once, and a fast loop plays them back. New plans are blended in smoothly, and the robot holds still if plans stop arriving.

VLA (vision-language-action) model
A model that takes images and an instruction and outputs robot actions.
Action chunk
A sequence of future actions predicted in one model run.
Control rate
How often the low-level controller sends a command, such as 50 times a second.
Temporal ensembling
Averaging the actions that several overlapping chunks predict for the same moment.
Staleness

Real-time loop
