2 · MENTAL MODEL

A vision-language-action (VLA) model takes camera images and an instruction and outputs robot actions. These models are large, so one inference may take 50–300 ms, while a robot arm's controller needs a new command every few milliseconds. The common bridge is action chunking: each inference predicts a chunk of the next H actions (say 50 steps at 50 Hz, one second). A low-level controller runs at its own fast rate, following the chunk, while the next inference runs in the background. Three problems appear. Latency: by the time a chunk arrives, its first actions are already in the past. Skip the actions for elapsed time so the robot doesn't jerk backwards. Discontinuities: switching from one chunk to the next can cause a jump. Temporal ensembling (from the ACT work on action chunking) averages all chunks that cover the current time, weighting older predictions more or less with an exponential factor, which smooths motion. Staleness: if inference stalls, the robot keeps executing an old plan. The executor must detect that the current chunk is used up or too old and command a safe hold. Keep the fast loop real-time: no memory allocation, no locks that can block, and fixed-size buffers.

MAKE IT STICK

A tour guide who walks ahead plotting the next stretch of the route while the group follows the last one. When a new plan arrives, the group blends into it instead of turning sharply; if the guide goes silent, the group stops rather than walking off a cliff.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The arm that twitches every second

A team deploys a VLA policy on a 7-joint arm. Inference takes 180 ms, chunks are 50 steps at 50 Hz, and the arm jerks visibly each time a new chunk arrives. Once, when the inference server hiccuped, the arm kept moving past its target.

1 · Latency

Each chunk was played from its first action on arrival, 9 ticks late, so the arm jumped back in time. Indexing by ticks since the observation removes most of the jump.

2 · Smoothing

Temporal ensembling averages the overlapping chunks. Motion becomes smooth, at the cost of slightly slower reaction to new instructions.

3 · Stale plans

When no chunk covers the current tick, the executor returns 'hold', and the arm's controller holds position. A watchdog also checks inference health.

4 · Real-time hygiene

The control loop uses fixed buffers and a lock-free handoff from the inference thread. Worst-case loop time is measured and logged.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

An AI that drives a robot can make mistakes, so a simple safety checker watches every command. If a command would get too close to a person or object, the checker takes over and stops the robot. The AI gets control back only after things are safe for a while.

Simplex architecture
A learned controller plus a simple, verified safety controller, with a switch between them.
Safety envelope
The set of states and commands known to be safe.
Stopping distance
How far the robot moves before it can stop: reaction distance plus braking distance.
Fallback controller
The simple controller that brings the robot to a safe state.
Intervention rate
How often the safety layer overrides the learned policy.
Hysteresis
Requiring a calm period before switching back, to avoid flickering.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A learned policy can't be fully verified, but a robot near people must have guarantees. The Simplex architecture handles this with three parts. An advanced controller (the learned policy) proposes commands. A simple, verifiable safety controller (stop, brake, retreat) can always bring the robot to a safe state. A decision module checks every proposed command against a safety envelope, and switches to the safety controller if the command would leave it. Envelope checks are simple physics: speed limits near humans, joint and workspace limits, and stopping distance. At speed v with deceleration a and reaction time t_r, the robot needs v·t_r + v²/(2a) to stop. If the distance to the nearest obstacle is less than that plus a margin, the proposed command isn't safe. Switch back to the learned policy only after a period inside the envelope (hysteresis), or the robot flickers between modes. Log every intervention: the intervention rate is a key safety and quality metric for learned behaviors. Safety standards such as ISO 10218 (industrial robots) and ISO/TS 15066 (collaborative robots) shape the limits for real products.

MAKE IT STICK

A learner driver with an instructor who has their own brake pedal. The learner drives; the instructor only brakes when the car would get too close to something, then lets the learner continue once things are calm.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A mobile robot in a busy lab

A learned navigation policy drives a mobile manipulator through a lab with people. It's usually smooth, but twice it approached a person faster than staff were comfortable with.

1 · Add the envelope

A supervisor checks each proposed speed against the stopping distance to the nearest obstacle from the depth sensors, with a margin and a speed cap near people.

2 · Fallback

On violation, a simple controller brakes at a known deceleration. It is small enough to review line by line and test exhaustively.

3 · Hysteresis

Control returns to the policy after 20 calm cycles. Without this, the robot stuttered at doorways as it flipped between modes.

4 · Metrics

Interventions per hour are logged with sensor snapshots. They feed back into policy training data and form a release gate (lesson 35.3).

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Robot tests are slow and costly, so we only get a few trials. A small number of trials leaves a lot of uncertainty about the true success rate. This lesson only promotes a new robot policy when it is clearly better on every important task.

Success rate
Share of trials where the robot completed the task.
Confidence interval
A range likely to contain the true value, given the data.
Wilson interval
A confidence interval for proportions that works well with small samples.
Lower bound
The bottom of the interval; a cautious estimate.
Task suite
A fixed set of tasks and conditions used for every evaluation.
Sim-to-real gap
The difference between results in simulation and on real robots.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Robot policies are judged by success rate on a set of tasks, but real-robot trials are expensive, so sample sizes are small. 18 successes in 20 trials isn't 90% with certainty. A confidence interval shows the uncertainty. For proportions, the Wilson interval behaves well with small samples and rates near 0 or 1. Gate decisions should use the interval's lower bound: a new policy is promoted only if its lower bound beats the current one's point estimate, or if the difference is clearly positive. Evaluate on a task suite that covers the variety you care about: different objects, lighting, positions. Report per task, because a gain on easy tasks can hide a loss on hard ones. Simulation gives thousands of trials cheaply, but the sim-to-real gap means sim results may not transfer. Track the correlation between sim and real scores, and use sim to screen candidates and real trials to decide. A release gate checks several things together: success with confidence, no regression on any critical task, safety intervention rate (lesson 35.2) not worse, and latency within budget.

MAKE IT STICK

Judging a new recipe from 20 taste tests. 18 of 20 liked it, but with so few tasters you'd say 'somewhere between about 70% and 97%'. Before replacing the old recipe, you want the low end of that range to beat it, for every type of customer.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 'better' policy that wasn't

A new manipulation policy scores 92% versus the current 85% on 25 real trials each. The team wants to ship it. A week later, operators report it fails often on transparent objects.

// Wilson score interval for k successes in n trials (z = 1.96 for ~95%).

Interval wilson(int k, int n, double z = 1.96) {
10

11
  double p = static_cast<double>(k) / n, z2 = z * z;
12

13

14

15
  return {std::max(0.0, c - half), p, std::min(1.0, c + half)};

}

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

This lesson explains what the Anthropic role involves and how its interviews are reported to work. It then practises a typical hands-on problem: a job queue where workers borrow jobs for a limited time. Jobs that keep failing go to a separate list for people to check.

Lease
Temporary ownership of a job that expires unless renewed or completed.
Ack (acknowledge)
A worker's message that a job is finished.
Fencing token
A number issued with each lease so stale owners can be rejected.
Dead-letter queue

2 · MENTAL MODEL

What the role really is. One requisition covers SF, NYC and Seattle (POSTED); the two LinkedIn cards are the same job. You interview for the Infrastructure organization, and team placement happens after the interview (POSTED). So prepare broadly: training and serving reliability, clusters, scheduling, data systems. The loop. Anthropic's application form says it does not run LeetCode-style interviews and wants practical coding in your best language (POSTED). Third-party guides report a recruiter call, a technical screen and about 4–5 rounds: coding, system design, a project deep dive, a hiring-manager/behavioral round and a culture/values round (PUBLIC, reported). Coding is reported to grow in stages, adding concurrency and failure cases as you go. Practice problem. A work queue with leases is a classic practical exercise. A worker leases a job for a fixed time. It must ack before the lease expires, or the job returns to the queue. Each lease gets a token, so a slow worker's late ack can't complete a job that someone else now owns. After too many attempts, the job goes to a dead-letter queue for humans to inspect. Mapping your Poly experience. Staff-level stories show scope, numbers and influence. Frame driver debugging as reliability ownership: the failure rate you measured, the root cause you proved, and the fleet-level result. The 6-week plan is in the sim.

This lesson explains the Qualcomm platform role and how its interviews are reported to work. It then practises classic chip-level C: setting bits inside a hardware register, and packing a message header with an error check.

Bitfield
A group of bits inside a larger value that holds one setting.
Mask
A value with 1s where the field's bits are, used to isolate or clear them.
Endianness
The byte order of multi-byte values: big-endian puts the most significant byte first.
CRC-32
A 32-bit checksum that detects accidental changes in data.

This lesson explains the Microsoft robotics role and its reported interviews. Then it builds a small message bus like the one robot software uses. Each listener chooses whether it must get every message, or only the newest few.

Topic
A named channel that publishers send messages to and subscribers listen on.

Settings that control delivery guarantees and buffering.

Messages are not dropped; the publisher waits or retries.

Messages may be dropped under load.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

What the role really is. A principal-level technical staff role in Microsoft Robotics. It covers bringing vision-language-action models to real robots, ROS 2 and Nav2, sim-to-real, safe-autonomy boundaries with human-in-the-loop fallback, evaluation and validation gates, and ML serving (POSTED). The posting lists Microsoft's values: respect, integrity, accountability and growth mindset (POSTED). Practice problem. ROS 2 passes messages over topics with QoS (quality of service) settings. Reliable delivery retries until received; best effort may drop. History depth (keep last N) bounds memory: when a slow subscriber's queue is full, the oldest message is dropped. 1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Senior interviews ask for stories about your past work. This lesson gives ten common questions with fill-in templates, using only your real experience. It also shows how to check that an improvement you claim is real and not luck.

STAR
Situation, Task, Action, Result: a structure for telling work stories.
Scope
How far your work reached: your team, several teams, or the whole company.
Depth ladder
Follow-up questions that go one level deeper each time.
Bootstrap
Estimating uncertainty by resampling your own data many times.
Confidence interval
A range likely to contain the true value.
Placeholder

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Every one of these loops is reported to include a behavioral, leadership or project deep-dive round. At staff and principal level, interviewers look for scope (beyond your own team), ambiguity (you defined the problem), influence (others changed what they did), and measured results. The STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result) keeps stories tight: two sentences of situation, one of task, most of the time on your actions, and a result with a number. The bank in the sim has 10 prompts with templates. The brackets are placeholders: fill them only with things you actually did and can defend under questioning. Deep dives then go down a depth ladder: what you did, why, what else you considered, what went wrong, and what you'd do now. Prepare each story to the fourth level. Honest numbers. 'Failures fell 40%' invites the question 'how sure are you?'. A bootstrap confidence interval answers it: resample your before and after data many times, recompute the difference each time, and report the middle 95% of results. If the interval includes zero, say the improvement isn't established. That honesty is itself a staff-level signal.

MAKE IT STICK

A courtroom witness. Tell the story in order, say exactly what you did, and back the key claim with evidence that holds up under cross-examination.

Chips are tested before they ship and when they come back broken. Memory tests follow a fixed walk through every address, writing and reading patterns in both directions. This lesson builds that walk, injects realistic defects, and shows which ones each step catches.

Fault model
A precise description of how hardware can be broken, such as a bit stuck at 1.
Stuck-at fault
A memory bit that always reads the same value, whatever is written.
Transition fault
A bit that can't change in one direction, for example from 1 back to 0.
Coupling fault
Writing one cell (the aggressor) changes a different cell (the victim).
March test
A sequence of passes over all addresses, each doing a small read/write recipe at every address, in a set direction.
Manufacturing screen
A fast test run on every unit to decide whether it ships, and in which bin.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A diagnostic test answers a narrow question quickly: is this part good enough to ship, and if not, where is it broken? Memory is the classic example. Real defects follow a few fault models. A stuck-at fault is a bit that always reads 0 or 1. A transition fault is a bit that can't change in one direction (it can go 0→1 but not 1→0). A coupling fault is when writing one cell (the *aggressor*) flips another (the *victim*). Address-decoder faults make two addresses hit the same cell. Writing random data and reading it back misses many of these. March tests do better: a fixed sequence of *march elements*, each walking every address up (⇑) or down (⇓) and doing a short read/write recipe at each one. March C- is ⇕(w0); ⇑(r0,w1); ⇑(r1,w0); ⇓(r0,w1); ⇓(r1,w0); ⇕(r0). That is 10 operations per cell (10N), and it detects all stuck-at, transition and unlinked coupling faults. The direction matters: a coupling fault where a low address disturbs a high one is caught going up, and the reverse going down. In production the same idea scales to a whole SoC. Stress tests push power, temperature and bandwidth to the edges (power-virus kernels, DMA storms, all cores at max frequency). Screening decides pass/fail/bin from the results. A good framework logs the first failing address, the element and the expected vs actual value, because that pattern (one bit in every word, one row, one bank) points to the root cause: a bad cell, a bad row driver, or a signal-integrity problem on one data line.

Checking every seat in a stadium by having a usher walk each row forwards, then backwards, asking each seat to stand up and sit down. Walking both ways catches the seat that only collapses when its neighbour on one particular side stands up.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The module that failed only when it was hot

A batch of SoC modules passes the factory memory test, but a data-center customer reports rare corrupted results after a few hours under load. Returned modules pass the same test on the bench.

1 · Why the old test passed

The factory test wrote every cell, then read every cell back, once, at room temperature. If writing a lower cell flips a higher one, the victim is rewritten afterwards and the flip is hidden.

2 · Reproducing the failure

Run March C- in both directions inside a thermal chamber while a power-virus kernel loads the cores. March C- reads each cell before writing it, so the disturbed value is seen: the test fails in element 1 at addresses that share one row, with one bit wrong.

3 · Root cause from the pattern

One row, one bit, only when hot: a weak cell coupled to its neighbour, made worse by temperature. That points at the memory vendor's lot, not the board design.

4 · Changing the screen

Add March C- at hot temperature to the manufacturing screen, bin marginal parts, and log first-failure records so field returns can be matched to factory data.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

GPU designers predict speed with simulators before any chip exists. The key effect is that the GPU switches to another group of threads whenever one is waiting for memory. This lesson builds a tiny cycle-by-cycle simulator and checks it against a simple formula.

Warp
A group of 32 GPU threads that execute the same instruction together.
SM (streaming multiprocessor)
One GPU core block with its own schedulers, registers and shared memory.
Latency hiding
Keeping the hardware busy by running other warps while one waits.
Occupancy
Resident warps divided by the maximum the SM can hold.
Performance model
A program that predicts how many cycles hardware takes, not just what it computes.
Scoreboard
Hardware that tracks which registers are still waiting for results, so dependent instructions stall.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

GPU architects test ideas in simulators long before silicon exists. A functional model says *what* the hardware computes; a performance model says *how long* it takes. The core idea of a GPU is latency hiding. A streaming multiprocessor (SM) holds many warps (groups of 32 threads that run one instruction together). When one warp waits for memory, the warp scheduler issues an instruction from another ready warp, so the pipeline stays busy. Suppose each warp does m compute instructions and then a memory load that takes L cycles. One warp keeps the issue slot busy only m/(m+L) of the time. With W warps the best case is about min(1, W·m/(m+L)). So you need roughly (m+L)/m warps to keep it busy. Occupancy (resident warps / maximum warps) is limited by registers and shared memory per thread block, so using more registers per thread can *lower* performance by reducing warps. A cycle-level simulator makes this concrete: every cycle, pick one ready warp, issue its next instruction, and if it is a load, mark it busy until cycle + L. Count issued cycles / total cycles. Real simulators add many more details: several schedulers per SM, a scoreboard for register dependencies, cache hit rates, memory bandwidth limits and bank conflicts. The method doesn't change: model the simple thing exactly, check it against the analytic formula, then add one effect at a time and validate against silicon or RTL.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The kernel that got slower with more registers

An engineer unrolls a loop so each thread keeps more values in registers. The kernel does fewer instructions but runs 30% slower on the target GPU.

1 · The occupancy drop

Registers per thread went from 64 to 128. The SM's register file is fixed, so the number of resident warps halved. Each warp still waits about 400 cycles per memory load.

2 · Modelling it

With m = 20 compute instructions per load and L = 400, one warp is busy about 5% of the time. 32 warps reach full use; 16 warps reach only about 80%. The simulator shows the same drop the profiler does.

3 · The fix

Limit registers with launch bounds so occupancy returns, or increase the work per load (larger m) by reusing data from shared memory. Measure both in the model before rewriting the kernel.

4 · Architect's view

The same model answers hardware questions: how much would a bigger register file help, or a cache that cuts L to 200 for this workload? That is what performance models are for.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Chip designs are huge collections of rectangles. Many calculations, like how much area is covered, need careful sweeping across the shapes. To run on many machines, the design is cut into tiles, and each tile also reads a thin border from its neighbours. This lesson checks that the tiled answer matches the single-run answer.

Rectilinear polygon
A shape whose edges are all horizontal or vertical, typical in chip layouts.
Sweep line
An algorithm that moves an imaginary line across the plane and updates a running state at each event.
Coordinate compression
Replacing coordinates by their rank among all distinct values, so arrays can be indexed by them.
Tile
One rectangular piece of a large layout processed independently.
Halo
An extra border around a tile, copied from neighbours, so local operations near the edge see everything they need.
Computational lithography
Simulating and correcting how patterns print on silicon, a huge geometry and optics workload.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A modern chip layout is billions of polygons, mostly rectilinear (all edges horizontal or vertical). Manufacturing steps such as optical proximity correction, design-rule checks and lithography simulation are geometry computations over these shapes. Computational lithography is the NVIDIA cuLitho area. Two ideas carry most of the weight. Sweep lines: to compute the area covered by a set of overlapping rectangles, sort the x-edges and sweep left to right. Between two consecutive x values, the covered length on the y-axis is constant, so area = Σ covered_y × Δx. With coordinate compression and a counter per y-interval, this is O(n²) simply or O(n log n) with a segment tree. Tiling with halos: one layout is far too big for one machine, so cut it into tiles and process tiles in parallel (on GPUs, across a cluster). An operation that looks at neighbours within distance r (an optical kernel's radius, a spacing rule) needs shapes from just outside the tile. So each worker reads its tile plus a halo of width r, computes, and keeps only results inside its core tile. That gives exactly the same answer as a single huge run, which you can test. The trade-offs are classic distributed-systems ones. Smaller tiles mean more parallelism but more halo overhead: the ratio is about 4r/T for tile side T. Uneven density causes stragglers, so split dense tiles further. And because jobs run for millions of compute hours, tiles must be idempotent and restartable.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The tile seams that showed up on the wafer

A distributed lithography-correction job splits a layout into tiles across a GPU cluster. Results look right in each tile, but checks find mismatched corrections along tile boundaries.

1 · The cause

The correction at a point depends on all shapes within the optical radius r. Workers read only their own tile, so shapes just across the boundary were invisible and edge corrections were computed from incomplete data.

2 · The fix: halos

Each worker now reads its tile plus a halo of width r, computes, and writes only results inside its core. The seams disappear, and a regression test checks that the tiled output equals a single-tile run on small layouts.

3 · The cost

With tile side T and halo r, extra work is about 4r/T. Tiles that are too small waste time on halos; tiles that are too large reduce parallelism and make stragglers worse. Dense regions get split further.

4 · At scale

Tiles are idempotent tasks with content-addressed inputs, so a failed task is just rerun. Progress, retries and straggler detection are what keep a million-GPU-hour job on schedule.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Some cloud sites have no internet connection at all. They still need updates, so the provider builds its own Linux: chosen packages, a carefully configured kernel, and signed update bundles carried in. This lesson builds the two core tools: a package resolver and a kernel config merger.

Linux distribution
A complete, curated set of kernel, packages and tools that are built, tested and updated together.
Dependency resolution
Choosing package versions that satisfy every package's requirements, then installing in a valid order.
Topological order
An ordering where every package comes after the packages it depends on.
Kconfig / CONFIG_ option
The Linux kernel's build options, such as CONFIG_SECURITY_SELINUX=y.
Config fragment
A small file of CONFIG_ settings merged on top of a base configuration.
Air-gapped
A network with no connection to the internet; updates arrive on physical media or a one-way transfer.
Rollback protection
Refusing to install an older (possibly vulnerable) version than the one already trusted.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A cloud that runs air-gapped (no internet, for governments and regulated customers) still needs security updates. So the provider maintains its own Linux distribution: a curated set of packages, a kernel with a controlled configuration, and an update pipeline that works without network access to the outside. Four skills matter. Package resolution: each package declares dependencies with version constraints ("libssl >= 3.0"). The resolver picks one version per package that satisfies every constraint, then installs in dependency order (a topological sort), and it must report conflicts and cycles clearly. Real resolvers (libsolv for dnf and zypper, apt's solver) treat this as a satisfiability problem. A greedy "highest version that fits" works for most cases and is what you can write in an interview. Kernel configuration management: kernels are configured by thousands of CONFIG_ options. Teams keep a small defconfig plus fragments (security.cfg, debug.cfg, hardware.cfg) merged in order, later ones winning. The kernel's own merge_config.sh does this and warns when a value is overridden. Then *make olddefconfig* fills in dependencies, and a check confirms that every option you asked for actually survived, because Kconfig silently drops options whose dependencies aren't met. Kernel updates: track a long-term-support (LTS) branch, apply stable patches, rebuild out-of-tree modules, and roll out through canary nodes with an A/B image so a bad kernel rolls back (see 34.1). Air-gapped delivery: updates ship as a signed bundle (packages plus repository metadata). The site verifies signatures against keys it already trusts, rejects old bundles (rollback protection via a monotonically increasing version), and mirrors the bundle internally. Reproducible builds let a customer rebuild and compare hashes.

MAKE IT STICK

Running a pharmacy on a remote island. You stock only medicines you've checked, each prescription must be compatible with the others the patient takes, and new stock arrives in sealed, signed crates on a ship, never by phone order.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The security option that quietly disappeared

A team adds CONFIG_SECURITY_LOCKDOWN_LSM=y to a security fragment for the air-gapped node image. The kernel builds, ships to a test site, and an audit finds lockdown isn't enabled.

1 · What happened

The option depends on another setting the base defconfig had turned off. make olddefconfig quietly dropped the request. Nothing failed, so nobody noticed.

2 · The guard

The build now compares the requested fragments against the final .config and fails if any requested value didn't survive. Fragment overrides are logged, so reviewers see when debug.cfg turns off something security.cfg turned on.

3 · Shipping the fix to an air-gapped site

The fixed kernel and packages go into a signed bundle with a higher version number. The site verifies the signature with a key it already trusts, refuses any bundle older than what it has, and mirrors it internally.

4 · Rolling out

Canary nodes boot the new image in the B slot; health checks pass; the rest follow in waves. A failed boot falls back to slot A automatically (34.1).

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Cloud customers each get a private network, even though they all share the same cables. The trick is to wrap each customer packet inside another packet addressed between servers. This lesson builds that wrapper, the table that knows where each customer machine lives, and the size limit that trips up many teams.

Overlay network
A virtual network built by wrapping packets inside other packets that travel over the real network.
VXLAN
A standard wrapper that puts an Ethernet frame inside a UDP packet with a 24-bit network ID (RFC 7348).
VNI
VXLAN network identifier: which customer network a packet belongs to.
VTEP
VXLAN tunnel endpoint: the host or NIC that wraps and unwraps packets.
FDB (forwarding database)
A table mapping a MAC address (and VNI) to where to send frames for it.
MTU
Maximum transmission unit: the largest packet a link carries without fragmenting.
Netlink
The Linux socket API that tools such as ip and bridge use to configure the kernel's networking.
SmartNIC
A network card with its own processor, often running Linux, that handles packet work in hardware.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Clouds give every customer a private network on top of shared physical wires. Oracle calls it a VCN and Amazon calls it a VPC. The usual trick is an overlay: wrap the customer's Ethernet frame inside a UDP packet that travels between hosts. VXLAN (RFC 7348) is the standard wrapper. The outer packet is Ethernet (14 bytes) + IPv4 (20) + UDP (8, destination port 4789) + VXLAN header (8), so it is 50 bytes larger than the inner frame. The VXLAN header carries a 24-bit VNI (virtual network identifier, about 16 million networks), with flags byte 0x08 meaning "VNI is valid". Each host runs a VTEP (VXLAN tunnel endpoint). Its forwarding database (FDB) maps (inner MAC, VNI) → remote VTEP IP. Entries are learned from received packets or programmed by the SDN controller, and they age out. MTU math is the most common real bug. If the physical MTU is 1500, the inner MTU must be 1450, or the underlay must use jumbo frames (9000). Otherwise large packets are dropped, and TCP connections hang after the handshake, because small packets work and big ones vanish. On Linux you build this with netlink (the kernel's configuration socket API, used by *ip link add vxlan0 type vxlan id 42 dstport 4789*), bridges and the FDB (*bridge fdb*). For speed, the per-packet work moves to a fast path: tc or XDP eBPF programs in the kernel, or a SmartNIC that does encapsulation in hardware. That is the "card" in OCI's card management: the NIC runs its own embedded Linux, which needs provisioning, monitoring, firmware updates and troubleshooting like any other device.

MAKE IT STICK

Posting a letter inside a larger envelope. The inner envelope has the customer's own addresses; the outer one has the building-to-building addresses and a room number (the VNI). The outer envelope takes up space, so the inner letter must be a little smaller to fit through the same mail slot.

INTERACTIVE LAB

IN PLAIN WORDS

THE TECHNICAL VERSION Full-size VM packets cross the overlay.

Small packets work and big ones vanish. Shrink the inner packet size limit to 1450 or use jumbo frames underneath.
Term: MTU black hole
START WITH THE INCIDENT
SSH connects, then freezes

After a new overlay network goes live, customers can ping and open SSH sessions to their VMs, but the session freezes as soon as they run a command with lots of output. File copies stall.

1 · Small works, big fails

Ping and the TCP handshake use small packets. Bulk data uses full-size 1500-byte frames. Add 50 bytes of VXLAN and the outer packet is 1550 bytes on a 1500-byte underlay, so it is dropped.

2 · Why it isn't obvious

VXLAN packets usually have the IPv4 don't-fragment bit set, and the ICMP 'too big' message often goes back to the host, not the VM. The VM never learns to send smaller packets.

3 · The fix

Either set the VM's interface MTU to 1450 through DHCP, or run the underlay with jumbo frames (9000) so 1500-byte inner frames fit. Add a monitoring probe that sends a full-size packet across every new tunnel.

4 · Preventing it next time

The SDN controller rejects configurations where the inner MTU plus 50 exceeds the underlay MTU, and the SmartNIC exports drop counters by reason, so 'too big' drops show up on a dashboard.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Security sensors watch everything a computer does: programs starting, files opening, network connections. They link events into a family tree of processes and match suspicious patterns. Their detection rules are updated daily, and a bad update can crash every machine at once. This lesson builds the tree, the pattern check, and the validator that stops bad rules.

Endpoint sensor
Security software on each computer that watches activity and can block threats.
Process tree
The parent-child chain of which program started which.
Behavioural rule
A detection that matches a pattern of actions rather than a known bad file.
Ring buffer
A fixed-size queue that wraps around; when full, new events are counted as dropped instead of blocking.
Content update
New detection rules or templates sent to sensors without changing their code.
Staged rollout
Sending an update to a small group first, checking health, then widening.
eBPF
Small verified programs that run inside the Linux kernel at hook points.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An endpoint sensor has three parts. Collection happens in privileged hooks: eBPF programs on Linux tracepoints and LSM hooks, kernel callbacks and ETW on Windows, and the EndpointSecurity framework on macOS. The core card is 4.4. Correlation happens in user space: events are joined into a process tree (who launched whom), and behavioural rules look for patterns such as "a document editor launched a shell that opened an outbound connection". Response blocks, kills or isolates on the box, and sends telemetry to the cloud. Three engineering rules keep it safe. Bounded cost per event: thousands of events per second arrive. Use a fixed-size ring buffer between kernel and user space, count drops instead of blocking, and keep ancestry walks bounded. Process-tree hygiene: PIDs are reused. Key processes by (pid, start time), and keep exited parents briefly so children can still be attributed. Safe content updates: detection logic changes daily through content (rules, templates), not code. Content is input to privileged code, so it needs the same care as code. On July 19, 2024, a faulty content update to the Windows sensor crashed about 8.5 million machines. CrowdStrike's public root-cause analysis describes a mismatch between the input fields a template defined (21) and the fields the sensor supplied (20), which led to an out-of-bounds read. The fixes it lists are bounds checks in the interpreter, a content validator that checks field counts, and staged deployment of content through canary rings with customer control. These apply to anyone shipping data into privileged code.

MAKE IT STICK

Airport security with a rulebook delivered every morning. The guards (sensor) must keep the queue moving, know which traveller came with whom, and never follow a page of the rulebook that refers to a checkpoint that doesn't exist. New pages are tried at one gate before every airport.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
A rule update reaches every machine at once

A detection team ships a new rule template that references one more input field than the sensor passes in. Tests passed because the test harness supplied every field. The update goes to all customers within minutes.

1 · What fails

The interpreter reads the missing field past the end of the array. In user space that's a crash; in a kernel driver loaded at boot, it's a crash on every boot. This is the class of failure CrowdStrike's public July 2024 root-cause analysis describes (PUBLIC).

2 · Validation

The content validator now checks every field reference against the field count the deployed sensor version supplies, and the interpreter bounds-checks every access anyway (defence in depth).

3 · Staged deployment

Content goes to internal machines, then a small canary ring, then wider rings, with crash and heartbeat telemetry gating each step. Customers can choose how early they receive content.

4 · Recovery

The sensor tracks repeated crashes after a content load and falls back to the previous known-good content on the next boot, so a bad update can't loop forever.

WHICH JOB NEEDS THIS
Anthropic · Staff + Sr. Software Engineer, Scaling (Seattle)
POSTED: 'Maximize compute efficiency and optimize cost across the fleet by autoscaling and orchestrating production, research, and experimental workloads across multiple cloud providers'; routing 'across thousands of accelerators'.

1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

AI models run on expensive chips that cost money even when idle. The fleet should grow when many requests arrive and shrink when they don't, but new servers take minutes to start. This lesson builds the scaling rule, the delay that stops it from shrinking too quickly, and the choice of which pool of machines to use.

Autoscaler
A control loop that changes the number of replicas based on load.
Target tracking
Scaling so a metric per replica (such as requests in flight) stays near a target.
Stabilization window
When scaling down, use the highest recommendation over a recent period, so brief dips don't remove capacity.
Cold start
The time a new replica needs before it can serve: image pull, weight loading, warm-up.
Headroom
Spare capacity kept on purpose to absorb bursts while new replicas start.
Preemption
Evicting lower-priority work to free capacity for higher-priority work.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Serving a model costs accelerator time whether or not anyone is using it, so the fleet must grow and shrink with demand. CPU utilisation is a poor signal for inference. The better signals are queue depth or in-flight requests per replica and latency SLOs (time to first token, p99). Target tracking: if each replica handles about q requests in flight, then desired = ceil(total_in_flight / q), clamped to [min, max]. Three details decide whether this works in practice. Asymmetry: scale up fast, scale down slow. A stabilization window uses the *maximum* desired value over the last few minutes when scaling down, so a brief dip doesn't remove capacity you'll need a minute later. That is how Kubernetes' HPA behaves (its default scale-down stabilization is 300 s). Cold starts: a new replica must pull a large image and load tens or hundreds of GB of weights onto accelerators, which takes minutes. So scale on a forecast or keep headroom, warm pools or pre-loaded weights, and don't count replicas as capacity until they pass a readiness check. Multi-pool placement: capacity lives in many pools (accelerator types, regions, clouds) with different cost, availability and performance per model. Place new replicas in the cheapest pool that has capacity and meets latency, and fall back to the next pool. Keep production above research when capacity is tight (priority and preemption: research jobs on spare capacity are evicted first). Anthropic's posting adds routing on top: the router sends each request to a replica with room. Chapter 26.2 covers prefill/decode and KV-cache-aware routing, so this lesson focuses on the scaling and placement loop.

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant that calls in cooks when the queue at the door grows. Cooks take twenty minutes to arrive, so you call early, and you don't send anyone home the moment the queue shrinks for a minute.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The fleet that shrank right before the morning peak

Traffic dips for two minutes at 8:58 a.m. The autoscaler removes a third of the replicas. At 9:00 traffic doubles, and new replicas need eight minutes to load weights. Latency SLOs are missed for ten minutes.

1 · Why it happened

The scaler used the current recommendation for both directions. A short dip looked like lower demand, and capacity that takes minutes to restore was removed in seconds.

2 · Stabilization

Scale-down now uses the maximum recommendation over the last 10 minutes; scale-up still reacts immediately. The 8:58 dip no longer removes anything.

3 · Cold starts

Replicas count as capacity only after readiness checks pass. A small warm pool with weights preloaded absorbs bursts while new replicas start, and a daily forecast pre-scales before known peaks.

4 · Placement under pressure

When the cheapest pool runs out, replicas go to the next pool that meets the SLO; if every pool is full, research jobs on borrowed capacity are preempted before production misses its SLO.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Kubernetes has a new version every few months, and companies run many clusters. Upgrades must follow strict version rules, never take down too many copies of an app at once, and work around jobs that run for days. This lesson writes the checks and the planner that decides which machines to upgrade now.

Version skew policy
Kubernetes' rules on how far apart component versions may be.
Control plane
The API server, scheduler, controllers and etcd that run the cluster.
Kubelet
The agent on each node that runs pods; it may lag the API server by up to three minor versions, never lead it.
Cordon / drain
Stop new pods from landing on a node, then evict the pods already there.
PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)
A limit on how many replicas of an app may be voluntarily disrupted at once.
Node image pipeline
The build that produces tested OS + kernel + runtime + kubelet images for nodes.
GitOps
Keeping desired cluster state in Git and letting controllers apply it.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Running one cluster is a project; running dozens across data centers and clouds is a lifecycle that never ends. Kubernetes releases a minor version about every four months and supports each for about a year, so upgrades never stop. The rules come from the official version skew policy. The control plane upgrades one minor version at a time (1.29 → 1.30 → 1.31, never skipping). The kubelet on nodes may be up to three minor versions older than the API server (since 1.28), but never newer. Upgrade order: control plane, then nodes. Node upgrades usually mean replacing the node image (OS, kernel, container runtime, kubelet) built in a node image pipeline, then cordon → drain → replace → uncordon. Draining respects PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs): a PDB says how many replicas of an app may be down at once, and eviction is refused if it would be exceeded. Here's the hard part named in NVIDIA's posting: EDA jobs and GPU training jobs run for days and can't be drained on demand. So upgrades must be job-aware. Mark busy nodes, upgrade idle ones first, stop scheduling new long jobs onto nodes due for upgrade, and pick up the rest when their jobs finish or at agreed maintenance windows. Upgrades go out in waves by fault domain: canary cluster, then one cluster per site, then the rest, with health checks (API latency, node readiness, error rates) gating each wave. Everything is declared in Git (GitOps, e.g. Argo CD): the desired version lives in the repo and controllers converge to it, so a manual change is a drift alert, not a fix.

Renovating a hospital without closing it. You redo one ward at a time, never more beds than the rules allow, and you wait for long-stay patients to be discharged before working on their rooms.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Big companies collect traces, metrics and logs from thousands of services. OpenTelemetry is the standard way to do that. Storing everything costs too much, so you keep every trace that shows a problem and only a sample of normal ones. You also cap how many label combinations each metric may have. This lesson builds both decisions.

OpenTelemetry (OTel)
An open standard and toolkit for traces, metrics and logs.
Span / trace
A span is one timed operation; a trace is the tree of spans for one request.
Collector
A service that receives telemetry, processes it (batch, redact, sample) and exports it to backends.
Tail sampling
Deciding whether to keep a trace after seeing all its spans, so errors and slow requests are kept.
Cardinality
The number of unique label combinations for a metric; each is a separate time series.
Telemetry contract
Agreed rules for names, required attributes and allowed labels, checked automatically.
Monitoring-as-code
Dashboards, alerts and maintenance windows defined in version-controlled files.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Every service should report how it is doing in the same format. OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the open standard for that: traces (the path of one request through services, as a tree of spans), metrics (counters, gauges and histograms) and logs, all tagged with resource attributes (service.name, deployment.environment). Apps use an OTel SDK (auto-instrumentation plus manual spans) and export over OTLP to a Collector. The Collector is a pipeline of receivers → processors → exporters. Processors do batching, attribute redaction (strip card numbers before anything leaves a bank's network), memory limiting and sampling. Then it sends to whatever backend the company uses (Dynatrace, Splunk, Grafana, Datadog). Changing vendors means changing an exporter, not every app. Two cost problems decide whether a big rollout succeeds. Sampling: storing every trace is too expensive. *Head sampling* decides at the start (keep 1%), which is cheap but drops the rare slow or failed requests you most want. *Tail sampling* buffers all spans of a trace until it completes, then keeps every trace with an error or high latency and a small percentage of the rest. The decision must be consistent per trace ID (hash-based), and all spans of a trace must reach the same Collector, which is done with a load-balancing exporter keyed by trace ID. Cardinality: each unique combination of metric labels is a separate time series. Putting user_id or request_id in a label creates millions of series and huge bills. Set a cardinality budget per metric, and fold overflow into an "other" bucket. Telemetry contracts (required attributes, naming conventions, allowed labels) checked in CI, plus monitoring-as-code (dashboards and alerts in Git), keep a large enterprise consistent.

MAKE IT STICK

A bank's mailroom. Every letter (span) gets a standard envelope (OTel). The mailroom (Collector) shreds account numbers, keeps every letter about a problem, and keeps only a sample of routine ones, so storage doesn't overflow.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The observability bill that tripled in a month

A bank rolls out OpenTelemetry to 300 services. Within a month the vendor bill triples, and during an incident engineers can't find the failing requests because head sampling at 1% dropped them.

1 · Cardinality

One team added customer_id as a metric label. A single histogram became four million series. The limiter now caps each metric at a budget and folds the rest into 'other', and a CI contract check rejects ID-like labels.

2 · Sampling

Head sampling kept 1% of traces chosen at random, so most failed requests were dropped. The Collector tier now tail-samples: every error and every trace over the SLO threshold is kept, plus 2% of the rest.

3 · Routing traces

Tail sampling needs every span of a trace in one place, so a first Collector layer uses a load-balancing exporter keyed by trace ID to send all spans of a trace to the same sampling Collector.

4 · Adoption

Teams onboard with a template: SDK config, required resource attributes, a standard dashboard and alerts in Git. Maintenance windows are code too, so planned work doesn't page anyone.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

When one action must update a database and tell other systems, crashes in between cause lost or phantom orders. The fix is to save the message in the same database transaction and send it later, safely retrying. Multi-step workflows across services undo earlier steps if a later step fails. This lesson builds both patterns.

Dual write
Writing to two systems (database and queue) separately, which can leave them inconsistent after a crash.
Transactional outbox
Saving outgoing events in a table in the same transaction as the data change, then publishing them later.
At-least-once delivery
Every message is delivered, but possibly more than once.
Idempotent consumer
A receiver that produces the same result if it gets the same message twice.
Saga
A multi-step workflow across services where each step has an undo (compensation).
Compensation
An action that reverses an earlier step, such as a refund for a charge.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A delivery order touches many systems: the order database, payment, a flight planner that reserves an aircraft and airspace, and partner notifications. The classic bug is the dual write: the service commits the order to its database, then publishes an "order created" event to a queue. If it crashes in between, the order exists but nobody hears about it. If it publishes first and the commit fails, everyone hears about an order that doesn't exist. Transactional outbox: in the *same* database transaction as the order, insert a row into an outbox table. A separate relay reads unpublished outbox rows, publishes them, and marks them sent. The commit is now the single source of truth. The relay can crash and retry, so delivery is at least once, which means consumers must be idempotent: record processed event IDs (in the same transaction as their own effect) and skip duplicates. Change-data-capture tools such as Debezium implement the relay by tailing the database log. Sagas handle workflows that span services, where no single transaction is possible. Each step has a compensation (reserve aircraft ↔ release aircraft; charge ↔ refund). If step k fails, run the compensations for steps k−1 … 1 in reverse. Compensations must themselves be idempotent and retryable, and some steps can't be undone (a drone already launched), so put those last. Workflow engines (Temporal, AWS Step Functions) persist saga state so it survives restarts. Schema design supports all of this: an order state machine (CREATED → PAID → SCHEDULED → IN_FLIGHT → DELIVERED / CANCELLED) with valid transitions enforced in code and constraints, plus an idempotency key on every external request (see 06 c28).

MAKE IT STICK

A restaurant writes each order on a ticket and pins it to the rail in the same motion. A runner takes tickets from the rail to the kitchen; if a ticket is delivered twice, the kitchen recognises the number and ignores the copy. If the dessert can't be made, the waiter undoes the earlier steps in reverse: cancels the main, then refunds the starter.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Orders that paid but never flew

A few times a week, a customer is charged for a drone delivery that is never scheduled. Logs show the order committed, then the service restarted during a deploy before publishing the event to the flight planner.

1 · The dual write

Commit then publish has a crash window. Deploys restart pods often enough that the window is hit every week.

2 · Outbox

The order and an outbox row are written in one transaction. A relay publishes unsent rows and marks them sent. A crash means a re-publish, never a loss.

3 · Idempotent planner

The flight planner records each event ID with its reservation in one transaction, so duplicates do nothing. Duplicate deliveries are now harmless and visible in metrics.

4 · Saga for cancellations

If airspace isn't available, the saga releases the aircraft reservation and then refunds the payment. Launch, which can't be undone, is the last step and happens only after every reversible step succeeds.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Privacy laws say people control how their data is used. In code that means recording what each person agreed to, checking it on every use, deleting data on schedule, and keeping some data inside a region. This lesson builds those four checks.

GDPR / CCPA
EU and California privacy laws that give people rights over their personal data.
Consent
A person's recorded agreement to a specific use (purpose) of their data, which they can withdraw.
Purpose limitation
Using data only for the purposes it was collected and agreed for.
Data minimization
Collecting and keeping only the data a purpose actually needs.
Retention period
How long a kind of data may be kept before it must be deleted or anonymized.
DSAR
Data subject access request: a person asking for a copy of their data, or its deletion.
Data residency
A requirement that data is stored and processed in a particular region.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Privacy laws in Europe (GDPR) and California (CCPA) turn into concrete system requirements. Consent is a record, not a checkbox: who agreed to what purpose (analytics, marketing, personalisation), when, under which policy version, and when they withdrew. Store it as an append-only ledger and take the latest entry per (subject, purpose). That gives you an audit trail for free. Purpose limitation: every data access names a purpose, and the check is "does this subject currently consent to (or is there another lawful basis for) this purpose?" Data minimization: collect only what a purpose needs, and drop or pseudonymize the rest early. Retention: each data category has a retention period, and a scheduled job deletes or anonymizes expired records, including derived copies, caches, search indexes and backups (backups usually expire on their own schedule). Data subject requests (DSARs): users may ask for a copy of their data or its deletion (GDPR generally allows one month to respond). This only works if you keep a data map of where each subject's data lives. Residency: some customers require data to stay in a region. Enforce it at write time (reject or route), not by policy documents. Osano sells consent and privacy tooling, so for them these aren't side concerns; they are the product. One more rule from the posting: customer and personal data stays out of AI tools except through approved, privacy-safe paths.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The marketing email after an opt-out

A user withdraws marketing consent on Monday. On Wednesday they receive a campaign email. The campaign tool read a nightly copy of a 'consented=true' column that had been overwritten, not appended.

1 · The data model

A single boolean per user lost history and timing. The consent store becomes an append-only ledger; the latest event per (subject, purpose) is the current state, and every change is auditable.

2 · Check at use

The email service calls Allowed(subject, 'marketing', now) right before sending, not from a stale copy. No record means no send.

3 · Retention and copies

The campaign tool's nightly copy had no retention rule. The sweeper now flags data categories without a rule, and copies expire within a day.

4 · Proving it

For a regulator or a SOC 2 auditor, the ledger shows when consent changed and the send logs show each check, so the fix is demonstrable, not just claimed.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

AI agents call tools: search, create a ticket, send an email. At work, every call is checked and risky ones need a person to approve. Repeats must not run twice, and every agent change is tested on real tasks before release. This lesson builds that tool gate and the test gate.

MCP (Model Context Protocol)
An open protocol for exposing tools, resources and prompts to AI applications.
Tool schema
The description of a tool's inputs (names, types, required fields) that calls are validated against.
Human-in-the-loop
A step where a person must approve before the agent's action happens.
Idempotency key
A unique key for a request so that repeating it doesn't repeat the effect.
Evaluation harness
A program that runs the agent on a fixed set of test tasks and scores the results.
Regression gate
A rule that blocks a release if scores drop compared with the current version.
Prompt injection
Text in data (a web page, an email) that tries to make the agent follow the attacker's instructions.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Core lessons 6.1–6.3 introduce agents, MCP and evals. This lesson is the production version both postings ask for. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol: an MCP server exposes tools (functions with JSON-schema inputs), resources and prompts, and an MCP client inside the agent host calls them. Because the protocol only *describes* capabilities, the host and server still enforce authorization, validation and side-effect control. A production tool layer has four checks before any tool runs. (1) Schema validation: required arguments are present and typed, and unknown arguments are rejected. (2) Risk tier: read-only tools run freely, while tools that write, send or spend need a human-in-the-loop approval unless policy allows them. (3) Idempotency keys for side-effecting tools, so an agent retry doesn't send two emails or create two tickets. (4) Audit log of every call with inputs, decision and result. RAG grounding (ch5) applies to answers: cite retrieved sources and refuse when retrieval finds nothing relevant. Evaluation decides whether a change ships. Keep a test set of real tasks with expected outcomes, grouped by category (happy path, ambiguous, adversarial/prompt injection, should-refuse). Score each run, compare with the baseline, and gate the release on overall pass rate *and* no regression in safety categories. Track business impact separately (time saved, adoption), which the Google posting asks you to quantify with SQL.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The helpful agent that emailed a customer twice

A support-automation agent drafts and sends follow-up emails. After a model update, a customer gets the same email twice, and a red-team test shows the agent will follow instructions hidden in a customer's message.

1 · Duplicate side effects

The agent retried after a tool timeout. The send tool had no idempotency key, so the retry sent again. Every side-effecting tool now requires a key, and the gate skips duplicates.

2 · Approval and audit

Sending to customers moves to the 'needs approval' tier until the eval set shows it's safe to automate; every call and decision goes to an audit log with the trace ID.

3 · Evals that block

The eval set gets an adversarial category with prompt-injection cases. The new model scored higher overall but worse on that category, and the gate now blocks that release.

4 · Impact

Adoption and time-saved are measured from the audit log with SQL: tasks completed, approvals per task and edits before sending. These numbers decide which workflows to automate next.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Garmin devices search maps with very little memory and power. Instead of checking every place, the map is cut into a grid; a search looks at nearby squares first and spreads outward only as needed. Names are kept sorted so a prefix search is a quick binary search. This lesson builds both.

POI (point of interest)
A place on a map, such as a café or water fountain, with coordinates and a name.
Spatial index
A structure that finds things by location without checking every item.
Uniform grid
Dividing the map into equal squares and listing which POIs fall in each.
Nearest neighbour (k-NN)
Finding the closest item, or k closest items, to a point.
Quadtree / R-tree
Tree indexes that split space unevenly (quadtree) or group rectangles (R-tree).
Z-order / geohash
Ways to turn a 2-D cell into one number so nearby cells are near each other in storage.
Front coding
Compressing a sorted word list by storing only what differs from the previous word.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A watch has little memory, slow storage and a small battery. Map search must still answer "nearest water fountain" or "cafés starting with *Ber*" in well under a second. Two ideas do most of the work. Spatial indexing: a naive search checks every point of interest (POI): O(n) per query and far too many flash reads. A uniform grid buckets POIs by cell (cell = floor(x / size), floor(y / size)). A nearest-neighbour query searches the query's cell, then rings of cells around it, and stops once the best distance found is smaller than the distance to the next ring. That's exact and usually touches a handful of cells. Quadtrees adapt cells to density (dense cities, empty deserts). R-trees index rectangles such as roads and areas. Geohash or Z-order (Morton) codes turn 2-D cells into 1-D keys, so nearby places sort near each other on flash, and that's how map data is tiled. Compact prefix search: name lookup over sorted strings uses binary search (lower_bound on the prefix) and needs no extra memory. Tries are faster but use more memory unless compressed. Front coding (store only the suffix that differs from the previous word) shrinks sorted name lists a lot. Memory budget thinking separates senior answers: estimate bytes per POI (coordinates as 32-bit integers in fixed units instead of doubles, an index into a string table instead of a pointer), count the flash pages a query reads, and keep the hot index in RAM while records stay on flash. Integer squared distances avoid floating point and square roots on small cores.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 'nearest' search that drained the battery

A new cycling computer firmware adds 'nearest water' search across a whole country's POIs. Searches take three seconds and visibly drain the battery on long rides.

1 · Measuring

Each query scanned all 400,000 POIs from flash, reading thousands of pages. CPU time was small; flash reads and wake time dominated energy.

2 · A grid index

POIs are bucketed into 1 km cells sorted by Z-order on flash. A query reads its cell and expands rings until the best distance beats the next ring. Typical queries touch fewer than 10 cells.

3 · Memory

The cell directory (cell key → flash offset) stays in RAM: a few bytes per non-empty cell. Records stay on flash. Coordinates are 32-bit integers; names are offsets into a front-coded string table.

4 · Result

Median query time drops to under 50 ms and flash reads by about 100×. A test compares the grid answer with a brute-force scan on random queries, so the index is proven exact.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Aircraft software must be certified. Every requirement is tested and every line traces back to a requirement. For the most critical code, you must prove each condition in a decision can change the result on its own. This lesson writes the checker for that last rule (MC/DC) and explains how flight software shares a processor safely.

DO-178C
The standard used to certify airborne software.
DAL (Design Assurance Level)
A to E: how severe a failure would be, which sets how much evidence is required.
Traceability
Links from requirements to code to tests, in both directions.
MC/DC
Modified condition/decision coverage: each condition shown to independently change a decision's outcome.
Independence pair
Two tests that differ only in one condition and give different decision results.
ARINC 653
A standard for partitioned RTOSes: fixed memory and time windows per application.
WCET
Worst-case execution time: the longest a task can take, proven by analysis or measurement.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Aircraft software is certified under DO-178C, *Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification*. Each function is assigned a Design Assurance Level (DAL) from A to E by how bad a failure would be: A is catastrophic, E is no safety effect. Higher levels require more objectives, many satisfied with independence (someone else verifies). The process is requirements-driven: high-level requirements → low-level requirements → code, with bidirectional traceability. Every requirement has tests, every line of code traces to a requirement, and nothing is untraced (no dead or extra code). Structural coverage proves the requirement-based tests exercised the code: statement coverage for Level C, plus decision coverage for B, plus MC/DC (modified condition/decision coverage) for A. MC/DC means every condition in a decision has been shown to independently affect the outcome: there is a pair of tests that differ only in that condition and give different results. For a decision with n conditions, MC/DC needs at least n+1 tests (versus 2ⁿ for all combinations). Supplements cover tools (DO-330 tool qualification), model-based development (DO-331) and object-oriented technology (DO-332). Partitioning: avionics often runs several applications of different DALs on one processor, under an ARINC 653 RTOS such as INTEGRITY-178 or VxWorks 653. Each partition gets fixed memory and fixed time windows in a repeating major frame, so a fault or overrun in one can't starve another. Timing analysis shows each task's worst-case execution time (WCET) fits its window. Coding standards such as MISRA C/C++ remove undefined behaviour. In interviews for these roles, explaining MC/DC precisely and showing traceability habits stands out more than any algorithm.

Proving each switch on a cockpit panel actually matters: for every switch, show two flights identical except for that switch, where the outcome changes. If you can't, either the switch is useless or your tests are.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The condition nobody could prove mattered

A Level A display function has the decision (weight_on_wheels && !override) || maintenance_mode. Requirement-based tests pass, but the coverage tool reports MC/DC is missing for one condition.

1 · Finding the gap

The tests never had a pair that differed only in override and changed the outcome, because every test with weight_on_wheels true also had maintenance_mode true, masking the effect.

2 · Back to requirements

Instead of writing a test just to hit coverage, the team asks which requirement describes override's behaviour when not in maintenance mode. The requirement existed, but its test case was incomplete; a new requirement-based test closes the gap.

3 · Why not 2ⁿ tests

Three conditions need at least four tests for MC/DC, not eight. Choosing the pairs deliberately keeps the test set small and every test traceable.

4 · Partitioning and timing

The display partition runs in a fixed 5 ms window of a 25 ms major frame. WCET analysis shows the function fits with margin, so an overrun elsewhere can't delay it.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Military aircraft connect their computers with a bus where one controller asks and each device only answers when asked. Every message takes a precise time, so the controller follows a fixed timetable that repeats. This lesson encodes the bus words and builds that timetable, checking that nothing runs over.

MIL-STD-1553B
A 1 Mbit/s, dual-redundant command/response data bus used in military aircraft.
Bus controller (BC)
The one device that starts every message on the bus.
Remote terminal (RT)
A device on the bus (up to 31) that answers the BC.
Command / status / data word
The three 20-bit word types: what to do, how it went, and the values.
Subaddress
A 5-bit field choosing which buffer or function inside the RT a message is for.
Major / minor frame
The repeating schedule period (major) made of fixed slots (minor).
Mode code
A special command for bus management, such as synchronize or transmit status.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

MIL-STD-1553B is the command/response data bus used on military aircraft since the 1970s, still everywhere for its determinism. It runs at 1 Mbit/s over a dual-redundant twisted pair (buses A and B). One bus controller (BC) commands up to 31 remote terminals (RTs); no RT speaks unless asked. There are three 20-bit word types (3-bit sync, 16 data bits, 1 parity bit), so each word takes 20 µs. The command word packs RT address (5 bits), transmit/receive (1), subaddress or mode (5) and word count or mode code (5). A word count of 0 means 32 words, and subaddress 0 or 31 means a mode code (e.g. synchronize, transmit status). The status word carries the RT address and flags: message error, service request, busy, subsystem flag, terminal flag. Data words carry up to 32 × 16-bit values. A BC→RT transfer is command + data words, then after a short response time (4–12 µs) the RT's status word, then an intermessage gap. So message time is about 20·(n+2) µs plus gaps. Bus software is a cyclic schedule. Messages repeat at fixed rates (e.g. 50 Hz attitude, 10 Hz fuel). The BC runs a major frame (often 1 s or the least common multiple of the periods) made of minor frames (e.g. 20 ms at 50 Hz). A message at rate r appears every (minor-rate / r) minor frames, and each minor frame's total bus time must fit with margin, which is a direct timing analysis. Offsets spread slow messages across minor frames to balance load. Engineers check traffic with analysers (AltaView, as the posting mentions) the way Ethernet engineers use Wireshark.

MAKE IT STICK

A strict classroom teacher who calls on students by number. A student speaks only when called, says exactly how many sentences were asked for, then confirms with a fixed reply. The lesson plan repeats every period, and the teacher spreads the long questions across the week so no period runs over.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The minor frame that ran long

After adding a new 10 Hz sensor message, a bus analyser shows the BC occasionally starting the next minor frame late, and a 50 Hz attitude message jitters.

1 · The load table

All 10 Hz and 5 Hz messages had offset 0, so they landed in the same minor frame as every 50 Hz message. That frame needed 19.2 ms of a 20 ms slot, and the new message pushed it over.

2 · Spreading with offsets

Giving the slow messages different offsets spreads them across the five or ten minor frames in their period. The worst frame drops to 11 ms, and the schedule check passes with margin.

3 · Checking on the wire

The analyser capture now shows every 50 Hz message starting at the same offset within its minor frame, so the jitter is gone.

4 · Evidence

The schedule table and worst-case frame time become part of the timing analysis record, re-run whenever a message is added.

#include <stdint.h>

3
/* Command word, 16 data bits (MSB first on the wire): RT(5) T/R(1) SA(5) WC(5). WC 0 means 32 words. */
4
uint16_t cmd_encode(unsigned rt, int transmit, unsigned sa, unsigned wc) {
5
  return (uint16_t)(((rt & 31u) << 11) | ((transmit ? 1u : 0u) << 10) | ((sa & 31u) << 5) | (wc & 31u));
6
}
7
typedef struct { unsigned rt, transmit, sa, words, mode; } Cmd;
8
Cmd cmd_decode(uint16_t w) {
9
  Cmd c;
10
  c.rt = (w >> 11) & 31u; c.transmit = (w >> 10) & 1u; c.sa = (w >> 5) & 31u;
11
  c.mode = (c.sa == 0 || c.sa == 31);
12
  c.words = c.mode ? 0 : ((w & 31u) ? (w & 31u) : 32u);
13
  return c;
14
}
15
 
16
/* Status word flags (bit 1 = MSB in the standard's numbering). */
17
enum { ST_MSG_ERROR = 1 << 10, ST_SERVICE_REQ = 1 << 8, ST_BUSY = 1 << 3, ST_SUBSYS = 1 << 2, ST_TERMINAL = 1 << 0 };
18
int status_ok(uint16_t st, unsigned expect_rt) {
19
  if (((st >> 11) & 31u) != expect_rt) return 0;
20
  return (st & (ST_MSG_ERROR | ST_BUSY | ST_SUBSYS | ST_TERMINAL)) == 0;
21
}
22
 
23
/* Approximate BC->RT message time: command + n data + status, 20 us each, plus response time and gap. */
24
unsigned msg_time_us(unsigned n_words, unsigned response_us, unsigned gap_us) { return 20u * (n_words + 2u) + response_us + gap_us; }
25
 
26
typedef struct { unsigned rate_hz, words, offset; } Msg;
27
 
28
/* Fill per-minor-frame bus time. minor_hz is the minor frame rate; each rate must divide it.
29
   Returns 0 if any frame exceeds capacity_us, else 1. load[] has minor_hz entries (one major frame = 1 s). */
30
int build_schedule(const Msg *m, int n, unsigned minor_hz, unsigned capacity_us, unsigned *load) {
31
  for (unsigned f = 0; f < minor_hz; f++) load[f] = 0;
32
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
33
    if (m[i].rate_hz == 0 || minor_hz % m[i].rate_hz) return 0;
34
    unsigned every = minor_hz / m[i].rate_hz;
35
    for (unsigned f = m[i].offset % every; f < minor_hz; f += every) load[f] += msg_time_us(m[i].words, 12, 4);
36
  }
37
  for (unsigned f = 0; f < minor_hz; f++) if (load[f] > capacity_us) return 0;
38
  return 1;
39
}

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

First principles means you start from facts you can measure (pixels, bits, frames per second, watts, milliseconds) and calculate what's actually needed. You don't start from what the last project did. The 5-step order keeps you from polishing things that should be deleted. Interviewers test both: they hand you a fuzzy problem and watch whether you reach for numbers.

First principles
Reasoning up from basic, verifiable facts (physics, measured numbers) instead of from precedent or analogy.
Requirement owner
The named person who asked for a requirement. Musk's rule: every requirement needs one, so it can be questioned.
Back-of-envelope estimate
A quick calculation with round numbers that tells you the order of magnitude: is it 5 MB/s or 500 MB/s?
`constexpr`
C++ keyword: the value or function can be computed at compile time, so mistakes get caught before the code runs.
`static_assert`
A compile-time check. If the condition is false, the build fails with your message.
`constexpr double`
A function or variable the compiler can evaluate at compile time, so the bandwidth math costs nothing at runtime and can feed a static_assert.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Tesla leaders describe two habits again and again. The first is first-principles reasoning: break a problem down to physics and hard numbers instead of copying what's been done before. The second is a 5-step design order Musk calls "the algorithm": 1) make the requirements less dumb, 2) delete the part or process, 3) simplify or optimize, 4) speed up the cycle time, 5) automate. The order matters. The classic mistake is optimizing or automating something that shouldn't exist. In an interview this shows up as estimation questions ("how much bandwidth do 8 cameras need?") and "why did you do it that way?" follow-ups. You're expected to answer from constraints you've calculated, not from "that's how the vendor BSP does it."

TESLA CONTEXT · PUBLIC SOURCES ONLY
Musk's 5-step "algorithm" (question requirements → delete → simplify → accelerate → automate) was described in his 2021 Starbase tour with Everyday Astronaut. PUBLIC (interview); summarized by Aviation Week
AI Day 2021: eight cameras, 1280×960, 12-bit, ~36 Hz feed the vision stack. PUBLIC-TESLA (AI Day 2021)
Seen in sampled postings:

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 4-lane camera nobody needed

Picture a board built for a feature nobody actually asked for. A camera board for a robot head was specified with a 4-lane MIPI link, an extra SerDes and a dedicated DMA engine "for future 4K". The board was late and over budget. When asked, nobody could name who required 4K. The perception network ran at 1.2 MP. Deleting the requirement removed two parts and a week of bring-up.

1 · Make the requirement less dumb

Every requirement should have a person's name on it, not a department's. Ask what it's for and calculate whether it's needed. "Future-proofing" with no owner is the most common dumb requirement in hardware bring-up.

2 · Delete before you optimize

A rule of thumb Musk is widely quoted on (e.g. in Walter Isaacson's 2023 biography): if you never have to add anything back, you didn't delete enough. In firmware terms, remove dead code paths, unused modes and redundant copies before you profile anything.

3 · Then simplify, accelerate, automate

Only after deletion: simplify the data path (zero-copy), speed up the iteration loop (faster flashing, HIL rigs), and finally automate (CI on hardware). Automating a broken process just makes it fail faster.

The Tesla job map: Optimus vs FSD vs AI infra vs firmware

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Before you prepare, decide which family of jobs you're aiming at. Your camera, driver and C/C++ background maps almost directly onto Autopilot camera software and Optimus embedded roles. Controls and inference roles need extra study. The code below scores how well a skill profile matches a role, which is the same thing the lab does visually.

Role family
A group of postings that share most required skills (e.g. Optimus embedded firmware).
`std::map`
A sorted key→value container from the C++ standard library. Lookups are O(log n).
Structured binding
auto& [key, value] : m unpacks each map entry into two named variables (C++17).
`find()` vs `[]`
m.find(k) only looks a key up. m[k] inserts a default value if the key is missing, a classic bug.
Weight
How important a skill is for a role. Here it's an integer from 1 to 3.
`const auto&`
Loop by reference to const: no copy of each element, and the compiler stops you from modifying it by accident.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

"Tesla AI" job postings cluster into a few families, and each one needs a different skill stack. Optimus embedded/firmware: MCU and RTOS firmware, Linux BSPs and drivers, CAN/EtherCAT/Ethernet, sensor bring-up, safety management. The hardcore interview: loop format, depth ladders and the C phone screen

INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Expect two kinds of pressure: deep follow-ups on your own stories, and fast, precise C. Bit manipulation is the most common embedded warm-up because it shows whether you think in hardware terms: masks, shifts, registers. Learn the five patterns below until you can write them without thinking.

Depth ladder
Repeated "why/how exactly?" follow-ups on one story, used to test real ownership.
Mask
A number whose 1-bits select the bits you care about, e.g. 0x0F selects the low 4 bits.
`x & (x - 1)`
Clears the lowest set bit of x. It's the basis of fast popcount and power-of-two tests.
Read-modify-write
Read a register, change some bits, write it back. Not atomic if an ISR touches the same register.
`static inline`
C: a function local to this file that the compiler may paste in at the call site to avoid call overhead.
Two's complement
The standard signed-integer encoding: negate by inverting all bits and adding 1. It's why x & -x isolates the lowest set bit.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

This describes the interview steps as others report them, not an official process. Tesla's loop is publicly reported (third-party guides and candidate accounts, so treat it as unconfirmed and team-dependent) to run: recruiter or automated screen → hiring-manager call (often early) → online coding assessment → a live coding screen → a 3–5 round panel covering coding, a domain deep dive, system design and behavioral. Two things are distinctive. First, the depth ladder: Musk has said publicly that he asks people about the hardest problems they solved and then drills into detail, because "the person who had to struggle with the problem really understands it." Second, embedded teams ask C: bit manipulation, volatile, ISR rules, ring buffers and register fields. The code below shows the bit tricks that come up most.
