1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Keep two copies of the firmware, so if a new one fails, the device falls back to the old one. There are two copies of the firmware (slot A and slot B), each with a small header saying its version, whether it's verified, whether it's been confirmed working, and how many trial boots are left. At power-on, the bootloader picks the newest slot that is valid and either confirmed or still has trial boots left. If the new one fails too many times, it automatically goes back to the old one.

A/B slots
Two firmware partitions; update the inactive one, keep the active one as a fallback.
Secure boot
Only cryptographically signed images are allowed to run.
Trial boot / tries counter
A limited number of boots for an unconfirmed image before rollback.
Confirm / commit
The app marks the slot good after passing self-tests.
Torn write
Power loss mid-write leaves partial data, detected via CRC or magic.
Rollback protection
A minimum version counter preventing downgrade to vulnerable images.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Tesla updates cars over the air, and a fleet of robots will be updated the same way. An update that bricks a robot (or leaves it half-updated) is unacceptable, so firmware uses A/B (dual-slot) updates. The new image is written to the inactive slot while the active one keeps running, its signature is verified (secure boot: only images signed by the manufacturer can run), it's marked pending with a limited number of trial boots, and the device reboots into it. The application then runs self-tests and confirms the slot. If it crashes or never confirms, the bootloader decrements the trial counter and falls back to the known-good slot. Headers carry their own CRC, so a torn write is detected. Every step must be safe against power loss at any instant. Tesla's firmware postings ask for bootloaders, secure boot and update flows across Linux/RTOS/bare-metal, and Tesla's OTA practice for vehicles is publicly well known.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The update that bricked 2% of devices

A fleet of devices updated in place (single slot). Units that lost power during the 40-second flash write were left with half an image and no way to boot, so 2% needed a technician. The redesign used A/B slots, wrote the header last, required a signature check before marking an image bootable, and added three trial boots plus app-side confirmation after self-tests. Fleet bricking went to zero across the next 30 releases.

1 · Order of operations

Install the update in the spare slot, check it, give it a few trial boots, and only then mark it good. Download to the inactive slot → verify hash and signature → write the header with bootable = 1, confirmed = 0, tries = 3 (header last, CRC-protected) → reboot → the bootloader decrements tries and persists it → the app self-tests → confirmed = 1. Power loss at any step leaves either the old slot or a trial-limited new slot.

2 · Security

Each boot stage checks the next one's signature, like a chain of ID checks. Secure boot chain (ROM → bootloader → app), signature verification with keys in fuses or a secure element, anti-rollback version counters, and encrypted images if needed. Never trust an image that wasn't verified.

3 · Fleet operations

Staged rollouts (1% → 10% → 100%), health telemetry gating each stage, automatic halt on regression, and per-device logs of update results. Robots also need a 'safe to update' state, like a car parked and not charging.

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

For an arm with two segments, the distance from shoulder to target fixes the elbow angle (law of cosines). Then the shoulder angle is the direction to the target minus a correction for the bent elbow. If the target is farther than both segments combined, there's no solution. The code returns 'nothing' then, and also includes forward kinematics to check the answer.

Forward kinematics
Joint angles → end-effector position (unique).
Inverse kinematics
End-effector target → joint angles (0, 1, 2 or ∞ solutions).
Workspace
Set of reachable end-effector positions.
Jacobian
Matrix mapping joint velocities to end-effector velocities.
Singularity
A configuration where the Jacobian loses rank: some directions become unreachable or need infinite joint speed.
Redundancy
More joints than task dimensions: infinite IK solutions, allowing secondary goals.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

To reach for a box or place a foot, a robot must convert between joint space (angles) and task space (positions of the hand or foot). Forward kinematics (FK) is easy and unique: chain the link transforms. Inverse kinematics (IK) asks which joint angles put the hand at a given target. It may have zero solutions (out of reach), two (elbow up or down) or infinitely many (redundant arms like a 7-DoF human arm). For a planar 2-link arm, IK has a closed-form solution from the law of cosines. For full humanoid limbs, solvers use the Jacobian (how small joint changes move the hand) iteratively, with damping near singularities (e.g. a fully stretched arm), plus joint limits and secondary objectives. Optimus postings explicitly list IK, forward/inverse dynamics and state estimation. IK is also a classic whiteboard problem.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The elbow that flipped mid-reach

A robot arm reaching along a straight line suddenly flipped its elbow from down to up halfway through, sweeping through a nearby shelf. The IK solver returned whichever solution was numerically closest to a default seed, not to the current configuration. Choosing the solution nearest the current joint angles (and enforcing continuity) fixed it.

1 · Closed form vs numerical

Simple chains (2-link planar, 6-DoF arms with spherical wrists) have closed-form IK. General chains use iterative Jacobian methods: Δq = J⁺·Δx, damped least squares near singularities, plus joint limits.

2 · Multiple solutions and continuity

Pick the solution nearest the current state, respect limits, and avoid branch switches mid-motion. For redundant limbs, use the null space for secondary goals (avoid limits, stay away from obstacles, keep posture natural).

3 · Humanoid specifics

Legs need IK for foot placement relative to the pelvis. Whole-body control solves many tasks at once (hands, feet, balance) with priorities, often as a QP at hundreds of hertz to 1 kHz.

// Analytic IK for a planar 2-link arm (link lengths l1, l2), target (x, y).
8
std::optional<Angles> ik2(double x, double y, double l1, double l2, bool elbow_up) {
9
  const double r2 = x * x + y * y;
10
  double c2 = (r2 - l1 * l1 - l2 * l2) / (2.0 * l1 * l2);         // law of cosines
11
  if (c2 < -1.0 - 1e-9 || c2 > 1.0 + 1e-9) return std::nullopt;    // out of reach
12
  c2 = std::clamp(c2, -1.0, 1.0);                                  // absorb rounding
13
  const double s2 = (elbow_up ? -1.0 : 1.0) * std::sqrt(1.0 - c2 * c2);
14
  const double q2 = std::atan2(s2, c2);
15
  const double q1 = std::atan2(y, x) - std::atan2(l2 * s2, l1 + l2 * c2);
16
  return Angles{q1, q2};
17
}
18
 
19

20
void fk2(const Angles& a, double l1, double l2, double& x, double& y) {
21
  x = l1 * std::cos(a.q1) + l2 * std::cos(a.q1 + a.q2);
22
  y = l1 * std::sin(a.q1) + l2 * std::sin(a.q1 + a.q2);
23
}

LESSON T7.2 · C++17 · +20 XP
Balance: the linear inverted pendulum and the capture point
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

The robot's body is modeled as a point mass on a massless leg. If the body is ahead of the foot's pressure point, it accelerates further forward, like a falling stick. The capture point adds 'where I'm heading' (speed divided by the pendulum's natural rate) to 'where I am'. If that point is under the foot, the ankle can catch the fall; if not, you need a step.

CoM
Center of mass: the weighted average position of the robot's mass.
CoP / ZMP
Center of pressure (zero moment point): where the net ground reaction force acts, always within the support polygon.
Support polygon
Convex hull of the foot contact areas.
ω (omega)
√(g/z0): the pendulum's natural rate (≈3.1 rad/s at z0 = 1 m).
Capture point
ξ = x + ẋ/ω, where to place the CoP or a foot to stop.
Ankle vs stepping strategy
Recover with ankle torque (small pushes) or by taking a step (large pushes).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

A standing or walking humanoid is an inverted pendulum: its center of mass (CoM) sits high above small feet. The linear inverted pendulum model (LIPM) keeps the CoM at a constant height z0 and gives a beautifully simple equation: ẍ = (g/z0)·(x − p), where p is the center of pressure (CoP), the point under the foot where the ground force acts. The CoP can only be moved within the foot (by ankle torque), so the robot can push the CoM back only so much. The capture point ξ = x + ẋ/ω (ω = √(g/z0)) is where the CoP must be for the robot to come to rest. If the capture point is inside the foot, ankle torque alone recovers. If it's outside, the robot must step (or use hip strategies). This model underlies much classic humanoid control, including ZMP walking and capture-point stepping. Optimus postings list inverted pendulum, state estimation and locomotion. Modern RL controllers learn balance, but these models remain the vocabulary and the sanity checks.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The push that needed a step

In a demo, a researcher gave a humanoid a firm shove. The ankle controller saturated at the toe and the robot tipped forward. The capture point had jumped 12 cm beyond the toe within 50 ms, so no ankle torque could save it. Adding capture-point-based stepping (trigger a step when ξ leaves a margin inside the foot) let it recover from pushes 3× larger.

1 · Why it's unstable

ẍ = ω²(x − p) has solutions growing like e^{ωt}. Balance means continually placing p so the divergent component (the capture point) stays bounded. The CoP is limited to the support polygon, so control authority is finite.

2 · Capture point control

The capture point obeys ξ̇ = ω(ξ − p), so the CoP pushes ξ away from it. Keep ξ inside the foot with margin, and if it leaves, step so the new foot's CoP region covers ξ. Step timing matters: the longer you wait, the further ξ runs.

3 · Beyond the model

Real robots add angular momentum (hip/arm strategies), height changes, swing-leg dynamics and contact uncertainty. RL policies (named in Optimus RL postings) learn these behaviors in simulation, and LIPM-based metrics still help evaluate and debug them.

2
 
3
struct ComState { double x, xd; };   // horizontal CoM position (m) and velocity (m/s)
4
 
5
// LIPM dynamics: x'' = (g / z0) * (x - p), with p the center of pressure.
6
ComState lipm_step(ComState s, double p, double z0, double dt) {
7
  const double w2 = 9.81 / z0;
8
  const double xdd = w2 * (s.x - p);
9
  s.xd += xdd * dt;                  // semi-implicit Euler: velocity first
10
  s.x  += s.xd * dt;
11
  return s;
12
}
13
 
14
// Capture point: CoP location that brings the CoM to rest.
15
double capture_point(const ComState& s, double z0) {
16
  return s.x + s.xd / std::sqrt(9.81 / z0);
17
}
18
 
19
// Ankle-only recovery is possible iff the capture point lies within the foot.
20
bool ankle_can_recover(const ComState& s, double z0, double heel, double toe) {
21
  const double cp = capture_point(s, z0);
22
  return cp >= heel && cp <= toe;
23
}

text:
LESSON T7.3 · C++17 · +20 XP
Impedance control: touching the world safely
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Instead of forcing the hand to a position, the controller computes a force like a virtual spring (pulling toward the target) plus a virtual shock absorber (resisting fast motion). Hitting a wall then just compresses the virtual spring, so the force is limited and predictable. A saturation limit adds a hard cap.

Impedance
The dynamic relation between motion and force (spring + damper + mass).
Stiffness K
N/m (or Nm/rad): force per unit position error.
Damping D
N·s/m: force per unit velocity error.
Critical damping
D = 2√(K·m): fastest response without overshoot.
Admittance control
The dual: measure force, command motion (for stiff position-controlled robots).
Feed-forward force
A known force added directly (e.g. gravity compensation).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Position control says 'be exactly here', which is disastrous when the hand meets a table or a person: the controller pushes harder and harder against the obstacle. Impedance control says 'behave like a spring and damper around this target': F = K·(x_des − x) + D·(v_des − v) + F_ff. The stiffness K sets how hard the robot pushes per meter of error, and damping D removes oscillation (critical damping D = 2√(K·m)). With low stiffness the robot is compliant: safe contact, tolerance of position errors, natural interaction. With high stiffness it's precise but harsh. Contact force is predictable: pressing a target 2 cm into a wall at K = 500 N/m gives 10 N. It requires torque-controllable joints (good current/torque control or torque sensors), which ties back to T6 actuators and FOC. Optimus simulation postings list impedance and torque control explicitly.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The table that pushed back

A robot placing a box with a stiff position controller slammed into a table that was 1.5 cm higher than its map said. The joints drove to full torque trying to reach the commanded height and tripped overcurrent protection. With impedance control at K = 800 N/m and a 30 N cap, the same error produced a gentle 12 N contact, detected via the force estimate, and the placement completed.

1 · Choosing K and D

Low K (100–500 N/m) for contact and human interaction, high K for free-space precision. D near critical, based on effective mass. Vary them by task phase: stiff while moving, soft at contact.

2 · Requirements on hardware

Soft, springy control needs joints that can feel force, which high gearing hides. Impedance control needs accurate joint torque: transparent actuators (low friction and reflected inertia) or torque sensors, plus a fast inner current loop. High gear ratios hide external forces, which links back to T6.1.

3 · Contact detection and safety

Estimate external force (torque residual from the model or sensors), detect contact, and switch modes. Cap forces and energy for human safety (as in collaborative robot standards like ISO/TS 15066).

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Before each simulated training episode, pick random values for the robot's mass, foot friction, motor strength, control delay and sensor noise from chosen ranges. The policy has to work across all of them. A helper checks whether the real robot's measured values fall inside those ranges. If they don't, expect the policy to struggle on hardware.

Sim-to-real gap
Performance drop from simulation to hardware due to modeling mismatch.
Domain randomization
Training across randomized physical and sensor parameters.
System identification
Estimating real parameters (mass, friction, latency) from measurements.
Policy
The learned controller: observations → actions.
Reward shaping / curriculum
Designing rewards and progressively harder tasks to guide learning.
Imitation learning
Learning from demonstrations (e.g. teleoperation data).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Many robot skills are now learned in simulation, but the simulator is never quite like the real world. Modern humanoid controllers increasingly come from learning: reinforcement learning (RL) in massively parallel simulation, and imitation learning from human demonstrations (teleoperation or video). The catch is the sim-to-real gap: the simulator's masses, friction, motor behavior, latency and sensor noise never exactly match the real robot, so a policy that walks perfectly in simulation may fall on hardware. Domain randomization trains across wide random ranges of these parameters, so the real robot looks like 'just another sample'. Other tools include system identification (measure the real parameters and narrow the ranges), actuator networks (learned motor models), latency modeling, and observation noise. Tesla's Optimus RL postings explicitly ask for sim2real, domain randomization, learned dynamics, curricula, reward design and massively parallel simulation (IsaacLab/mjlab). Third parties have reported that some Optimus demos involved teleoperation, which is also how imitation data is commonly collected.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Perfect in sim, falling on hardware

A locomotion policy trained in simulation walked flawlessly there but stumbled on the real robot within seconds. Logs showed ~18 ms of actuator latency on hardware vs 0 ms in sim, and foot friction lower than the simulated value on the lab floor. Randomizing latency (5–25 ms) and friction (0.4–1.2), plus adding observation noise, produced a policy that transferred on the first try.

1 · Where gaps come from

Here are the things a simulator usually gets wrong; measure them on the real robot first. Actuator dynamics (torque limits, friction, backlash, bandwidth), latency and control rate, mass and inertia errors, contact and friction models, sensor noise and bias, and unmodeled compliance. Measure the real values (system ID) before choosing ranges.

2 · Randomize wisely

Cover the identified values with margin, but not absurdly wide (training gets harder and policies get timid). Use curricula to widen ranges over training. Validate policy robustness per parameter in sim before trying hardware.

3 · Imitation and data

Teleoperation and human video give demonstrations for manipulation. RL refines locomotion and robustness. Both need good data infrastructure (T3.5), evaluation suites and safe hardware testing (T4.4).

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Each worker has its own list of gradient numbers. We want every worker to end up with the sum of all lists. Split each list into P pieces. In each step, every worker sends one piece to the next worker, who adds it to its own. After P−1 steps, each worker has one fully summed piece. Then P−1 more steps pass the finished pieces around until everyone has all of them. This code simulates that exactly.

Data parallelism
Same model on every worker, different data, gradients averaged.
All-reduce
Collective operation leaving every worker with the sum or average of all inputs.
Reduce-scatter
Phase 1: each worker ends up with one fully reduced chunk.
All-gather
Phase 2: distribute every reduced chunk to all workers.
NCCL
NVIDIA's collective communications library (ring and tree all-reduce).
Bandwidth-optimal
Data sent per worker approaches the theoretical minimum (2·(P−1)/P·N).

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Training FSD-scale networks on video needs thousands of accelerators working together. The workhorse is data parallelism: every worker holds a copy of the model, processes a different slice of the batch, computes gradients, and then all workers average their gradients so the copies stay identical. That averaging is an all-reduce. The naive approach (everyone sends to one server) bottlenecks on that server's link. Ring all-reduce arranges P workers in a ring and splits the gradient into P chunks. In a reduce-scatter phase (P−1 steps) each worker passes one chunk to its neighbor, which adds its own. After that, each worker owns one fully summed chunk. An all-gather phase (P−1 more steps) circulates the finished chunks. Each worker sends only 2·(P−1)/P × the gradient size, nearly independent of P, which makes the ring bandwidth-optimal. Libraries like NCCL implement this (and tree variants). Tesla's Distributed Training posting asks for multi-GPU scaling, NCCL and CPU/GPU profiling. Tesla has publicly described large GPU clusters and the Dojo system for training.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
Adding GPUs made training slower

A team scaled a video model from 8 to 64 GPUs and saw the step time get worse. Gradients were averaged through a single parameter server whose network link saturated. Switching to NCCL ring/tree all-reduce and overlapping communication with the backward pass restored near-linear scaling up to 64 GPUs.

1 · Cost model

Big messages are limited by link speed and small ones by per-hop delay, so group gradients into medium-size bundles. Ring all-reduce time ≈ 2·(P−1)/P · N / BW + 2·(P−1)·latency. Bandwidth dominates for large gradients and latency for small ones (where tree algorithms win). Bucket gradients (e.g. 25 MB) to balance the two.

2 · Overlap

Start all-reducing the last layers' gradients while backward is still computing earlier layers (DDP buckets). Good overlap hides most communication. Profile to confirm (T8.4).

3 · Beyond data parallel

Huge models get split across chips in several ways, and the wiring decides which ways are fast. Huge models add tensor parallelism (split layers), pipeline parallelism (split stages) and sharded optimizers (ZeRO/FSDP). Hardware topology (NVLink, InfiniBand, or a custom mesh like Dojo's) decides which collectives are fast.

6

7
void ring_allreduce(std::vector<std::vector<float>>& data) {
8
  const int P = static_cast<int>(data.size());
9
  const size_t n = data[0].size();
10
  const size_t chunk = (n + P - 1) / P;                       // ceil(n / P)
11
  auto range = [&](int c, size_t& b, size_t& e) {
12
    b = std::min(n, static_cast<size_t>(c) * chunk);
13
    e = std::min(n, b + chunk);
14
  };
15
  // Phase 1, reduce-scatter: at step s, worker r sends chunk (r - s) to r + 1, which adds it.
16
  for (int s = 0; s < P - 1; ++s) {
17
    const auto snap = data;                                    // all sends happen "simultaneously"
18
    for (int r = 0; r < P; ++r) {
19
      const int c = ((r - s) % P + P) % P, dst = (r + 1) % P;
20
      size_t b, e; range(c, b, e);
21
      for (size_t i = b; i < e; ++i) data[dst][i] += snap[r][i];
22
    }
23
  }
24
  // Phase 2, all-gather: circulate each finished chunk around the ring.
25
  for (int s = 0; s < P - 1; ++s) {
26
    const auto snap = data;
27
    for (int r = 0; r < P; ++r) {
28
      const int c = ((r + 1 - s) % P + P) % P, dst = (r + 1) % P;
29
      size_t b, e; range(c, b, e);
30
      for (size_t i = b; i < e; ++i) data[dst][i] = snap[r][i];
31
    }
32
  }
33

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Chips in a grid pass messages hop by hop to neighbors. The route rule here is simple: first move horizontally until the column matches, then vertically. The time to send a message is roughly the number of hops times the per-hop delay, plus the time to push all the bytes through one link.

2D mesh
Nodes in a grid, each linked to up to 4 neighbors.
Hop
One link traversal between neighboring nodes.
XY (dimension-order) routing
Route fully in X, then in Y; deadlock-free on meshes.
Network-on-chip (NoC)
On-die packet network connecting cores.
Placement
Assigning work and data to nodes to minimize communication.
Bisection bandwidth
Bandwidth across a cut splitting the network in half, a key scalability metric.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

Tesla's Dojo (AI Day 2021/2022, Hot Chips 2022) took a different path from GPU clusters. The D1 chip packs 354 training cores, each with 1.25 MB of SRAM, connected in a 2D mesh network-on-chip. Training tiles join 25 D1s (5×5) with high-bandwidth edges into one ~9 PFLOPS unit, and tiles join into larger meshes (6 tiles per tray, 120 tiles in an 'ExaPOD', as announced). Tesla said it deliberately dropped virtual memory and cache coherency for scalability. Software (the compiler) decides explicitly where data lives and how it flows. In a mesh, communication cost depends on distance (hops) and link congestion, so placement and routing matter. Dimension-order (XY) routing sends packets along X first, then Y. It's simple and deadlock-free on meshes. Dojo's status has changed: Bloomberg reported the team was disbanded in August 2025, and Musk later announced 'Dojo3' work; a September 2026 kernel posting mentions Dojo3. Treat the concepts (SRAM-centric dataflow, mesh routing, explicit placement) as durable, and the product details as fluid.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The hotspot in the corner

In a mesh-based accelerator prototype, a parameter-gathering phase sent all partial results to the node at (0,0). Links near that corner saturated while the rest of the mesh sat idle, and the phase took 9× longer than the bandwidth math predicted. Spreading the reduction (a tree or ring over the mesh, with the result owner chosen in the middle) restored the expected time.

1 · SRAM-centric dataflow

With no automatic memory sharing, the compiler must plan every data move in advance. With large distributed SRAM and no hardware coherency, the compiler plans data placement and movement explicitly: which core holds which weights and activations, and when they stream to neighbors. That is predictable and scalable, but places the burden on software.

2 · Mesh communication

Latency ∝ hops; throughput is limited by the busiest link. Nearest-neighbor patterns (convolution halos, pipeline stages) are cheap. All-to-one and all-to-all are expensive. Map computation so communication stays local.

3 · Durable lessons

Whatever happens to Dojo, the same memory and data-movement skills still apply. Whether Dojo itself continues, kernel and compiler postings (MLIR, roofline, Dojo3, AI5/AI6) show the same skills apply: explicit memory hierarchies, data movement analysis and placement.

18

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Threads hand work to each other through a queue with a maximum size. If it's full, the producer waits. If it's empty, the consumer waits. Waiting uses condition variables, which let a thread sleep until another thread signals that something changed. 'close()' wakes everyone up at shutdown so no thread waits forever.

Producer–consumer
Threads that create work and threads that process it, connected by a queue.
Bounded queue
Fixed maximum size; blocks the producer when full.
Backpressure
A slow consumer naturally slows producers via full queues.
Mutex
Mutual-exclusion lock protecting shared data.
Condition variable
Lets threads sleep until notified that a condition may be true.
Bottleneck
The stage with the lowest throughput; it sets the whole pipeline's rate.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

An accelerator that waits for data is wasted money. Training on fleet video means reading clips from storage, decoding video, augmenting, batching and copying to devices, all fast enough to keep GPUs busy. The same structure appears onboard: camera capture → ISP → inference → planner → logging. These are producer–consumer pipelines: stages connected by bounded queues. Bounded is essential. When a downstream stage is slow, the queue fills and the upstream stage blocks (backpressure) instead of growing memory without limit. Throughput equals the slowest stage's rate (workers ÷ time per item), so you find the bottleneck and add workers or optimize it. Thread-safe queues use a mutex plus condition variables (sleep until 'not empty' or 'not full'). For hot onboard paths, single-producer/single-consumer lock-free rings (T9 gym) avoid locks entirely. Tesla's C++ Generalist posting describes high-performance IPC buffers, logging and replay for the onboard vision stack, and the Distributed Training posting mentions CPU–GPU profiling.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
GPUs at 35%

A training job's GPUs averaged 35% utilization. Profiling showed GPU kernels finishing quickly and then idling, waiting on the data loader. Video decode ran on 4 CPU threads at ~45 ms per clip, while the GPUs could consume a clip every ~8 ms. Raising decode workers to 24, moving decode to hardware decoders and enlarging the prefetch queue brought utilization to 92%.

1 · Throughput math

Each stage's rate = workers / time_per_item. Pipeline rate = min over stages. Utilization of the accelerator = pipeline rate / accelerator consumption rate. Find the min, fix it, repeat (the bottleneck moves).

2 · Queues and backpressure

Bounded queues cap memory and latency and propagate slowness upstream. Unbounded queues hide problems until memory runs out. Size queues to absorb jitter (a few items), not to store the world.

3 · Onboard vs training

In the car, freshness wins; in training, total throughput wins. Onboard pipelines optimize latency (small queues, drop stale frames, zero-copy IPC buffers). Training pipelines optimize throughput (prefetching, many workers, large batches). The same primitives, tuned differently.

LESSON T8.4 · C++17 · +20 XP
Profiling and efficiency: RAII timers, step breakdowns and MFU
1
PLAIN LANGUAGE
2
MENTAL MODEL
3
CODE, LINE BY LINE
4
PRACTICE
5
INTERVIEW + JOB

1 · PLAIN LANGUAGE

PLAIN LANGUAGE FIRST

Create a Profile object at the start of a block of code. Its constructor notes the time. When the block ends, for any reason, its destructor adds the elapsed time to a table under the block's name. At the end, print each section's time and share. MFU then tells you what fraction of the chip's peak math you actually used.

RAII
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: tie setup and cleanup to an object's lifetime.
steady_clock
Monotonic clock, unaffected by wall-clock changes; the right choice for durations.
Step-time breakdown
Share of each phase (data, fwd, bwd, comm, optimizer) in one training step.
MFU
Model FLOPs utilization: achieved model FLOPs/s ÷ peak FLOPs/s.
Mixed precision
BF16/FP16 math with FP32 master weights, roughly doubling throughput.
Overlap
Running communication or data loading concurrently with compute.

2 · MENTAL MODEL

You can't optimize what you don't measure. For training jobs, the key metric is model FLOPs utilization (MFU): the model's useful FLOPs per second divided by the hardware peak. Typical well-tuned large-scale training reaches 30–60%. Low MFU has a cause you can find with a step-time breakdown: data loading, forward, backward, communication (all-reduce), optimizer, synchronization. Fixes follow from the breakdown: overlap communication with backward, use mixed precision (BF16) to double math throughput, prefetch data, fuse kernels, raise batch size. In C++ systems (onboard or infrastructure), lightweight instrumentation uses RAII: a timer object starts in its constructor and records in its destructor, so every exit path (including early returns and exceptions) is measured. Combine it with sampling profilers (perf), GPU timelines (Nsight) and counters. Tesla's postings repeatedly ask for profiling across CPU/GPU, latency/throughput optimization and roofline analysis.

Illustrative numbers: 8 accelerators, 2.4 PFLOP per step. The score is called MFU. It always compares against the chip's top speed in BF16 mode. So slower FP32 runs score lower on purpose.

START WITH THE INCIDENT
The 18% MFU job

A large training run sat at 18% MFU. The step breakdown showed 35% of the time in all-reduce (not overlapped), 20% waiting on data, and FP32 math. Turning on gradient bucketing with overlap, BF16 mixed precision and a deeper prefetch queue raised MFU to 47%, cutting the projected training time from 19 days to 7.

1 · Instrument first

Use a mix of timers and profilers, and always look at the slow cases, not just the average. RAII scoped timers for coarse phases, sampling profilers (perf) for CPU hotspots, GPU timelines for kernels, gaps and overlaps, and counters for memory bandwidth and cache misses. Measure p50/p99, not just means.

2 · Read the breakdown

Big data-wait share: fix input pipelines (T8.3). Big comm share: overlap, bucketing, topology (T8.1). Compute-heavy but low MFU: mixed precision, fusion, better kernels and layouts (T4.3).

3 · Report impact

Tie efficiency to cost and time: MFU 18 → 47% means 2.6× fewer accelerator-hours. That's the 'evidence of excellence' framing from T1.

unit: #home
text:
LeetCode-style prep for staff/principal systems interviews
In plain words
This is a gym, not a textbook. Each problem starts as a closed box: you read it, start the timer, and try it yourself — no AI, no peeking. Hints come in three small steps. Only when you click Reveal do you get the analogy-first explanation, the animated walkthrough, code in C#, Java and C++, and a step-by-step execution visualizer that shows the call stack.

110 coding problems · 28 system design questions · 31 narrated concept videos · 25 company pages. Every solution was compiled and tested in all three languages; every execution trace was recorded from a real run of the instrumented solution (C++ for all problems, plus Java and C# for many — pick the language on the Run tab).

Start coding practice → · System design → · Concept videos → · Mock interview → · Companies →

Where these come from

Questions are adapted from (1) cvpeceee/systems-career-learning-hub: the 36-chapter main tutorial (interview rooms, gym problems, staff-level design drills, role playbooks for NVIDIA, Anthropic, Google, Roblox, Qualcomm, Microsoft Robotics), the Tesla FSD/Optimus track and the Skills Academy sims; and (2) cvpeceee/interview-mastery-courses: 8 company courses (Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA, OpenAI) and 3 systems courses (Systems & AI Infrastructure, Specialized Systems Roles, Storage Systems), which list the high-frequency patterns (arrays/hash maps, trees, graphs BFS/DFS/topological sort/shortest path, DP, intervals, sliding window, LRU cache, rate limiter, concurrency) and design prompts (rate limiter, top-K, storage, inference serving, safe OTA, telemetry/monitoring). LeetCode numbers are listed only for well-known problems.

Suggested order
Watch Big-O and Recursion & the Call Stack.
Do one problem per pattern (filters on the Coding tab).
Do a design question every weekend; time it at 45 minutes.
From week 3, run a mock interview twice a week.
